title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text: Every model’s expected error on a new point decomposes into three parts: bias² (systematic wrongness), variance (sensitivity to the training sample), and irreducible noise. The U-curve of 4.1 is this decomposition plotted against flexibility. Here you derive it, then watch it move under your own simulations.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
1. Basic Concept
At a fixed query point \(x_0\), with training set \(T\) treated as random:
\[\mathbb{E}_{T}\big[(y_0 - \hat{f}_T(x_0))^2\big] = \underbrace{\big(f(x_0) - \mathbb{E}_T[\hat{f}_T(x_0)]\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{V}\text{ar}_T\big(\hat{f}_T(x_0)\big)}_{\text{variance}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\varepsilon)}_{\sigma^2}\]
Derivation (one completing-the-square trick): write \(\hat f_T(x_0) - y_0 = (\hat f_T - \mathbb{E}\hat f) + (\mathbb{E}\hat f - f) - \varepsilon\). The cross-terms vanish because ε is independent of T and mean-zero, and \(\mathbb{E}_T[\hat f - \mathbb{E}\hat f] = 0\). Averaged over \(x_0\): total test MSE = bias² + variance + σ².
Empirical decomposition — bias and variance are measurable with many training sets:






Averaged over the grid, the three curves and their sum:

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
2. Concept Questions

Where does the irreducible σ² term come from in the formula, and why can no model remove it?
KNN: as k → 1 and as k → n, state the bias/variance limits at a fixed x₀.
Your colleague says “the bias–variance trade-off means you should always pick the middle.” Give a dataset property that pushes the optimum to the flexible end, and one that pushes it rigid.
Why does more training data decrease variance but (mostly) leave bias unchanged — and which classical model is the exception where data shrinks bias too?
Bootstrapped bagged trees average many trees trained on resamples. In decomposition language, what does the averaging buy, and what doesn’t it fix? (Preview of Part 7.)



Answers


ε enters the prediction target \(y_0 = f(x_0) + \varepsilon\); since ε is independent of the training set, its variance adds in full. No function of the training data can predict ε — it’s the noise floor of 2.1.
k = 1: \(\hat f(x_0) = y_{\text{nearest}} = f(x_{\text{near}}) + \varepsilon_{\text{near}}\) — bias ≈ f(x_near) − f(x₀) ≈ 0 for dense data (low bias), variance = Var(ε) plus neighbor-identity jitter (high). k → n: prediction → global mean \(\bar y\) — maximal bias (|f(x₀) − f̄|) and variance → Var(ȳ) ≈ σ²/n → 0.
Flexible-friendly: large n, low noise, complex wiggly f (bias dominates rigid models). Rigid-friendly: small n, high noise, simple f — or high dimension d ≫ n, where variance of flexible models explodes (2.9/3.5 curse).
Variance is estimation noise: more points pin each parameter/local average tighter (∝ 1/n effects). Bias is structural — wrong model class — so extra data from the same process doesn’t help. The exception: KNN and other local methods — more data shrinks neighborhoods, reducing approximation (bias) too; that’s why nonparametric methods converge to truth.
Averaging i.i.d.-ish model fits cuts variance (∝ 1/B for uncorrelated members; less for correlated trees) while leaving each member’s bias intact. Bagging fixes instability, not mis-specification — and boosting (Part 7) attacks bias by sequential fitting instead.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build bias_variance(model_factory, make_data, x0, reps=1000) returning bias, variance, and total MSE at point x0 for any sklearn-style model. Apply it to KNN with k ∈ {1, 5, 25, 100} on the sinusoid (n = 100, σ = 0.3); produce the k-vs-(bias², variance) table. Verify: total − σ² = bias² + variance within Monte Carlo error, and identify the MSE-minimizing k.


Solution







The table shows the trade exactly: k = 1 has tiny bias, large variance; k = 100 (≈ mean model at n = 100) has huge bias, vanishing variance; the MSE-optimal k sits between. Note bias isn’t monotone in a trivial way at one point — averaging over x (as in Section 1) smooths the picture.

Exercise 2. Noise and flexibility interact: rerun the degree-sweep decomposition (Section 1’s second figure) at σ = 0.05 and σ = 0.6. For each noise level, report the MSE-optimal degree. Write the one-line design rule linking noise to the flexibility you can afford, then connect it to why 2.10’s equal-variance violations matter for model choice and not just inference.


Solution







Low noise → optimal degree near the true complexity (variance is cheap); high noise → optimal degree drops hard (each estimated parameter imports σ² worth of variance). Rule: affordable flexibility scales inversely with noise. Heteroscedasticity (2.10) makes noise region-dependent — so flexible features are locally affordable, one motivation for adaptive smoothers (Part 6) and variance-aware likelihoods (GLMs, 3.6).

Exercise 3. The data-rescue curve, decomposed: fix degree 9 (overparameterized for n = 30) and rerun the decomposition at n ∈ {30, 100, 300, 1000}. Report bias², variance, and total at each n. Which component dies with data, which refuses, and what does the surviving component’s floor equal (compute it analytically for reference)?


Solution







Variance collapses roughly like (number of effective parameters)/n as n grows; bias² barely moves (degree 9 can represent the sinusoid, so its residual bias is small from the start — try degree 2 to see bias refuse to die). The floor is σ² = 0.09, exactly the irreducible term. Data cures variance; only a richer model class cures bias — the two diseases, two medicines.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The decomposition is for squared loss — classification’s 0-1 loss has bias/variance notions but they’re subtler (multiple decompositions exist; correlations between bias and variance signs). Don’t force the additive story onto accuracy or AUC.
Bias and variance need not trade monotonically at every point — the trade is an average statement; at particular x₀, or with correlated estimators, both can move together (and modern double-descent breaks the U entirely beyond interpolation — hold the classical picture for classical models).
Ensembles exploit the decomposition, not vibes: bagging attacks variance (averaging correlated fits helps less — trees’ correlation is why random feature subsampling (Part 7) works), boosting attacks bias (sequentially fitting residuals).
Regularization (Part 5) is variance purchase with bias currency: ridge shrinks coefficients (bias ↑, variance ↓); the penalty is the exchange rate. Every Part 5 method is a point on this dial.
Estimating the decomposition from ONE training set is impossible — bias and variance are properties of the estimator across training sets (4.1 Exercise 1); single-fit diagnostics speak to residuals, not to the decomposition.
σ² estimation matters for everything downstream: RSE (2.4), Cp/AIC penalties, and “are we at the floor” verdicts all consume σ̂²; a biased σ̂ (from a mis-specified model) corrupts the whole accounting.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “bias-variance analysis” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Bootstrap resamples of ONE training set measure stability-to-resampling of that fit — not the estimator’s sampling variance across training sets (it underestimates it and confounds data noise with fit jitter).
Training MSE ≠ test MSE (4.1) — on 30 points degree 9 interpolates: ≈ 0. Fix with fresh evaluation data.
Bias is defined against f, not against a noisy realization — regressing toward interpolated noise corrupts the target. Bias needs the true f (known in simulation) or a principled proxy.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the decomposition rigorously: define \(\bar{\hat f}(x_0) = \mathbb{E}_T[\hat f_T(x_0)]\), expand \(\mathbb{E}_T[(y_0 - \hat f_T(x_0))^2]\) by adding and subtracting \(\bar{\hat f}(x_0)\), and show both cross-terms vanish — one by independence of ε from T, one by the definition of expectation. Then explain where the proof fails for 0-1 loss (why no clean additive decomposition exists there).


Hint

E[(A + B + C)²] with A = ȳ-type zero-mean term, B = bias, C = −ε; check E[A] = 0, E[AC] = E[A]E[C] = 0 by independence.



Solution

Let \(A = \bar{\hat f} - \hat f_T\), \(B = \bar{\hat f} - f(x_0)\), \(C = -\varepsilon\). Then \(y_0 - \hat f_T = A + B + C\). Squaring and taking \(\mathbb{E}_T\): E[A²] = Var, B² = bias², E[C²] = σ². Cross-terms: E[AB] = B·E[A] = 0; E[BC] = B·E[C] = 0 (ε mean-zero, independent of everything T-derived); E[AC] = E[A]E[C] = 0 by independence. Sum = bias² + var + σ². For 0-1 loss the indicator \((y_0 \ne \hat f_T)\) doesn’t expand into squares — bias and variance interact (high variance can correct systematic boundary bias — “variance cancels bias” — which squared loss forbids). That’s why classification intuition sometimes rewards instability, and why the clean U-curve is a squared-loss picture.

Q2. Double descent, demonstrated small: with n = 40 points and a linear model in k random Fourier features (X → sin/cos features), sweep k from 5 to 300 and plot train and test MSE. Identify the interpolation threshold (train MSE ≈ 0) and describe test error’s behavior around and beyond it. Then explain in bias/variance language why the classical U-curve story needs extending — and why you should still not casually interpolate your next dataset.


Solution







Around p ≈ n the minimum-norm interpolating fit is unstable — test error peaks (the classical story ends at this wall). Beyond it, the minimum-norm solution among infinitely many interpolants becomes smoother/more benign as p grows, and test error descends again. Bias/variance language extends via “effective capacity” and norm-based complexity rather than parameter count. Practical stance: the descent region requires specific (min-norm/implicit-regularized) solvers and lots of features — for classical tabular work, the U-curve and its remedies (Part 5) remain the operating manual.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (bias–variance × 2.6–2.7 model classes). Three nested model classes for one truth with group-specific slopes: additive (shared slope), interaction (two slopes), saturated (per-group curvature). For each class and n ∈ {40, 200, 1000}, measure test MSE by multi-training-set simulation. Produce the 3×3 table and read it in decomposition language: which cell’s error is bias-dominated at n = 40 but variance-dominated at n = 40 for the saturated class, and how does the ranking of classes change with n?
C2 (bias–variance × 4.6 tuning preview). The decomposition explains what CV’s minimum finds: rerun Exercise 1’s KNN sweep while recording the decomposition; overlay the empirical test-MSE minimum k with the k minimizing (bias² + variance) from the ground-truth simulation. How often (across 100 dataset draws) does CV pick within ±1 neighbor of the decomposition-optimal k? The frequency you observe is the empirical content of “CV approximates the bias-variance optimum” — and its failure cases are your introduction to why tuning needs care.

title: 4.4 The Bias–Variance Trade-off
text:
7. Summary

Test MSE = bias² + variance + σ²; the proof is one completing-the-square; σ² never leaves.
Flexibility buys bias down at variance’s price; the U-curve is that exchange plotted.
More data kills variance, not bias; local (nonparametric) methods are the exception — neighborhoods shrink.
Noise sets the flexibility budget: high σ ⇒ rigid optima (Exercise 2).
Bagging/boosting/regularization are the decomposition’s applied children: variance-, bias-, and exchange-machines.
The decomposition is a squared-loss, classical-model story — 0-1 loss and interpolation-threshold regimes need amended maps.
With error anatomy understood, the bootstrap gives it standard errors without new theory: 4.5 The Bootstrap.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text: Cross-validation (CV) keeps the validation idea but recycles the data: split into K folds, hold each out in turn, average. Every row is validated exactly once and trains K−1 times — more precise estimates from the same data, at K times the compute. It is the default referee of applied machine learning.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
1. Basic Concept
K-fold protocol: partition rows into K disjoint folds (shuffled, ideally stratified). For k = 1..K: fit on all folds except k, predict fold k, record the metric. Report the mean (and spread) of the K values.






The full loop, explicitly, then the one-liner that does the same:






Classification needs stratified folds (class proportions preserved per fold — 0.5):






LOOCV — the K = n extreme: every point validated once, training on n−1. Nearly no bias from undertraining, but expensive and with correlated folds:

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
2. Concept Questions

What exactly does “5-fold CV estimate = 0.31 ± 0.04” estimate, and which model (trained on what fraction of data) does the ± describe?
Why is K-fold CV not K times more precise than a single validation split, despite using K folds?
LOOCV is nearly unbiased for the error of models trained on n−1 points. Name its two practical costs.
You’re comparing two models with fold-wise CV errors. Why must the fold splits be identical across models, and what test formalizes the comparison?
Repeated CV (e.g., 10× 5-fold) — what does repetition add, and what doesn’t it fix?



Answers


It estimates the expected test error of the procedure “fit this model type to 4/5 of data” — i.e., of models trained on 80% of the data. The final deployed model (trained on 100%) will typically be slightly better; the estimate carries that small pessimism (4.2).
The K fold errors share training data (any two training sets overlap in K−2 folds) and evaluate on the same finite dataset — the fold errors are strongly positively correlated, so their mean’s variance doesn’t shrink like independent estimates would (no 1/K). Repetition with fresh shuffles reduces, but never eliminates, this.
Compute (n fits, each on n−1 rows — infeasible for expensive models) and high fold-correlation: the LOOCV mean has low bias but its variance isn’t correspondingly tiny, so per-fold SEs are misleading. Also no stratification granularity at K = n for classification (some folds have 1 positive).
Fold difficulty (which easy/hard rows land together) shifts all models’ scores on a given split — pairing cancels it. With identical folds, compare fold-wise differences with a paired t-test (3.7); with different random splits, you’re comparing two noisy marginals.
Repetition with different shuffles averages out partition luck, tightening the estimate (the SD across repeats estimates the partition-noise). It does NOT fix: selection inflation (picking the winner among many models by CV), leakage, or distribution shift — those are pipeline diseases, not partition noise.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Variance anatomy: estimate the true test error of a degree-3 model (fit on 80% of n = 120) via (a) one 5-fold CV, (b) 20 repeats of 5-fold CV, (c) 200 independent 80/20 splits. For each, report the estimate and an empirical SD across 300 repetitions of the whole scheme. Which scheme’s repetition-SD is smallest, and what does the comparison say about what CV does and doesn’t recycle?


Solution







All three estimate nearly the same thing and their means agree; the SD ranking (single split worst, one 5-fold in the middle, 20× repeats best) quantifies the partition-noise that CV partially — but not fully — recycles. Diminishing returns set in: 20 repeats ≈ 100 fits for a modest tightening, because folds within a repeat are correlated.

Exercise 2. Model selection by CV, done right and wrong: among degrees 1–12 on sinusoidal data (n = 100), (a) select the degree minimizing 5-fold CV MSE; (b) report that minimum as the performance; (c) also compute the true error of the CV-selected degree (big fresh test). Repeat over 200 datasets: compare the distribution of (b) against (c), and against the true error of the fixed degree-3 model. Quantify the optimism of (b) and the quality of CV as a selector.


Solution







The reported minimum sits below the selected model’s true error — that gap is selection optimism, paid for searching 12 candidates. Meanwhile CV-as-selector works well: the selected degrees’ true errors beat (or nearly match) fixed degree-3, because CV’s noise per candidate is small enough that the true winner usually scores near the top. Two hats, one tool: a good selector, an optimistic reporter — never let it wear both hats at once (4.6 formalizes the fix).

Exercise 3. Grouped biological data done properly: 40 patients × 5 visits (200 rows); the signal is at the patient level. Compare three evaluation schemes for a logistic model: (a) row-level StratifiedKFold(5) — patients split across folds; (b) GroupKFold(5) by patient; (c) GroupKFold with LOO-patients (40 folds). Report each scheme’s mean CV AUC and across-fold SD, then evaluate the winning-by-(a) model’s performance on truly unseen patients. Which scheme’s number would you put in a paper claiming “generalizes to new patients”?


Solution







Scheme (a) lets each patient’s rows appear in both train and validation — the model memorizes patient-level drift and reports inflated AUC (“generalizes” only to new visits of known patients). Schemes (b)/(c) answer the new-patient question and their numbers are visibly lower and more honest. The evaluation unit must match the deployment claim: row-level questions (rare in medicine) vs patient-level questions (the usual).

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

K choice folklore: K = 5 or 10 balance bias (training fraction 1−1/K) against compute and fold-correlation. K = 2 gives the most independent folds; LOOCV the least (and is noisier per-unit-cost for unstable learners).
Preprocessing belongs inside the folds — Pipeline + cross_val_score is the mechanical guarantee (0.5); a scaler fit before cross_val_score silently invalidates the whole table.
Fold-level SEs understate uncertainty (correlated folds); for error bars on the CV mean, use repeated CV across random partitions or bootstrap over rows — not sd(fold scores)/√K alone.
CV estimates procedures, not fitted models — after CV, refit on all data for deployment; the CV number is the performance claim, the full-data fit is the artifact (4.2 post-selection note).
Group/cluster leakage is the silent killer of biomarker papers: same patient, same batch, same unit across folds (0.5 bug #3, Exercise 3).
Time series: shuffle-free TimeSeriesSplit or rolling-origin schemes; random K-fold CV on temporal data answers a question nobody deploys against.
Feature selection inside CV only: screening features on the full dataset before CV is leakage — the fold must not know which features exist until it trains (2.8 Exercise 3).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Pre-CV scaling: every fold’s training statistics include validation rows. Pipeline inside CV.
Unshuffled folds on sorted data: some folds see one class only; several folds can’t even fit. Shuffle (or stratify).
Feature selection outside CV: the folds’ validation rows voted on which features matter — leakage. Selection must live inside the fold pipeline.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Estimate the fold-correlation of 5-fold CV errors empirically: generate 400 datasets; for each, compute the 5 fold MSEs of a fixed model; extract the average pairwise correlation of fold errors. Use the observed ρ to explain why the SE of the CV mean is √((1 + 4ρ)/5)·SD(fold)/√5-ish rather than SD(fold)/√5, and compute the inflation factor at your measured ρ.


Hint

For the mean of K equicorrelated estimates, Var(mean) = (σ²/K)(1 + (K−1)ρ).



Solution

Measure the correlation across datasets: standardize each dataset’s fold errors, pool, and correlate fold positions.






Typical ρ lands well above 0 — folds share rows and the same underlying fit. The naive SD/√K understates the CV mean’s uncertainty by the inflation factor; repeated-CV or bootstrap-over-rows error bars are the honest alternative (Q2 of 4.2 for the single-split analogue).

Q2. You have n = 80 rows, an unstable learner (KNN k = 1), and must choose between LOOCV and 5-fold repeated 10 times as your error estimator. Simulate the truth (fresh test sets) and compare both estimators’ bias and variance across 200 datasets. Confirm or refute the folklore “LOOCV has low bias but high variance for unstable learners” and state which you’d use for (a) unstable learners, (b) stable learners (linear regression).


Solution







For the unstable k = 1 learner, LOOCV trains on n−1 ≈ n (low bias) but its per-fold predictions are maximally jumpy and folds nearly identical — high variance across datasets. Repeated 5-fold trades a hair of bias (training on 80%) for substantially lower variance — better for unstable learners, matching the folklore. For stable learners (linear regression), the variance difference largely evaporates and LOOCV’s minimal bias is attractive (compute permitting). The estimator must be matched to the learner’s stability — one more decision CV forces you to own.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (CV × 3.7 comparison × 12.x multiplicity preview). Ten models, five-fold CV, pairwise McNemar on pooled out-of-fold predictions = 45 comparisons. Simulate null data (no signal) and count how many pairs come out “significant” at p < 0.05. Apply Bonferroni (α/45) and re-count. Connect the result to why model-comparison tables in the wild overclaim — and write the protocol sentence your future papers will include.
C2 (CV × 2.4 R²). Out-of-sample R² from K-fold CV: implement fold-wise \(R^2 = 1 - \text{MSE}_{fold}/\text{Var}_{fold}(y)\) vs pooled \(1 - \sum \text{resid}^2 / \sum (y - \bar{y}_{pooled})^2\) on the same CV predictions. Show the two can differ noticeably on small folds, decide which is the defensible summary for (a) balanced folds, (b) drifting fold composition, and produce the exact sklearn-equivalent computation (cross_val_predict + r2_score) to check your arithmetic.

title: 4.3 Cross-Validation
text:
7. Summary

K-fold CV: every row validated once; report mean fold error ± honest uncertainty (fold correlation!, repeats).
Stratify classification folds; group by patient/batch when deployment means new groups; never shuffle time.
Preprocessing, feature selection, everything data-dependent lives inside the fold pipeline.
CV is a fine selector and an optimistic reporter of its own minimum — separation of hats is [4.6]’s law.
LOOCV: low bias, high compute, high estimator variance for unstable learners; 5/10-fold is the working default.
Fold-level SEs understate; repeat partitions or bootstrap rows for error bars.
The U-curve of 4.1 has a decomposition — bias² + variance + σ² — that explains why the minimum sits where it does: 4.4 The bias–variance trade-off.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text: Every model from Part 2–3 has dials you don’t fit from data: polynomial degree, KNN’s k, regularization strength, tree depth. Hyperparameter tuning chooses them by validation — and inherits every trap of 4.1–4.5 in concentrated form, because tuning is selection, and selection is optimism. This page builds the honest tuning machine: grids, pipelines, nested CV, and the reporting discipline that keeps the numbers true.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
1. Basic Concept
The separation of hats: hyperparameters are chosen on validation data (inner loop); performance of the whole choose-and-fit procedure is estimated on untouched data (outer loop). Conflating the hats — tuning and reporting on the same data — is the single most common inflated number in applied ML.






The tuning landscape itself — mean CV score per k with its fold spread:






Note the landscape’s flat top: neighboring k values are statistically indistinguishable — the one-standard-error rule (below) exists for exactly this reason.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is search.best_score_ NOT an unbiased estimate of the tuned model’s performance — describe the mechanism in one sentence.
State the one-standard-error rule and the philosophy behind preferring the simpler model within 1 SE of the best.
Grid vs random search: when does random win, and what property of real hyperparameter landscapes makes it so?
Your pipeline = scaler + feature-selector + model, all tuned. Why must the selector’s parameters also live inside the CV loop?
After nested CV selects and scores the procedure, what model do you deploy, and what number do you quote for its expected performance?



Answers


best_score_ is the maximum over candidates of noisy CV estimates — an order statistic. Even on pure noise it beats the true optimum; its expected value = true performance + selection bonus (measured in 4.1 Q2). Only an outer loop (or fresh test set) prices the selection itself.
Among models whose CV scores lie within 1 SE of the best, choose the most parsimonious (largest k, strongest penalty, fewest features). Rationale: those scores are indistinguishable from the best; the simpler model has less variance, better interpretability, and typically better deployment behavior — you give up nothing measurable and buy robustness.
When the grid is larger than a handful of dimensions or several parameters are irrelevant (low effective dimensionality of the response surface). Landscapes are usually dominated by a few parameters (e.g., k, learning rate) while others barely matter — random points find the important dimensions faster than a lattice that spends equal effort on all.
Because feature selection fits parameters to data (which features look informative): leaving it outside the loop means validation folds were pre-filtered using their own labels — leakage by another name (0.5, 4.3). The fold must contain the entire data-dependent chain.
Deploy the chosen configuration refit on all available data; quote the outer (nested) estimate as the expected performance of the procedure — not the inner best score, not the refit model’s training score.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Two grids, honestly compared: candidate A tunes KNN over k ∈ {1..30}; candidate B tunes k ∈ {1..30} and weights ∈ {uniform, distance} and p ∈ {1, 2} (180 combos). On the same outer 5-fold nested evaluation, compare the two procedures’ nested scores. Does the bigger grid win? By how much — and is the gain inside noise? Then relate the answer to the selection-inflation drill: which procedure pays more selection tax?


Solution







Typical result: grid B edges out A by a fraction of a percent — often within the outer-fold SD. The 6× larger search pays 6× the selection tax on its inner best score; the outer estimate, which prices that tax, shows the true (small) gain. Lesson: bigger grids mostly buy bigger reported inner numbers, not performance — tune what theory says matters, not what the grid can enumerate.

Exercise 2. The one-standard-error rule in action: from Section 1’s GridSearchCV, compute the SE of the best score’s folds, mark the 1-SE band, and list all k whose mean score falls within it. Choose the largest such k and compare its held-out test accuracy to the argmax k’s. Repeat over 30 different random states — how often does the 1-SE model match or beat the argmax on test?


Solution







The 1-SE model matches or beats the argmax most of the time despite (usually) being smoother — its test luck is comparable and it’s the model you’d rather deploy (larger k = stabler). The rule isn’t magic; it’s a tie-breaker that spends a tie on robustness.

Exercise 3. Build nested_compare(procedures, X, y, outer_k=5) where each procedure is an unfitted GridSearchCV — returning each procedure’s outer mean/SD plus a paired comparison of the top two (fold-wise differences, t-test). Demonstrate on (a) KNN with tuned k, (b) logistic with tuned C, (c) LDA (no tuning) on one dataset. Report the ranking, the paired p-value for the leaders, and the honest sentence you’d write about “the best model.”


Solution







Nested comparison answers “which procedure generalizes better,” with pairing across outer folds and a real test — and the usual outcome on modest data is “statistically indistinguishable,” which is a finding, not a failure: it licenses choosing by interpretability, cost, or simplicity (3.7’s ethic, formalized).

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The tuning metric must be the deployment metric — tuning accuracy to deploy a precision@k system optimizes the wrong thing; set scoring deliberately (roc_auc, average_precision, f1, custom).
Grid resolution is a bias-variance choice: coarse grids miss optima (bias), fine grids inflate selection tax and compute. Log-spaced grids for scale parameters (C, α, learning rate) are the efficient default.
Search over preprocessing counts too — imputation strategy, scaling flavor, selector’s k are hyperparameters and belong in the grid (inside the pipeline); anything data-dependent outside the loop is leakage.
Refit-on-all-data after selection (GridSearchCV does it by default: refit=True) — but the number you report is the outer/nested one, never best_score_.
Flat landscapes are informative: if a wide band of hyperparameters scores identically, the data cannot distinguish them — pick by parsimony/interpretability and say so, rather than reporting the argmax as if it were discovered.
Compute budgeting: nested CV multiplies fits (outer × inner × grid); for heavy models use coarse inner grids, random search, or successive halving — but never drop the outer layer: that’s the whole page.
Tuning on the test set via iteration (“we only looked at the test score a few times”) is optional stopping (1.4) — the test set’s budget is spent by attention, not by fit calls.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “tuning pipeline” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Scaling before split + tuning — leakage (scaler saw test rows) and the inner CV scores are computed on pre-scaled data. Pipeline + refit-per-fold.
Argmax on the test set across 7 Cs — the test set just became a training set; final_C is selection-on-test (4.1). The test set gets ONE evaluation of the frozen winner.
The reported number is the max of 7 noisy test numbers — pure order-statistic optimism. Report the frozen model’s single test score (or better, a nested CV estimate).

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive (or verify by simulation) the expected selection bonus for M candidates whose scores are i.i.d. N(μ, s²): it is μ + s·E[max of M standard normals] ≈ μ + s·√(2 ln M). Then measure the bonus empirically for M = 10, 100, 1000 with s = 0.02 and compare against the formula. What does the logarithmic growth imply about adding candidates to a search — and about the honesty of “we searched 10,000 configurations and found X”?


Hint

E[max] of M standard normals grows like √(2 ln M); the bonus scales with the noise s, not the effect sizes.



Solution







Agreement is close (√(2 ln M) is an asymptotic approximation, slightly high at small M). Implications: the bonus grows only logarithmically — 10× more candidates buys little extra inflation — but it grows without bound, and it scales with score noise s: noisy small-validation searches suffer most. A “10,000-configuration search” must therefore report performance from an outer/nested estimate; the search’s own best score is guaranteed flattery worth ≈ s√(2 ln M).

Q2. Successive halving / Hyperband-style tuning spends more budget on promising candidates. Design a miniature version for 60 KNN configurations (k ∈ 1..60) on a fixed dataset: start all on 2-fold CV over 200 rows, keep the top 20, then 4-fold over 400 rows, keep top 7, then full 5-fold on all rows. Compare the winner and total fit-count against exhaustive GridSearchCV (60 configs × 5 folds). Does the cheap scheme pick the same k? Implement and report — and state the failure mode it imports (which honest-estimator principle does the multi-stage scoring bend?).


Solution







The cheap scheme usually lands on the same k or a neighbor (flat landscape) at a fraction of the fits. The bent principle: candidates are compared on different amounts of data at different stages — early elimination can kill a config whose advantage only shows at full data (variance-vs-budget trade). Remedies: generous early stages, random restarts, or accepting a small probability of eliminating the true optimum — the same order-statistic humility as everything else on this page.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (tuning × 4.3 CV × 3.7 comparison). Design and run the full “honest bake-off”: 4 model families (logistic+C, KNN+k, random-forest-ish depth dial — use a shallow DecisionTreeClassifier with tuned max_depth, LDA fixed), each tuned by inner 5-fold over sensible grids, compared by outer 5-fold nested CV with paired fold-differences and a multiplicity-aware verdict (Bonferroni across the 6 pairs). Deliver the table, the pairwise p-value matrix, and the deployment sentence — this is the capstone artifact of Parts 2–4.
C2 (tuning × 12.x multiplicity preview). Show that hyperparameter search over M configurations is structurally identical to testing M hypotheses: simulate null data; for each of M = 100 random configurations compute a CV score and its (approximate) p-value vs a fixed baseline; count “significant improvements” at α = 0.05 raw and after Bonferroni. Write the paragraph connecting the family-wise-error view to the selection-bonus view of 4.1 Q2 — two languages, one phenomenon — and state which controls what in practice.

title: 4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
text:
7. Summary

Tuning is selection; selection is optimism; the outer loop (nested CV or a virgin test set) is the only honest scoreboard.
best_score_ is a marketing number; the nested estimate is the performance claim; deploy the refit-on-all-data winner.
Grid/random: log-spaced scales, few meaningful dimensions, random search for big spaces; the one-SE rule buys robustness for free.
Every data-dependent step — scaling, selection, imputation — lives inside the fold pipeline.
Selection bonus ≈ s·√(2 ln M): grows with score noise and candidate count; budget score noise (bigger validation folds) and candidate count deliberately.
Comparison of tuned procedures needs identical budgets, pairing, and multiplicity awareness — the 3.7 rules at full depth.
Parts 2–4 are complete: you can build models, price their uncertainty, and choose among them honestly. Next, Part 5 turns regularization into a first-class citizen — the shrinkage dials this page kept referencing.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the discipline of interrogating data before modeling: distributions first, relationships second, anomalies always. matplotlib is the plotting engine under nearly every Python plotting library (pandas plotting calls it, seaborn wraps it), so we drill it directly.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
1. Basic Concept
matplotlib has two layers: the pyplot state machine (plt.plot(...)) for quick plots, and the object-oriented interface (fig, ax = plt.subplots(); then ax.plot(...)) which is the right habit for anything non-trivial. Anatomy you should be able to name: Figure (the canvas), Axes (one plot panel), axis (with limits, ticks, labels), title, legend.






The three plots that carry 90% of EDA:






EDA is a loop, not a plot. The minimal protocol you should run on any new table:

.head(), .shape, .dtypes — what is this, actually?
.describe() and .isna().sum() — ranges, centers, holes.
Histogram of every numeric column — skew, multimodality, impossible values (negative ages).
Scatter/correlation for relationships you care about.
Boxplots by group — does grouping explain spread?

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
2. Concept Questions

In fig, ax = plt.subplots(), what is the type and role of ax?
Your histogram has one tall bar at 0 and a flat sea of bars to the right. What transform should you almost certainly try?
Why is alpha=0.3 or smaller essential when scatter-plotting thousands of points?
What does a boxplot’s whisker-cap convention actually mark, and what is plotted as individual points?
Name two questions a groupby + boxplot answers that describe() alone cannot.



Answers


ax is an Axes object — one panel. All plotting methods hang off it (ax.hist, ax.set_xlabel); the OO interface avoids pyplot’s hidden global state and is required for multi-panel figures.
A log transform (np.log10 / np.log1p). Mean ≫ median in .describe() is the numeric tell; a spike at zero with a long right tail is the visual tell.
Overplotting: with thousands of points, opaque markers hide density — the plot then shows only where points exist, not where they concentrate. Alpha (transparency) makes density visible as darkness.
Whiskers mark the most extreme data points within 1.5×IQR of the quartiles; points beyond are drawn individually as (candidate) outliers. The fence is a convention, not a definition of “outlier.”
Whether distributions differ in shape (not just center) between groups, and whether sample sizes are comparable (a tiny group’s mean is noise). describe() pools everything.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Small plotting reflexes. For each: predict the shape of the output, run, compare.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Full EDA pass on the simulated cohort in one figure: (a) 2×2 grid with histograms of age, log10(marker), a scatter of age vs log-marker, and a boxplot of log-marker by group. Every panel titled and every axis labeled.


Solution







Note the log transform before plotting the skewed marker — the histogram becomes readable and the boxplot comparison becomes fair.

Exercise 2. Demonstrate bin-width sensitivity: plot the same 200-point sample as 5, 20, and 100-bin histograms side by side. Write one sentence on what the “right” number of bins depends on.


Solution







There is no “right” bin count — it depends on sample size and the question (rough guides: Sturges 1+log2(n), Freedman–Diaconis based on IQR). With n=200, 100 bins mostly display sampling noise; 5 bins can hide bimodality. Look at several.

Exercise 3. Build a scatter matrix (pairplot by hand): for the 3 numeric columns of the cohort, produce a 3×3 grid, diagonal = histograms, off-diagonal = scatter. No seaborn.


Solution







This double loop is the whole idea of a pairs plot (R: GGally::ggpairs). You will later recognize PCA and clustering as ways to make such grids interpretable in high dimensions.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Y-axis truncation exaggerates differences. Bar charts starting at non-zero are a classic misleading visual (and a classic reviewer complaint). For line charts truncation is fine; for bars, don’t.
Dual axes are a lie amplifier. Two independent y-scales let you manufacture any “correlation.” Prefer two stacked panels sharing an x-axis.
Log scales with zeros/negatives break (log(0) = -inf): use symlog or transform with np.log1p after checking for non-positives.
Histograms are model statements: bins impose structure that may not exist (bimodality can appear/vanish with bin width — Exercise 2).
Correlation plots lie under nonlinearity: r ≈ 0 says “no linear relation,” nothing more (see 1.2 Relationships).
Colorblind-safe palettes (tab10, viridis) and direct labeling beat red-green pairs and remote legends.
matplotlib in Pyodide: always end with plt.show(); set fig-width/fig-height cell options (inches) rather than figsize when you want consistent embedding.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated figure has four problems (three visual, one data). Run it, list them before opening the solution.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Truncated bar axis (y from 9.0): turns a modest mean difference into a towering bar. Bars must start at 0 — or better, show the distribution instead of two means.
Unlabeled, indistinguishable scatter series: same color/marker for both groups, no legend, x-axis meaningless. Need labels + legend + real x (e.g. strip/jitter plot).
Wrong Axes: the histogram is drawn on the bar chart’s panel (axes[0]), overwriting the bars. Use the intended panel (axes[1] or a third).
State-machine mixing: plt.show() after building with fig, axes is fine, but any further plt.hist-style calls would target the current figure implicitly. Stay in one interface.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. A colleague says: “the histogram is bimodal, so there are two subpopulations.” Give three alternative explanations and describe the EDA you would run to distinguish them.


Hint

Think: sampling noise (Exercise 2), mixtures of process regimes (batch), and transform artifacts.



Solution


Sampling noise: with small n, bin counts fluctuate into a fake second mode — re-draw with different bin widths/seeds (Exercise 2 logic) and bootstrap the histogram. (b) Batch/technical structure: data collected in two runs, sites, or instruments — color the histogram by batch; check within-batch shape; a two-sample test across the suspected split (1.4 Statistical inference) should vanish within batch. (c) Transform artifact: e.g. log of a mixture of a point-mass at zero plus positives, or periodic rounding (integer counts). Plot untransformed, check value granularity. Also consider a genuine mixture — but the burden of proof is after (a)–(c) are excluded: overlay a fitted two-component normal mixture and check the gap depth.


Q2. Explain why ax.set_yscale("log") often “fixes” a scatter where the vertical spread grows with x, and what that visual pattern implies for modeling choices later (name the variance structure).


Solution

Funnel-shaped residuals — spread proportional to the mean level — indicate multiplicative noise: y = f(x)·ε rather than y = f(x) + ε. Multiplicative error becomes additive and roughly homoscedastic after a log transform, which is why log axes tidy such plots. Modeling consequence: fit the model to log(y) (or use a GLM with a log link and variance proportional to mean², gamma/Poisson-style), rather than vanilla least squares which weights the large-y points overwhelmingly. The EDA observation is literally a specification diagnostic for Part 2 regression.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (EDA × 0.3 pandas). Using groupby + the plotting drills, construct the “small multiples” figure: one histogram per group on a shared x-range. Which two pandas/matplotlib mechanics make shared scales essential for honest comparison, and what does each group’s count tell you about how much to trust each panel?
C2 (EDA × 1.1 Descriptive statistics). Generate lognormal data, then plot mean and median of increasing samples (n = 5, 10, 50, 200, 1000, each resampled many times) as dot strips. Which estimator’s strip narrows faster, and how does the histogram shape you saw in Section 1 predict that result? Connect: skew → sampling distribution of the mean vs median → why “median for skewed data” is a precision claim, not just an aesthetic one.

title: 0.4 Visualisation & Exploratory Analysis
text:
7. Summary

EDA protocol: head/dtypes → describe/isna → distributions → relationships → by-group comparisons.
Use the OO interface (fig, ax = plt.subplots()); label everything; end cells with plt.show().
Alpha and jitter reveal density; truncated bar axes and dual y-axes manufacture stories.
Transform skewed data (log) before comparing and plotting — mean ≫ median is the flag.
Bin width is an assumption; look at several before claiming structure.
Boxplots compare distributions; scatter matrices compare everything pairwise.
Pictures suggest; only inference decides — next page sets up the train/test discipline that makes model evaluation honest: 0.5 Data splitting.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text: Every model in this course will be judged by one rule: performance on data it did not see during training. The mechanics of splitting data seem trivial — and that’s exactly why leakage bugs are so common. This page drills the mechanics so they’re automatic before Part 2 builds models on top of them.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
1. Basic Concept
The test set estimates how a model performs on new data. The core failure mode is leakage: any information from the test set (or from future data) influencing the training process inflates that estimate.
The basic protocol with sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split:






random_state seeds the shuffling: same seed → identical split → reproducible results. It does not make the split “better.”
For classification with imbalanced classes, use stratify=y so each split preserves class proportions:






One split gives one noisy number. K-fold cross-validation averages over K splits — every sample is in a validation fold exactly once:

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must the test set be used once, at the end — what exactly is lost if you peek repeatedly?
What does stratify=y protect you from, and when is it useless?
Why does random_state matter in research code even when results “should” be stable?
In 5-fold CV, how many times is each sample used for validation, and how many times for training?
Your test R² is better than your training R². Give one benign explanation and one suspicious one.



Answers


Repeatedly peeking at test performance and making choices (features, hyperparameters, stopping) based on it trains on the test set through you: the estimate stops being out-of-sample and becomes optimistically biased. The test set’s value is spent by adaptation.
It preserves class proportions across splits — essential for rare classes (a 2% class can be absent from a small test split). Useless/unnecessary for regression (continuous y), and it can’t fix too small data: if a class has fewer members than folds, even stratified splitting fails.
Same seed → same split → run-to-run reproducibility, which is what makes bug fixes, reviewer requests, and controlled comparisons possible. Unseeded splits confound “different partition” with “different method.”
Exactly once for validation; K−1 = 4 times for training (in different combinations).
Benign: the test split happens to be easy, or training metrics are computed on a regularized objective (e.g. penalized loss) while test R² is unpenalized. Suspicious: leakage — test information reached training (scaled together, duplicated rows, feature derived from the outcome). Investigate, don’t celebrate.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Simulate a small classification dataset (500 samples, 2% positives), split it badly (no stratify, seed chosen “unluckily”) and well (stratify). Report positives in each test set. Then quantify: repeat the unstratified split 500 times and report the range of positive counts in the test set.


Solution







A test set with zero positives makes recall, AUC, and AUPRC literally undefined. Stratification is not cosmetic.

Exercise 2. Write a 5-fold CV loop by hand (KFold + explicit fit/predict on a LinearRegression) for the synthetic regression data from Section 1, collecting validation R² per fold. Report the mean and the standard deviation across folds — then explain why that SD, not just the mean, matters.


Solution







The mean estimates expected performance; the SD across folds estimates how stable that number is. Mean ± SD ≈ 0.85 ± 0.06 and mean ± SD ≈ 0.85 ± 0.30 are very different claims about your model — an unstable CV is a red flag for high variance (see 4.4 Bias–variance trade-off).

Exercise 3 — the leakage lab. Build a dataset where one feature is derived from the outcome (leaky = y + noise). Compare (a) a model trained with the leaky feature vs (b) without, using a proper split. Then do it “wrong”: scale X on the full dataset before splitting. Which comparisons change? Quantify each difference.


Solution







Read the results: the leaky feature produces near-perfect accuracy by construction — the single most common way “too good to be true” results reach publication. Pre-split scaling is the same crime at lower dose: test-row means/variances shaped the training inputs.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Leakage taxonomy: (1) feature leakage — a column derived from y (outcomes aggregated into features, “post-treatment” variables); (2) preprocessing leakage — scaling/imputation/feature selection fitted before the split; (3) duplication leakage — the same patient/sample appearing in train and test; (4) temporal leakage — shuffling time series so the model trains on the future.
The fix for (2) is always the same shape: fit the transformer inside the training fold only — StandardScaler().fit(X_tr), then .transform(X_te). In pipelines: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge()) + cross_val_score does this mechanically and correctly.
Duplicate rows before splitting: drop_duplicates / group-aware splitting by patient ID (GroupKFold) — not by row.
test_size semantics: float = proportion, int = absolute count. Tiny test sets (n < ~30 per class) make every performance estimate mostly noise (4.1 The generalization problem).
shuffle=False is the correct default for time-ordered data — train_test_split shuffles by default, which is wrong for temporal splits.
Reproducibility chain: seed the split and any stochastic model; a notebook is only reproducible if every source of randomness is pinned.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation pipeline contains three bugs, two of them leakage. Run it, then fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Pre-split scaling — test statistics leaked into training inputs. Fit the scaler on X_tr only.
No stratification — with ~48% positives here it’s tolerable, but the code must not depend on luck; make stratify=y unconditional.
Evaluating on training data — score(X_tr, y_tr) measures memorization, not generalization. Score on X_te, y_te.







Test ≤ train, and both are believable — that’s what an honest pipeline looks like.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. A reviewer asks why your cross-validation used shuffle=True, random_state=42. Justify both choices, and explain when shuffle=True would be wrong.


Hint

What order were the rows in? What does an unshuffled KFold fold look like if the table is sorted by group or by time?



Solution

shuffle=True protects against order artifacts: real data frames are often sorted (by site, date, or outcome), and unshuffled KFold then makes folds that are systematically different from each other — e.g. sorted-by-class data can place an entire class in one fold, making it a training-only class for other folds. random_state makes the shuffling deterministic so the estimate is reproducible and comparable across code changes. shuffle=True is wrong when row order carries information: time series (train must precede test — use TimeSeriesSplit), spliced biological batches where you want to generalize to a new batch (use GroupKFold/leave-one-batch-out instead), and grouped data where rows share a subject (shuffle splits subject’s rows across train/test — leakage). The seed is part of the protocol, like the test set itself.

Q2. Your test set has 200 samples and true accuracy 80%. What is the standard error of the measured accuracy, and what does that imply about differences of 1–2 points between two models’ test scores?


Hint

Binomial SE = √(p(1−p)/n). Compute it for p = 0.8, n = 200.



Solution

SE = √(0.8·0.2/200) = √0.0008 ≈ 0.028 (2.8 percentage points). Two models measured 81% vs 83% on this test set differ by ~0.7 SE — indistinguishable from partition noise. Implications: (1) report uncertainty with test metrics, not just points; (2) prefer cross-validation for comparisons (averages over splits); (3) reserve the biggest test set you can afford; (4) resist leaderboard-grade conclusions from small test sets. This is the bridge to 4.1 The generalization problem and 4.3 Cross-validation.

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (splitting × 0.4 EDA). Construct a dataset where the test set’s marginal distribution differs visibly from training’s (e.g. sample y-dependent data, then split unstratified). Plot both test histograms. Then explain, quantitatively, how a covariate-shifted test set changes the meaning of every metric you compute on it — and why stratify/shuffling fixes the estimation but not a genuinely shifted deployment population.
C2 (splitting × 1.5 Resampling). Repeated train/test splitting (50 random 80/20 splits) gives a distribution of test R². Compare its spread to the K-fold spread from Exercise 2. Which estimator has lower variance here, and what does each split in the repeated scheme share with the others that K-fold handles differently? (This previews why repeated CV and bootstrap (4.5 Bootstrap) exist.)

title: 0.5 Data Splitting
text:
7. Summary

Test data answers one question — “how does this do on new data?” — and must be spent once.
train_test_split(test_size, random_state, stratify=y): stratify classes, seed everything.
K-fold: every sample validated once; report mean and across-fold SD.
Leakage has four faces: y-derived features, pre-fit preprocessing, duplicate subjects, shuffled time.
The universal fix: fit preprocessing inside training folds — or just use a Pipeline.
Small/imbalanced test sets produce undefined metrics and noisy numbers; SE of accuracy ≈ √(p(1−p)/n).
Part 0’s toolkit is complete. Next, Part 1 builds the statistical language — centers, spread, probability, and inference — that turns those splits and plots into claims: 1.1 Descriptive statistics.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text: NumPy is the foundation of the entire Python scientific stack: pandas, scikit-learn, statsmodels, and PyTorch all speak NumPy arrays. The core skill is not memorizing functions — it is learning to think in whole-array operations instead of element-by-element loops.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
1. Basic Concept
A NumPy ndarray is an N-dimensional grid of values that are all the same type (dtype), stored in one contiguous block of memory. Because the data is homogeneous and contiguous, operations can be dispatched as compiled loops over memory — this is vectorization, and it is typically 10–100× faster than a Python loop.
Three attributes define an array’s shape story:






Vectorization replaces loops. Here is the same computation both ways:






Broadcasting is how NumPy applies operations between arrays of different but compatible shapes. Rule: compare shapes from the right; each dimension pair must be equal or one of them must be 1; missing (left) dimensions are treated as 1.






This is how you normalize a matrix by column means without writing a loop:

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
2. Concept Questions

What are the three attributes that describe an array’s structure?
Why is np.array([1, 2, 3]) * np.array([10, 20, 30]) not the dot product, and what is it?
Which shapes can broadcast together: (4, 3) with (3,)? (4, 3) with (4,)?
What does axis=0 mean when calling .sum() on a 2-D array?
a = np.arange(5); b = a[::2]; b[0] = 99 — did a change? Why?



Answers


shape (size per axis), dtype (element type), ndim (number of axes).
* on arrays is elementwise multiplication → [10, 40, 90]. The dot product is a @ b → 140.
(4, 3) with (3,): yes — (3,) is treated as (1, 3) and broadcasts across rows. (4, 3) with (4,): no — right-aligned, 3 vs 4 conflict → ValueError. Fix by making it a column: x[:, None] or x.reshape(-1, 1).
Collapse axis 0, i.e. reduce across rows, producing one value per column.
Yes. Basic slicing returns a view sharing memory with a, so writing to b writes to a. Use b = a[::2].copy() when you need independence.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict each output before running.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Given the expression matrix below (4 genes × 6 samples), z-score each gene (each row) using vectorized code — no loops.


Solution







The keepdims=True keeps shape (4,1) so broadcasting subtracts the right mean from the right cells. Without it, (4,) broadcasts across the wrong axis and NumPy raises an error — or worse, silently “works” on a square matrix.

Exercise 2. Simulate 1,000 experiments of 100 fair coin flips each. Estimate the probability that an experiment yields more than 60 heads. Do it with one function call, no loops.


Solution







Sanity check against theory: P(X > 60), X~Binomial(100, 0.5) ≈ 0.0176 — (flips > 60).mean() estimates it via Monte Carlo. The trick (condition).mean() — counting by averaging booleans — is used constantly in simulation work.

Exercise 3. Compute all pairwise Euclidean distances between the rows of a (5, 2) coordinate array using broadcasting only.


Solution







The (i, 1, k) - (1, j, k) pattern broadcasts every row against every row simultaneously. This exact pattern reappears inside KNN, K-means, and kernel methods later in the course.

Exercise 4. One-hot encode the integer labels [2, 0, 3, 1] into a 4-column binary matrix without loops.


Solution







np.eye(4) is the 4×4 identity; fancy-indexing its rows by labels selects row 2, row 0, etc. Same output as sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder, in one line.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Views vs copies. Slicing returns a view (memory shared, mutating it mutates the parent); fancy indexing and boolean masking return copies. Silent aliasing bugs look like “my data changed itself.”
Integer overflow is silent. np.array([127], dtype=np.int8) + np.int8(1) wraps to -128 with no warning. NumPy does not upcast like Python ints.
NaN poisons aggregates. np.mean of an array with one NaN is NaN. Use the nan* family (np.nanmean, np.nansum) — but think about why values are missing before averaging around them (see 9.3 Missing values later in the course).
rng.integers(low, high) is high-exclusive; rng.random() spans [0, 1). Off-by-one here produces subtly wrong simulations.
Broadcasting errors vs broadcasting bugs. Shape mismatches raise loud errors, but compatible misaligned shapes (e.g. (4,1) vs (4,)) broadcast “successfully” into something semantically wrong. Print .shape when results look insane.
np.round uses round-half-to-even, unlike naive expectations (np.round(2.5) → 2.0). Same rule as Python’s built-in round.
Floating-point comparison: (a - b) == 0 fails for computed floats; use np.isclose / np.allclose for arrays.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “normalizer” has three bugs. Run it, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Wrong axis / loop mindset: it claims to normalize rows but computes statistics over X[:, j] — columns. For this square matrix the result is column z-scores, exposed by the two checks: row means are not 0, column SDs are 1. (On a non-square matrix the claim and code would diverge even more visibly.) The double loop is also exactly what NumPy exists to avoid.
No invariant check in the original: whoever ran this trusted it because column-SD printed 1s — a check that passes while testing the wrong axis. Always assert the invariant that matches the claim (row means ≈ 0 for row normalization).
int8 overflow: values are within int8 range at construction, but adding 10 in int8 arithmetic wraps past 127 into negatives, silently. Cast to a wider dtype first.







And the honest one-liner replacing the whole loop: (X - X.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / X.std(axis=1, keepdims=True).

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Why is x[:, None] the standard fix when (n,) fails to broadcast against (n, m)? Explain using the right-to-left alignment rule, and give the two operations for which this asymmetry matters most (column-scaling and row-scaling).


Hint

Draw (n,) as (1, n) after alignment and ask which axis it then stretches along.



Solution

Right-aligned, (n,) behaves like (1, n): it varies along columns, so M + v adds v[j] to every row’s j-th entry (row-constant). To scale/shift per row (statistics across columns), you need a (n, 1) array: x[:, None] inserts an axis so the vector varies down rows and broadcasts across columns. It matters most in (1) M - M.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)-style centering and (2) distance computations A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :]. The general discipline: every broadcast bug is a shape bug — print shapes, don’t guess.

Q2. np.arange(0, 1, 0.1) and np.linspace(0, 1, 10) look like they should produce the same thing. Explain the actual difference and why linspace is preferred for evenly spaced sampling in continuous ranges.


Hint

How does each decide the step size, and which endpoint is excluded?



Solution

arange(start, stop, step) computes values as start + k*step and excludes stop, accumulating floating-point step error along the way — so np.arange(0, 1, 0.1) yields 10 points ending at ≈0.9 (and can even produce a surprising extra point when the step doesn’t divide the range cleanly). linspace(start, stop, num) takes the count of points and includes both endpoints by default, placing them by index division so spacing is as even as binary floats allow. Rule of thumb: arange for integer steps (e.g. np.arange(10)), linspace for float sampling of an interval.

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (NumPy × 0.5 Data splitting). Using only rng.permutation and slicing, implement train_test_split(X, y, frac=0.8, seed=0) yourself. Then verify it agrees with sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split in spirit (same sizes, same seed → same partition) — where do the implementations necessarily differ? What does this exercise teach you about what random_state actually guarantees?
C2 (NumPy × 9.2 PCA preview). Center a random (100, 3) matrix column-wise, compute its covariance with np.cov(Z, rowvar=False), and take np.linalg.eigh of it. What is the sum of eigenvalues, and how does it relate to np.trace of the covariance and to the total variance Z.var(axis=0, ddof=1).sum()? This identity (total variance = trace = sum of eigenvalues) is the backbone of PCA’s “explained variance ratio.”

title: 0.2 NumPy
text:
7. Summary

An ndarray is a homogeneous, contiguous grid: shape, dtype, ndim describe everything.
Vectorization pushes loops into compiled code — think in whole-array expressions.
Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right; 1s stretch; make column vectors with x[:, None].
Slices are views, masks/fancy indices are copies; keepdims=True keeps broadcasting honest.
Booleans sum as 1/0: (cond).mean() is an estimator, not a trick.
Watch int8 overflow, NaN-poisoned aggregates, exclusive high in integers, and banker’s rounding.
Arrays hold the numbers; labeled data with mixed types needs pandas — next page.

Next: 0.3 pandas puts names, labels, and mixed types on top of this machinery — and introduces its own selection and grouping semantics that you must drill separately.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text: Every previous clustering page deferred the same questions: how do I choose k defensibly, which validation do I report, what do I do about mixed data types, outliers, and the fact that clustering is an optimization game with many legitimate answers? This page assembles the practical machinery — stability, internal indices, external validation — into one honest workflow.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
1. Basic Concept
The validation triad, defined precisely:

Internal — silhouette, inertia-based indices: does the partition fit the chosen metric? (necessary, never sufficient)
Stability — do partitions reproduce under resampling/perturbation/seed changes? (reproducibility evidence)
External — do clusters align with domain-known variables (outcomes, batches, replicated cohorts)? (the only truth-adjacent evidence)







Stability as the workhorse — the full implementation (revisited from 9.1 Exercise 2, now with per-k curves):

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
2. Concept Questions

Silhouette’s formula rewards which geometry, and what truth-shape makes it systematically misleading?
Stability selects reproducible partitions. Construct (in one sentence) the case where a partition is perfectly stable and scientifically wrong.
External validation correlates clusters with outcomes. What does a strong cluster–outcome association not prove (two answers: one statistical, one causal)?
Mixed data types (continuous + categorical): why does one-hot + Euclidean quietly distort, and what does the distortion favor?
You report “we found 4 clusters (silhouette-selected among k = 2..9).” Name the two selection games you just played and the evidence a reviewer should demand.



Answers


Silhouette = (b − a)/max(a, b): cohesion-to-nearest-other-neighbor ratio. It rewards convex, well-separated, similarly-sized clusters and penalizes elongated/ring/uneven truths even when perfectly recovered (9.4’s rings; spectral methods score “poorly” on silhouettes they solve perfectly).
Stable-but-wrong: K-means with k = 4 on two true blobs at a strong scale artifact — resamples reproduce the same 4-way artifact every time (stability measures the procedure, the truth lives outside it — 9.1 Q2).
Statistical: no multiple-testing control (you tested many clusterings/covariates until one “worked” — 12.x stub). Causal: cluster membership is a derived feature; association with outcome may ride on the same confounders that shaped the clustering — clusters are not interventions.
One-hot categorical columns contribute 0/1 coordinates whose scale (k levels → unit spacing) silently weights them against standardized continuous features (or for them, with many levels); distances become an accidental blend. Favor: whichever block the encoding happened to amplify — dominant-axis behavior (9.1’s sensitivity, encoded).

The k-selection game (9 values tried, best reported — the 4.6 selection bonus); (2) the index-selection game (silhouette chosen from the index zoo). Demanded: stability at reported k, index-agreement, external validation, and all tried values disclosed.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The full k-selection tribunal: implement select_k(X, k_range, B=40) producing a DataFrame with, per k: inertia, silhouette, bootstrap stability (mean ARI), and the gap-style null comparison (mini). Run it on (a) 4 planted blobs, (b) null uniform data. Report both tables. Define the selection policy you’d pre-register (e.g., “k must maximize ≥2 indices, achieve stability > 0.8, and beat the null silhouette by ≥ 0.1”) and check what each dataset yields.


Solution







Pre-registered policy example: “k must have stability ≥ 0.75, silhouette within 0.05 of the max, and gap > 0.1; ties resolved toward smaller k.” Planted data: k = 4 passes all gates; null data: nothing passes (stability low, gap ~0) — the pipeline’s most important output is often refusing to claim clusters. That refusal must be a pre-registered outcome, not a failure.

Exercise 2. External validation done right: on a dataset with a known binary covariate (treatment arm) and a known continuous outcome, cluster into k = 3 and test cluster–treatment (chi-square) and cluster–outcome (ANOVA/Kruskal) associations with multiplicity control over k ∈ 2..6 (report best p-value vs Bonferroni threshold). Then invert the causal framing: the clusters were built from features including the outcome-correlated ones — what does that contaminate? Rebuild excluding those features and re-test. Write the association-claim sentence that survives.


Solution







The leaky features manufacture cluster–outcome association by construction (the outcome shaped the clustering) — no causal or even associational claim survives; the multiplicity correction alone doesn’t save it. Rebuilt without outcome-correlated features, any surviving association is at least arguable. Surviving sentence: “Clusters derived from baseline features (excluding outcome-correlated measurements) were associated with the outcome at Bonferroni-corrected p = …, requiring replication in an independent cohort” — associations, replicated, with the construction disclosed.

Exercise 3. Mixed-type and outlier-safe workflow: on a cohort with 3 numeric + 2 categorical features (some rows also outliers), implement (a) one-hot + standardized-numerics K-means with categorical weight as a tuned parameter (compare weight 1 vs √(levels)), (b) outlier screen (IsolationForest or IQR) before clustering with the removed rows reported separately, (c) full validation battery on the final k. Report the pipeline’s choices as a reproducible spec — the “methods paragraph” for mixed-data clustering.


Solution







Methods paragraph: “Numeric features were standardized; categorical features were one-hot encoded and weighted at w = √(levels) (comparable total mass to the numeric block; w tuned by silhouette sensitivity). Isolation-forest outliers (n = …) were flagged and analyzed separately. K was selected by combined silhouette/stability criteria over k = 2–4, and the resulting partition was tested against treatment and outcome associations with multiplicity correction.” Every number in that paragraph came from a check you’ve now implemented — that’s what makes it reproducible rather than narrative.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The index zoo is not the law: dozens of internal indices (Davies–Bouldin, Calinski–Harabasz, …) exist; they disagree systematically by geometry — pre-commit to your index set and policy, or report the zoo (12.x stub’s multiplicity, again).
Subsampling changes k: stability curves can cross — k stable at bootstrap B₁ unstable at B₂ means your “clusters” live at one sampling density; report the stability curve, not one point.
Outliers both create and destroy clusters: one outlier = one hijacked centroid; a dense outlier pocket = a “real” cluster of artifacts. Detect, report, and decide by mechanism (7.2’s ledger for trees; here for points).
Batch effects outrun biology (5.6): audit clusters against batch/site first — a cluster that’s 95% one batch is a process finding, not a discovery.
Clustering ≠ classification of a latent truth unless you validate externally: the “confusion matrix” against a known labeling is a bonus analysis (ARI), not the definition of success (9.1 Q1’s impossibility).
Reproducibility spec: algorithm, version, distance, scaling, k (and how chosen), initialization/restarts, seed, outlier policy — a clustering without this spec is a rumor.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “validated clustering” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Argmax over the k × metric zoo: the selection bonus (4.1 Q2) plus index-shopping — report all tried values and pre-commit the policy.
Validation by the selection metric: circular by construction; validation must be a different evidence family (stability, external).
Cluster–batch agreement rebranded as subtypes: high agreement means the clustering reproduced the artifact. Audit, disclose, batch-correct, and re-cluster — then look for structure that isn’t the batch.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the silhouette–stability independence: construct two datasets with identical mean silhouette for k = 3 but different bootstrap stability (one with a genuinely separated 3-group geometry, one with three coin-flip partitions of uniform data). Implement both and verify. What does this construction prove about composing internal and stability evidence — and why is the composition necessary rather than redundant?


Hint</summary»
Silhouette is a fixed-dataset geometric average; stability is a resampling property. Uniform data can be carved into 3 well-separated-by-chance regions in one draw.



Solution</summary»
Uniform data’s one draw can show decent silhouette by luck (three separated-looking patches from the triangulation of randomness), while resampling reshuffles the patches — stability collapses. Conversely a stable partition can have modest silhouette (elongated truth). Construction:






The composition is necessary because the two evidences measure orthogonal failure modes: internal indices can’t detect sampling fragility; stability can’t detect geometry mismatch with the truth. Any single-number validation claim (“silhouette 0.6, good clustering”) commits at least one of the two errors this construction isolates.

Q2. Consensus clustering, built and judged: implement the consensus matrix for K-means across 200 subsampled runs at a given k — C_ij = fraction of runs where i and j co-occur. Visualize C (sorted by consensus ordering) for the planted-blob dataset at k ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}: the true k shows a clean block-diagonal C, others show ragged off-blocks. Define the summary statistic (mean within-block vs between-block consensus gap) and verify it peaks at the true k. Then state the one caution: consensus measures clustering-algorithm agreement, not truth — connect to 9.1 Q1.


Solution







The gap peaks at the planted k: within-consensus near 1, between near 0 only when k matches the true block structure. Caution: consensus quantifies how self-consistently the algorithm partitions this dataset — a memorizable-but-wrong structure is equally capable of high consensus (stable-artifact case, 9.1 Q2). Consensus is the strongest internal reproducibility evidence available; external validation still outranks it.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (practical × 7.x ensembles × 9.2). Ensemble-clustering pipeline: build a co-association matrix from 100 K-means runs (varying seeds, subsamples, feature subsets) instead of one run; cluster the co-association matrix (hierarchical, ward) for the final partition. On planted data with an ambiguous k, compare consensus-ensemble partition vs single-run K-means by ARI and stability. Quantify the ensemble dividend, name its cost (compute + lost per-run interpretability), and connect to why bagging works for trees (7.3) — variance reduction by averaging unstable structures.
C2 (practical × 2.5 confounding × 9.1). Clusters as covariates, honestly: derive cluster dummies from an unsupervised run, then use them as covariates in a regression predicting an outcome. Simulate data where (a) clusters genuinely moderate the outcome-gradient and (b) clusters are pure noise. Compare: treating cluster dummies as fixed known covariates (ignoring the estimation of clusters) vs the uncertainty-aware view (clusters are estimated — the classic classification-measurement-error issue). Quantify the SE overconfidence of the naive route across 300 simulations, and write the reporting sentence that acknowledges the two-stage estimation.

title: 9.6 Practical Clustering Issues
text:
7. Summary

Validation is a triad: internal (metric fit), stability (resampling reproducibility), external (domain evidence) — claims need the members their language implies.
Silhouette rewards convex geometry; stability rewards procedure reproducibility; neither certifies truth — compose them and add external evidence.
Choose k by pre-registered multi-evidence policy; refusal (“no defensible clusters”) is a publishable outcome.
Mixed data: encoding weight is a hyperparameter; outliers are audited before k; batch is audited before biology.
Consensus/co-association matrices are the strongest internal reproducibility evidence — algorithm agreement, not truth.
Clusters as downstream covariates are estimated quantities: their uncertainty propagates; disclose the two-stage design.
The unsupervised toolkit is complete. From here the course’s remaining parts (survival analysis, multiple testing, LLMs) lean on it — and on everything Parts 0–8 drilled: this was the checklist chapter.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
Everything so far had answers in the data. Unsupervised learning removes them: find structure — clusters, directions, patterns — with no labels to score against. The mindset shift is profound: there is no test set for truth, so validation becomes stability, interpretability, and usefulness — and every choice (k, scaling, distance) is a建模 statement you must own.
The shift, demonstrated: same data, two legitimate structures:
Structure-finding with no labels — two classic moves previewed (deep dives: 9.2, 9.4):

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
2. Concept Questions

Without labels, what replaces test-set accuracy as the criterion for “this decomposition/clustering is good”?
Why do unsupervised results depend more on preprocessing than supervised ones? Name the two preprocessing choices that matter most.
Your PCA finds “PC1 = 60% variance = patient severity.” What’s the hidden inferential leap in that sentence?
In what sense is clustering a modeling decision rather than a discovery? Give two datasets where the same algorithm yields different legitimate clusterings.
How can unlabeled data still improve a supervised pipeline? Name three distinct mechanisms.



Answers


External validity: stability under resampling (1.5 logic), interpretability by domain experts, downstream usefulness (does the structure predict outcomes you care about? — a supervised check after the fact), and internal indices (silhouette, explained variance) — each necessary, none sufficient. The honest claim is always conditional: “given k = 3 and these distances.”
Because structure IS the output: scaling changes distances → changes clusters (0.5’s standardization law, now generative rather than cosmetic); feature selection changes what “similar” means. Also: transformations (log for skewed counts) reshape geometry wholesale.
“PC1 captures 60% of variance” is a mathematical fact; “PC1 = severity” is an interpretation — it holds if loadings align with severity markers and survives validation against external severity measures. Variance ≠ importance (5.5’s low-variance-signal lesson at full strength).
Clustering imposes a structure family (K distinct spherical groups) and reports the best fit of that family. Same algorithm, different legitimate answers: elongated/gappy data (K-means sees 2 vs 4 depending on scale), multi-scale data (clusters within clusters). The algorithm answers “what does k-means see,” not “what clusters exist.”

Pretraining/representation: PCA directions as features (5.5); (b) semi-supervision: cluster labels as weak features; (c) leakage-free structure for stratification/normalization (batch detection, 9.3) — plus anomaly detection feeding quality control.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The preprocessing sensitivity exhibit: generate 3 elongated Gaussian blobs at different scales. Run K-means (k = 3) on (a) raw data, (b) standardized data, (c) whiten-and-rotate data.
