Compare cluster assignments against the true blob membership (ARI). Report the 3×1 table and explain which preprocessing choice encoded which assumption about what “similar” means.


Solution







Raw data: the wide-scale axis dominates distances — clusters smear. Standardizing equalizes axes (assumes both features equally important). The ARI table is the preprocessing-as-assumption lesson: no choice is “correct” — each defines similarity differently, and the right one matches the domain’s notion (9.6 returns to this with full machinery).

Exercise 2. Stability as validation: build a pipeline that measures clustering stability: bootstrap-resample rows 50×, refit K-means (k = 3), and compute the mean pairwise ARI between the resulting partitions (evaluated on the shared rows via prediction). Apply it to (a) clearly separated blobs and (b) one uniform blob with k = 3. Report both stabilities. What does the stability number license you to claim?


Solution







High stability (blobs) licenses: “the data support a 3-group partition reproducibly.” Low stability (uniform): the partition is an artifact of initialization — you may still use it operationally, but discovery language is forbidden. Stability validates reproducibility, never truth: a stable wrong clustering (e.g., two true blobs split by a scale artifact) remains stable.

Exercise 3. Structure ≠ truth, shown twice: (a) run K-means with k = 6 on 3 well-separated blobs and report how the algorithm happily splits true blobs (over-segmentation with high stability!); (b) run K-means with k = 2 on two concentric circles (make_blobs-style construction by hand) and report ARI ≈ 0 despite visually obvious “clusters.” Write the two failure modes’ names and the tool each demands (validation-set k choice; non-spherical-shape methods).


Solution








Over-segmentation: k larger than the truth yields stable, fine partitions — stability alone can’t catch it (compare 9.6’s stability discussion). (b) Shape mismatch: K-means carves by distance-to-centroid — it cannot represent rings; spectral/density methods are the cure. Both failures say the same thing: the algorithm’s assumptions are the hypothesis being tested.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Unsupervised “validation” is a family, not a number: stability, internal indices, expert interpretability, downstream-task usefulness — report the ones your claim needs (9.6 organizes them).
The reification trap: “K-means found 4 patient subtypes” — the algorithm found 4 centroids minimizing inertia given your scaling; the subtypes exist as model outputs. Clinical translation requires external validation (outcomes, replication cohorts) — always.
Scaling, outliers, skew: each reshapes distance geometry silently; robust scaling or transformations belong in the unsupervised pipeline as modeling choices (0.4’s skew transforms, now structural).
Curse of dimensionality hits hardest here: distances concentrate (2.9), variance spreads everywhere — dimension reduction (9.2) usually precedes clustering in wide data.
Batch effects masquerade as structure: the strongest “cluster” in biological data is often the processing batch — unsupervised methods find it before biology (5.6’s warning, sharpened).
Multiple testing’s cousin — multiple clusterings: trying k = 2..10 and several algorithms then reporting the “interesting” one is the same selection game (4.1, 12.x stub); pre-specify or correct.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “unsupervised discovery” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled clustering lets the batch-dominated feature decide everything — the “subtypes” are likely batches. Scale, and audit clusters against known artifacts (batch, site) before biological naming.
Inertia as k-selection: it decreases monotonically — it cannot select k; use stability/silhouette/elbow-with-eyes (9.4, 9.6).
Discovery language without validation: cross-check against batch labels, report stability, and only then hypothesize — the claim needs external validity to graduate from “partition” to “subtype.”

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Formalize “no free validation”: prove that for any partition P of a dataset and any rival partition P′, there exists a distance metric under which P is the exact K-means solution (construct the metric from P’s indicator structure). What does this impossibility result imply about unsupervised model selection — and which external ingredient breaks the circularity?


Hint

Define distances: 0 within P-groups, huge between; K-means with k = |P| recovers P exactly under it.



Solution

Given P, set d(x, x′) = 0 if same P-cluster, 1 otherwise; all within-cluster variances vanish and between-cluster distances dominate → K-means (and most criteria) select P exactly. Symmetrically for P′. So “the best clustering” is metric-relative — any partition can be crowned by some reasonable-sounding geometry. Implication: internal criteria can’t, even in principle, arbitrate between structurally different partitions; the circularity breaks only with external reference — outcomes, stability across independent datasets, expert validity, or downstream-task performance. This is the precise reason Part 9’s validation chapter (9.6) leans so hard on stability and external checks rather than internal indices alone.

Q2. Design an end-to-end unsupervised analysis protocol for a new 2,000-patient, 50-feature clinical cohort: (a) preprocessing decisions and their justifications, (b) structure-finding methods to run and their assumption families, (c) the validation battery (internal, stability, external), (d) the pre-registered reporting standard (what gets reported regardless of how results look). Implement the skeleton (code structure with the key calls) and annotate each step with the pitfall it prevents — drawing on every Part 9 assumption you can name.


Solution







The deliverable of unsupervised analysis is the protocol plus evidence, not a partition: (a) prevents geometry artifacts, (b) spans assumption families so conclusions aren’t algorithm-shaped, (c) substitutes for the missing test set, (d) blocks the garden-of-forking-paths (4.1, 12.x selection games). Every pitfall from this part reappears as a checklist line — that’s the curriculum compressed.

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (mindset × 0.3–0.4 toolkit). Exploratory-data-analysis as unsupervised learning in disguise: take the cohort table from 0.3 and run the full Part 9 pipeline (scale → PCA → K-means k ∈ {2, 3, 4} → stability) treating the EDA outputs as findings to validate. Which EDA observation (skew, correlation, group imbalance) becomes which unsupervised structure? Write the mapping table — EDA view ↔︎ unsupervised formalization — and note where the formalization changed your belief versus merely quantified it.
C2 (mindset × 12.x multiple testing stub × 4.6 tuning). The selection-game census: enumerate every selection act in a typical unsupervised analysis (k, metric, scaling, features, transformations, algorithm, batch-correction flavor) and estimate the multiplicity. Then design the control: either pre-registration (fix choices from domain theory), selection-frequency reporting (5.1), or external validation — and implement the one you can run today on simulated data where the truth is known (plant 3 clusters; measure how often your full pipeline “discovers” them vs noise).

title: 9.1 The Unsupervised Mindset
text:
7. Summary

No labels ⇒ no test truth: validation becomes stability, interpretability, external checks, downstream usefulness.
Preprocessing is the model: scaling, transforms, feature choice define similarity — own them explicitly.
Structure claims are conditional on the algorithm’s assumptions; reification (“discovered subtypes”) requires external validation.
Stability licenses reproducibility, not truth; internal indices are evidence, never verdicts.
Batch effects and dimensionality are the two ambient hazards of real unsupervised work.
The selection game is alive here too — pre-specify, report everything, validate externally.
First formal tool, the workhorse of dimension reduction everywhere: 9.2 Principal component analysis.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text: Real data has holes: dropped measurements, failed assays, unanswered questions. What you do with them is a modeling decision — delete cases, fill with means, model the missingness, or exploit low-rank structure — and each choice encodes an assumption about why the values are missing. This page builds the taxonomy and the toolkit.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
1. Basic Concept
The missingness taxonomy (Rubin):

MCAR — missing completely at random: the hole is independent of everything (a scanner glitch).
MAR — missing at random: the hole depends on observed variables only (young patients skip a costly scan).
MNAR — missing depends on the missing value itself (the sickest patients’ values are unmeasurable).

The mechanism determines the remedy: deletion is unbiased only under MCAR; imputation models must capture MAR dependencies; MNAR needs explicit missingness modeling (or honesty about limits).






The basic toolkit on one matrix:

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
2. Concept Questions

Complete-case (listwise) deletion: under which mechanism is it unbiased, what does it cost even then, and when is it catastrophic?
Mean imputation’s two distinct sins — one statistical (variance), one geometric (for distances/clustering)?
KNN imputation: what structure does it exploit, and what happens to it as dimension grows (2.9)?
Why is “impute, then treat imputed values as real” in downstream inference dishonest — and what’s the standard fix’s name?
A recommender-style matrix (users × items) is 98% missing. Which paradigm applies, and why is this not an imputation problem in the usual sense?



Answers


Unbiased under MCAR only. Cost even then: smaller n and wider SEs — you paid data for holes. Catastrophic under MAR/MNAR with systematic missingness (e.g., all severe cases missing one assay): the “complete” sample is a biased population (1.1’s summary trap, dataset edition).
Statistical: imputed values are the mean — zero deviation — so variances/correlations shrink toward 0 (n identical contributions). Geometric: every imputed row sits exactly on the mean-point, corrupting distances and cluster structure (9.1’s geometry law).
It exploits local correlation structure: a missing value is filled from similar rows’ values — works while neighbors are informative; under high dimension, neighborhoods blow up and “nearest” becomes meaningless (curse of dimensionality, 2.9).
Imputed entries are guesses with model-derived uncertainty; treating them as observations understates every SE and overstates every p-value — the imputation model’s uncertainty must propagate. The classical fix: multiple imputation (Rubin) — draw several imputations, analyze each, pool with Rubin’s rules. (Modern shortcut: models that treat missingness natively, 7.6.)
Low-rank matrix completion (Netflix problem): the matrix’s rank structure (users × items have few latent factors) makes recovery possible from sparse entries — the goal is predicting held-out entries, not filling a covariate matrix for a model. Different objective, different machinery (SVD-based, Exercise 3).

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Deletion vs imputation under three mechanisms: build y = 2x + ε and censor x (30%) under MCAR, MAR (missing when another observed variable z > 0), and MNAR (missing when |x| large). For each: fit OLS on complete cases and on mean-imputed data; compare slope estimates to truth. Which mechanism breaks deletion? Which breaks naive imputation worse? Write the decision rule.


Solution







Reading: deletion is fine under MCAR, biased under MAR (dropping by z distorts x’s range) and MNAR; naive mean-imputation is acceptable-ish under MCAR, but under MNAR it fabricates average-x values for exactly the extreme cases — often the worse distortion. Decision rule: diagnose the mechanism first (is missingness related to observed data? to itself?); delete freely only under MCAR; under MAR use imputation that models the observed-data dependencies; under MNAR, no mechanical fix — model the missingness explicitly or report the limitation.

Exercise 2. KNNImputer vs IterativeImputer on structured data: build a 4-feature matrix with two correlated pairs (x₂ ≈ x₁ + noise; x₄ ≈ −x₃ + noise) and 20% MCAR holes. Compare fill quality (MAE on held-out true values) for mean, KNN (k ∈ {2, 5, 15}), and IterativeImputer (round-robin regression). Which wins, and what data property does its win exploit?


Solution







Iterative (and small-k KNN) win by exploiting the pairwise correlation structure — each imputation is a mini-regression on the other features, exactly what the correlated pairs make learnable. Large k blurs toward the mean; the mean ignores structure entirely. The property exploited: conditional correlation among observed features — the more structure your matrix has, the more sophisticated imputation pays.

Exercise 3. Low-rank matrix completion by alternating SVD: build a ratings-like matrix with true rank 3 (users × items via 3 latent factors), mask 80% at random. Implement iterative SVD completion: initialize missing entries with the matrix mean; repeat {SVD at rank 3, replace missing entries with reconstruction} until convergence. Report recovery error on held-out entries vs the mean-fill baseline. Then verify the impossibility intuition: rerun on a full-rank (random) matrix — recovery collapses.


Solution







The alternation works because a low-rank matrix is determined by far fewer entries than it contains — the SVD projection strips noise from the guessed entries and the observed entries anchor the truth, iterating toward consistency. Random matrices have no such compression: completion is impossible, and the algorithm honestly fails. This is the Netflix-problem paradigm: recovery from structure, not imputation from covariates.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Diagnose before treating: build missingness indicators and test them against everything observed (chi-square/logistic) — discovered structure means MAR and exploitable signal; undiagnosed MNAR silently biases everything downstream (1.4’s assumption discipline).
The missingness indicator trick (drill 4): adding “was-missing” as a feature lets tree/boosting models use the pattern — legitimate under MAR-ish mechanisms, and standard practice in Kaggle-grade pipelines; but it assumes the pattern is informative, which MNAR can violate subtly.
Impute inside pipelines: imputers are fitted statistics (means, neighbor structure, regression coefficients) — fit per fold, transform test (0.5 law); fitting the imputer on all data leaks.
Dropping columns with high missingness is also a modeling decision: threshold-based dropping (“>40% missing → drop”) is arbitrary unless tied to mechanism reasoning; a column that’s missing because of the outcome is informative, not broken.
sklearn’s IterativeImputer is experimental (enable_iterative_imputer import) — it’s MICE-flavored; still single-imputation: uncertainty propagation needs multiple draws (or a native-NaN model like 7.6’s boosters).
Matrix completion ≠ imputation: completion predicts held-out entries of one big low-rank matrix (no response variable); imputation fills covariates for downstream models. Choose by what the filled values are for.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated imputation pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Imputer fit before split: means/structure from test rows entered training — leakage (0.5). Imputer inside the pipeline.
Mean-impute-then-cluster: imputed rows sit at the mean point, corrupting distances and fabricating a “central” mega-cluster (Concept 2b); use KNN-imputation, native-NaN models, or missingness-aware clustering.
Dropped informative column: missingness correlated with y is signal — dropping it discards mechanism information; keep it with an indicator, or model the mechanism (drill 4).

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove mean-imputation’s variance shrinkage: for x with variance σ² and fraction p missing-at-random imputed with x̄, the imputed vector’s variance is (1−p)σ² (+ a p(1−p)x̄-level correction of order 1/n). Verify by simulation across p ∈ {0, .25, .5, .75}, and derive the same shrinkage for correlations between two independently-imputed columns. What does this imply for downstream PCA/clustering on naively imputed matrices?


Hint

Imputed entries contribute zero deviation from the mean by construction; compute Var = (1/n)Σ(observed deviations² + p·0²).



Solution

Imputed entries equal x̄ exactly, so Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² accumulates only over the (1−p)n observed rows: Var ≈ (1−p)σ² (exactly, for MCAR, in expectation). For two columns independently imputed, imputed positions are mean-valued in both — cross-products with imputed rows contribute 0 in deviation — correlations shrink toward 0 similarly. Simulation:






Downstream consequence: naively mean-imputed matrices show shrunken variances and correlations — PCA underestimates structure, clusters blur toward the centroid, loadings flatten (9.2). Every structure-seeking method sees a demorphosed world; the fix is uncertainty-aware imputation or methods treating missingness natively.

Q2. Missingness-forest vs MICE-style imputation on MAR data: simulate MAR missingness (probability of missing x₁ increases with observed x₂) with x₁ genuinely needed downstream; compare (a) KNN/Iterative imputation then logistic, (b) HistGradientBoosting with native NaN (7.6), (c) mean-impute + missingness-indicator logistic. Report downstream test accuracy/AUC. Which approach captures the MAR information, and what does the native-NaN win tell you about where imputation models actually earn their keep?


Solution







All imputation-and-indicator approaches capture most of the MAR information (the pattern is observable in x₂ and indicators); native-NaN boosting matches without maintaining an imputation model — its per-split missing-branch learns the pattern where it matters for the decision. The broader lesson: imputation models earn their keep by preserving the joint structure (correlations, mechanism) that the downstream task uses — when the downstream learner can ingest missingness natively and the pattern is simple, the elaborate imputer is optional; when inference (not prediction) is the goal, MICE-style multiple imputation remains the principled standard.

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (missingness × 0.5 splitting × 4.6 tuning). The full missing-data pipeline audit: build a pipeline (imputer-choice tuned + model tuned) under 25% missingness; evaluate three protocol variants — (a) imputer fit on all data (leaky), (b) imputer per-fold (honest), (c) per-fold imputer with imputation strategy also tuned — by nested CV. Quantify each gap and write the audit checklist item that would have caught (a) in review.
C2 (missingness × 9.2 PCA × 5.6). PCA of incomplete wide data: n = 150, p = 300, 30% MCAR. Compare (a) mean-impute → PCA, (b) IterativeImputer → PCA, (c) native low-rank completion → rank-3 scores, by recovery of the planted 3-factor structure (subspace angle to true loadings). Which preserves structure, which shrinks it (recall Q1’s variance shrinkage), and what does this imply for omics-style workflows where >50% of values are missing at low abundance?

title: 9.3 Missing Values & Matrix Completion
text:
7. Summary

Missingness has mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR); the mechanism, not convenience, picks the remedy.
Deletion: unbiased only under MCAR, always costly; catastrophic under systematic missingness.
Mean imputation: shrinks variance and correlations, wrecks geometry — a placeholder, not a method.
KNN/Iterative imputers exploit observed-feature structure; fit them inside CV folds; uncertainty needs multiple imputation or native-NaN models.
Missingness indicators turn holes into features — legitimate when the pattern is informative; an assumption when it isn’t.
Low-rank completion solves the sparse-matrix problem (Netflix) from rank structure — impossible without it.
Every choice here is a missingness-mechanism assumption — diagnose the holes before modeling them.
Structure found, holes filled — now partition it: 9.4 K-means clustering.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text: The lasso (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) penalizes the sum of absolute coefficients. The kink at zero that ‖β‖₁ introduces does something ridge never does: it sets coefficients exactly to zero — shrinkage and variable selection in one convex problem, and the workhorse of p ≫ n data.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
\[\hat{\beta}^{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j |\beta_j| \Big\}\]
No closed form in general (the absolute values aren’t differentiable at zero) — solved by coordinate descent: iterate coefficients one at a time, each update a soft-threshold of the OLS-style partial fit. For orthonormal X the solution is explicit and illuminating:
\[\hat\beta_j = S_\lambda(b_j) = \text{sign}(b_j)\,\max(|b_j| - \lambda,\ 0)\]
— shrink small things to zero, shrink large things by λ:






Against sklearn’s lasso (standardized data, orthonormal-ish case), the same logic appears as zeros you can count:






The lasso path — coefficients entering and leaving the model as λ decreases:






Watch x₀ and x₁ (the near-duplicates): the lasso typically admits one of them and ignores the other — feature selection among twins by coin flip.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the L1 penalty produce exact zeros while L2 never does? (Use the soft-threshold formula’s kink.)
sklearn’s LassoCV selects alpha by CV. What does that alpha optimize, and what does it not optimize?
Two features are near-perfect duplicates and both truly matter. What does lasso do, and is the resulting model wrong?
Your lasso selects 4 features; you then report those 4 features’ p-values from a fresh OLS on just them. What’s still wrong?
As n grows with fixed true sparsity, what happens to lasso’s selection consistency — and which condition on the design can break it (the “irrepresentable” idea, in one sentence)?



Answers


For βⱼ near 0, the L2 penalty’s gradient 2βⱼ → 0 — nothing forces an exact zero (flat, smooth approach). The L1 gradient near zero is sign(βⱼ)·λ — a constant push through zero; the optimum sits at 0 unless the data strongly objects. Zero is a corner, and optima sit at corners.
It optimizes prediction error (default MSE) estimated by CV over the alpha grid. It does not optimize the selected set’s correctness, coefficient unbiasedness, or any inferential property — a good predictive alpha can over- or under-select features relative to the truth.
It picks (essentially) one of the duplicates and zeros the other. The model is not wrong predictively — the kept twin carries the shared signal. It’s wrong interpretively if you conclude “feature A matters, feature B doesn’t”: B is shadowed, not exonerated (2.5’s collinearity in L1 clothing).
The selection step used y (through the lasso), so the refit p-values still condition on a data-chosen set — naive OLS inference after selection is invalid (5.1’s post-selection problem; lasso doesn’t escape it, it’s just smoother). Options: split-sample selection/inference, or selective-inference machinery.
With n → ∞, lasso can consistently recover the true support if the design satisfies the irrepresentable condition — loosely, no feature outside the support may be too correlated with the selected set (the signal must be unambiguous). With strongly correlated “shadowed” features, lasso selection stays inconsistent even as n grows.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Derive the soft-threshold update: for a single coefficient βⱼ with residual partial correlation fixed (others held), write the objective as a quadratic in βⱼ plus λ|βⱼ|, minimize over βⱼ > 0 and βⱼ < 0 separately, and show the solution is \(S_\lambda(z_j)\) where \(z_j = x_j^\top r_{-j} / (x_j^\top x_j)\) (r₋ⱼ = partial residuals). Then implement one full coordinate-descent pass on a small dataset and verify the objective decreases at every step.


Solution

Holding other coefficients fixed, the objective in βⱼ is \(\frac{1}{2}x_j^\top x_j\,\beta_j^2 - z_j'\beta_j + \lambda|\beta_j| + \text{const}\) (where z′ absorbs the current partial residual). For βⱼ > 0 the minimizer is (z′ − λ)/(xⱼᵀxⱼ); for βⱼ < 0 it’s (z′ + λ)/(xⱼᵀxⱼ); if the unconstrained optimum lies within ±λ, the corner βⱼ = 0 wins — assembling to the soft-threshold.






Each coordinate’s update is the exact minimizer along that coordinate, so convexity guarantees the objective never rises — the guarantee coordinate descent rides on. (The threshold is λ/(xⱼᵀxⱼ) in coefficient units: bigger columns pay proportionally less — one reason practitioners standardize.)

Exercise 2. Lasso vs ridge on sparse truth with junk: n = 80, p = 40, truth uses 3 features. Fit ridge (α tuned by CV) and lasso (LassoCV); compare test MSE on fresh data AND the number of nonzero coefficients. Then flip the truth to dense (all 40 features with small effects) and re-run. Which method wins under which truth, and what does the loser’s nonzero count say about it?


Solution







Sparse truth: lasso’s MSE is competitive-or-better and its nonzero count ≈ the truth — the interpretability win is free. Dense truth: ridge typically edges out lasso on MSE, and lasso’s nonzero count shows it dropped many small-but-real effects (bias on dense signals). The methods embody priors about the world; pick by which prior matches, verified by CV — never by leaderboard reflex.

Exercise 3. The relaxed lasso (post-lasso refit): run LassoCV to select a support; then refit plain OLS on the selected features only. Compare on fresh test data: lasso’s predictions, the relaxed fit’s predictions, and (a) MSE, (b) the relaxed coefficients vs the truth (when you know it). Why does the refit usually reduce shrinkage bias without reintroducing much variance — and when could it blow up?


Solution







Once the support is (mostly) right, refitting OLS on p_support ≪ n parameters removes the lasso’s deliberate shrinkage bias at little variance cost — that’s the relaxed lasso idea. It blows up when the support is wrong or barely stable: the selected set’s near-duplicates recreate collinearity, and selection noise propagates into the refit (which is why the relaxed variant should itself be CV’d against plain lasso, and why 5.1’s selection-uncertainty warnings still apply).

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Standardize before lasso, always — the penalty counts coefficient magnitudes; unstandardized lasso selects by units, not information.
sklearn’s Lasso may not converge silently on correlated data at small alphas — watch ConvergenceWarning, raise max_iter, and prefer LassoCV (which handles warm starts and selection).
Alpha’s scale is objective-dependent (sklearn uses 1/(2n)·RSS + α‖β‖₁): alphas are not portable across n, feature scaling, or libraries — retune everywhere.
Selection ≠ inference: lasso p-values require selective-inference methods or sample splitting (5.1); a selected feature’s “significance” from a naive refit is doubly data-used.
Under correlation, lasso’s choice among twins is unstable — selection frequencies across bootstraps (5.1 drill) are the honest report; elastic net (5.4) is the structural fix.
The oracle doesn’t always appear: lasso consistency needs the irrepresentable condition; under violation it selects extras or misses features even at huge n. Don’t promise “lasso finds the true variables” in any write-up.
Orthonormal-case intuition is honest intuition: soft-thresholding explains every qualitative behavior (zeros, uniform shrinkage, twin coin-flips via correlated columns breaking orthonormality).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated lasso workflow has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled lasso: feature 5’s tiny coefficient (units!) escapes the penalty while genuinely informative standardized features get taxed — selection by measurement unit. Standardize.
Inherited alpha: α is n-, scale-, and objective-dependent (Advanced pitfalls); it must be re-tuned (LassoCV) per dataset.
Naive refit p-values: the support was chosen with y’s help; these p-values double-dip the data. Use split-sample selection→inference or selective inference; at minimum, disclose that inference is post-selection.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the orthonormal-case soft thresholding: for X with orthonormal columns, the lasso objective separates across coordinates into \(\frac{1}{2}(b_j - \beta_j)^2 + \lambda|\beta_j| + \text{const}\) where \(b_j = x_j^\top y\). Solve each 1-D problem by cases and assemble \(S_\lambda(b)\). Then state precisely what breaks when columns are merely correlated: which step of the separability argument dies, and what replaces it (coordinate descent on coupled problems).


Hint

Orthonormality makes Xᵀy the OLS estimate coordinatewise and decouples βⱼ’s; correlated columns couple the coordinates through off-diagonal XᵀX entries.



Solution

With \(X^\top X = I\): completing the square gives \(\frac{1}{2}\|\beta - b\|^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_1 + \text{const}\), which is a sum of independent 1-D problems \(\frac{1}{2}(\beta_j - b_j)^2 + \lambda|\beta_j|\). Case |b_j| ≤ λ: minimum at βⱼ = 0 (the V’s corner). Case b_j > λ: optimal βⱼ = b_j − λ; symmetric below. Assemble: \(\hat\beta = S_\lambda(b)\) — shrink everything by λ, drop anything smaller. With correlated columns, XᵀX has off-diagonal mass: βⱼ’s objective depends on the other β’s through them, separability dies, and the solution is characterized by KKT conditions (subgradient of ‖·‖₁ balanced with gradient of RSS) — solved iteratively by coordinate descent, each step a soft threshold of a partial residual estimate. The twins coin-flip lives exactly here: two near-identical columns share one z, and ties break to whichever coordinate descends first.

Q2. Lasso’s degrees of freedom equal the number of selected features (for the Lasso at a given λ). Verify by simulation: compute the covariance-based degrees-of-freedom estimate, \(\text{df} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\text{Cov}(\hat\mu_i, y_i)\) over many training draws (use σ known), for a small problem at several λ, and compare to the nonzero count. What does df = |support| buy you conceptually (Cp-style penalties on the lasso path), and why is it surprising (a discontinuous model can have a smooth, integer-valued complexity)?


Hint

Zou/Tibshirani/Efron: for the lasso, E[df] = E[#nonzeros] under regularity — testable with the covariance formula.



Solution







The two agree to Monte Carlo noise — the lasso’s degrees of freedom is its support size. Conceptual payoff: you can price lasso models on the Cp scale (RSS + 2σ̂²·|support|) — a bridge between 5.1‘s subset penalties and penalized fitting. The surprise: the fit jumps discontinuously as features enter/leave, yet its expected complexity moves smoothly with λ and equals an integer statistic — one of statistics’ cleaner magic tricks.

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (lasso × 5.1 selection instability). Quantify the twin coin-flip at scale: p = 30 features where x₂ = x₁ + small noise and both are truly active with equal coefficients. Run LassoCV selection on 200 bootstrap resamples; report the joint selection frequency of {x₁, x₂} and each individually. Then rerun with elastic net (α_mix = 0.5, 5.4) and compare — the resulting table is the empirical case for the elastic net’s existence.
C2 (lasso × 4.4 bias–variance × 4.1 optimism). Measure lasso’s bias–variance profile across λ with the multi-training-set protocol from 4.4 (300 training sets, n = 60, sparse truth, fixed evaluation grid). Overlay: bias², variance, and the number of selected features per λ. Interpret the three panels jointly — where in λ does variance collapse (sparsity kicks in) relative to where bias starts climbing, and how does that gap explain LassoCV’s typical conservative choice?

title: 5.3 Lasso Regression
text:
7. Summary

L1 penalty → exact zeros: shrinkage and selection in one convex fit, solved by coordinate soft-thresholding.
Standardize; tune α by CV (LassoCV); α is not portable across n/scales/libraries.
Lasso selects twins by coin flip — great for prediction, hazardous for narratives; report selection frequencies.
Post-lasso refit (relaxed lasso) trades a little variance for the shrinkage bias back — when the support is stable.
At most n features survive in p ≫ n; df of the lasso = its support size.
Selection still invalidates naive p-values — the post-selection problem wears a smoother costume.
Ridge groups, lasso splits — the compromise that groups and sparsifies: 5.4 Elastic net.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text: Ridge groups correlated features but never zeroes them; lasso zeroes features but coin-flips among correlated twins (5.2, 5.3). The elastic net mixes both penalties, getting sparsity and grouping — and introduces a second hyperparameter that captures a real modeling question: how much do you believe features are interchangeable?

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
1. Basic Concept
\[\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \big( \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2 + \alpha\|\beta\|_1 \big) \Big\}\]
Two dials: λ (overall penalty — sklearn’s alpha) and α (the L1 share — sklearn’s l1_ratio). Endpoints recover the classics: α = 1 → lasso, α = 0 → ridge.






The grouping experiment — correlated twins: lasso splits them, the net keeps them together:






Tuning both dials with ElasticNetCV over a grid:

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
2. Concept Questions

In sklearn’s parameterization, what do alpha = 0.1, l1_ratio = 0.7 mean — and what does alpha = 0 give you exactly, regardless of l1_ratio?
Why does the ridge component stabilize selection among correlated twins? Explain via the penalty’s geometry (edges vs corners).
The elastic net has two tuning parameters. What does the CV surface over (λ, α) typically look like, and what does a flat ridge along α tell you?
Your lasso selects 3 of 30 features; the net selects 8 (including near-duplicates). Which model would you deploy for (a) a $1-per-feature measurement budget, (b) pure prediction with no measurement cost?
Why does elastic net sometimes select more features than n (unlike lasso’s ≤ n cap)? When does that matter?



Answers


The objective penalizes 0.15·‖β‖² + 0.7·‖β‖₁ (times λ = 0.1): mostly-L1 with a ridge floor. alpha = 0 zeroes the whole penalty → plain OLS at any l1_ratio — the ratio only matters when a penalty exists.
The L1 diamond has sharp corners/edges where optima sit — among equal twins the fit picks one edge/vertex (a winner). The L2 ball’s boundary is round: moving along the twin-subspace costs (nearly) nothing, so both twins can share the coefficient smoothly. Ridge’s grouping + L1’s sparsity = twins selected jointly with shrunken, stable values.
Typically a long, flat valley along λ at moderate-to-high α: many (λ, α) pairs score within noise (4.6’s landscape flatness). A flat ridge along α says the data doesn’t care about the mixing share — pick by parsimony of the selected set, not the argmax.

The 3-feature lasso — measurement cost is real money and the twins carry no extra signal. (b) Either on prediction grounds (indistinguishable by CV); the net is safer under future drift/collinearity because it doesn’t bet everything on one twin.

The ridge component lets correlated groups enter jointly; a group of size g can share one “selection ticket” per member, so p_selected can exceed n. It matters when you’re interpreting support size as complexity, or in extreme p ≫ n where the net’s support can balloon — cap with stronger λ.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Map the two-dial landscape by hand: on a fixed dataset (n = 120, p = 25, 4 true signals, one duplicated pair), fit ElasticNet over α ∈ logspace(−3, 0, 10) × l1_ratio ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0}, recording 5-fold CV MSE and support size per cell. Display the two heatmaps side by side. Locate: (a) the MSE argmin, (b) the smallest support within 1 SE of the best MSE. How different are their supports?


Solution







The landscape is the familiar flat valley (4.6): many cells tie within noise; the parsimony pick usually has a third of the support at statistically identical MSE — the one-SE rule, two parameters deep.

Exercise 2. The grouping staircase: build 8 features in 4 correlated pairs (within-pair ρ = 0.95, between pairs independent), with one pair truly active. Trace each method’s selected set across α (lasso: l1_ratio = 1) vs net (l1_ratio = 0.3) at matched CV-chosen λ. Report the “family selection rate”: how often does each method select both or neither member of the active pair, over 100 bootstrap resamples? This number is the operational definition of grouping.


Solution







The lasso’s rate hovers near coin-flip territory (it takes one twin and ignores the other), while the net’s rate approaches 1 — it treats the pair as the atom. When features come in natural groups (gene pathways, duplicate sensors), that rate is the property you’re buying.

Exercise 3. Method bake-off with honest evaluation (4.6): on one dataset (p = 40, sparse truth with a duplicated pair), compare OLS-with-top-k-filter (5.1), ridge, lasso, and elastic net — each tuned by inner 5-fold CV — evaluated by outer 5-fold nested CV. Report nested test MSE per procedure and the paired fold differences between the winner and runner-up. Write the two-sentence conclusion for a methods section.


Solution







Typical outcome: the penalized methods cluster within fold noise while filter+OLS trails (hard selection pays a variance tax). The write-up writes itself: “All shrinkage procedures performed equivalently (paired CV p > 0.05); we selected [method] for its [sparsity/stability] properties rather than predictive superiority.”

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Two dials, twice the selection tax: tuning (λ, α) jointly searches a bigger space than either parent — expect a slightly larger selection bonus and use nested CV accordingly (4.6).
sklearn’s alpha rescales with l1_ratio (the mixing formula divides by 1 − α/2-terms): comparing alphas across l1_ratio values is meaningless — compare CV scores, not parameter values.
l1_ratio = 1 is lasso, 0 is ridge — but tiny nonzero ratios aren’t pure anything: a 0.95 net is “lasso with insurance”; a 0.05 net is “ridge with occasional zeros.” Name the operating point, don’t just cite the class.
Standardization remains mandatory — the mixed penalty still counts coefficient magnitudes.
Groups need not be prescribed: the net groups correlated features automatically; for known groups (pathways), the group lasso exists beyond sklearn’s core — same spirit, structured penalty.
Support size ≠ degrees of freedom for the net: with twins jointly selected, df grows less than support (shared signal) — don’t reuse the lasso’s df = |support| identity here (5.3 Q2).
Convergence warnings matter: the mixed penalty is harder to optimize; watch max_iter, and prefer the CV wrappers that warm-start across the path.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated net workflow has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled net: feature 3’s tiny coefficient dodges both penalties — selection by units again. Standardize inside a pipeline.
The dials swapped: l1_ratio = 0.1 is mostly ridge (few zeros expected); the sparsity knob is l1_ratio near 1. Reading support size off the wrong dial produces confident nonsense.
Test-set tuning: the reported score is an order statistic over 4 tries. Tune with ElasticNetCV on training; spend the test set once.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Geometric derivation: draw (for p = 2) the lasso diamond, ridge disk, and the elastic net’s rounded diamond. Show that the net’s boundary has (a) corners on the axes (producing exact zeros like lasso) and (b) straight edges between corners that are flattened arcs (allowing twins to ride together like ridge). Explain why a fit at an edge gives equal coefficients to twins while a fit at a diamond’s edge forces |β₁| + |β₂| = c — one winner.


Hint

The penalty region {(β₁,β₂): λ[(1−r)/2·‖β‖² + r‖β‖₁] ≤ c} mixes the diamond’s linear edges with quadratic arcs; the L1 part dominates near axes, the L2 part dominates near the diagonal.



Solution

The net’s constraint region is a superellipse between diamond and disk. Near an axis (one coefficient large), the L1 term’s linear boundary dominates → sharp corner → solutions sit at β₂ = 0 exactly (sparsity). Along the diagonal (equal coefficients), for twins the L1 term still contributes 2r·λ|β| but the L2 arc’s curvature — driven by (1−r)/2·(β₁²+β₂²) — rounds the boundary; a tangency with correlated data’s elliptical RSS contours can occur mid-edge with β₁ = β₂ ≠ 0 (grouping). The pure diamond’s edge is dead straight: its tangency logic forces the fit to a vertex (one twin zero). Geometry is the whole story: corners select, curves share, and l1_ratio interpolates the boundary.

Q2. Design and run the stability-driven α choice: for the twins dataset, choose α_mix not by CV-MSE argmin but by maximizing selection stability (Jaccard overlap of supports across 50 bootstrap resamples) among candidates whose CV MSE is within 1 SE of the best. Report the chosen α_mix, its CV MSE vs the argmin’s, and the stability scores of both. When does this procedure change the answer, and what principle is it an instance of?


Solution







High-α (lasso-like) values show lower overlap — the twin coin-flip decorrelates supports; mid ratios stabilize. The procedure only changes the answer when the CV valley is flat (elsewhere it wastes stability on worse fits); it is the one-standard-error rule (4.6) with a second-order criterion swapped in: among statistically tied models, pick by a property you actually care about — here, reproducibility of the selected set.

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (net × 2.5 collinearity × 5.2–5.3). Build a truth with 5 blocks of 4 highly-correlated features each (2 blocks active). Compare ridge, lasso, and net (α tuned) on: prediction MSE (outer CV), true-block recovery rate, and within-block coefficient equality (max/min ratio). Produce the 3×3 summary table and write the guidance sentence for a biologist whose features are pathway members — which method answers which scientific question.
C2 (net × 0.5 splitting × 4.3). The full pipeline audit: implement the net workflow (standardize → tune (λ, α) by inner CV → refit → predict) and wrap the entire thing in an outer CV, tracking per-fold selected supports. Report (a) outer MSE, (b) how many folds agree on the support, (c) the Jaccard distance between per-fold supports. What does the support disagreement across folds predict about the stability of your final published feature list — and what are your two honest options (report frequencies; fix α by domain reasoning and disclose)?

title: 5.4 Elastic Net
text:
7. Summary

Elastic net = λ[(1−r)/2·‖β‖² + r‖β‖₁]: sparsity from L1, grouping from L2; r = l1_ratio interpolates the parents.
Two dials mean two-dial selection tax and flatter CV valleys — one-SE/parsimony reasoning applies twice over.
Twins: lasso splits, net shares — the family-selection rate is the operational difference.
Endpoint sanity: l1_ratio 1/0 recover lasso/ridge exactly; alpha = 0 is OLS at any ratio.
Compare CV scores across (λ, α), never parameter values; standardization is still law.
Stability-driven choice of α (within 1 SE) buys reproducible supports when prediction can’t decide.
What if you never regress on features at all — regress on their principal directions instead? 5.5 PCR and PLS.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text: Ridge regression keeps every feature but shrinks its coefficient toward zero, buying variance down with bias up. It is the canonical answer to collinearity (2.5) and the first stopping point on the regularization dial that Part 5 spends three pages exploring.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
Ridge replaces least squares with penalized least squares:
\[\hat{\beta}^{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2 \Big\}\]
Excluding the intercept from the penalty (as above — always, in practice): the center of the data shouldn’t be regularized. The solution has a closed form:
\[\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y\]
λ > 0 makes the matrix invertible even when \(X^\top X\) is not — ridge exists precisely where OLS breaks (2.5’s singular design). The closed form, verified against sklearn (on centered data, so no intercept needed):






Bias–variance in action (4.4): λ buys variance down:






The coefficient path — every coefficient shrinking smoothly as λ grows (the visual signature of ridge, vs lasso’s sharp zeros in 5.3):

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is ridge not scale-equivariant, and what preprocessing does that force on you?
λ = 0 recovers which estimator? λ → ∞ recovers which prediction rule?
Show from \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}\) why ridge is computable when p > n while OLS is not.
Your colleague ridge-fits and then reports “effect of xⱼ = β̂ⱼ, p < 0.05.” Two problems with that sentence?
In the bias–variance decomposition at fixed x₀, what does increasing λ do to each term — and why does total error eventually rise?



Answers


The penalty Σβⱼ² depends on coefficient magnitudes, so multiplying xⱼ by 10 (dividing βⱼ by 10) changes the penalty for the same fit. Standardize features first — the penalty then says “each SD of signal costs equally.”
λ = 0 → OLS (exact). λ → ∞ → coefficients → 0 → predictions collapse to ȳ (the mean-model of 2.1) — ridge interpolates between OLS and the null model.
\((X^\top X + \lambda I)\) adds λ to every eigenvalue; even if \(X^\top X\) has zero eigenvalues (p ≥ n or perfect collinearity), all become ≥ λ > 0 — invertible. OLS needs \(X^\top X\) itself invertible.

β̂ⱼ is shrunk — it underestimates the effect by design; quoting it as an effect size biases every claim toward zero. (2) The usual SEs/p-values don’t apply to penalized fits (4.6’s warning) — ridge is for prediction; for inference use OLS on selected/refit models or Bayesian machinery.

Variance falls (shrunk coefficients wobble less across training sets), bias² rises (systematically short of the truth), σ² untouched. Total = U-shaped in λ: the sweet spot is where marginal variance savings stop exceeding marginal bias cost.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Prove the closed form: expand \(\sum(y - X\beta)^2 + \lambda\beta^\top\beta\), differentiate in β, set to zero, solve. Then verify numerically that the ridge solution equals OLS on the augmented dataset obtained by appending rows of zeros y=0 (a trick: penalized = unpenalized with pseudo-data). What does each pseudo-row “say” to the fit?


Solution

Objective: \((y - X\beta)^\top(y - X\beta) + \lambda\beta^\top\beta\). Gradient: \(-2X^\top(y - X\beta) + 2\lambda\beta = 0 \Rightarrow (X^\top X + \lambda I)\beta = X^\top y \Rightarrow \hat\beta = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\). The augmentation: appending √λ·I as rows with targets 0 makes the unpenalized RSS on the augmented data exactly RSS + λ‖β‖² — so OLS-on-augmented = ridge.






Each pseudo-row whispers: “imagine an observation where all features are √λ and the outcome is 0 — a fit with large coefficients would miss it.” That’s the prior in data clothing (and the Bayesian MAP connection of Complex C2).

Exercise 2. The collinearity payoff, priced: build y = 2x₁ + ε with x₂ = x₁ + noise (heavy collinearity, n = 60). For λ ∈ {0, 0.1, 1, 10, 100}: (a) record the variance of β̂₁ across 500 training sets (fix the scale by standardizing), (b) record test MSE on fresh data. Produce the two-row table. Which λ minimizes variance, which minimizes test MSE, and how does the OLS row (λ = 0) illustrate 2.5’s “coefficients see-saw”?


Solution







SD of β̂₁ collapses monotonically as λ grows (variance cure), while test MSE bottoms around λ ≈ 1–10 and rises at λ = 100 (bias takes over) — the U-curve in one table. At λ = 0, note how unstable the standardized coefficient is despite the model predicting fine: collinearity wrecks interpretation, not prediction — and ridge is the interpretation-preserving compromise.

Exercise 3. Tune λ honestly (4.6): with RidgeCV and with GridSearchCV-in-pipeline, select α on training data over a log grid; report the chosen α, its CV score, and a nested outer estimate of the whole procedure. Then compare the nested estimate against the naive best_score_ — quantify the selection optimism you now expect.


Solution







best_score_ sits above the nested estimate by the usual order-statistic margin — now predictable, because you’ve measured this gap three ways (4.1 Q2, 4.3 Exercise 2, here).

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Standardize first — no exceptions. Unscaled ridge penalizes measurement units, not information; the pipeline is the enforcement mechanism (0.5).
Ridge coefficients are biased by construction — never quote them as effect sizes or feed them to inference machinery. If you need effects after shrinkage: post-ridge OLS refit on the (all) features with honest caveats, or Bayesian ridge with credible intervals.
The intercept is unpenalized (sklearn’s fit_intercept=True default) — centering by the intercept handles the mean; penalizing it would fight the data’s level for no reason.
λ’s meaning is n-dependent: sklearn minimizes \(\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|^2 + \alpha\|\beta\|^2\)-style objectives, so “α = 1” means different shrinkage at n = 100 vs n = 100,000. Tune per dataset, never copy alphas between studies.
Ridge keeps all p features — if p ≫ n and most features are dead, ridge’s predictions can still be good but its weight spread is ugly; that’s lasso territory (5.3).
The SVD view: ridge divides each principal-component direction’s contribution by (1 + λ/sᵢ²) — low-variance directions (9.2 preview) are shrunk hardest. Ridge is soft PCR, which is exactly 5.5’s comparison.
Correlated groups share credit smoothly — two near-duplicates get similar shrunken coefficients (no coin-flip), which is often the scientifically honest answer, and exactly where lasso behaves worse (5.4).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated ridge pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled ridge penalizes columns by their units — the big-variance feature is shrunk least regardless of signal. StandardScaler inside a pipeline.
Test-set alpha shopping — the test set spent on tuning (4.6). Tune with RidgeCV/GridSearchCV on training folds.
Shrunken coefficient as “effect” — it’s biased toward zero by construction; and no p-value can accompany it. Report it as a model parameter of a predictive model, or do inference separately.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Using the SVD \(X = U S V^\top\), derive the ridge fit as \(\hat y = U\, \text{diag}\!\left(\frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\right) U^\top y\) and conclude: (a) ridge shrinks each principal direction by the factor \(s_i^2/(s_i^2 + \lambda)\); (b) directions with tiny \(s_i\) (near-collinearity) are crushed first. Verify numerically on a rank-deficient design that ridge’s fitted values are finite and stable while OLS’s minimum-norm solution swings wildly across resamples.


Hint

OLS fitted values are \(U U^\top y\) (projection); ridge replaces the indicator \(1\{s_i > 0\}\)-style weights with smooth shrink factors.



Solution

\(\hat\beta = V\,\text{diag}\!\left(\frac{s_i}{s_i^2+\lambda}\right)U^\top y\), so \(\hat y = X\hat\beta = U\,\text{diag}\!\left(\frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2+\lambda}\right)U^\top y\): each SVD direction passes through with a shrink factor — small-\(s_i\) directions (where OLS divides by \(s_i\), amplifying noise) are suppressed. Verification:






The near-collinear second column makes OLS’s fitted surface (here, its 1-var analogue’s slope estimate) jitter; ridge’s shrink factor on the small-\(s\) direction stabilizes it. This SVD picture is also the precise link to PCR (5.5): PCR truncates small directions (hard), ridge damps them (soft).

Q2. Bayesian ridge: with a Gaussian prior \(\beta \sim N(0, \tau^2 I)\) and Gaussian likelihood, show the MAP estimate equals ridge with \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\). Verify numerically that Ridge(alpha)’s solution matches the posterior mode from a simple Gaussian-prior least-squares objective. What does this buy you (credible intervals, prior knowledge encoding) and what does it cost (name the assumption)?


Hint

Maximize the log posterior: log-likelihood − ‖β‖²/(2τ²); match coefficients with the ridge objective.



Solution

Log posterior ∝ \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y - X\beta\|^2 - \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\beta\|^2\). Multiplying by \(2\sigma^2\): \(\|y-X\beta\|^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\|\beta\|^2\) — ridge with \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\). The MAP of “Gaussian likelihood + zero-mean Gaussian prior” IS ridge.






Buy: a principled reading of λ (prior variance ratio), credible intervals from the posterior (Gaussian: covariance \((X^\top X/\sigma^2 + I/\tau^2)^{-1}\)), and a place to encode genuine prior knowledge (e.g., effects near zero and bounded). Cost: the prior assumption itself — credible intervals are statements conditional on Gaussianity of effects, and treating the prior as “just regularization” while quoting Bayesian intervals is having it both ways.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (ridge × 4.4 bias–variance). Measure the full decomposition across λ: 300 training sets (n = 40, p = 20, 5 real features), record bias²/variance of predictions on a fixed grid for λ ∈ {0.01, 1, 100}. Show the variance curve falling monotonically, bias² rising, and the sum bottoming between — then locate the λ that CV chose on one representative dataset and mark it on the decomposition. How close is CV’s choice to the decomposition optimum?
C2 (ridge × 9.2 PCA stub × 5.5 preview). Construct the classic pathological direction: y driven by a component whose variance is smallest (signal in the noise directions of X). Show ridge (which damps low-variance directions) underperforms OLS-with-selectkbest or PLS here, and quantify the gap by CV. This is the “ridge fails when variance ≠ relevance” experiment — the exact motivation for supervised direction methods, and the reason 5.5 exists.

title: 5.2 Ridge Regression
text:
7. Summary

Ridge = least squares + λ‖β‖²; closed form \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\); λ > 0 rescues singular problems.
Bias for variance: paths shrink smoothly, never to zero; λ interpolates OLS → mean-model.
Standardize first; leave the intercept unpenalized; tune α by CV inside a pipeline; nested CV for claims.
Shrunken coefficients are parameters, not effect sizes — no naive p-values.
SVD view: each direction damped by \(s_i^2/(s_i^2+\lambda)\) — soft, stable, blind to direction relevance.
Collinear groups share credit smoothly — honest under duplication, unlike coin-flip subset selection.
Shrink-to-zero is often what you actually want — sparsity next: 5.3 Lasso regression.

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text: The laziest classifier is tempting: encode the classes as numbers (0/1) and run the Part 2 machinery. This page shows precisely what breaks — and the surprisingly defensible uses of the resulting “linear probability model” — so that logistic regression’s logit link (3.3) earns its complexity honestly.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
1. Basic Concept
Fit \(p(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) by OLS on 0/1 outcomes. Three structural problems, none fixable by more data:

Out-of-range predictions: a line is unbounded; probabilities must live in [0, 1]. Near the data’s edges (where decisions matter!) the line exits the unit interval.
Heteroscedasticity by construction: with y ∈ {0,1} and mean p(x), \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x) = p(x)(1 - p(x))\) — variance maximal at p = 0.5, vanishing at the extremes (2.10 Q1). Every classical SE is wrong, automatically.
Wrong error family: Gaussian errors on 0/1 outcomes is a category error; the Bernoulli likelihood is the honest one.







The heteroscedasticity signature, live:
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is a predicted probability of −0.2 or 1.3 not merely “slightly wrong” but unusable for decisions built on probabilities?
The heteroscedasticity of the linear probability model is structural. Why can’t a variance-stabilizing transform of y fix it?
For multi-class data encoded 0, 1, 2, what extra assumption does OLS smuggle in beyond the binary case’s problems?
Despite everything, econometricians use linear probability models. Name two properties that make them tolerable in their niche.
Your LPM gives slope 0.06 for a binary predictor. Translate that into the sentence a stakeholder understands.



Answers


Decisions multiply probabilities: expected cost = p × cost; posterior updating; risk thresholds (“treat if p > 0.2”). Negative probability or probability > 1 breaks the arithmetic that decisions are made of — it’s not a small inaccuracy, it’s a type error.
y is 0 or 1; there is nothing to transform (log of 0, arcsine of a constant…). The variance is a function of the mean’s position — only a model whose variance follows the mean (Bernoulli GLM) or robust SEs can cope; no y-transform exists.
Ordinal spacing: coding {control=0, drugA=1, drugB=2} forces the mean response to be linear in the codes — asserting drugB’s effect is exactly double drugA’s and that the categories are ordered at all. Nominal labels have no arithmetic; OLS invents one.

The coefficient is directly interpretable as a percentage-point change in probability per unit x — no odds-ratio translation needed. (b) With mid-range probabilities (0.2–0.8) and modest extrapolation, the line is a decent local approximation, and OLS’s robustness/diagnostics ecosystem applies. (Plus: interaction effects and panel-data fixed-effects machinery are simple in LPM.)

“Moving from the predictor’s 0 to 1 raises the probability of the outcome by 6 percentage points, on average.” (For small probabilities, odds ratios would say something different — this honesty about which summary you’re quoting is the whole game.)
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Quantify the damage: for the simulation below (steep truth), compute (a) the fraction of the x-range where the LPM predicts outside [0, 1]; (b) the classification error rate of thresholding the LPM at 0 vs 0.5 vs 1 (treating clipped values); (c) the same for clipping predictions into [0,1]. Where does clipping help, where does it silently distort?


Solution







Clipping rescues hard decisions but keeps lying about probabilities — any downstream cost arithmetic (Exercise 2 of 3.1) still consumes nonsense. Classification hides LPM’s sin; probability uses expose it.

Exercise 2. The LPM’s one honest superpower — marginal effects: simulate a logistic truth with modest slope, fit (a) logistic regression and (b) LPM. Compute the logistic model’s average marginal effect (mean over data of dp/dx = p(1−p)·β), and compare it with the LPM slope. Write the sentence explaining why practitioners sometimes prefer the LPM coefficient for reporting.


Solution







For gentle slopes, p(1−p)·β is nearly constant, so “the logistic model’s average effect” ≈ “the LPM slope” — but the LPM gets there with no iteration and reads directly off the coefficient table. That convenience is worth having when the probability range is mid-span; it evaporates near 0 or 1, where the LPM’s line can’t follow the logistic curve.

Exercise 3. Multi-class misuse: simulate three groups with distinct means on x and class labels (control/drugA/drugB) where drugB’s shift is not double drugA’s. Fit OLS on 0/1/2 codes and on one-hot dummies (2.6); show the coded model’s predictions are constrained to a line in code-space while the dummy model’s are not, and quantify the prediction error of each against group means.


Solution







The coded fit is dragged by its fake arithmetic: it must place drugB at exactly twice drugA’s offset. With nominal categories the one-hot model is correct by construction (it’s just group means). Coded-label regression is not a shortcut; it’s a different (wrong) model.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The LPM’s coefficient is on the probability scale; logistic’s is on the log-odds scale. Cross-model coefficient comparisons without conversion (e^β, or AMEs) are meaningless — a perennial review-report error.
LPM + HC3 robust SEs fix inference but not the range violations or efficiency losses; it remains an approximation whose quality is a function of how far p sits from 0/1.
Don’t diagnose-and-patch an LPM into a GLM manually — weighting by 1/(p̂(1−p̂)) (“iterated WLS”) is the historical pre-GLM trick; modern practice fits the Bernoulli likelihood directly.
Zero-one-inflated outcomes (p pinned near 0 for most x) make LPM slopes collapse toward 0 and R² meaningless (never above ~prevalence·(1−prevalence)); the rare-event regime is logistic’s home turf.
Thresholding an LPM at 0.5 implicitly equates FP and FN costs — classification thresholds are decision theory (3.1 Exercise 2), not model byproducts.
Why not least squares on probabilities “estimated” from bins? That’s just the binned drill from 2.8 — it works descriptively but has no likelihood, no efficient SEs, and bin boundaries are arbitrary.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated model has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Out-of-range probabilities as deliverables: reporting “P = 1.18” — a number that cannot exist — to stakeholders. Use logistic regression for probability outputs, or at minimum clip-and-disclose (and never feed unclipped values into cost arithmetic).
Classical SEs under structural heteroscedasticity: wrong by construction (2.10 Q1); minimum fix cov_type="HC3", real fix Bernoulli likelihood.
Nominal codes as intensity: “drugB = 2× drugA” was inserted by the encoding, not learned from data (see Exercise 3). Dummies or multinomial logistic, never ordinal codes on nominal labels.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x) = p(x)(1 - p(x))\) for a 0/1 response, and use it to show that OLS’s Gauss–Markov efficiency claim fails for binary data: construct (in simulation) an estimator with lower variance than OLS — e.g., the MLE from logistic regression — and quantify the variance ratio as a function of the probability range in the data.


Hint

Gauss–Markov requires homoscedastic errors; binary data violate it structurally. The Bernoulli MLE is (asymptotically) efficient for its model.



Solution

ε = y − p(x) takes values 1−p (prob 1−p… wait: y=1 w.p. p ⇒ ε = 1−p) and −p (prob 1−p): Var = p(1−p)² + (1−p)p² = p(1−p). Since this varies with x, homoscedasticity fails and OLS is not BLUE for binary data. Simulation:






Wider x-ranges (probabilities pushed toward 0/1, variance collapsing at the extremes) increase the LPM’s relative inefficiency — the Bernoulli MLE exploits the variance function OLS ignores.

Q2. The thresholded-LPM classifier is not insane: threshold the linear fit at 0.5 and it often classifies nearly as well as logistic regression. Construct the regime where they differ maximally (steep sigmoid, wide x-range), show the classification agreement rate, and explain why classification metrics hide what probability metrics expose — connecting to the calibration discussion your 3.1 answer promised.


Solution







Both models place the 0.5-crossing near the same x (monotone scores, same ranking locally), so hard labels agree almost everywhere and accuracy/ROC-type views see little difference. But probability-valued outputs — costs, PPV statements, risk tiers — diverge wildly at the extremes (−0.4 vs 0.03!). Classification metrics are invariant to monotone score warping; probability correctness is not. That’s the calibration axis from 3.1 Q5, and it’s why “same AUC” never means “same model.”
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (LPM × 2.7 Interaction). In an LPM, interaction coefficients are differences of probability effects — directly interpretable as percentage-point moderation. Fit LPM and logistic (with AME-style interpretation) to the same data with a true interaction; show where the two reports agree (mid-range) and disagree (tail). Which would you present to a clinical audience and why — and what does the “one number per moderation” convenience cost in fidelity at the tails?
C2 (LPM × 3.6 GLMs preview). Write the Bernoulli log-likelihood for data (xᵢ, yᵢ) under (a) the linear-probability model p = β₀+β₁x (where you must clamp/penalize parameter values that push p outside [0, 1]) and (b) the logistic model p = σ(β₀+β₁x). Fit both by direct optimization (scipy.optimize.minimize) and compare each MLE against the plain OLS solution. The punchline to verify: OLS is not even the right fitting criterion for the LPM’s own probabilistic story — report how far apart they land and why.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
7. Summary

OLS on 0/1 labels: unbounded predictions, variance = p(1−p) (heteroscedastic by design), wrong likelihood.
Classification metrics can hide all of this; probability uses and costs expose it.
The LPM survives as a local approximation with direct percentage-point readings — defensible mid-range, dangerous at the tails.
Nominal multi-class labels must never be numerically coded: codes fabricate order and spacing (2.6).
Robust SEs patch inference, not probabilities; clipping patches decisions, not probabilities.
The honest machine for binary responses puts the Bernoulli likelihood and a bounded mean function together — logistic regression: 3.3 Logistic regression.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text: Logistic regression models P(y = 1) as a sigmoid of a linear score — bounded, Bernoulli-likelihood-honest, and the workhorse classifier of applied statistics. Its coefficients speak in log-odds, which is either its greatest interpretive feature or its greatest PR problem, depending on how well you’ve drilled this page.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The model:
\[p(x) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \log\frac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
The logit (log-odds) is linear in x; the sigmoid maps it back to [0, 1]. Coefficients are log-odds ratios: \(e^{\beta}\) multiplies the odds of the outcome per unit of x. Fitting maximizes the Bernoulli log-likelihood — no closed form, solved by iteration (Newton/IRLS):
\[\ell(\beta) = \sum_i \big[ y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i) \big]\]






Note penalty=None: sklearn’s default penalizes the fit (C = 1.0) — worth knowing before comparing coefficients against statsmodels’ unpenalized MLE:






The decision boundary and probability surface, drawn:

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

β = 0.693 for a binary treatment. Translate twice: once into odds, once into a sentence a patient understands.
Where is the decision boundary in terms of the linear score, and why does moving β₀ shift it but moving β₁ rotate it?
sklearn’s default C = 1.0 penalizes coefficients. What happens to the fitted coefficients as C → ∞ and as C → 0, and what real-world failure does the C → 0 extreme prevent?
Logistic regression has no closed-form solution. Why (in one sentence), and what does the algorithm actually optimize?
Your model’s predicted probabilities are well-ranked but poorly calibrated (everything too extreme). Which metric family is blind to this, and what might have caused it?



Answers


Odds multiply by e^0.693 = 2.0 — treatment doubles the odds. For a patient: “if your baseline chance were 1-in-10 (odds 1:9), treatment moves you to about 2-in-9 ≈ 18% chance.” (Odds doubling ≠ probability doubling — the translation must go through the patient’s baseline.)
Boundary = where p = 0.5 = where linear score = 0 (a line, β₀ + β₁x = 0). β₀ shifts the line (offset); β₁ changes its direction/steepness (in 2-D: the normal vector). β₁’s magnitude sets how quickly probability transitions across the boundary.
C → ∞ = no penalty = unpenalized MLE (coefficients as large as likelihood demands); C → 0 = coefficients crushed toward 0 (predicting base rate everywhere). Small C prevents coefficient blow-up under separation or p ≫ n — a ridge penalty in disguise (Part 5).
The log-likelihood is nonlinear in β (β sits inside a sigmoid), so no algebraic zero exists; software maximizes ℓ(β) iteratively — Newton–Raphson/IRLS — the same machinery statsmodels’ summary then reuses for SEs (inverse Hessian).
AUC/AP (3.1, 3.1.5) — rank-based, calibration-blind. Causes: training/serving prevalence mismatch, regularization, resampled training data (oversampling positives), or a drifted population — the fixes live in 3.7’s calibration section.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Hand-compute a prediction: given fitted β₀ = −4.0, β₁ = 0.8 (age, in years) for disease status — compute P(disease) at ages 40, 50, 60 by hand (sigmoid), the odds at each age, and verify the odds ratio between consecutive ages equals e^0.8 ≈ 2.23. Then compute the risk ratio between ages 50 and 60 and explain why it differs from the odds ratio.


Solution







The odds ratio is constant (2.23 per 5 years — the model’s defining constraint); the risk ratio depends on the baseline (here ~3.9 at age 60 vs 50). Odds ratios are portable and log-symmetric; risk ratios are what many audiences think they’re hearing — always know which one you quoted.

Exercise 2. The separation problem: construct x where all y = 1 for x > 0 and y = 0 for x < 0 (perfect separation). Fit unpenalized (penalty=None) and watch the coefficients; then fit with C = 0.1 and C = 100. Report coefficient magnitudes, and explain why the MLE “does not exist” here and what the small-C fit is implicitly doing about it.


Solution







Under perfect separation, likelihood increases forever as the slope grows (the model can approach zero training error by steepening the sigmoid) — the MLE diverges to ±∞. The penalty (small C) caps the climb, acting as the prior/regularization that makes the problem well-posed: a finite, conservative boundary. Symptoms in the wild: “convergence warnings” + absurdly large coefficients + predicted probabilities at exactly 0/1 — fix with regularization or better data, not more iterations.

Exercise 3. Logistic regression in a pipeline with honest tuning: build make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)), tune C over a log grid with 5-fold CV (GridSearchCV), and report (a) the chosen C, (b) CV AUC, (c) test AUC on a held-out set, and (d) the odds ratios from the refit model. Then re-run everything with random_state changed — how stable are (a)–(d)?


Solution







Everything is stable to ~a decimal place except C’s exact position on the grid (neighboring Cs perform nearly identically — see the one-standard-error discussion in 4.6). The pipeline guarantees scaling is fit per-fold; the test set answers once, at the end.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Odds ratios vs risk ratios vs percentage points — three languages for one coefficient. e^β multiplies odds; converting to risk changes requires knowing the baseline (Exercise 1); quoting “30% increase” for e^β = 1.3 is wrong unless p is small.
sklearn penalizes by default — penalty=None (or huge C) for MLE-comparable inference; statsmodels Logit for SEs/p-values. Mixing the two without checking is a silent-model-swap bug.
Regularized coefficients are biased — their SEs are not the inverse-Hessian values; statsmodels-style inference on a penalized fit is invalid (bootstrap if you must).
Separation/quasi-separation → diverging coefficients and zero-width CIs; recognize the convergence warnings, regularize or collect data (Exercise 2).
Complete-data quirks: sklearn’s classes are order-sensitive in coef_ sign conventions; predict_proba[:, 1] is P(class 1) — with string labels, “class 1” is classes_[1], alphabetically determined. Check model.classes_.
Logistic is additive in log-odds — interactions and nonlinearities enter exactly as in Part 2 (2.7, 2.8) but their interpretation happens on the odds scale, which multiplies rather than adds.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated classifier has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Penalized coefficients read as MLE odds ratios: default C = 1 shrinks the coefficient, so the “odds ratio” understates the association. Use penalty=None for interpretable coefficients (or disclose the penalty).
Saturated probabilities described with certainty language: predicted probabilities are never “100% risk” — 0.9997 ≠ certainty; and the 0.5 threshold has no clinical meaning by default. Report ranges and set thresholds from costs (3.1).
Unit-dependent coefficient comparison: multiplying x by 1000 divides the coefficient by 1000 — neither magnitude means anything without units. Standardize (per-SD odds ratios) to compare.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the gradient of the Bernoulli log-likelihood for logistic regression and show it equals \(X^\top (y - p)\) — the same form as linear regression’s normal equations. Two consequences to explain: (a) why Newton–Raphson for logistic = iteratively reweighted least squares, (b) why a perfect-separation dataset makes both the gradient and the Hessian misbehave (relate to Exercise 2).


Hint

ℓ = Σ[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]; dp/dz = p(1−p) with z = x^Tβ; then differentiate ℓ in β via the chain rule.



Solution

With z_i = x_i^Tβ and p_i = σ(z_i): ∂ℓ/∂β = Σ (y_i − p_i) x_i = X^T(y − p). Setting it to zero mirrors OLS’s X^T(y − Xβ) = 0, but p depends on β through sigmoids, so the equation is transcendental — no closed form. Newton–Raphson needs the Hessian H = −X^T W X with W = diag(p(1−p)); the update solves the weighted least-squares problem X^TWX β_new = X^TW z_working — IRLS: iteratively reweighted least squares with working response z = x^Tβ + (y−p)/(p(1−p)). Under separation, as ‖β‖→∞, p_i → 0/1 matching y_i, the gradient X^T(y−p) → 0 along the diverging direction while the log-likelihood itself → its supremum: the iteration drifts to ‖β‖ = ∞ and W’s entries vanish (Hessian degenerates) — numerically rendered as “failure to converge,” statistically as a non-existent MLE.

Q2. LDA vs logistic — the famous equivalence: for two Gaussian classes with shared covariance, both models yield parallel linear boundaries, and their coefficients are proportional. Verify numerically (fit both, compare coefficient directions), then break the equivalence twice — (a) unequal covariances, (b) heavy-tailed features (t-distributed) — and report which model degrades more in each case and why (generative assumption vs discriminative flexibility).


Solution







Equal covariances: directions align (cos ≈ 1) — the two are near-proportional estimates of the same boundary. Unequal covariances: LDA’s shared-covariance assumption is false → its single pooled boundary is mis-specified (QDA is the fix), while logistic, modeling only P(y|x), flexibly fits some linear boundary (though now the Bayes boundary itself is quadratic — both are limited). Heavy tails: LDA’s means/covariances are moment-based and outlier-driven; the logistic likelihood, depending only on y given the score, is typically more robust. Moral (Efron/Friedman): generative models win when their density assumptions hold (faster convergence, fewer parameters); discriminative models are safer when assumptions are questionable.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (logistic × 2.6–2.7). Build a treatment × biomarker model: logit(P(response)) ~ treatment * biomarker_high. (a) Fit and interpret each coefficient in odds-ratio language, including the interaction. (b) Convert the interaction into a difference of log-odds — then show numerically that a positive interaction in log-odds can correspond to a negative difference in absolute risk change at high baselines. What does this imply for presenting “effect modification” to non-statistical audiences?
C2 (logistic × 4.6 Tuning × 1.3 Bayes). Train on a case–control dataset with 50% positives (sampled prevalence ≠ population prevalence of 5%). Show that (unpenalized) logistic regression estimates coefficients consistently but its intercept — hence all predicted probabilities — is miscalibrated by the sampling ratio; correct it with the logit-offset correction (subtract log(sampling odds)) and verify calibration before/after on a population-prevalence test set. This intercept-transport trick is standard in epidemiology and worth owning.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
7. Summary

p = σ(linear score): bounded probabilities, Bernoulli likelihood, MLE by IRLS.
Coefficients are log-odds ratios — translate consciously (odds ≠ risk), and standardize before comparing.
sklearn penalizes by default; statsmodels gives unpenalized MLE inference — know which model you fitted.
Separation breaks the MLE; regularization is the practical answer, warnings the tell.
Boundary: score = 0; intercept shifts it, slopes rotate it; probabilities are smooth across it.
Additivity holds in log-odds: interactions multiply odds, not risks — mind the audience.
Discriminating classes without a parametric story is next: 3.4 Generative classifiers (LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes).

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text: Classification predicts a categorical response. The output of a classifier is really two things: a score (a probability-like number per case) and a decision rule (a threshold converting scores to labels).
