Confusing the two is the root of most classification-metric confusion — this page separates them and builds the metric toolkit: confusion matrix, sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall, F1, and ROC.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
1. Basic Concept
Every classifier worth using exposes scores. The confusion matrix tabulates decisions vs truth:




Predicted +
Predicted −




Actually +
TP (hit)
FN (miss)


Actually −
FP (false alarm)
TN (correct rejection)



From it, the quartet that all others are ratios of:
\[\text{Sensitivity/Recall/TPR} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad \text{Specificity/TNR} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}\] \[\text{Precision/PPV} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad \text{FPR} = \frac{FP}{FP + TN}\]
Accuracy folds everything into one number — and hides everything, too (3.1.5 is dedicated to that trap).






Scores + threshold. Moving the threshold slides cases across the decision boundary — trading recall for precision/specificity along a fixed frontier:






ROC sweeps the threshold and plots TPR against FPR; the area under it (AUC) has a beautiful interpretation — the probability a random positive is scored above a random negative:

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
2. Concept Questions

A screening test has sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.90. In plain words, what do those two numbers promise — and what do they not tell you about a positive result?
Why can accuracy be uninformative while sensitivity/specificity stay excellent? Construct the extreme case.
Your classifier’s scores get monotonically squashed (e.g. all scores squared, order preserved). Which metrics change: accuracy at t = 0.5? AUC? AP?
Precision and recall pull in opposite directions as the threshold moves. State what each one’s denominators “cost” and why no single number captures both.
Two models have identical AUC. Are they interchangeable? Name one axis on which they can differ.



Answers


Promise: 99% of diseased people test positive (few misses); 90% of healthy people test negative. Not promised: that a positive result means disease — that’s PPV, which depends on prevalence (the Bayes result of 1.3: at 0.1% prevalence it’s ~1%… here: 0.99·0.001/(0.99·0.001+0.10·0.999) ≈ 0.98%).
Extreme case: 1% prevalence, “always predict healthy” — accuracy 99%, sensitivity 0. The two class-conditional rates (sensitivity/specificity) are computed within true classes, so they’re immune to prevalence; accuracy isn’t. Report both families or use prevalence-aware metrics.
Squashing destroys the absolute score scale but not the ranking. Accuracy at a fixed threshold can change arbitrarily (t = 0.5 lands somewhere new); AUC is invariant (it uses ranks only); AP likewise (rank-based). Threshold-dependent metrics care about calibration; ranking metrics don’t.
Precision’s denominator (TP+FP) pays for every false alarm the threshold admits; recall’s (TP+FN) pays for every miss. Loosening the threshold admits both more TPs and more FPs — recall ↑, precision typically ↓. Their trade-off is the operating curve; F1 summarizes it at one point, losing the shape.
No — AUC measures ranking quality only. They can differ wildly in calibration (does 0.8 mean 80%?), which matters for cost decisions and downstream probability uses; also in score distribution (threshold placement) and per-region behavior (one may win high-specificity operating points, the other high-sensitivity).

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. From the ranked list below, compute by hand (paper or code, no sklearn) the confusion matrix at threshold 0.5, then TPR/FPR at every possible threshold, the full ROC, and AUC via concordant pairs. Verify every number against sklearn.


Solution







The sweep logic — walk down the ranked list, accumulating hits and false alarms — is the same walk every ROC/PR implementation takes. Owning it once demystifies the curves forever.

Exercise 2. Show the threshold-cost trade in dollars: a screening context has FN cost = $2000 (missed disease), FP cost = $100 (needless follow-up), TN/FN-free = $0. Using the scores from Section 1, compute expected cost at thresholds 0.1–0.9 (step 0.1) and find the cost-optimal threshold. Compare it to the Youden-optimal threshold (max TPR − FPR) and explain when/why the two disagree.


Solution







Youden treats error types symmetrically; real costs almost never are. With FN 20× costlier than FP, the optimal threshold drops (screen loose, confirm hard). Metric choice is a decision-theory choice — there is no threshold-free “best.”

Exercise 3. Cross-validated metric honesty: generate a moderate-signal classification dataset (n = 300, 20% positives), and compare in-sample vs 5-fold-CV values of accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1, and AUC for a logistic classifier. Which metric’s in-sample–CV gap is largest, and why does AUC’s gap behave differently from accuracy’s?


Solution







All in-sample numbers are optimistic; the ranking of metrics is preserved but the gaps differ with each metric’s sensitivity to the specific borderline cases the model tuned on. AUC’s gap tracks the same overfitting — the lesson is not “trust one metric” but “compute every metric out-of-sample,” the discipline Part 4 industrializes.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

confusion_matrix row/column convention: sklearn rows = true, columns = predicted. Transposed matrices are a classic silent error — print it once, label it forever.
AUC pairs with ties count 0.5 (the hand formula above); scores from a coarse model (few distinct values, e.g. a 5-bin risk score) lose AUC resolution through ties.
predict vs predict_proba: predict uses the (possibly inappropriate) 0.5 threshold; decision problems usually want predict_proba + your own threshold from costs (Exercise 2).
Macro vs micro vs weighted averaging of F1 across classes: macro treats a 2% class equally with the 98% class (each class one vote); micro ≈ accuracy. Know which your library reports by default.
AUC ignores calibration — great for ranking, dangerous if someone downstream multiplies your scores into decisions as if they were probabilities; calibration gets its own treatment in 3.7.
Class imbalance doesn’t bias AUC as an estimate of ranking skill, but its sampling noise grows as the positive count shrinks — with 10 positives, one swap changes AUC by 0.02+ (1.4 logic applies to metrics too).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Accuracy on 2%-positive data is ~98% even for a coin-flip classifier — the number certifies nothing. Use prevalence-aware metrics (recall/precision/F1/AP — see 3.1.5) alongside.
Recall is 0 — the “model” catches no positives at all; the line as printed would show it, but the ‘excellent!’ framing (bug 1) hides the contradiction. Never let one flattering metric sit next to a damning one without comment.
AUC on hard 0/1 predictions throws away the ranking within thresholds — with 0/1 scores, AUC degenerates to balanced accuracy and ties dominate. Feed continuous scores to ranking metrics.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive AUC as the Mann–Whitney U statistic: show that AUC = U/(n₊n₋) where U counts concordant positive-negative pairs (ties as ½), and use this to (a) prove AUC = 0.5 under exchangeable scores, (b) construct the null SD of AUC (≈ √((n₊+n₋+1)/(12·n₊·n₋))) and compute how many positives you need for AUC ± 0.05 at n₋ = 500.


Hint

Each positive-negative pair contributes 1, ½, or 0 to the numerator; under the null each pair is a fair coin.



Solution

By definition of the empirical ROC, each threshold pair (TPR, FPR) increment is (1/n₊, 1/n₋); the area integrates the fraction of pairs with score₊ > score₋ — exactly U/(n₊n₋). (a) Under H₀ (scores exchangeable across labels) each pair is concordant/discordant with probability ½ ⇒ E[AUC] = ½. (b) Var per pair ≈ 1/12 (variance of a fair three-way ±1/½/0 trial scaled); SD(AUC) ≈ √((n₊+n₋+1)/(12n₊n₋)). Setting 1.96·SD ≤ 0.05 with n₋ = 500: n₊ ≈ 1.96²·501/(12·500·0.05²) ≈ 128 positives. Moral: the 10-positive biomarker studies quoted with 3-decimal AUCs are noise — cite the interval, not the point.

Q2. A colleague argues: “We shouldn’t fix the threshold at 0.5; we should report sensitivity and specificity at their best threshold on the test set.” Give the two failures of this plan (optimism and interpretation), then implement the honest version: choose the threshold on a validation split, freeze it, report test-set sensitivity/specificity at the frozen threshold, and compare the two procedures’ reported numbers over 200 resamples.


Solution

Failures: (1) Selection optimism — picking the threshold that maximizes test performance then reporting that same performance is tuning on the test set (0.5); the reported best point is an extreme order statistic, biased upward. (2) Interpretation — the “best” point is noise-selected per dataset; across studies the reported sensitivity/specificity are not the same operating point, so they’re not comparable or replicable. Honest version:






The frozen threshold generalizes; the per-dataset-max procedure would report visibly rosier pairs on average (run both to see the gap). One threshold, chosen where tuning is allowed, applied where it isn’t — the Part 4 ethic in miniature.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (metrics × 1.3 Bayes). A classifier has sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.95. Plot PPV as a function of prevalence from 0.1% to 50% (log x-axis). Mark the prevalence at which PPV crosses 50%, and connect the curve to the F1-vs-AP discussion in 3.1.5: which metric family bakes prevalence in, and which keeps it out — and which does your reporting audience actually need?
C2 (metrics × 0.5 Splitting × 4.3 preview). Generate a dataset with 2% positives and fit logistic regression; compute recall at the 0.5 threshold on (a) the full training set, (b) each of 10 stratified CV folds, (c) 10 folds without stratification. Report the spread of recall across folds in (b) vs (c) and tie it to the stratification lessons of 0.5 — then predict what happens to the unstratified recall when prevalence drops to 0.5%.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
7. Summary

A classifier = scores + threshold; the confusion matrix is where decisions meet truth.
Sensitivity/specificity are prevalence-immune; precision and accuracy are not — know which question each answers.
AUC = probability a random positive outranks a random negative; rank-based, threshold-free, calibration-blind.
Thresholds are decision-theory: costs set them, validation selects them, test sets only measure them.
On imbalanced data, accuracy flatters; balanced accuracy/F1/AP keep you honest.
All metrics inherit sampling noise — small positive counts make small AUC differences meaningless.
When positives get truly rare, even ROC starts flattering: the precision–recall view is next — 3.1.5 AUPRC for skewed datasets.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text: You now own five classifiers (logistic, LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes, KNN). Choosing between them is where careless pipelines go to lie to themselves: comparing on one split, one metric, or — worst — the metric that was also used to tune. This page builds the honest comparison protocol: same folds, paired tests, calibration checks, and decision-aware selection.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three principles of fair comparison:

Same folds, paired evaluation — models see identical train/test partitions; differences are then within-fold, far less noisy than independent estimates.
Metrics match the decision — AUC/AP for ranking, calibration for probabilities, operating-point metrics for budgets (3.1, 3.1.5).
Uncertainty on differences, not just points — a 0.01 AUC gap between two models on one split is noise until tested.

The canonical setup, all five models on identical CV folds:






Paired comparison — the same fold’s differences, tested. For two models’ predictions on the same test rows, McNemar’s test asks whether the disagreement pattern is asymmetric:






Calibration — do predicted probabilities mean what they say? The reliability diagram:

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is a paired comparison (same folds) so much more powerful than comparing two independent 5-fold means?
Two models have AUC 0.81 and 0.83. List, in order, the three facts you need before believing the second is better.
What does a model above the diagonal in a reliability diagram (observed > predicted) indicate, and name one common pipeline step that causes systematic miscalibration.
Why can Naive Bayes have a worse Brier score but nearly identical AUC to logistic — and when would you still ship NB?
You tuned model A’s hyperparameters by CV and want to compare against untuned model B. What does honest comparison require?



Answers


Fold-to-fold difficulty dominates variance (easy folds flatter everyone). Pairing differences out that shared noise: Var(diff) = Var(A) + Var(B) − 2Cov(A,B), and the fold-correlation makes the covariance term large — paired tests see the signal that independent-mean comparisons drown in. The same logic as paired t-tests (1.4).

Uncertainty: is 0.02 within fold/seed noise (paired fold-wise test)? (2) Same preprocessing/tuning budget for both? (3) Does the metric match the deployment question — and does the gap replicate on a held-out set or fresh data?

Observed frequency exceeds predicted probability → the model is systematically underconfident in that region. Causes: training on resampled/oversampled data (case–control sampling shifts the intercept — 3.3 C2); regularization that shrinks logits toward the base rate in the wrong direction; score warping in NB under feature correlation.
Brier scores squared-error penalties punish NB’s overconfident probabilities (3.4); AUC, being rank-based, is blind to that inflation. Ship NB when you consume rankings (top-k retrieval) and cost nothing by probability errors — its speed and small-sample stability then win.
Either tune B with the identical CV protocol (same folds/grid budget) or evaluate both with an outer CV layer untouched by tuning — nested evaluation (4.6). Comparing a tuned model’s selection-optimized number against an untuned model’s plain number conflates selection luck with model quality.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build compare_models(models, X, y, k=5, seed=0) returning a DataFrame of mean±SD accuracy, AUC, AP plus pairwise McNemar p-values on pooled out-of-fold predictions. Run it on the five classifiers of Section 1; identify (a) the statistical leader, (b) the pair whose difference is not significant, (c) which metric(s) disagree with accuracy’s ranking.


Solution







Caveat carried forward: pooled out-of-fold predictions are not fully independent across folds for the McNemar counts (models refit per fold), but the paired structure is preserved — for publication-grade claims, repeat across outer resamples (4.3). The table + test pattern is the deliverable regardless.

Exercise 2. Calibration repair: the NB probabilities from Section 1’s reliability data are inflated. Implement a simple Platt-style fix: fit a 1-D logistic regression mapping NB’s logit-scored output to the true labels on a validation split, apply to test. Show Brier before/after and the reliability diagrams side by side. Confirm AUC is unchanged (rank-preserving map) — then state when this fix is not legitimate (which data it must not touch).


Solution







The calibration map is fit on a dedicated split that played no role in training the NB — touching the test set (or the original training set) for calibration would re-introduce optimism (0.5). AUC is invariant (monotone map); Brier collapses toward the logistic’s. This split discipline — fit, calibrate, test on three disjoint samples — is the production-grade pattern.

Exercise 3. Decision-theoretic selection: two models, fixed budget of 100 follow-ups per 5,000 screened (1% prevalence). Compute for each model the expected number of true hits in its top-100 (per 10 bootstrap resamples of the screening population), with a CI on the difference. Also compute each model’s precision@100. Which model wins the deployment question, and does it match the AUC winner?


Solution







The bootstrap CI on hits-in-top-100 is the deployment metric with uncertainty attached. If it excludes 0, the decision is made regardless of what AUC says — models with similar AUC can differ sharply in the head of the ranking, and budgets only ever buy the head.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The comparison protocol IS the result: same folds, same preprocessing (pipelines), same tuning budget, paired tests, uncertainty on differences. Deviating from any of these resets the table to anecdote.
Pooled out-of-fold predictions (Exercise 1) preserve pairing but fold-refitting leaks mild dependence across folds — fine for exploration; use repeated outer resampling for claims.
McNemar’s exact test is binomial on discordant pairs — b and c only; concordant pairs carry no comparison information. Low discordance = low power, whatever the accuracies say.
Brier vs AUC rank: fixing calibration never changes AUC (monotone maps) — which is why “we recalibrated and AUC didn’t move” is expected, not suspicious.
Multiple models ⇒ multiple comparisons: 5 models = 10 pairwise tests; control family-wise error (Bonferroni ×10) or pre-specify the primary comparison (12.3–12.4 preview).
Selection on the comparison metric: if the winner’s metric then becomes the reported performance, the number is selection-inflated — the nested-CV discipline of 4.6 applies with full force.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “model selection” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Model selection on the full dataset including the evaluation rows — the test set is spent tuning (0.5). Select by CV inside training only.
Training accuracy as final performance: KNN(k=1) scores 1.0 — pure memorization crowned winner. Report held-out/CV.
Single-split gap declared decisive: one split’s difference is noise (4.1); use repeated/paired CV and a McNemar-style test before naming a winner.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The “no free lunch” caveat says no classifier dominates universally. Construct two 2-D problems — one where logistic beats KNN decisively, one where KNN beats logistic — with identical n and noise. Report both test-accuracy tables and explain each winner’s edge in terms of assumption alignment (linear boundary vs local structure). What legitimate conclusion is possible about “the best classifier” for a new problem before looking at its data?


Solution







Linear truth: logistic’s inductive bias matches the boundary — it wins. Spiral: the boundary is wildly nonlinear; KNN’s local votes trace it while logistic caps out at linear. Conclusion about a new problem, pre-data: none about which wins — only about the procedure (honest CV over a small, diverse candidate set) that finds out. Model choice is an empirical property of the problem, which is why Part 4’s machinery exists.

Q2. You must compare k=7-KNN and logistic and report a p-value for “A is better.” Walk through the construction of a paired, replicated comparison: (a) why fold-wise paired t on 5 folds is weak (df = 4, dependence), (b) how repeated 5×2-fold CV (or 20 random 80/20 replications) restores power, (c) what exactly the unit of analysis is (a replication’s difference), and (d) the multiplicity caveat if 8 models enter the same protocol. Implement (b) for two models and report the CI for the accuracy difference.


Solution








5-fold paired t has df = 4 and folds share training rows — dependence inflates the nominal Type I error (the famous Dietterich point). (b) Each replication is a fresh split: differences are far less correlated across replications; 40 replications give a stable CI. (c) The unit is the replication-level difference — treat replications as the sample. (d) Eight models ⇒ 28 pairwise CIs; multiplicity control (Bonferroni/Holm) or a pre-registered primary comparison keeps the family-wise error honest (12.3 preview).

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (comparison × 0.5 splitting × 4.3 CV). Build the full “league table” experiment: 6 classifiers × 20 repeated stratified 5-fold CVs, recording accuracy, AUC, and Brier per repeat. Produce (a) a ranked mean table with per-model CIs, (b) a paired heatmap of p-values (all pairs), (c) a stability statement — which model’s variance across repeats is worst and what does that imply for reproducibility of a published winner? This deliverable is the reusable template for every future model-selection question in the course.
C2 (comparison × 3.1.5 AUPRC × 1.3 Bayes). Two hospitals each evaluate your two models; hospital A has 2% disease prevalence, hospital B has 25%. Show empirically that model rankings can flip by metric family (AUC stable, AP and precision@budget flip or compress) across the two prevalences, then write the reporting paragraph that tells both hospitals which model to deploy and why — in language that survives their different baselines.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
7. Summary

Compare models on identical folds, paired; differences need uncertainty, points don’t settle arguments.
McNemar for hard labels; paired fold differences for scores; replicate for power.
Rank metrics (AUC/AP), probability metrics (Brier, calibration), and operating-point metrics answer different questions — pick per decision, report several.
Calibration is a separate axis: Platt/isotonic fixes on dedicated data; AUC is blind to it, Brier isn’t.
Same tuning budget for every candidate; selection metrics must never double as reported performance.
With several candidates, multiple-comparisons discipline applies — previewing Part 12.
Comparison done honestly is model selection’s foundation: Part 4 formalizes the machinery — starting from why held-out error is the only currency: 4.1 The generalization problem.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text: Bagging (bootstrap aggregation) fits many models on bootstrap resamples and averages them. Its entire logic is the variance decomposition of 4.4: averaging B unstable fits divides variance by ~B — and trees are the perfect fuel, unstable enough to benefit, cheap enough to grow hundreds.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
1. Basic Concept
Given B bootstrap samples, fit \(\hat f^{(b)}\) on each and predict by the average (regression) or majority vote (classification):
\[\hat f_{\text{bag}}(x) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat f^{(b)}(x)\]
Why it works — for (approximately) uncorrelated, identically-distributed estimators:
\[\text{Var}(\hat f_{\text{bag}}) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2\]
where ρ is the pairwise correlation between trees. Averaging kills the second term; ρ (shared signal structure) sets the floor.






The B-curve: test error falling with ensemble size, then plateauing:

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must bagging use bootstrap resamples rather than k fresh splits of the data — what does each replicate lose, and what does it gain?
In Var = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, what sets ρ, and which later method attacks ρ directly?
Bagging is said to “reduce variance while leaving bias roughly unchanged.” Why roughly — when does bagging actually change bias?
What is the out-of-bag (OOB) estimate, and which CV concept is it a bootstrap-flavored cousin of (4.3)?
Your bagged tree ensemble extrapolates flat outside training x — same as one tree. Which property survived averaging (per 7.2)?



Answers


Bootstrap resamples share rows (≈ 63% distinct) — each replicate is worse (trained on a sample of a sample) but available in quantity from one dataset. Fresh splits would give better individual models but you’d need a k× bigger dataset. Bagging trades per-model quality for ensemble quantity — a bargain only because averaging punishes independent noise, not individual skill.
ρ = pairwise correlation between trees’ predictions — set by how strongly the same signal structure dominates every bootstrap fit. Random forests (7.4) attack ρ by forcing trees to consider random feature subsets, decorrelating them at the cost of slightly worse individual trees.
The bagged average lives in the convex hull of the base fits — for squared loss, averaging can’t add bias outside the single-model bias pattern, but it can smooth the staircase into something closer to the truth (jaggedness was partly bias-like misfit of the piecewise-constant approximator), so effective bias often drops slightly — most visibly for unstable approximators of smooth truths.
Each bootstrap fit never saw ≈ 36.8% of rows; predicting those OOB rows and aggregating gives a test-error estimate without a separate holdout — the bootstrap cousin of CV, free with the fit (4.5).
Averaging preserves each base model’s support — predictions remain convex combinations of leaf means, so outside training x the ensemble is as flat as its members. Ensembles fix variance, not bias; the axis-parallel and no-extrapolation biases are inherited (7.2’s ledger).

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement bagging from scratch (no sklearn ensemble classes) and verify it matches BaggingRegressor behavior: same B, same bootstrap draws (same rng pipeline), compare test MSEs within tolerance. Then decompose: report the average single-tree test MSE, the bagged test MSE, and the mean pairwise tree correlation ρ — check the variance formula ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B approximately holds using σ² = mean single-tree squared-deviation.


Solution







The scratch version lands beside sklearn’s (differences: rng streams and sklearn’s internal bootstrap details). The variance story checks out to first order: bagged variance ≈ ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B — and since ρ ≈ 0.6–0.9 for full trees, the floor ρσ² dominates — the number random forests exist to crush.

Exercise 2. Instability → benefit mapping: for stability-ranked learners (linear regression, depth-3 tree, full tree), bag each with B = 100 and measure the relative test-MSE improvement (single vs bagged). Report the 3-row table. Then state the bagging selection rule: which base learners deserve bagging, and what does the linear row predict about “bagging everything” as a workflow?


Solution







Improvement ordering is exactly the instability ordering: full tree gains hugely, depth-3 moderately, linear ~zero (sometimes slightly negative — averaging stable learners adds nothing and the bootstrap samples’ mild quality loss can dominate). Rule: bag unstable, low-bias learners; don’t bag a stable model for accuracy (do it only for uncertainty quantification via OOB, or to parallelize).

Exercise 3. OOB as an honest validator: for one dataset, compare (a) the ensemble’s OOB score, (b) 5-fold CV of the same bagging procedure, and (c) true test error on fresh data. Repeat over 100 dataset draws; report mean and SD of each estimator’s error-in-estimating-the-truth. How does OOB’s accuracy as an estimator compare with 5-fold CV, and at what compute price?


Solution







OOB tracks the truth nearly as well as 5-fold CV while costing zero extra fits — the bootstrap samples are already there. (Details differ: OOB is R²-based by default and uses ≈63%-sized training sets like 4.5’s .632 discussion.) For ensembles specifically, OOB is the default internal referee — with nested CV still required when the procedure itself is tuned (4.6).

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

More trees never hurt (accuracy-wise): bagged test error decreases monotonically in B and plateaus — B is a compute dial, not a tuning dial (7.5 breaks this rule: boosting can overfit with B).
ρ is the enemy: bagging full-grown trees on wide data yields highly correlated trees (the strong feature wins every bootstrap) — the variance floor stays high. max_features < 1 decorrelates and becomes… a random forest (7.4).
OOB subtleties: OOB estimates each row’s prediction from ≈ B·0.368 trees (not all B) — slightly noisier and more pessimistic than the full ensemble; fine for monitoring, tuned-claim rules still apply.
Averaging kills calibrated-by-construction class fractions: bagged classification votes are fractions of trees, not of data — probability calibration still needs checking (3.7).
Bagging linear models ≈ feature subspace ensembling — occasionally useful for stability selection vibes, useless for accuracy (drill 4/Exercise 2’s law).
Bias interactions: because bootstrap trees are trained on ≈63% distinct rows, each is weaker; for stable-but-high-bias learners, bagging can even hurt — measure, don’t assume.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated bagging pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Bagging stable learners: the improvement is ~0 (Exercise 2’s law) — the base learner must be unstable (trees) for averaging to pay.
B = 2 is not bagging: two trees average to two trees; the comparison “bagging hurts” is an artifact of B too small to average anything. Use B ≥ 50–100 and watch the B-curve (Section 1).
Stumps bagged silently: depth-1 trees have high bias; bagging can’t fix bias — the mush is bias, measured by nothing in the snippet. Report single vs bagged with the same base learner, across B, with an honest test set.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the bagged-variance formula: for B i.i.d. estimators with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, show Var(mean) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, and hence the plateau as B → ∞ is ρσ². Then verify by simulation for bagged trees: estimate ρ and σ² from an ensemble’s prediction matrix, predict the B → ∞ plateau, and compare against the empirical B = 500 error. What does this decomposition predict about the relative value of adding trees to a forest with B = 10 vs B = 1000?


Hint

Var(mean) = (1/B²)[Bσ² + B(B−1)ρσ²]; divide and split into diagonal + off-diagonal terms.



Solution

Var(mean) = (1/B²)(Bσ² + B(B−1)ρσ²) = σ²/B + ρσ²(1 − 1/B) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B — diagonal variance dies as 1/B; the correlated floor ρσ² never does. Simulation:






The marginal value of a tree decays like (1−ρ)σ²/B: at B = 10 each addition still matters; past a few hundred, more trees buy smoothness of the OOB aggregate, not accuracy — spend compute on ρ (random forests) or on sequential bias-fitting (boosting, 7.5) instead.

Q2. Bagging and bias for smooth functions: theory says averaging convex combinations can’t increase squared bias, but for trees it often decreases it. Verify: measure bias² of a single depth-unlimited tree vs a B = 200 bag of them (multi-training-set protocol of 4.4) on the sinusoid, and explain the mechanism — averaging piecewise constants with different cutpoint locations approximates a smoother function whose expected value lands nearer f. Then state when bagging would leave bias untouched.


Solution







Different bootstrap trees cut at slightly different x’s; their average has cutpoints spread — an effective finer partition whose mean function tracks the smooth truth better. Bagging leaves bias untouched when the base model is stable (linear models: the bootstrap fits barely differ, so the average equals one fit) or when the truth is itself piecewise-constant aligned with typical cuts. The headline: bagging changes the bias/variance mix in practice — “variance-only” is the textbook simplification, not the measurement.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (bagging × 4.4 bias–variance). Decompose bagging across B: with the multi-training-set protocol, estimate bias²/variance for B ∈ {1, 5, 25, 200} bagged full trees. Confirm variance falls ~ (ρ + (1−ρ)/B) while bias² drifts slightly down; overlay the total. Then answer: at which B does adding trees stop mattering for your data, and how does that B scale with the base tree’s instability?
C2 (bagging × 3.7 comparison × 9.x). Bagged classifiers and calibration: fit a bagged tree classifier (B = 200 vote fractions) on an imbalanced problem; evaluate AUC, Brier, and a reliability diagram against a single tree and a logistic model. Explain mechanistically why vote-averaging improves the Brier score (votes average out leaf-fraction noise) yet still trails logistic calibration — and design the calibration step you’d add before deployment.

title: 7.3 Bagging
text:
7. Summary

Bagging = bootstrap + average: variance ÷ B for the independent part, ρσ² floor for the correlated part.
Works exactly as well as the base learner is unstable — trees are the canonical fuel; linear models don’t benefit.
B is compute, not tuning; the plateau is set by ρ, which random forests (7.4) attack directly.
OOB gives a free internal validation estimate — the bootstrap’s gift to ensembles (4.5).
Bias is roughly preserved — and measurably slightly improved for unstable approximators of smooth truths.
Inherited unchanged: axis-parallel bias, flat extrapolation, vote-fraction calibration caveats.
The floor ρσ² is the target now: force trees to disagree — 7.4 Random forests.

title: 7.2 Advantages and Limitations of Trees
text: Before averaging trees into powerhouses, inventory what a single tree gives and costs — because the ensembles of 7.3–7.6 inherit every item on this list, transformed. Knowing which properties survive averaging (and which don’t) is the difference between using forests well and misreading them.

title: 7.2 Advantages and Limitations of Trees
text:
1. Basic Concept
The ledger, demonstrated rather than asserted:






The data-type flexibility advantage — mixed scales, missing-value tolerance via surrogates, monotone transforms invariance:

title: 7.2 Advantages and Limitations of Trees
text:
2. Concept Questions

List four tree properties that survive bagging/boosting, and two that are transformed or lost.
Why is “trees capture interactions automatically” only half-true in shallow trees?
Trees are insensitive to outliers in y for classification but not for regression — explain precisely.
Name a setting where a single small tree is the right deliverable, and what you sacrifice.
Which limitation is fixed by averaging many trees, and which is merely hidden by it?



Answers


Survive: scale-invariance, mixed/unnormalized data handling, axis-parallel boundary bias, automatic interaction handling (given depth), no extrapolation (flat leaves). Transformed/lost: single-tree interpretability (a forest is not readable), instability (averaged away — the point), piecewise-constant roughness (averaging smooths it).
Interactions require depth: an interaction between x₁ and x₂ needs splits on both — reachable at depth 2 only in the best case, and greedy search may not find the pair at all (7.1 Q1). “Automatically” = “reachable given depth and data volume,” not “guaranteed.”
Classification: a huge y-outlier is just another correctly-classified point — impurity measures don’t see magnitude. Regression: leaf means are arithmetic averages, so one enormous y in a leaf drags every prediction in it (1.1’s mean-vs-median story; robust leaves exist but aren’t default).
Clinical/policy triage rules, credit-decline reasons, A/B guardrail rules — anywhere a human must read and apply the rule verbatim. Sacrificed: accuracy vs ensembles/linear models on smooth truths, and stability of the exact thresholds.
Fixed by averaging: variance/instability (and much of the jaggedness). Hidden, not fixed: axis-parallel bias (all trees in the ensemble share it — ensembles approximate diagonal boundaries as finer and finer staircases, not lines), and no-extrapolation.

title: 7.2 Advantages and Limitations of Trees
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The stability experiment, quantified: for 100 bootstrap resamples of one dataset, fit (a) a depth-3 tree, (b) depth-3 tree with max_features=1 (random split choice), (c) a linear regression. Measure prediction SD at fixed test points and the disagreement rate between fits (fraction of test points where two fits differ by > 0.5·noise). Rank the three by instability and connect to why 7.3’s averaging works best on the unstable ones.


Solution







Linear regression barely moves (stable learner — averaging buys ~nothing, as 7.3 Q2 will show formally); random-split trees wobble most; plain trees sit between. Bagging’s payoff is a function of instability — that’s the entire design logic of the next two pages.

Exercise 2. Interpretability deliverable: fit a depth-3 classification tree on the cohort-style data below and produce (a) the text rules, (b) a one-paragraph “policy explanation” a non-statistician could follow, (c) the same explanation from a 200-leaf tree — then reflect on what “interpretable” means operationally. Verify the small tree’s predictions on 3 hand-traced patients.


Solution







The depth-3 tree’s rules are literally readable (“marker above ~11 AND age above ~55 → positive”), each prediction traceable by hand — the deliverable in clinical/policy settings. The 200-leaf tree’s “explanation” is a document no human reads; interpretability is a property of the fitted size, not the class. That’s why small trees remain legitimate tools despite inferior accuracy — and why ensembles export separate explanations (importances, partial dependence) rather than rules.

Exercise 3. Limitation stress-test: three data pathologies — (a) smooth trend with time (y = 0.5t + noise), (b) linear boundary at 45°, (c) heavy-tailed y in regression — each evaluated for a pruned tree vs its natural rival (linear model / logistic / median-regression-style robust tree via criterion="absolute_error"). Report the paired test-MSE/accuracy gaps and write the “when not to use a tree” checklist.


Solution







Checklist: don’t reach for a single tree when (i) the signal is smooth/linear/trending — linear models interpolate it for free while trees staircase and flatline; (ii) the boundary is oblique — axis-parallel greediness pays a staircase tax; (iii) regression y is heavy-tailed — squared-error leaf means chase outliers (the absolute-criterion tree is the in-class remedy); (iv) the deliverable is calibrated probability or extrapolation — neither is native. Each limitation has an ensemble-level patch, but patches work on the ensemble, not the story you tell about a single tree.

title: 7.2 Advantages and Limitations of Trees
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Bias list (survives ensembling): axis-parallel splits; no extrapolation; leaf-mean predictions; greedy (not optimal) split search. Variance list (averaging fixes): instability to resamples, threshold jitter, jaggedness.
“Nonparametric” ≠ “assumption-free”: trees assume piecewise-constant regions and axis alignment — smooth diagonal truths violate both, and ensembles only approximate the violation at computational cost.
Categorical levels: high-cardinality categoricals get greedy advantage in impurity ranking (many ways to split); group rare levels first (5.1 instability note).
min_samples_leaf as uncertainty honesty: leaf means from 3 observations are noise; set it to keep every prediction defensibly backed — or report leaf sizes alongside predictions.
Missing values: sklearn’s trees don’t accept NaN (except HistGradientBoosting, 7.6); imputation choices interact with splits — keep them inside the pipeline (0.5).
The reading trap: export_text on a deep tree looks interpretable (it’s just rules) but no human tracks 200 nested conditions — interpretation budget is a function of size, not syntax.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “interpretable model” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unconstrained “interpretable”: hundreds of leaves — syntax readable, semantics impossible. Constrain to the size a reader can actually verify (max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf), and quantify what the constraint costs in accuracy.
Training accuracy as performance: the full tree memorized — report held-out.
Leaf fractions as calibrated risks: a leaf’s class fraction with 8 samples is a crude estimate, uncalibrated across leaves; if risks matter, calibrate (3.7) or use a model with smoother probability output.

title: 7.2 Advantages and Limitations of Trees
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Formalize scale-invariance: prove that applying any strictly increasing transform to feature j changes neither the set of possible splits on j nor any impurity computation — hence the fitted tree (up to threshold relabeling) is identical. Contrast with ridge/PCA/KNN, citing the specific mechanism each uses magnitudes for. What residual role does scaling play in tree pipelines (name one real reason you might still standardize)?


Hint

Splits are thresholds x_j > c; a monotone transform maps thresholds bijectively and preserves orderings — sorting is all the algorithm uses.



Solution

Trees sort feature j and evaluate candidate cuts between consecutive values; g monotone increasing permutes nothing in that order and maps cut c to g(c), preserving both partitions and impurity sums — the tree is invariant. Ridge penalizes β_j (unit-dependent), PCA ranks variance (scale-dependent), KNN distances (scale-dependent): all magnitude-users, all scale-sensitive. Residual reason to standardize trees: numerical reproducibility of tie-breaking, and pipeline uniformity when tree ensembles sit beside linear members (stacking) — never for the tree’s own benefit.

Q2. Tree stability as a function of n: for n ∈ {30, 100, 400}, fit depth-3 trees on 200 bootstrap resamples each and record (a) the SD of predictions at fixed test points, (b) the probability that the root feature is the same across resamples. Sketch both against n and connect the root-stability curve to the sampling-variability of a correlation estimate (1.2 Exercise 3) — why does the root stabilize faster than the full tree’s predictions?


Solution







Root-feature agreement climbs quickly with n (the dominant signal asserts itself — like a correlation estimate whose sign stabilizes faster than its value), while prediction SD declines much more slowly (every leaf threshold keeps wobbling). The asymmetry explains a practical pattern: trees agree on which drivers matter long before they agree on what they predict — a distinction to respect when reporting importances vs predictions.

title: 7.2 Advantages and Limitations of Trees
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (limitations × 7.3–7.6 preview). Build the “inheritance table”: for each property (scale-invariance, axis-parallel bias, no extrapolation, interaction reach, instability, single-model interpretability), mark whether bagging, random forests, and boosting preserve, hide, or transform it — justifying each cell from the algorithm’s mechanics (you may peek at the next pages’ docs). This table is the conceptual map of Part 7; revisit it after each page and revise.
C2 (limitations × 6.x smoothness). Smoothness repair options compared: on a smooth 1-D truth, approximate with (a) a depth-6 tree, (b) the same tree’s leaves refit with linear models (piecewise-linear tree — implement manually), (c) bagged depth-6 trees (7.3), (d) a cubic spline (6.4). Report CV MSE and plot fits. Rank the repairs of the staircase artifact by MSE-per-interpretability, and note which repairs are available to ensembles but not single trees.

title: 7.2 Advantages and Limitations of Trees
text:
7. Summary

Assets: scale-invariance, mixed data, automatic interactions (with depth), interpretable when small, robustness in classification.
Liabilities: instability, axis-parallel bias, no extrapolation, jagged regression fits, poor calibrated probabilities.
Bagging/boosting transform the liability sheet — but axis-parallel bias and flat extrapolation are inherited, not cured.
“Interpretable” is a statement about the fitted size; export_text on a maze is not interpretability.
Classification is outlier-blind; regression leaf means are outlier-sensitive — pick criteria accordingly.
Single trees remain the right deliverable when a human must execute the rule.
The instability that plagues single trees is exactly what averaging consumes: 7.3 Bagging.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text: Boosting flips bagging’s logic: instead of fitting independent trees to resampled data in parallel, fit trees sequentially, each to the residuals the previous ones left behind. Each weak tree contributes a small correction; the sum climbs toward the truth. Gradient boosting generalizes the idea to any differentiable loss — and introduces the first ensemble in this course that can overfit with more trees.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
1. Basic Concept
For squared-error loss, gradient boosting is plain residual fitting:
\[f_m(x) = f_{m-1}(x) + \nu \cdot h_m(x), \qquad h_m = \text{tree fitted to } (y_i - f_{m-1}(x_i))\]
ν (the learning rate) shrinks each step; the general “gradient” version fits \(h_m\) to the negative gradient of any loss — which for squared loss is exactly the residual, and for other losses (deviance, absolute error) is the loss-specific pseudo-residual.
Hand-rolled on 1-D data — watch the staircase grow:






sklearn’s version, with the staged test-error curve — the overfitting watch:

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
2. Concept Questions

Contrast the roles of B: why is “more trees” safe for forests but a tuning parameter for boosting?
What exactly does the learning rate ν trade — and what is the classic ν × M coupling rule of thumb?
For absolute-error loss, what is the “gradient” that each tree fits? What does this buy over the squared version?
Why are boosting’s base trees kept shallow (depth 3–5) while forest trees grow deep?
Two features are perfectly correlated. How do forest importances and boosting importances behave differently — and why does sequential fitting encourage early features to monopolize credit?



Answers


Forest trees are i.i.d.-ish draws: averaging more draws monotonically reduces variance toward the ρσ² floor — no overfitting mechanism. Boosting trees are sequentially adapted to the current error: later trees encode increasingly specific structure of this dataset (including noise), so past the optimum test error turns up — B must be tuned (or early-stopped).
ν scales each correction; small ν (0.01–0.1) with large M gives gentle, stagewise refinement — better test error, more compute. Coupling: smaller ν wants proportionally larger M (M ≈ a few/ν as folklore) — tune ν·M as a pair.
The negative gradient of absolute loss is −sign(residual): trees fit the sign pattern of errors — robust to outliers (magnitude-blind), the boosting version of 1.1’s median-vs-mean. sklearn exposes it as loss=“absolute_error” (Huber for in-between).
Each boosting tree corrects what’s left — a small, structured residual. Deep trees would refit noise wholesale in one step (large ν-equivalent) and erase the stagewise refinement; shallow trees force the ensemble to spread learning over many steps, which is what makes the shrinkage work.
Forest trees are independent draws — twins split importance stochastically (7.4). Boosting is greedy-sequential: the first tree to grab a correlated pair’s signal takes it, the second finds little residual to justify itself — credit concentrates in the earlier feature, an order-dependence forests don’t have. Importances remain advisory.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The ν × M coupling, mapped: fit boosters on the sinusoid over the grid ν ∈ {0.5, 0.1, 0.02} × M ∈ {50, 200, 800}. Report a 3×3 table of test MSEs. Verify the folklore “small ν + big M beats big ν + small M at equal compute” — and locate the one cell that is dangerous (high ν, high M) and explain its failure in stagewise terms.


Solution







The table’s sweet corner is small ν + large M (each small step averages over many refinements — variance tamed by shrinkage); the dangerous cell is ν = 0.5, M = 800: each tree makes aggressive corrections to already-aggressive fits, and the ensemble chases noise late into training. ν·M coupling: (0.5, 50) ≈ (0.1, 200) in fit quality — pick small ν for accuracy, scale M, and early-stop on validation.

Exercise 2. Boosting vs bagging head-to-head, with the 7.3 contrast you now own: on (a) the noisy sinusoid and (b) pure-noise data (null), compare single tree, bagged trees (B = 200), and boosted trees (tuned shallow) by test MSE (with early stopping via staged predictions for boosting). Report the 3×2 table. Which method degrades more gracefully on the null — and what does that say about their variance budgets?


Solution







On signal, boosting usually edges bagging (its sequential bias-reduction suits the smooth truth). On the null, boosting’s early stopping limits damage but its tuned optimum still fits noise structure the bag never looks for — bagging’s variance-only budget degrades most gracefully. Boosting’s power is bias-attacking; on nulls that power is aimed at nothing.

Exercise 3. Early stopping, industrialized: use validation_fraction, n_iter_no_change, and tol (sklearn’s built-in early stopping) vs your manual staged-prediction stop, on the same data. Compare (a) chosen M, (b) test MSE, (c) compute (fit time). Then explain what the validation split costs relative to staged stopping on ALL training data — and when each is the right tool.


Solution







The built-in early stop holds out a validation slice inside training, watches it, halts — deployable and automatic. Staged prediction over the test set diagnoses the curve but is not a legitimate stopping rule for reporting (it’s tuned-on-test). Cost: the validation split trains on 80% of data — the same pessimism trade as 4.2; CV-wrapped early stopping is the fully honest version.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The dials and their defaults: learning_rate (ν, 0.01–0.1), n_estimators (tune with early stopping), max_depth (2–5: interaction depth), subsample (0.5–0.8 stochastic boosting — bagging-flavored variance reduction inside boosting).
Boosting ≠ parallelizable like forests: trees depend on predecessors; the sequential dependence is the algorithm (distributed variants exist but lose the simple story).
Loss choice matters: squared (default), absolute_error (robust), Huber (robust + smooth), deviance for classification — the pseudo-residual changes, everything else identical (2.1’s loss-matching principle, automated).
Overfitting signature: staged test error U-curve — always plot it before trusting a fit; the trained n_estimators is part of the model spec.
Feature importances inherit the sequential-greedy bias (7.1‘s note): early features absorb correlated partners’ credit; permutation importance on held-out data for claims.
Interactions via depth: max_depth = 2 allows pairwise interactions per tree; the ensemble composes higher orders through accumulation — check whether your truth needs depth or just more trees.
Scale-invariant like all trees, but subsample and early stopping make forests-of-seeds matter: pin random_state for reproducibility.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated boosting pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Aggressive everything: ν = 0.5 with depth 8 over 1000 steps is a noise-chaser — train R² ≈ 1, test collapses. Small ν, shallow trees, early stopping.
M tuned on test: the staged/test-peeking selection is diagnosis, not protocol; choose M via validation split or CV.
Depth ≠ interactions here: with one feature, “interactions” don’t exist; depth 8 just overfits wiggles. Depth is the interaction-order dial (2.7 vocabulary), meaningful in multivariate problems.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive why fitting trees to residuals equals gradient descent in function space: parameterize the model as f(x) = Σₘ ν·hₘ(x); the squared-loss gradient w.r.t. f(xᵢ) is −2(yᵢ − f(xᵢ)); hence “fit the negative gradient” = “fit the residual.” Then verify numerically that one gradient-boosting step with squared loss reproduces the residual fit exactly, and state what changes for Huber loss (which points’ pseudo-residuals shrink?).


Hint

Gradient descent in “function space”: the “parameter” at each training point is the function’s value there; the tree approximates the descent direction.



Solution

With loss L = Σᵢ L(yᵢ, f(xᵢ)), gradient descent updates f(xᵢ) ← f(xᵢ) − ν·∂L/∂f(xᵢ). For squared loss ∂L/∂f(xᵢ) = −2(yᵢ − f(xᵢ)) — the negative gradient IS the residual vector, so “fit a tree to residuals” is exactly “take a tree-approximated gradient step.” Verification:






For Huber loss, pseudo-residuals equal plain residuals for small |r| but are clipped at δ·sign(r) beyond it — large errors contribute bounded direction, not magnitude: boosting with Huber loss is robust regression built from trees.

Q2. Stochastic boosting’s variance attack: subsample = 0.7 fits each tree on a random 70% — inject bagging into the sequence. Design and run the 2×2 (subsample ∈ {1.0, 0.7} × ν ∈ {0.1, 0.05}) comparison with early stopping, on the noisy sinusoid, reporting test MSE and the M at stopping. Which cell stops earliest, which generalizes best, and what does the exercise teach about combining variance-reduction within the bias-attacking algorithm (4.4 both dials at once)?


Solution







Subsampling typically stops later (each tree sees noisier residuals → gentler progress) but generalizes better — the injected randomness decorrelates successive trees, a ρ-reduction inside the bias-attacking algorithm. The 2×2 confirms the two dials are complementary, not redundant: shrinkage (ν) controls step size; subsampling controls step diversity — the mature boosting configuration uses both.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (boosting × 7.3–7.4 × 4.4). The ensemble family portrait: single tree, bagged trees, random forest, boosted trees on the same truth (sinusoid + interaction feature) — all honestly evaluated (nested CV for tuned members). Produce the accuracy table and a bias/variance annotation for each member (from the 4.4 protocol where feasible). Write the “family reasoning”: given a new tabular problem, what diagnostics would tell you which member to try first?
C2 (boosting × 3.1 metrics × 7.6 preview). Boosted classification with deviance loss: fit GradientBoostingClassifier to an imbalanced problem (5% positives); evaluate staged AUC and staged log-loss on validation. Do their optima coincide? Connect the divergence to what each metric rewards (ranking vs probability sharpness), and predict what calibration step (3.7) the deployed model needs at the AUC-optimal M.

title: 7.5 Gradient Boosting
text:
7. Summary

Boosting = sequential trees on negative gradients (residuals, for squared loss): bias attacks with shrunken steps.
ν small + M large + shallow trees: the canonical configuration; ν·M couple; early stopping or CV sets M.
Unlike forests, boosting can overfit with more trees — the staged curve is the instrument panel.
Loss choice is a dial (squared/absolute/Huber/deviance): the same machinery, different pseudo-residuals.
Subsample injects bagging into the sequence: variance reduction inside bias correction.
Sequential greediness concentrates importances in early features — advisory only.
The ideas graduate to industrial libraries with histogram speeds and native NaN handling: 7.6 Modern boosting libraries.

title: 6.7 Generalized Additive Models
text:
With many features, one multivariate smooth is hopeless (“curse of dimensionality”), but one smooth per feature, added together scales beautifully:
\[g\big(\mathbb{E}[Y]\big) = \beta_0 + s_1(x_1) + s_2(x_2) + \cdots + s_p(x_p)\]
Generalized additive models (GAMs) combine Part 6’s smoothers with Part 3’s GLM likelihoods: flexible per-feature curves, additive structure, interpretable partial effects — the workhorse between linear/GLM models and black boxes.

title: 6.7 Generalized Additive Models
text:
1. Basic Concept
No GAM library ships in Pyodide, so we build the core object ourselves — and in doing so learn what a GAM is: (1) a smoother per feature, (2) a backfitting loop that coordinates them, (3) a GLM link when the response demands it.
Backfitting by hand (Gaussian response): iterate — fit each feature’s smoother to the current residuals, sweep out its contribution, repeat:






The GLM connection — additive logistic, via spline features in any linear classifier:

title: 6.7 Generalized Additive Models
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does the additive assumption exclude, in one sentence — and why is that often a feature, not a bug?
Why does backfitting converge (when it does)? Connect to coordinate descent (5.3).
In the additive logistic model, how do you interpret \(s_1\)’s curve on the log-odds scale — and what would you plot for a clinical audience?
Why is a GAM with p = 50 features viable while a full 50-dimensional smooth is not?
Your GAM’s \(s_3\) looks flat. What are the two possible realities, and which tool distinguishes them?



Answers


It excludes interactions: no term like \(s_{12}(x_1, x_2)\) — the effect of x₁ is one fixed curve regardless of x₂. Feature: effect estimates are stable, each smooth is plottable, and estimation needs O(p) smooths, not one product-basis monster (2.7 for when that assumption must be tested).
Each step solves exactly the same kind of subproblem as lasso’s coordinate update: minimize the objective over one function holding the rest fixed. The objective (least squares + smoothing penalties) is convex and separable-ish across functions given residuals, so the cyclic minimizer descends to the (unique, for identifiability-fixed) optimum.
\(s_1(x_1)\) is that feature’s additive contribution to log-odds — a unitless score. For clinicians: transform to the probability scale at meaningful covariate values (plot predicted P(y=1) vs x₁ with x₂ fixed at reference values, with bands).
The curse bites per-smooth, not jointly: each 1-D smooth needs only its own ~df, and estimation error adds across features linearly instead of exponentially (2.9’s curse avoided by construction).

x₃ truly has no effect; (b) the smoother over-penalized (λ too big) or the effect is real but confounded/cancelled. Distinguish: refit with a much looser smoother — if \(s_3\) stays flat, believe null; if it explodes, your penalty was the story.

title: 6.7 Generalized Additive Models
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Finish the GAM: wrap backfitting + a query-time predictor into a small class MyGAM with fit(X, y) (one spline per column, centered) and predict(X_new) (evaluate each stored spline — UnivariateSpline objects are callable at new x). Fit on 3-feature data (sin, linear, noise), report test MSE vs linear regression, and verify that predict equals the training-time fitted values at training points (self-consistency).


Solution







predict outside training x-ranges uses the frozen curves’ extrapolation — police ranges or clamp. The self-consistency check is the regression equivalent of “the pipeline reproduces its training predictions” — a cheap invariant worth asserting in any hand-rolled model.

Exercise 2. The additive-vs-interaction boundary: truth A: y = sin(x₁) + x₂² + noise; truth B: y = sin(x₁)·x₂/5 + noise. Compare (a) additive spline model, (b) tensor-product spline basis (SplineTransformer on both features jointly), by CV. Report the 2×2 table (model × truth). Quantify the additive model’s bias on B and the tensor model’s variance on A — then write the decision rule for adding a specific interaction term (e.g., test \(s_{12}\) only where domain theory says interactions live, per 2.7).


Solution







Additive truth: both fine (tensor pays a small variance tax). Interaction truth: the additive model’s bias floor is visible (it cannot bend with x₂), while the tensor model pays for its freedom on the additive truth. Decision rule: pre-specify candidate interactions from domain knowledge, add each as a tensor term for those variables only, and let CV arbitrate — never all-pairs by default (2.7’s discipline with smoother ingredients).

Exercise 3. Partial dependence, honestly: fit the additive logistic model (spline-basis logistic from Section 1) on the simulated cohort; produce the partial-dependence plot for x₁ — model predictions averaged over the empirical x₂ distribution as x₁ sweeps a grid — and compare it against the fitted \(s_1\) curve. They coincide because the model is additive; then break additivity (add a true tensor term to the data-generating process, refit the additive model) and show how the partial-dependence plot and \(s_1\) diverge. What does the divergence measure?


Solution







For a truly additive fitted model, partial dependence equals the fitted component function — the plot adds nothing but the probability-scale translation. When interactions exist but the model is additive, PD averages the model’s best additive compromise while any single-slice curve shows a slice — their divergence is a diagnostic of missed interaction (and motivates adding the tensor term for x₁×x₂).

title: 6.7 Generalized Additive Models
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Identifiability: additive functions are only defined up to constants that sum to zero — every implementation centers the smooths (your hand-rolled one drifts otherwise, drill 2); report curves centered so their mean is 0.
Smoothing parameter per feature: one global s imposes one prior flexibility on all features; tune per-feature (or at least per-feature-family) by CV — the same flat-landscape reasoning as 4.6.
Correlated features blur additive effects: with x₁ ⊥⊥ x₂ the backfit recovers clean components; under collinearity, the split of a joint signal between \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) is unstable (2.5’s warning in curve clothing).
Concavity of the penalized objective holds for Gaussian smoothers; for logistic-GAMs the coordinate updates are iteratively-reweighted — convergence is still well-behaved but slower; watch iteration counts.
Binary/counts: the right way is additive logit/log with the Bernoulli/Poisson likelihood (a true GAM); the spline-features-in-a-GLM shortcut used here is equivalent up to penalty details — declare which you ran.
Interactions are absent by default: if the science is interactive, GAMs are the wrong default — tensor terms, trees, or kernels (8.4) take over.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “GAM” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Uncentered components: f1 absorbed everything it could (including x2’s signal through correlation) and carries a nonzero level; the pair (f1, f2) is not identifiable and the plots are misleading. Center each component; backfit with partial residuals.
Single pass: one sweep is not the fixed point — residuals after one round still carry structure the second pass removes. Iterate until the residual SD stabilizes.
Per-feature penalties used as feature selection: a huge s on f2 forces it flat, then the flatness gets reported as “no effect” — the conclusion was installed by the dial (5.3’s penalty-as-prior, abused). Tune s per feature by CV; report null effects only after the loosest sensible smoother agrees.

title: 6.7 Generalized Additive Models
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove backfitting’s fixed point: at convergence, each \(s_j\) satisfies the normal-equation-like condition \(s_j = S_j(y - \sum_{k \ne j} s_k)\) (where \(S_j\) is feature j’s smoother matrix). Show that stacking these conditions gives \((I - \mathcal{S})\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{Q}y\) for block operator 𝒮, and explain why convergence requires the smoothing matrices to be “not too aggressive” (relate spectral radii to the λ’s — the additive-model version of 4.4’s stability intuition).


Hint

Backfitting is block coordinate descent / fixed-point iteration \(\mathbf{s}^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{Q}y) + \mathcal{S}'\mathbf{s}^{(t)}\)-style; convergence iff the iteration operator’s spectral radius < 1.



Solution

At the fixed point each component’s smoother applied to current partial residuals reproduces that component: \(s_j = S_j(y - \beta_0\mathbf{1} - \sum_{k\ne j} s_k)\). Stacking across j: \(\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{Q}y + \mathcal{A}\mathbf{s}\) where 𝒜 is the block operator with jk-block \(-S_j\) for k ≠ j. The backfitting iteration is \(\mathbf{s}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{Q}y + \mathcal{A}\mathbf{s}^{(t)}\), converging iff ρ(𝒜) < 1. Very small λ (aggressive smoothers, S_j ≈ interpolators) pushes 𝒜’s radius toward 1 — oscillating, slowly-converging backfits; heavy smoothing shrinks S_j and guarantees convergence but biases components toward zero — the smoothing-parameter choice is literally a convergence/stability choice, mirroring how ridge’s λ stabilizes correlated-coordinate descent.

Q2. Design the variable-selection GAM: with p = 12 features (5 real, various shapes), select features by per-feature df tuning + backfit-and-prune: run the full GAM, drop the feature whose removal least increases CV MSE, refit, repeat — record the removal order and the CV-MSE path. Compare against (a) lasso-on-spline-basis (5.3) and (b) marginal filters (5.1). Which method recovers the true 5, and what does the comparison teach about selection with nonlinear components?


Solution







Lasso-on-basis recovers most of the true 5 (its joint fit sees conditional contributions) but may keep spline-support extras; the marginal filter misses any feature whose signal is non-monotone or confounded. The lesson: with nonlinear components, selection must happen in the model class you’ll fit — basis-level penalization or per-component pruning, never univariate scores alone.

title: 6.7 Generalized Additive Models
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (GAM × 5.6 high dimensions). Scale test: n = 100 samples, p = 200 features (6 nonlinear signals). Compare (a) additive-spline lasso (your additive basis + LassoCV), (b) plain ridge on raw features, (c) PCR(5.5) — all nested-CV’d. Report test MSE and, for (a), the selected features’ overlap with truth. Write the guidance: when does the additive-sparse bet beat dimension reduction in the p ≫ n nonlinear world?
C2 (GAM × 7.4 random forests preview × 2.7). The interpretability trade, quantified: on a truth with 3 additive components + 1 interaction, compare GAM, GAM+one tensor term, and random forest by CV MSE and by recoverability of \(s_1\) (correlation of the fitted component with the truth, extracting the forest’s partial dependence for the same feature). Produce the 3×2 table (MSE, component-recovery) and write the two-sentence conclusion about what you sell when you sell interpretability.

title: 6.7 Generalized Additive Models
text:
7. Summary

GAM = GLM + one smooth per feature, added on the link scale: flexible, additive, interpretable.
Backfitting = coordinate descent over functions: iterate partial-residual smooths to the fixed point; center components.
The additive assumption excludes interactions by default — a stability/interpretability feature and a modeling commitment to test deliberately.
Per-feature smoothing penalties are priors: tune them; a flat s₃ is a conclusion only after the dial is honest.
Additive splines + L1 give nonlinear variable selection that respects the model class; marginal filters don’t.
With interactions confirmed, escalate deliberately: tensor terms, then trees (Part 7) — which grow the step-function world’s interactions automatically: 7.1 Decision trees.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text: The most local basis possible: cut the range of x into intervals and fit a separate constant to each. Step functions trade smoothness for robustness and interpretability — and make the knots (cutpoints) an explicit, debatable modeling decision instead of a hidden one.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
1. Basic Concept
Choose cutpoints \(c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_K\); build dummy columns \(C_k(x) = \mathbb{1}(c_{k-1} < x \le c_k)\) (plus the intercept as the first cell’s level, or all K cells with no intercept — the cell-means trick from 2.6). OLS on these columns fits the mean of y within each bin:






Bins as features in a predictive pipeline (with CV choosing the resolution):

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
2. Concept Questions

More bins = more flexibility. What are the two failure modes at K → ∞ and K = 1?
Uniform-width vs quantile bins: when does each starve?
Where do discontinuities come from, and when is a discontinuous model the right answer (name two real settings)?
Your step fit jumps at x = 5 but the scatter looks smooth there. What made the jump, and which alternative basis would remove it?
How does the step function’s bias behave within a bin, and why is it worst exactly where the true curve is steepest?



Answers


K → ∞: one observation per bin — the fit interpolates noise (zero bias, maximal variance; the k = 1 KNN of regression). K = 1: the global mean — maximal bias. Between them, the same U-curve as always.
Uniform bins starve where data is sparse (tails: bins with 2 points produce wild constants) and waste bins where data is dense; quantile bins equalize counts (stable constants) but let bin widths vary wildly, so the x-resolution is uneven. Match the strategy to the design: uniform for even designs, quantile for skewed designs.
From the basis’s own discontinuity at each cutpoint — the model cannot be smooth there. Right answer when the world genuinely steps: drug dosing tiers, tax brackets, age-risk categories, tissue types along an anatomical boundary.
The jump is bin-boundary arithmetic (adjacent constants straddling a steep true slope differ by slope × width) — not found structure. Continuous bases (6.4) trade away the discontinuity.
The constant equals the bin’s mean of f — bias at x is f(x) minus that mean: zero at the bin’s “center of mass,” growing toward the edges, maximal where |f′| is large (steep regions sweep across more f-values per bin).

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Piecewise-constant vs piecewise-linear: fit (a) 5-bin step function, (b) 5-bin piecewise-linear (bins + bin×x interaction within each bin — implement via KBinsDiscretizer + manual within-bin centering), on the sinusoid. Compare CV MSE and plot both. Which basis removes the edge bias without adding discontinuities within bins, and what’s the cost?


Solution







Adding (x − bin mean) within each bin upgrades constants to local lines: bias drops where the truth slopes, discontinuities at boundaries shrink (adjacent lines nearly meet), and the price is 2K parameters instead of K. This is, in fact, a crude linear spline — 6.4 does it with proper continuity.

Exercise 2. Quantile vs uniform under skewed x: x ~ lognormal, y = √x + noise. Compare 6-bin uniform vs quantile step fits by CV, and by worst-bin error (max |bias| over bins estimated on a dense grid). Explain the winner’s mechanism, and state when the loser’s strategy would flip to winning.


Solution







Quantile wins: lognormal x piles mass near 0, so uniform bins leave the extreme right tail with a handful of points (variance explosion) and the dense left region over-binned (wasted flexibility). Quantile bins equalize evidence per bin. The flip: if the true function bends most in the sparse tail, uniform bins’ finer resolution out there can win — bin strategy should follow where the curve is interesting, not just where the data is dense.

Exercise 3. The threshold hunt: simulate a true jump at unknown t* (y = 1 + 2·1(x > t) + noise, t = 6.3). Estimate t* by fitting step functions on a fine grid of candidate cutpoints and choosing the cut whose two-cell fit minimizes RSS. Report the estimate over 200 simulations (bias, SD). Then explain why this is change-point detection, how it relates to the basis view, and what the inference caveat is for the chosen t̂*.


Solution







The grid-of-cells fit is a two-bin step model — change-point detection is basis selection with the cutpoint as hyperparameter. Caveat: t̂’s sampling distribution is nonstandard (the cutpoint is a discrete argmin over candidate fits), so naive “±SE” statements about t̂ are unreliable; proper inference uses specialized change-point machinery, and reporting the estimate with a bootstrap distribution is the honest middle ground.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Cutpoint choice is a hyperparameter — chosen on validation data, never by staring at the scatter (4.6); bins chosen from the full data then CV’d leak (the 0.5 law, again).
pd.cut on test data with bins from training — freeze the edges: use KBinsDiscretizer fitted in-pipeline, or carry pd.cut(..., bins=frozen_edges); re-deriving quantiles on new data silently changes the basis.
Edge handling: include_lowest=True for the left edge; decide explicitly whether bins are (lo, hi]; off-by-one rows at boundaries are classic.
Empty or tiny bins produce unstable constants; enforce a minimum bin count (quantile strategy + n_bins sanity) or merge cells.
Trees are adaptive step functions (Part 7): they choose cutpoints from the data by RSS reduction — the machinery this page builds by hand, automated and greedy.
Dose responses and policy bands are genuinely discontinuous; forcing a smooth basis there underfits the phenomenon — mismatched smoothness is a modeling error in both directions.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated binner has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Edges re-derived per split: train and test are binned by different boundaries — the feature spaces differ; quantile edges must be frozen from training (that’s what KBinsDiscretizer.fit stores).
Cumulative dummies + intercept: indicators (x > e) are nested, and with an intercept the design is rank-deficient-ish (full redundancy at the outer cells); interpretability collapses. Use interval dummies (one per bin, drop-first or cell-means).
New data outside the training range: pd.cut returns NaN for x = 11 — a silent production crash. Clip, extend the edge bin, or refuse explicitly.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the step-function fit explicitly: with K cells and cell-means parameterization, show the OLS solution assigns each cell its sample mean, that the hat matrix is block-constant, and that tr(H) = K. Then prove the within-bin bias identity: E[μ̂_k] − f(x) = f̄_k − f(x) for x in cell k, and show the integrated bias² over a bin equals the variance of f within the bin (exactly the quantity minimized by optimal binning around steep regions).


Hint

Cell dummies are disjoint indicators; each cell’s normal equation decouples (the 2.6 Q1 argument, geometrically). For the bias: integrate (f̄_k − f(x))² over the bin.



Solution

Each row of the design has exactly one 1, so the normal equations decouple per cell: μ̂_k = mean of y in cell k, H is block-diagonal with (1/nₖ) blocks — tr(H) = K effective parameters. Bias at x ∈ cell k: E[μ̂_k] = f̄_k (mean of f over the cell under uniform-x), so bias = f̄_k − f(x); integrating its square over the bin gives ∫(f − f̄_k)²dx = nₖ·Var_bin(f) — the bin’s internal variance of the true function. Hence optimal bins concentrate boundaries where f′ is large: equalize f-variance, not point counts (the refined version of Exercise 2’s moral).

Q2. Step functions as the t = 0 limit of trees, and the CV consistency question: implement a one-split “stump” fit (threshold chosen to minimize RSS) on the sinusoid; compare its CV MSE against the best 5-bin step model. Then simulate 200 datasets: how often does the stump’s chosen threshold fall within ±0.2 of the bin boundary with the smallest within-bin bias? What does the answer say about data-driven cutpoints as estimators — consistent, noisy, or both?


Solution







The stump’s threshold estimate has SD ≈ 0.4–0.6 at n = 120 — noisy: single cutpoints are unstable estimators (the reason random forests average many trees’ cuts, Part 7). Meanwhile its 2-cell train MSE beats the fixed 5-bin fit because it’s chosen for this dataset — in-sample selection flattery again. Cutpoints are consistent only in that they concentrate near the steepest region; they are emphatically not stable point estimates, and any narrative built on a specific estimated threshold needs uncertainty attached (Exercise 3’s bootstrap).

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (steps × 2.6 categorical × 2.7 interaction). Two-group step surfaces: y depends on x through different step patterns per group. Fit (a) pooled bins, (b) bins + group, (c) bins + group + bin×group, comparing CV MSE. When does (c) beat (b), and what does the bin×group interaction matrix look like (the subgroup version of cell means)? Connect to how decision trees grow group-specific splits (7.1).
C2 (steps × 4.4 bias–variance). Decompose the K-bin step estimator’s error across K (protocol of 4.4, 300 training sets, n = 40): bias², variance, and total. Verify: variance ≈ K·σ²/n-scaled, bias² tracking the integrated f-variance within bins (Q1’s identity). Then overlay the same three curves for piecewise-linear bins (Exercise 1) and state the K-vs-basis trade in one sentence.

title: 6.2 Step Functions
text:
7. Summary

Step functions = dummies over intervals: maximal locality, minimal smoothness, K effective parameters.
Cutpoints are hyperparameters (frozen from training, chosen by CV); quantile vs uniform is an evidence-distribution decision.
Bias concentrates within bins in steep regions — the f-variance identity tells you where the basis hurts.
Discontinuities are basis artifacts unless the world truly steps (doses, brackets, boundaries).
One-split stumps are adaptive step functions — unstable cutpoints, the seed of Part 7’s trees.
Adding within-bin slopes fixes edge bias cheaply — the segue to proper splines.
Continuous local bases with enforced smoothness: 6.3 Basis functions generalizes, 6.4 Regression splines perfects it.

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text: Local regression fits the curve one query point at a time: at each x₀, fit a low-degree polynomial to the nearby points, weighted by distance, and read off the value. No global basis, no knots — just “fit locally, slide along.” It is smoothing at its most intuitive and the bridge between weighting (KNN) and global fitting.

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
1. Basic Concept
At query point x₀:

Take the s nearest points (span s — the dial), or all points within a bandwidth.
Weight them by a tricube kernel of their distance: \(w_i = (1 - |x_i - x_0|/d_{\max})^3_+\).
Fit weighted least squares (usually a line; LOESS = locally estimated scatterplot smoothing).
\(\hat f(x_0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_0\) from that local fit. Slide x₀ across the domain.

Hand-rolled, once:






The battle-tested version — statsmodels.lowess:

title: 6.6 Local Regression (LOESS)
text:
2. Concept Questions

Span vs bandwidth: what does each control, and what happens at span → 0 and span → 1?
Why weight by the tricube kernel rather than uniformly over the neighborhood — what changes visually?
