\(P(A\cup B) = 0.5 + 0.8 - 0.5\times0.8 = 0.9\).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — the full Bayes computation. Disease prevalence 0.1%, test sensitivity 99%, specificity 99%. Compute (a) P(disease | positive), (b) the same for prevalence 10%, (c) how high specificity must be at 0.1% prevalence for PPV ≥ 50%. State each result as one sentence.


Solution








9% — a positive result is usually false at 0.1% prevalence. (b) 92% — the same test is excellent in a high-risk population. (c) specificity ≈ 99.90% — the false-positive rate per healthy person must be driven below the true prevalence. Same machine, three different decisions — this is why screening policies depend on prevalence, not just on test quality.


Exercise 2 — Monte Carlo verification. Verify analytically-computed probabilities by simulation: (a) at least one six in 4 rolls; (b) P(Binomial(20, 0.3) ≥ 10); (c) P(Normal(0,1) within ±1.5). Report simulated vs exact to 3 decimals.


Solution







Note the pattern — sf(9, ...) for “≥ 10” (sf is P(X > k), so use k−1). Monte Carlo with N = 10⁶ carries ~0.05% MC error; agreement to 3 decimals is expected, and this verify-by-simulation habit will debug countless probability computations later.

Exercise 3 — the law of total probability in a lab setting. 1% of samples are contaminated. Contaminated samples fail QC 80% of the time; clean samples fail 2% of the time. What fraction of samples fail QC? Given a sample failed QC, what’s the probability it was contaminated?


Solution







Two-step structure: total probability pools the failure rate across the two sample types; Bayes re-weights to ask about the cause. Even a 40× higher failure rate for contaminated samples only gets you to 27% — because clean samples are 99× more numerous. Always ask what population produced this positive.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

P(A|B) vs P(B|A) — transposing the conditional is the prosecutor’s fallacy; DNA-match statistics are its most famous victim. Every Bayes computation should start by naming which conditional you have and which you want.
Independence is not “small correlation” and not “no obvious relationship” — it is \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) exactly. Rarely true for biological measurements (batch, relatedness, shared environment).
pdf values are not probabilities — stats.norm.pdf(0) ≈ 0.4 yet P(X=0) = 0; the density integrates to probability. Only CDFs and intervals carry probability meaning.
sf(k) = P(X > k) (strictly greater) — the classic off-by-one: P(X ≥ 10) = sf(9), not sf(10). Write the inequality before writing the function call.
Poisson has variance = mean; real count data routinely violates this (overdispersion) — the reason negative-binomial models exist in RNA-seq DE analysis (12.6).
CLT applies to standardized sums of many independent contributions — not to heavy-tailed data at small n, and not to highly skewed counts at n = 5.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “screening calculator” has three bugs. Run it, then fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Complement misuse: the stray “× 3” multiplies the none-detect probability by 3, producing a negative “probability”. The complement of “at least one” is “none”, full stop: \(1 - 0.9^3\).
sf off-by-one: sf(8) = P(X > 8) = P(X ≥ 9); for P(X ≥ 8) use sf(7).
pdf differences are not probabilities — subtracting densities is meaningless. Integrate: cdf(1.96) - cdf(-1.96).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the 9% PPV result symbolically and explain in terms of the Bayes numerator and denominator why increasing sensitivity barely helps at low prevalence, while increasing specificity helps enormously.


Hint

Write PPV \(= \frac{sp\,\pi}{sp\,\pi + (1-sc)(1-\pi)}\) and ask: which term shrinks when sens ↑ vs spec ↑, at \(\pi = 0.001\)?



Solution

PPV \(= \dfrac{\text{sens}\cdot\pi}{\text{sens}\cdot\pi + (1-\text{spec})(1-\pi)}\). At \(\pi = 0.001\): the numerator term is ≈ sens × 0.001 — small no matter how good sens is (bounded by prevalence itself). The denominator’s second term is \((1-\text{spec}) \times 0.999\) — nearly the whole healthy population times the false-positive rate. Raising sens 0.99 → 0.999 multiplies the numerator by ~1.009; raising spec 0.99 → 0.999 divides the false-positive term by 10. At low prevalence, PPV is governed by specificity — which is why screening programs chase specificity and why confirmatory (more specific) tests follow any positive screen.

Q2. Two independent watchtowers detect fires with probabilities 0.8 and 0.7 respectively. Given exactly one detection occurred, what is the probability it was tower 1? Compute symbolically and verify by Monte Carlo.


Hint

Enumerate the four detection outcomes with their probabilities; condition on the two “exactly one” outcomes.



Solution

Outcomes: both \(= 0.8 \times 0.7 = 0.56\); neither \(= 0.2 \times 0.3 = 0.06\); only-1 \(= 0.8 \times 0.3 = 0.24\); only-2 \(= 0.2 \times 0.7 = 0.14\). Given “exactly one”, it was tower 1 with probability \(0.24/(0.24 + 0.14) = 0.632\).






Note the method: enumerate + condition, or simulate — both beat formula-hunting when the event structure gets any more complicated.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (probability × 0.5 Data splitting). A test set has n = 50 samples with true accuracy p = 0.8. Compute the exact probability (binomial) that the measured accuracy is ≥ 0.9 (i.e., ≥ 45 correct). Now compute the same for n = 500. What does each number say about the credibility of “90% accuracy!” claims at the two sample sizes — and connect this to the binomial SE formula used in 0.5 Q2.
C2 (probability × 12.4 FDR preview). You test 10,000 genes for differential expression at α = 0.05; none are truly differential. (a) How many false positives do you expect? (b) What’s the probability of at least one? (c) If 100 are truly differential with 80% power, what is the positive predictive value of your “significant” list? This single calculation is the entire motivation for FDR correction — predict what q-values do before learning them.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
7. Summary

Complement turns “at least one” into “1 − none”; addition subtracts the double-counted intersection.
Conditional probability is the primary object; independence is \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\), not an adjective.
Bayes’ rule converts P(evidence|cause) to P(cause|evidence); at low prevalence, specificity dominates PPV.
Binomial = n trials; Poisson = counts in a window (variance = mean); Normal = the CLT’s destination.
pdf values are densities, not probabilities; CDF/sf carry probability, and sf is P(X > k) — mind the off-by-one.
Variances add for independent sums; SDs don’t.
Verify any analytic probability with a Monte Carlo one-liner — cheap, and it catches unit/interval bugs.
With probability as the language, the next step is the sentence structure of statistics: estimation and testing — 1.4 Statistical inference.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text: Descriptive statistics compress a sample into a few honest numbers: where is the center, how wide is the spread, what shape is the distribution. Every model diagnostic, every “significant difference,” every anomaly alert you will ever compute rests on these primitives — so the definitions (including the ones with silent variants, like population vs sample SD) must be reflexes.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
1. Basic Concept
Center. The mean \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i\) is the balance point; the median is the middle value by rank. They coincide for symmetric data; for right-skewed data, mean > median (a few large values drag the mean).
Spread. The variance is the average squared deviation from the mean. Two flavors:
\[s^2_{\text{pop}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \qquad s^2_{\text{sample}} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2\]
The \(n-1\) (Bessel’s correction) in the sample version compensates for the fact that \(\bar{x}\) was estimated from the same data — deviations from an estimated center are systematically too small. Standard deviation is the square root, back in data units.






Position and shape. Quartiles split the sorted data into quarters; the IQR (Q3 − Q1) is the spread of the middle half — robust to outliers. Skewness measures asymmetry (positive = right tail).






Robustness ranking (how much a single extreme value can move the statistic):

mean, SD — sensitive (breakdown point 0%)
median, IQR — robust (breakdown point 50%)
trimmed mean — tunable middle ground

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the sample variance divide by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\)?
Your gene-expression distribution has mean 210 and median 85. What shape do you suspect, and which two numbers would you report?
Is the IQR affected by multiplying all values by 10? By adding one extreme value?
When is the mode the most informative measure of center?
What does ddof=0 vs ddof=1 change in np.std, and which does pandas use by default?



Answers


Deviations are taken from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data; the fitted center absorbs part of the variability, shrinking deviations. Dividing by the degrees of freedom \(n-1\) unbias the estimate of the population variance (for normal data, exactly).
Strong right skew (a minority of very high values). Report median and IQR (robust pair); if you must report the mean, report it with the median so the skew is visible.
Multiplying by 10: IQR scales by 10 (it’s in data units). One extreme value beyond the fences: IQR is unaffected as long as it doesn’t cross the 25th/75th percentiles — that’s the point of quartile-based spread.
For categorical or discrete data (“most common category”), and for multimodal continuous data where mean and median both describe nothing real (“typical patient: bimodal, modes at X and Y”).
ddof = delta degrees of freedom subtracted from n. ddof=0 → population formula; ddof=1 → sample formula. NumPy defaults to 0, pandas to 1 — mixing pandas and NumPy without noticing this is a classic silent bug.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Write summarize(x) returning {"n", "mean", "sd", "median", "iqr", "min", "max"} using sample SD. Test it on normal data and on lognormal data; state which summary number changes most between the two and why.


Solution







The mean and SD blow up under lognormal data (they inherit the heavy tail), while median and IQR stay near their symmetric-data values — the empirical demonstration of robustness. Report median/IQR for skewed data.

Exercise 2. IQR outlier rule: flag values outside \([Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR},\ Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}]\) in the dataset below. Then compute z-scores and flag \(|z| > 3\). Compare the flagged sets and explain the disagreement.


Solution







The z-score rule uses the mean and SD — which the outlier itself inflates. One extreme value widened the SD so much that even the outlier isn’t 3 SDs out (masking). Quartile-based rules don’t have this self-blinding property: for small samples, prefer the IQR fence.

Exercise 3. Empirically verify Bessel’s correction: sample n = 5 points from a known distribution many times; for each sample compute variance with ddof=0 and ddof=1; average each. Which average converges to the true variance?


Solution







ddof=0 averages to \(0.8\sigma^2\) here (\((n-1)/n = 4/5\)) — a 20% underestimate, every time, silently. This is why the divisor choice is not a technicality.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

pandas vs NumPy ddof defaults disagree (pandas std/var use ddof=1; NumPy uses ddof=0). Numbers in mixed reports can differ by ~√(n/(n−1)) for no reason.
NaN handling differs: np.mean poisons, np.nanmean skips, pandas .mean() skips and warns differently — know which behavior produced a reported number.
Percentile interpolation: np.percentile linearly interpolates by default; small-n quartiles depend on this convention (9 conventions exist; R’s type=7 matches NumPy’s linear).
SD is not the “typical deviation” for skewed data: with a heavy right tail, most deviations are below the SD. IQR communicates spread more honestly there.
The mean minimizes squared error, the median absolute error — which is why least squares regression (Part 2) is mean-focused and least-absolutes-deviations is median-focused.
stats.mode behavior changed across SciPy versions (now returns a ModeResult object); pd.Series.mode is the stable, readable choice.
Descriptives ≠ inference: a summary is a claim about this sample; Part 1.4 is about claims regarding the population.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated summary function has three bugs. Run it on the test data and find them.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Population SD (ddof=0) — for a sample summary this underestimates spread; specify and use ddof=1.
No NaN policy — the function dies on the NaN (mean → nan, max → nan) without telling the caller whether NaNs were dropped. Make the policy explicit.
range on data containing NaN raises/propagates nan; also “range” is a fragile descriptives choice (a single typo’d value sets it) — min/max separately at most, or a robust span.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove (or verify by simulation) that the sample mean is the value \(c\) minimizing \(\sum_i (x_i - c)^2\), and the sample median minimizes \(\sum_i |x_i - c|\). What does each say about which errors the mean vs median take most seriously?


Hint

Differentiate \(\sum (x_i-c)^2\) in \(c\); for the absolute value, argue by moving \(c\) across data points and counting how many terms’ slope changes.



Solution

Mean: \(f(c)=\sum(x_i-c)^2\) has \(f'(c) = -2\sum(x_i-c)\), zero exactly at \(c=\bar{x}\) (second derivative \(2n>0\)). Median: \(g(c)=\sum|x_i-c|\) has slope \(= (\#\,\text{points} < c) - (\#\,\text{points} > c)\), which changes sign where the counts balance — the median. So the mean’s optimality is defined in squared error: a single far point contributes quadratically, dominating the objective — hence the mean chases outliers. The median’s objective is linear in each error: one far point costs the same as one near point — hence its robustness. This one paragraph explains robust statistics, why least-squares regression is outlier-sensitive, and why quantile regression exists.

Q2. Two labs each report SD ≈ 2.0 for the same assay. Lab A ran n = 5, Lab B ran n = 5,000. Construct a scenario where both reports are true, and explain which additional number distinguishes them (preview: it is not the SD).


Solution

Both labs can honestly report \(s \approx 2.0\) — SD describes individual measurement spread and barely depends on n. What distinguishes them is the precision of their estimated means: the standard error \(s/\sqrt{n}\) ≈ 0.89 for Lab A vs 0.028 for Lab B — a 30-fold difference. SD answers “how noisy is one measurement,” SE answers “how well do I know the center.” Confusing the two (reporting SD where SE is meant, or vice versa) is a notorious publication bug; the inference machinery that formalizes it arrives in 1.4 Statistical inference.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (descriptives × 0.4 EDA). For the lognormal samples from Section 1, produce side-by-side: (a) histogram of x, (b) histogram of log x with a normal-density overlay scaled to the log data. Which single transformation converts all the robust-vs-sensitive summary disagreements (mean/median, SD/IQR) into non-issues, and what does that imply about when those disagreements matter?
C2 (descriptives × 3.1.5 AUPRC preview). A screening cohort has 1% disease prevalence. Compute the mean/median of the binary label vector and explain, in descriptive-statistics language, why accuracy is a nearly useless summary for a classifier on this data (predicting all-healthy scores 99%). Which descriptive statistic of the confusion matrix would you report instead, and why is it robust to the prevalence imbalance?

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
7. Summary

Center: mean (balance, sensitive) vs median (rank, robust); skew shows as mean − median.
Spread: SD for symmetric data, IQR for skewed; ddof=0 vs 1 is a real bias, and pandas/NumPy disagree by default.
Quartiles + IQR fences detect outliers without being blinded by them; z-scores can be.
NaN policy is part of the statistic: nan-skipping is a decision, not a default to trust blindly.
Mean ↔︎ squared error, median ↔︎ absolute error: robustness follows from the loss function.
SD describes single measurements; SE describes the precision of a mean — next pages formalize this.
Summaries describe samples; to argue about populations you need probability and inference: 1.2 Relationships first asks how two variables move together.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text: How do two variables move together? Covariance and correlation quantify co-movement; regression (Part 2) will model it. The skill here is knowing what r measures, what it ignores, and the four ways it lies.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
1. Basic Concept
Covariance averages the products of paired deviations:
\[\text{cov}(x, y) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\]
Positive when variables move together, negative when opposed — but its magnitude depends on the units (expression levels in raw counts vs log-CPM give different covariances for the same relationship). The Pearson correlation fixes units by dividing both SDs:
\[r = \frac{\text{cov}(x,y)}{s_x s_y} \in [-1, 1]\]






Key reading: r measures linear association strength, not slope (slope lives in regression) and not agreement (r = 1 for y = x + 100, which disagrees by 100 everywhere).
Spearman correlation = Pearson correlation applied to ranks. It detects any monotone relationship and shrugs at outliers:






And the classical caution — curvature: quadratic data can have r ≈ 0 over a symmetric range even though the variables are perfectly dependent:

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is covariance useless for comparing relationships measured in different units, and what exactly does dividing by \(s_x s_y\) fix?
What is the relationship between r and the R² of simple linear regression?
Give two datasets where Spearman = 1 but Pearson < 1.
Does r = 0 mean “no relationship”? Does r = 0.9 mean “x causes y”?
One outlier flips your r from +0.6 to −0.6. Which coefficient is more trustworthy here, and why?



Answers


Covariance’s magnitude scales with the units of both variables (cov(x, y) = 5 for x in minutes is 300 for x in seconds). Pearson divides by the product of SDs — a pure number in [−1, 1] — so relationships are comparable across studies, units, and scalings.
For simple linear regression, \(R^2 = r^2\) — the fraction of y’s variance explained by the best straight line. r = 0.7 → the line explains 49%.
Any perfectly monotone but nonlinear pair: (x, eˣ), (x, x³) over positive x, (age, income) rising with diminishing returns. Ranks are identical; straightness is not.
No and no. r = 0 only rules out linear association (quadratics, U-shapes, interactions can be strong). r measures association; causation requires design (randomization, natural experiments) or much stronger modeling assumptions.
Spearman. A single point moved Pearson’s estimate violently because r is built from raw deviations — the outlier dominates both \(s_x\), \(s_y\) and the cross-products. Spearman caps any point’s influence at “one rank step.”

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — Anscombe’s quartet, cell 1. This classic dataset has 4 pairs with (nearly) identical mean, SD, r ≈ 0.816, and regression line — utterly different shapes. Build pair I and pair III, compute their summary statistics, and plot both.


Solution







Identical r, identical fitted line — because r and OLS are single-number summaries that different data structures can satisfy. Summary statistics compress away exactly the things you care about; plotting is not optional.

Exercise 2. Construct data where adding ONE observation flips the sign of Pearson r (from negative to positive), while Spearman barely moves. Report all three r values before/after.


Solution







The added point sits at the extreme corner, contributing huge cross-deviations \((x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\) — enough to outvote 40 points. Spearman only sees “new highest x, new highest y” — one rank step on each side. Any reported Pearson on real data should come with a scatterplot or a rank-correlation cross-check.

Exercise 3. For a bivariate normal sample (n = 30, true ρ = 0), empirically show the sampling distribution of r under the null, and verify that |r| > \(2/\sqrt{n-1}\) (rough 5% rule) happens about 5% of the time.


Solution







≈ 0.05: with n = 30, “noise correlations” of ±0.37 are routine. Two implications: small-n correlation claims need formal tests (1.4), and large correlation matrices (0.3 pandas drills) will always show impressive-looking r values somewhere — that’s multiplication of opportunities, not biology.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Correlation ≠ causation — and neither correlation nor its absence is about linear vs nonlinear: r ≈ 0 coexists with perfect functional dependence (the x² plot).
Range restriction and range enhancement: selecting only high-GPA applicants lowers r; mixing two clusters inflates it (Simpson’s paradox lives here — see Complex Questions).
Pearson needs rough linearity and tolerates outliers badly; Spearman needs only monotonicity but discards magnitude information (two datasets with identical ranks can have very different practical effect sizes).
Correlation matrices in high dimensions (10,000 genes → 50M pairs): extreme r values appear by chance alone (Exercise 3 logic × opportunities). Multiple-testing discipline (Part 12) applies to “top correlated pairs” lists.
Averaging correlations across groups is invalid (r is not on an additive scale — use Fisher z, or analyze per group).
Bootstrap or Fisher-z CI for r, never “r ± 0.05” from folklore. Formal test: stats.pearsonr returns the p-value alongside.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “correlation report” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


r ≠ slope and ≠ causation. The slope estimate is np.polyfit’s job, and “causes” needs design evidence, not correlation.
Averaging r across groups is invalid and hides sign flips; here group r’s may be +1 and −1, “averaging” to 0 while both groups have perfect (opposite) associations. Report per-group r (or Fisher-z average with justification).
r ≈ 0 ≠ no relationship. The U-shaped dependence is perfect; Pearson only tests the linear projection.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that for simple linear regression the fitted slope is \(b = r \cdot (s_y / s_x)\), and explain the two failure modes of “reading” r as if it were an effect size.


Hint

Write the OLS slope for standardized variables; then unstandardize.



Solution

Standardize both variables: \(\tilde x = (x-\bar x)/s_x\), \(\tilde y = (y-\bar y)/s_y\). For standardized data the OLS slope is \(\sum \tilde x_i \tilde y_i / \sum \tilde x_i^2 = (n-1)\,\text{cov}/(n-1)\,\text{var} = r\). Rescaling back multiplies by \(s_y/s_x\), giving \(b = r s_y/s_x\). Failure modes: (1) slope from r — r = 0.5 means nothing about units; a weak correlation with huge \(s_y/s_x\) can be a big effect. (2) r as slope — the same physical relationship yields different r if you restrict the x-range (range restriction lowers both spread and r) while the slope \(r s_y/s_x\) is more stable. Report both: r (strength of linear association), slope (effect per unit x), CI each.

Q2. The t-statistic for testing ρ = 0 is \(t = r\sqrt{(n-2)/(1-r^2)}\). Verify numerically that stats.pearsonr’s p-value matches the two-sided t-test with df = n−2, then explain what happens to that p-value’s meaning when you compute it for the largest of 10,000 gene-pair correlations.


Solution







The p-value is calibrated for one pre-specified pair. For the maximum over 10,000 pairs, the test is applied to the extreme order statistic of ~10,000 correlated tests: even under global null, the smallest p-value is routinely ≪ 0.05 (probability of at least one “significant” pair ≈ 1 − 0.95¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ ≈ 1). The honest procedure re-tests the selected pair in fresh data or applies family-wise/FDR correction — the entire subject of Part 12.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (relationships × 0.3 pandas — Simpson’s paradox). Build 3 groups where within every group r(y, x) is positive, but pooled over all groups r is strongly negative. (Give group intercepts very different levels and equal within-group slopes.) Then answer: which correlation should a model use — and how does adding group dummies (2.6 Categorical predictors) resolve the conflict?
C2 (relationships × 9.2 PCA preview). Generate 3 correlated variables, compute the correlation matrix, and its eigenvalues. What does the dominant eigenvalue/eigenvector tell you about how many “real directions” the data has? Relate this to why the scatter-matrix drill of 0.4 becomes unreadable at 50 variables and PCA becomes necessary.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
7. Summary

Covariance is direction × scale; Pearson r standardizes it to [−1, 1]; Spearman replaces values with ranks.
r describes linear association only: U-shapes hide at r ≈ 0; monotone curves lose r < 1.
r² is explained-variance for a straight line; slope is r·(sy/sx) — never confuse strength with effect size.
One outlier can flip Pearson; Spearman caps that influence — report both when data is dirty.
Sampling noise gives |r| ≈ 0.3 routinely at n = 30; scanning many pairs manufactures “discoveries.”
Per-group correlation, plots, and range questions come before any causal sentence.
Association is a description; deciding whether a pattern would reappear in new samples requires probability and inference — 1.3 Probability essentials.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text: Given linearly separable data, infinitely many hyperplanes classify it perfectly. The hard-margin SVM picks the one with the fattest cushion — the maximal margin between the classes — and identifies a handful of support vectors as the only points that matter.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
1. Basic Concept
The optimization, in the canonical form:
\[\max_{w, b} \; M = \frac{2}{\|w\|} \quad \text{subject to} \quad y_i (w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1 \;\; \forall i\]
— every point correctly outside its margin line; equivalently minimize ‖w‖²/2. The points with yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) = 1 are the support vectors: removing any non-support point changes nothing.






Only the support vectors matter — the experiment:

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the hard-margin SVM require separability — what happens to the constraint set when one point crosses the margin?
If a new data point lands far from the boundary on the correct side, how does the classifier change? What if it lands inside the margin?
Explain “the maximal-margin hyperplane depends only on the support vectors” both computationally and geometrically.
Two candidate hyperplanes both separate the data: one with margin 0.4, one with margin 1.2. Which does the SVM choose, and what implicit belief about future data justifies it?
A support vector sits exactly on the margin line. What is its value of yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b), and what does the constraint say about points beyond it?



Answers


The constraints yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 must be simultaneously satisfiable; one mispositioned point makes the feasible set empty — no solution exists, full stop. (The soft margin of 8.3 relaxes exactly this.)
Far-and-correct: nothing — it’s not a support vector, the classifier is unchanged (this is the SVM’s famous stability-to-far-points, the mirror image of 2.3’s leverage worries). Inside the margin: it becomes a support vector with a constraint violation — in the hard-margin world it would make the problem infeasible.
Computationally: the solution’s KKT conditions force non-support points’ multipliers to 0 — they appear nowhere in w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ. Geometrically: the fattest cushion is pressed against the closest points on each side — the boundary of the convex hulls; interior points don’t touch it.
Margin 1.2 — with the justification that future draws from the same distribution will, with high probability, fall in the cushion you measured on this sample (1.3’s logic applied to geometry): maximal margin is maximum-confidence classification under a stability assumption.
Exactly 1 — the constraint is tight (KKT: non-zero multiplier ⟺ tight constraint). Points beyond have yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) > 1 — slack constraints, zero multipliers, no influence.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Maximal margin by brute force: for a tiny 2-D separable dataset (6 points), enumerate a fine grid of candidate (w-angle, b) hyperplanes, keep the separating ones, and maximize the margin. Compare your brute-force winner to sklearn’s SVC(C=1e6) solution (normalize both to the ±1 convention first). This exercise is the SVM, before the optimization theory.


Solution







Scanning directions and centering the slab finds the same solution the QP does — the optimization theory is a fast, principled shortcut through exactly this search.

Exercise 2. The fragility experiment: take a separable dataset and its hard-margin SVM. Add one new point far away but on the correct side — measure the change in w, b, and predictions. Then add one point inside the margin (violating) — the hard-margin problem becomes infeasible; observe sklearn’s behavior with C = 1e6 (and connect to 8.3’s fix). Quantify both perturbations: which data points does the SVM care about?


Solution







Far-correct points: zero influence (the support-vector claim, demonstrated). Violating points: infeasibility for the true hard margin — C = 1e6 silently approximates it by allowing tiny slacks at enormous cost, which is exactly the tension the soft margin (8.3) makes explicit and tunable.

Exercise 3. Margin as confidence: for the hard-margin fit, plot decision_function magnitude against distance-to-boundary for 2000 fresh points from the same distribution, and estimate: P(correct classification | |score| > 1) vs P(correct | |score| < 0.2). Then explain in margin language why large-margin points are “safe” — and one way this intuition fails (distribution shift, e.g., the covariate-shift experiment of 4.2 Q2).


Solution







(|score|) is distance-to-boundary in canonical units: points with cushion almost never flip, borderline points flip often — the margin literalizes “confidence.” The failure: under covariate shift the boundary itself may be misplaced relative to the new distribution, and every confidence statement inherits that error — margins quantify position-in-sample geometry, not distributional safety.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Hard margin is a classroom object: real data has overlap; C = 1e6 is a soft margin pretending (8.3) — with numerical instability as a bonus. Use honest C tuning in practice.
C=1e6 ≠ hard margin: it’s soft with astronomically expensive slacks — sklearn may warn about convergence; the fix is the soft-margin formulation, not more iterations.
Support vector count and dimension: in p ≥ n separable data every point can be a support vector (5.6’s interpolation world) — the “only a few matter” intuition is a low-dimension luxury.
SVC’s decision_function is (wᵀx + b) in the canonical scale — margin units, thanks to the ±1 normalization; interpret |score| as cushion honestly only for linear kernels (kernels change the space, 8.4).
LinearSVC vs SVC(kernel="linear"): different solvers (liblinear vs libsvm), slightly different numerical answers, same geometry; LinearSVC scales to big n, SVC exposes support vectors directly.
Class imbalance: hard margins tilt toward the majority class’s geometry; class_weight rescales the constraints per class (3.1).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated SVM has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Overlapping classes + C = 1e6: the hard-margin assumption is false; the solver strains to satisfy near-impossible constraints (warnings, poor margin, borderline numerical behavior). Use tuned soft C.
“Margin” from slacked solutions: with slacks, 2/‖w‖ overstates the effective separation — violated support vectors sit inside the reported cushion. Report margins only with the slack picture (fraction violated, C).
Support-vector fraction misread: with heavy overlap, half the points become support vectors — the “efficient summary” story collapses; also SV-based prediction shortcuts are an implementation detail, not a data-efficiency claim.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the support-vector-only representation: the SVM dual has w = Σᵢαᵢyᵢxᵢ with αᵢ > 0 only for support vectors (KKT complementary slackness). Verify numerically that predictions via Σαᵢyᵢ(xᵢᵀx) + b (using only SVs) reproduce decision_function exactly, and explain why this representation is (a) the gateway to kernels (8.4) and (b) a statement about which data the model compresses.


Hint

KKT: constraints with slack have αᵢ = 0; tight constraints may have αᵢ > 0. w is a sum over αᵢyᵢxᵢ — zero terms vanish.



Solution

Complementary slackness ties each αᵢ to its constraint’s tightness: yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) > 1 ⇒ αᵢ = 0. So w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ sums over SVs only, and predictions need only inner products xᵢᵀx against SVs:







Replacing xᵢᵀx by a kernel k(xᵢ, x) gives nonlinear SVMs without ever materializing coordinates — the dual only ever sees inner products. (b) The model compresses the dataset to its boundary-adjacent skeleton: a data-efficiency statement in separable low-noise regimes, and a warning when everything is a support vector.


Q2. Maximal margin vs logistic boundary, geometrically: on separable data, fit both (SVC C=1e6; LogisticRegression) and compare boundary angles and margin widths across 100 resamples. Which boundary is stable, which drifts, and why does the logistic boundary depend on all points while the SVM’s doesn’t (7.2’s stability lens applied to geometry)? State the resulting division of labor.


Solution







Both boundaries wander (resampled data, overlapping tails), but the SVM’s direction is pinned by a handful of extreme points while logistic’s is pulled by the whole sample — different sensitivity profiles. Division of labor: SVM geometry when the boundary is what matters and data is separable-ish; logistic when probabilities, calibrated rankings (3.7), or full-data robustness are the product. Full comparison: 8.5.

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (max margin × 1.3 probability). Margin as a probability guarantee, stress-tested: for separable data with margin M, a classical result bounds future misclassification by (roughly) R²/M²-type ratios (R = data radius). Simulate: vary the noise level to produce margins M ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0}, measure test error over fresh draws, and plot error vs M. Does fatter margin → lower error hold empirically? Where does the monotonicity break (name the two competing effects: margin vs fit-to-distribution)?
C2 (max margin × 2.6 Simpson). The pooled-margin trap: two clusters with different internal geometries where the pooled maximal-margin boundary bisects neither. Construct the data, fit pooled vs per-cluster hard margins, and quantify boundary disagreement. When is a “single global margin” the wrong object — and does the kernel trick (8.4) or explicit group features (2.6) resolve it more honestly?

title: 8.2 The Maximal-Margin Classifier
text:
7. Summary

Hard-margin SVM: maximize 2/‖w‖ s.t. every point sits outside its margin line — solvable only when separable.
Support vectors (yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) = 1) fully determine the classifier; all other points are deletable.
Far-correct points cost nothing; margin-violating points break feasibility — the soft margin’s reason to exist.
Margin = measured cushion = confidence geometry — valid in-sample, conditional on the distribution.
The dual representation (predict via inner products with SVs) is the on-ramp to kernels.
Overlap and p ≥ n dissolve the clean story — tune softness, expect many SVs.
Real data overlaps: pay for slack, tune the price — 8.3 The soft-margin classifier.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text: SVMs live and breathe linear algebra: hyperplanes, normals, projections, distances, margins. This page drills the geometric vocabulary — every SVM statement in 8.2–8.6 is one of these objects in costume.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
1. Basic Concept
A hyperplane in d dimensions is \(\{x : w^\top x + b = 0\}\) — defined by a normal vector w (its direction) and offset b. The signed distance from a point x₀ to the hyperplane is
\[d(x_0) = \frac{w^\top x_0 + b}{\|w\|}\]
— the quantity SVMs classify by (its sign) and maximize (its magnitude):






Projections — the foot of that perpendicular — and the margin between two parallel hyperplanes:

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the same hyperplane described by (2w, 2b) define a different SVM margin — and what convention fixes w’s scale?
What does the sign of wᵀx₀ + b encode, and what does its magnitude encode before scaling?
Two parallel hyperplanes wᵀx + b = ±1: derive the distance between them geometrically (pick one point on one, compute its distance to the other).
In 2-D, a hyperplane is a line; in 3-D, a plane. What is it in 1-D — and does the SVM machinery care about the dimension?
Why do SVMs standardize features despite being geometric — name the quantity that units distort.



Answers


(2w, 2b) is the same zero-set (same line) but the margin formula 2/‖w‖ halves — margins are only comparable in the canonical convention wᵀx + b = ±1 at the support vectors, which pins ‖w‖ (SVMs solve for w up to this constraint, so the scale ambiguity is absorbed).
Sign = which side (the class in SVMs: +1 vs −1). Raw magnitude = distance scaled by ‖w‖ — proportional to true distance but unit-dependent until normalized.
Take x₊ on {wᵀx + b = +1}: wᵀx₊ + b = 1. Distance to {wᵀx + b = −1}: |wᵀx₊ + b + 1|/‖w‖ = |1 + 1|/‖w‖ = 2/‖w‖. That’s the margin the SVM maximizes.
In 1-D a “hyperplane” is a point (w, b as scalars, w·x + b = 0); the algebra — sign, distance, margin 2/‖w‖ — is dimension-blind. Everything here works in any d, which is why kernels (8.4) can.
Distance and margin are computed in raw coordinates: a feature measured in millimeters vs meters changes ‖w‖ and the geometry of “closeness.” Standardization puts all axes in comparable units — the same law as 5.2, now geometric.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build signed_distance(X, w, b) returning distances for a matrix of points, and verify three properties numerically on random data: (a) distance of points on the hyperplane ≈ 0; (b) flipping (w, b) → (−w, −b) flips all signs but preserves magnitudes; (c) distances are invariant to adding multiples of w to… (design the check: move a point parallel to the hyperplane and confirm its distance is unchanged).


Solution







Property (c) is the geometric soul of the SVM: moving along the hyperplane costs nothing; only normal-direction movement changes the classification score — which is why the margin direction w is everything.

Exercise 2. From line to margin to classifier: given w = (−1, 4), b = 2, compute (a) the line y(x₂) as a function of x₁, (b) the two margin lines wᵀx + b = ±1, (c) the signed distances of (0, 0) and (3, 2), (d) which side the classifier assigns each. Then plot all four lines with the two points using matplotlib and check the distances visually (aspect=“equal”).


Solution







The three parallel lines are the whole linear-SVM story: classify by side (sign), measure confidence by distance, and the ±1 family is the margin whose width 2/‖w‖ the SVM maximizes (8.2).

Exercise 3. Norms and their margins: for w = (3, 4), compute ‖w‖₁, ‖w‖₂, ‖w‖∞, and the L2-margin 2/‖w‖₂. Then show numerically that among all vectors achieving the same classification of a fixed dataset, scaling changes ‖w‖₂ — and that adding a perpendicular component changes ‖w‖₂ without changing any sign. Which of these two operations would an SVM’s objective permit (relate to how the margin constraint pins the scale)?


Solution







Scaling changes ‖w‖ (and thus the nominal margin) without changing classifications; adding a perpendicular component changes ‖w‖ and keeps signs for this dataset. The SVM’s canonical constraint — margin lines at ±1 with the support vectors on them — pins the scale so the only freedom left is the direction of w; maximizing 2/‖w‖ then chooses the direction with the fattest cushion. The margin isn’t a formula, it’s the normalization that makes the formula meaningful.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The sign convention: +1 class sits on the wᵀx + b > 0 side by convention of the labels — sklearn’s decision_function sign follows classes_[1]; always check model.classes_ before interpreting signs (3.3’s ordering note).
‖w‖ appears in denominators everywhere — margins, distances, hinge geometry — so feature scaling is not optional for SVMs: raw-unit features tilt the geometry in invisible ways.
Hyperplane ≠ classifier: the zero-set classifies; the scaled (w, b) carries the margin information. Two codebases reporting different (w, b) for the “same” SVM may agree completely after normalization — compare decision_function values, not raw parameters.
Projections are linear algebra’s workhorse beyond SVMs: residuals (2.2), PCA scores (9.2), backfitting (6.7) — the same perpendicular decomposition everywhere.
d(x₀) = 0 points: points on the hyperplane are classified by tie-breaking convention — in practice measure-zero, but in engineered features (integers) it happens; know your library’s rule.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated geometry helper has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Not a distance: wᵀx₀ + b is the unscaled score; distances divide by ‖w‖. The printed “distance” changes under rescaling of w — distances don’t.
b doesn’t belong in the margin: the gap between the ±1 planes is purely 2/‖w‖; b shifts the pair, doesn’t widen it.
Classifier needs the label convention: sign gives the side, but which side is “class 1” is a training-time fact (classes_), not derivable from geometry alone.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the signed-distance formula: for hyperplane H = {x : wᵀx + b = 0} and point x₀, write x₀ = p + t·ŵ (p ∈ H, ŵ = w/‖w‖), solve for t, and confirm t = (wᵀx₀ + b)/‖w‖. Then derive the ±1-planes separation: for x₊ with wᵀx₊ + b = +1, dist(x₊, H₋) = 2/‖w‖. Finally explain why SVM optimization may equivalently maximize 2/‖w‖ or minimize ‖w‖²/2 — and why the quadratic form is preferred by solvers.


Hint

Enforce wᵀp + b = 0 on the foot point p; subtract the two plane equations for the margin.



Solution

Substituting x₀ = p + tŵ: wᵀx₀ + b = (wᵀp + b) + t‖w‖ = t‖w‖, so t = (wᵀx₀ + b)/‖w‖ — the formula, proved. For the margin: x₊ satisfies wᵀx₊ + b = 1; distance to H₋ is |wᵀx₊ + b + 1|/‖w‖ = 2/‖w‖. Maximizing 2/‖w‖ ⇔ minimizing ‖w‖; the objective ‖w‖²/2 is quadratic — smooth, strictly convex, differentiable everywhere (no square-root kink) — which makes the SVM a clean QP for standard solvers. Every SVM formulation you’ll meet is this geometry plus a slack budget.

Q2. Angles between hyperplanes: the cosine of the angle between two hyperplanes equals |w₁ᵀw₂|/(‖w₁‖‖w₂‖). Implement it, then investigate: for two hyperplanes both separating a given linearly-separable dataset, compute their pairwise angles — are all separating hyperplanes within a narrow cone? Connect the cone’s width to the data’s margin geometry, and explain what this predicts about how much freedom the SVM’s margin maximization actually has (foreshadowing why “the” maximal-margin hyperplane is unique).


Solution







All separating planes lie in a cone around the “true” boundary whose width is set by the data’s gap: wide margins → narrow cones (little freedom — the maximal-margin choice barely matters); narrow margins → wide cones (many hyperplanes fit, and the choice among them is genuine model selection). The SVM resolves this freedom by fiat — max 2/‖w‖ — which is why its solution is unique even when infinitely many hyperplanes classify perfectly.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (geometry × 2.x regression). Two views of one object: a linear regression fit ŷ = wᵀx + b also defines a hyperplane in feature space. On a 2-D dataset, fit OLS and draw (a) the regression’s prediction surface as a contour plot, (b) the zero-set hyperplane. For a constructed binary target (sign of a linear function), compare the OLS-zero-set to the maximal-margin hyperplane (8.2 preview — use sklearn’s LinearSVC with huge C). Quantify the angle between them and explain in margin terms why they differ.
C2 (geometry × 6.4 splines × 8.4 kernels preview). Bases make geometry flexible: expand x = (x₁, x₂) into the quadratic basis (x₁², x₂², √2·x₁x₂, x₁, x₂, 1) — a hyperplane in the expanded space is a conic section in the original. Verify numerically: fit a linear hyperplane in the expanded space to XOR-like data, map its decision boundary back to the original 2-D plane (contour of φ(x)ᵀw = 0), and observe the ellipse/hyperbola family. This is the kernel trick’s entire promise — hyperplanes upstairs, curves downstairs — and the reason 8.4 never materializes the basis.

title: 8.1 Geometry Essentials
text:
7. Summary

Hyperplane = w (normal) + b (offset); zero-set classifies; signed distance = (wᵀx + b)/‖w‖.
Canonical convention: support vectors at wᵀx + b = ±1 → margin = 2/‖w‖ — scale pinned by constraint.
Maximizing 2/‖w‖ ⇔ minimizing ‖w‖²/2 — the quadratic objective solvers love.
Signs classify; scaled magnitudes score; both are unit-sensitive — standardize.
Separating hyperplanes form a cone; margin maximization picks its unique fattest member.
Basis expansion moves hyperplanes upstairs — curves downstairs, kernels to come.
The first SVM proper: make the margin maximal on separable data — 8.2 The maximal-margin classifier.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text: Binary SVMs answer “this class or that one?” — real problems ask “which of k?” Two standard extensions compose binary machines into multiclass classifiers: one-vs-rest (OvR: k machines, each against everyone) and one-vs-one (OvO: k(k−1)/2 machines, each on a pair). SVC runs OvO internally; knowing what that means for scores, calibration, and imbalance is this page’s job.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
1. Basic Concept
OvR: train fₖ(x) = “class k vs not-k” for each k; predict argmaxₖ fₖ(x). OvO: train f_{kl} on classes k and l only; predict by pairwise-vote majority (decision_function returns the k(k−1)/2 vote margins).






SVC’s built-in OvO and its decision-function shape:

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
2. Concept Questions

OvR with 1% positive class: what happens to each rest-vs-one machine’s training balance, and which page’s remedy applies to each binary subproblem?
OvO trains on only 2/nᵏ-ish of the data per machine. Why is that fine for SVC specifically (name the scaling behavior it dodges)?
decision_function for SVC multiclass returns 3 scores for 3 classes. Are these probabilities? Are they comparable across rows?
When do OvR and OvO disagree most, and give one dataset property favoring each.
Your 10-class problem needs calibrated probabilities for downstream cost decisions. What is the two-step pipeline, and which model class makes it trivial?



Answers


Each OvR machine sees ~1% positives vs 99% rest — the imbalanced binary problem k times over. Apply class weights / stratified folds / PR-metric evaluation per machine (3.1); the argmax across machines then compares scores trained on different balances — a known OvR wart.
SVC’s dual training scales roughly between n² and n³; restricting each machine to 2·(2n/k) rows slashes total cost for large k — OvO is the scaling-friendly choice for kernel-SVC multiclass (sklearn’s default for exactly this reason).
No and no. They’re pairwise vote margins in arbitrary per-machine scales (each pair’s SVM has its own w‖); comparable within a row for voting, not calibrated probabilities across rows or samples (8.5’s probability caveat, k-fold worse).
Disagreement peaks near class boundaries and under imbalance (OvR’s rest-class dominates its machine; OvO’s votes fragment). Favor OvO: large k with kernel-SVC (compute); favor OvR: few classes, per-class interpretability (“class k’s own machine”), or sparse outputs.
Model that emits real per-class probabilities (multinomial logistic — softmax, 3.3 extension) then calibrate + apply costs (3.7); SVM route: OvR/OvO scores → probability calibration (extra layer, extra caution).

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. OvR vs OvO vs multinomial, three ways: fit LinearSVC(OvR), SVC(OvO), and LogisticRegression(multinomial softmax) on a 5-class Gaussian problem; compare CV accuracy, fit time, and prediction agreement rates. Then answer: where do OvR and softmax disagree most — and which disagreement is “probability-shaped” vs “margin-shaped”?


Solution







Softmax differs from the SVMs on confidence geometry: it’s the one producing comparable per-class probabilities, so its “disagreements” with margin models concentrate where probabilities (not margins) would rank classes differently — near boundaries between close pairs. Margins answer “which side,” softmax answers “how much of each” — related questions, different answers, choose per downstream need.

Exercise 2. Imbalance across 4 classes (1%, 4%, 15%, 80%): compare SVC-OvO with and without per-pair class_weight="balanced" by macro-F1 and per-class recall (3.1). Which classes get sacrificed by default, and does balancing fix every class or shift the sacrifice? Write the deployment rule for imbalanced multiclass problems.


Solution







Unweighted OvO sacrifices the 1% class almost entirely (recall ≈ 0) and leans on the 80% class; class_weight="balanced" rescales each pair’s penalties, rescuing rare-class recall at the cost of the majority’s precision — recall mass moves, it doesn’t appear. Deployment rule: imbalanced multiclass needs per-class recall targets set by the costs of missing each class, encoded via class weights (or resampling), and evaluated by macro-averaged metrics — never by accuracy or micro-F1 alone.

Exercise 3. Codebook features vs native multiclass: build a 6-class problem where classes sit on a hierarchy (2 supergroups × 3 subclasses). Compare (a) flat 6-class SVC, (b) a two-level strategy: supergroup SVM → subclass SVC within predicted supergroup. Report flat vs hierarchical accuracy (overall and per-subclass). When does the hierarchy help (signal lives at the top level), when does it double-punish (early error propagates), and what does this preview about structured prediction?


Solution







The hierarchy helps when the top split is real and clean (supergroups well separated) — each subproblem becomes easier; it hurts when supergroups overlap, because one wrong top-level call guarantees a wrong subclass — error compounding. Same trade as any structured/sequential prediction: decompose only along genuinely strong boundaries, and measure the top level’s accuracy before trusting the cascade.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

decision_function shape is the tell: (n, k) → OvR scores (LinearSVC, LogisticRegression); (n, k(k−1)/2) → OvO votes (SVC). Code that assumes k columns breaks silently when swapping SVC/LinearSVC.
OvR’s scale non-comparability: each rest-machine has its own w scale; argmax compares apples to slightly different apples — probability calibration or shared-margin formulations fix it if scores must travel.
OvO’s vote ties: with even class counts, votes can tie; sklearn breaks them by a deterministic rule — for audit-sensitive applications, inspect decision_function rather than trusting the tiebreak.
Compute crossover: LinearSVC OvR ≈ k fast primal fits (scales to big n); SVC OvO = k(k−1)/2 dual fits on small pairs (scales to big k with kernels) — the reason SVC defaults to OvO.
class_weight semantics per strategy: OvR applies it per binary machine; OvO per pair — the effective weighting of rare classes differs; verify with per-class recalls, not the API name.
Calibration multiclass: calibrating k OvR machines independently doesn’t calibrate the argmax distribution — use proper multiclass calibration if probabilities matter (3.7).

What’s wrong, and the fix


Vote margins ≠ probabilities: SVC’s decision_function returns k(k−1)/2 pairwise scores; calling them class probabilities misstates both count and meaning. Use probability=True (Platt) — or a softmax model.
Flat accuracy on 25:5:1 imbalance hides total sacrifice of class 2 — macro-F1 + per-class recall (Exercise 2).
Vote margins aren’t cross-row comparable confidence: each pair-machine normalizes differently. Calibrated probabilities (or per-row softmax-style rescaling with validation) are the comparable currency.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Count and compare the training cost of OvR vs OvO for k classes, n rows, kernel-SVC at ~n²-per-fit: derive O(k·n²) vs O(k²·(2n/k)²) = O(4n²) — OvO is constant in k while OvR grows linearly! Verify empirically for k ∈ {3, 6, 12} on fixed-size data, then explain why OvO’s advantage strengthens exactly when n per class also grows (and when OvR’s simplicity wins anyway).


Hint

OvO: k(k−1)/2 machines, each on 2n/k rows → cost per machine ∝ (2n/k)²; multiply out.



Solution

OvR: k machines on n rows → k·n²-scale. OvO: k(k−1)/2 ≈ k²/2 machines on 2n/k rows each → (k²/2)·(2n/k)² = 2n²·(k²/k²)·… = O(4n²) — independent of k.






Fit time grows mildly with k (more machines, smaller each) — the flat-in-k prediction holding. OvO’s advantage strengthens when n is large (n² dominates everything) and kernels make dual training unavoidable; OvR wins when interpretability of per-class machines matters, when using linear primal solvers (already linear in n), or when k is small enough that the difference is noise.

Q2. Design multiclass calibration properly: you have OvR scores from a 4-class SVM and need probabilities for a cost matrix (misclassification costs differ per class pair). (a) Show why independently calibrating each OvR machine breaks (probabilities needn’t sum to 1). (b) Implement a fix: normalize (softmax over calibrated scores) or use a validation-set multiclass calibration, and evaluate proper multiclass calibration via log-loss before/after. (c) State which confusion-matrix entries the cost matrix should reweight, and where the thresholds live now (not in the model — in the decision layer).


Solution








Independent per-class calibrators produce k numbers with arbitrary sums — “probabilities” that violate the probability simplex. (b) A downstream softmax (or a validation-fitted multiclass calibrator) restores the simplex and measurably improves log-loss. (c) The cost matrix lives in the decision layer: given calibrated p, choose the class minimizing Σⱼ C(predicted j, true k)·pⱼ — thresholds become cost-weighted argmax rules, tunable without refitting the SVM. This separation — calibrated model + explicit decision layer — is the clean architecture for any cost-sensitive deployment.

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (multiclass × 3.7 comparison × 7.4 forest). The k-way bake-off: 6-class problem with per-class different geometries (one linear, one radial, one XOR-ish, three Gaussian). Compete SVC-OvO (tuned), LinearSVC-OvR, multinomial logistic, and random forest by macro-F1 (nested CV) plus per-class recall. Which classes does each method sacrifice, and what does the per-class pattern tell you about matching model geometry to class geometry rather than picking one global winner?
C2 (multiclass × 9.4 K-means preview). Clusters as pseudo-labels: run K-means with k = 6 on unlabeled data, then treat cluster IDs as classes for an SVC-OvR. Compare (a) supervised accuracy against true labels, (b) the stability of cluster-to-class mappings across seeds. What breaks when clusters ≠ classes (split/merged clusters), and what does this thought experiment teach about the unsupervised→supervised handoff coming in Part 9?

title: 8.6 Multiclass SVM
text:
7. Summary

Two compositions: OvR (k machines vs the rest; argmax scores) and OvO (k(k−1)/2 pairwise machines; vote majority — SVC’s default).
decision_function shapes differ ((n,k) vs (n,k(k−1)/2)); neither is probability — calibrate for that.
Compute: OvO is flat-in-k for kernel-SVC; OvR is simple and interpretable; LinearSVC makes OvR scale.
Imbalance: per-machine/per-pair class weights, macro metrics, per-class recall — accuracy lies at k > 2 too.
Hierarchical/structured decompositions help only when the top boundary is real; early errors compound.
Probabilities and cost-sensitive decisions live in the calibration + decision layer, not the SVM.
Part 8’s geometry chapter is done. Everything so far had labels — Part 9 removes them: 9.1 The unsupervised mindset.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text: Two linear classifiers, one hinge loss, one log loss. They agree on most datasets and diverge in exactly the dimensions that matter for deployment: probabilities, outlier sensitivity, margin geometry, and scalability. This page makes the comparison a decision procedure rather than a preference.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
Same linear score f(x) = wᵀx + b, different training losses:
\[\text{SVM: } \frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2 + C\sum_i \max(0,\, 1 - y_i f_i) \qquad \text{Logistic: } \frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2 + C\sum_i \log(1 + e^{-y_i f_i})\]






The geometric consequence on overlapping data:

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

State what each loss does with a far-correctly-classified point (score = 4, y = 1) — and the boundary consequence of the difference.
Both models output a signed score. Which one can you interpret as a log-odds, and why not the other?
Overlapping classes with heavy outliers: which method’s boundary is more robust, and which loss property delivers that?
Why does logistic regression scale to huge n more gracefully than SVC (two reasons — one statistical, one computational)?
Your stakeholder needs “probability of disease.” Which model, which step, and what must you check afterwards?



Answers


Hinge: loss 0 — the point vanishes from the fit (no gradient). Logistic: loss log(1 + e⁻⁴) ≈ 0.018 — small but nonzero, still pulling. Consequence: SVM’s boundary is set by frontier points only; logistic’s by every point, weighted by their surprise.
Logistic’s f(x) is the fitted log-odds (by construction: p = σ(f)) — exponentiate coefficients for odds ratios. SVM’s score is a margin distance in canonical units — no probability or odds semantics attached.
SVM — hinge’s linearity bounds any single outlier’s influence (its contribution grows linearly however far it strays), while logistic’s exponential tail lets extreme points dominate the gradient. (Robust variant: Huber/absolute-loss boosting, 7.5.)
Statistical: logistic is a smooth convex GLM — efficient IRLS/SGD variants, warm starts, and it doesn’t need the dual’s kernel trick to stay exact. Computational: hinge-SVM’s dual scales with n (SV count grows with overlap); logistic’s primal has no such n-dependence, and SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss") streams.
Logistic regression, then calibrate it (reliability check on held-out data — 3.7): logistic is the right starting point (native probabilities, no Platt detour), but calibration is still a checked property, not an assumption.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The outlier sensitivity dose-response: on separable data, add ONE mislabeled point at distance d ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8} beyond the boundary. For each d, record the boundary shift (perpendicular displacement of the zero-set) for SVM (C = 1) and logistic. Plot shift vs d. Verify: SVM’s shift saturates (linear-in-d influence), logistic’s grows without bound. State the robustness rule this supports.


Solution







The SVM’s displacement grows only linearly (hinge’s bounded tail — the point is “just another violator” once past the margin); logistic’s grows steadily with d (exponential tail amplifies distance). Rule: mislabeled extremes in the data → prefer margin-based losses or clean them first; logistic assumes labels are trustworthy at any distance.

Exercise 2. Probability quality, head-to-head: on a moderately overlapping dataset, compare (a) logistic’s native probabilities, (b) SVM + probability=True (Platt), (c) SVM’s raw decision_function rescaled by naive min-max — by Brier score, reliability curves, and AUC. Which wins calibration, which wins ranking, and does the ranking winner match the calibration winner? Conclude with the “probabilities vs scores” deployment rule.


Solution







AUC: identical or near-identical (monotone recalibrations preserve ranking). Brier/calibration: logistic and Platt-SVM are close; naive min-max rescaled scores are uncalibrated fiction. Rule: rank with whichever margin you like; probabilities require a model that produces them honestly (logistic) or an explicit calibration step (Platt/isotonic) — never a linear rescale of a margin.

Exercise 3. The scale-of-n crossover: generate datasets at n ∈ {500, 5,000, 50,000} (p = 10) and compare training time and test accuracy for LogisticRegression (liblinear/lbfgs) vs LinearSVC vs SVC(kernel=“linear”). Report the 3×3 table. Where does each become impractical, and what streaming/streaming-adjacent alternative (SGDClassifier with hinge/log losses) offers at 50k? Verify SGD’s accuracy is within ~1% of the batch solution.


Solution







Logistic and LinearSVC are both fast at these scales; SVC(kernel=“linear”) is the first to hurt (dual grows with n) — drop it for large n. SGD (hinge or log) trades a little accuracy for streaming-scale speed and stays within ~1% at 50k with a few passes. The scaling rule: probabilities + big n → logistic/SGD-log; pure decisions + big n → LinearSVC/SGD-hinge; SVC only when SVs themselves (or kernels) are the point.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Two regularizations, same λ-spirit: both penalize ‖w‖²; C (SVM) and C (logistic) are both 1/λ-style slack/tail prices — but their effects differ because the losses differ. Tune each on its own grid (4.6).
Hinge’s sparsity of influence is a feature (robustness, SV parsimony) and a bug (no per-point probability pressure, uncalibrated scores). Decide which you need before choosing the loss (3.1).
Logistic = canonical GLM: coefficients are log-odds ratios, inference exists (3.3); SVM coefficients are margin geometry, inference doesn’t (naively).
Both are linear: identical ceiling without feature engineering or kernels — the 6.3 dictionary, or 8.4’s trick, applies to both.
Class weighting differs subtly: SVM’s class_weight rescales slack prices; logistic’s resamples the loss — both fix imbalance directionally, verify with PR curves (3.1.5).
Multiclass paths differ: SVC does OvO (8.6); LogisticRegression does multinomial (softmax) by default — another semantic difference between “equivalent” pipelines.
