What’s wrong, and the fix


Accuracy at 8% prevalence is the prevalence in disguise (3.1); report AUC + AP/PR.
Margins ≠ probabilities: decision_function is unbounded geometry; Platt-calibrate if probabilities are needed (and validate the calibration).
AUC from hard predictions throws away ranking resolution (ties everywhere) — feed continuous scores: decision_function for SVM, predict_proba for logistic.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The regularized-loss unification: write both SVM and logistic as penalized ERM with the same L2 penalty and different losses. Show formally that as C → ∞ (no regularization), both maximize the margin-like quantity in their own metric, and that the only difference is the loss’s tail behavior past the margin. Then construct a dataset where the two fits produce orthogonal boundaries (hint: one dominant outlier vs clean data — reuse the geometry of 8.2 Exercise 2).


Hint

hinge’(f) = −y·1(yf < 1) — bounded support; logistic’(f) = −y·σ(−yf) — unbounded, decaying. Construct: two clean clusters + one mislabeled point at extreme distance; crank the loss weights and watch which boundary moves.



Solution

Both minimize (1/2)‖w‖² + CΣL(yᵢfᵢ): the tail past the margin is hinge = 0 vs logistic = e⁻^{|f|}-decaying-but-alive. A single extreme mislabeled point contributes zero SVM-gradient once outside the margin (boundary pinned by the rest) but a persistent logistic-gradient proportional to its distance (boundary dragged). Clean data: both boundaries converge to within a few degrees (the losses agree near the frontier). The construction demonstrates “loss tails = influence tails”: choose the tail you can defend given your labeling process — the entire 8.5 decision in one sentence.

Q2. Decision-theoretic selection: a screening program (1% prevalence, FN cost 50× FP) needs (i) a ranked list for follow-up budget and (ii) per-patient risk estimates audited by regulators. Design the model comparison: which metrics for (i) and (ii) (3.1, 3.1.5), which two models to compete, what calibration step the winner needs, and how the cost ratio enters threshold choice after modeling (3.1 Exercise 2). Implement the comparison on simulated data and report the decision.


Solution








Ranking for budget: AP/AUC on continuous scores — both models compete (SVM margins rank fine). (ii) Audited risks: logistic’s native probabilities + calibration check win (SVM needs Platt and still needs verification). Threshold: with FN:FP = 50:1, choose the cutoff from the cost-minimizing point of the chosen model’s ROC/PR trade — after modeling, on validation data, and reported with the confusion matrix it implies. Decision: logistic for the deployed risk model, SVM kept as the margin-consistency check.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (SVM × logistic × 5.x × 6.7 GAM). The four-way boundary study: on a dataset with 3 linear signals + 1 smooth nonlinear signal + 1 interaction, compare logistic-linear, SVM-linear, GAM-logistic (additive splines — 6.7), and RBF-SVM, all nested-CV’d. Report test AUC and each model’s recovery of the linear signals (coefficient/importance comparison). Which model when — write the routing rule a team should paste above their modeling notebook.
C2 (SVM × 0.5 leakage × 4.6 tuning). The optimistic-pipeline autopsy: a colleague reports “SVM (C, γ tuned) beats logistic 0.94 vs 0.91.” Audit: re-run their probable pipeline (scaler fit on all data, (C, γ) tuned on test) vs the honest nested version; quantify the inflation attributable to each bug separately. Then write the two-sentence review response you’d file — the reusable text for the next paper you review with this flaw.

title: 8.5 SVM vs Logistic Regression
text:
7. Summary

Same linear score, different loss tails: hinge (zero past margin, linear when wrong) vs log (never zero, exponential when wrong).
Probabilities: logistic native and interpretable; SVM via Platt — calibrate either way.
Robustness: hinge bounds outlier influence; logistic’s tail lets extremes pull — labeling quality decides.
Scale: logistic/LinearSVC/SGD for big n; SVC when SVs or kernels are the point.
Both are linear without engineering; both need scaling, honest tuning, and prevalence-aware metrics.
Multiclass paths differ (OvO vs multinomial) — see 8.6 next.
One family remains: SVMs for many classes at once — 8.6 Multiclass SVM.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text: Real classes overlap. The soft margin keeps the maximal-margin idea but lets points pay a price ξᵢ to violate it — turning “impossible” into “tunable”: C sets the exchange rate between a fat margin and a clean fit. It is the SVM you will actually use.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
1. Basic Concept
\[\min_{w, b, \xi} \; \frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2 + C \sum_i \xi_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i, \;\; \xi_i \ge 0\]
ξᵢ = how far point i intrudes into (or crosses) the margin; C = the price per unit of intrusion. C → ∞ recovers the hard margin; C → 0 lets the boundary ignore everything.






Hinge loss — the soft margin’s loss in unconstrained clothing: ξᵢ = (1 − yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b))₊:






C tuning, honestly (4.6):

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
2. Concept Questions

A support vector in the soft-margin world: which points get αᵢ > 0 now? Are they all on the margin?
C → ∞ and C → 0 endpoints: state both behaviors, including what the boundary does at C = 0.
How does the hinge loss differ from logistic loss at (a) correctly-classified far points, (b) misclassified points — and what does each difference do to the fitted boundary?
Your CV chooses C = 1000 on overlapping data. What is that telling you about the data — and is the resulting margin reportable?
Why does the soft-margin SVM remain scale-sensitive, and which quantity does a feature-unit change distort — C, ξ, or both?



Answers


In the hard margin, αᵢ > 0 ⟺ on the margin. Soft margin: αᵢ > 0 for points on the margin and all violators (ξᵢ > 0) — anything touching or crossing the band is load-bearing; far-correct points still don’t matter.
C → ∞: slacks become unaffordable → hard-margin behavior (infeasible if overlap exists — solver strains). C → 0: violations are free → ‖w‖ → 0 dominates, boundary collapses toward arbitrary/mean — practically untrained. C = 0 exactly is degenerate (w = 0 minimizes).

Hinge = 0 for far-correct points (no gradient, no influence — the margin geometry’s parsimony); logistic loss never reaches zero — every point pulls forever (smoother, no sparsity of influence). (b) Misclassified: hinge is linear in the violation (bounded influence of any single point), logistic is exponential-ish in the margin distance (a single extreme point can dominate the fit). Net: SVM boundary = geometry of the frontier; logistic boundary = a weighted average view of all data.

High C chosen on overlapping data says “the CV folds are (nearly) separable under heavy penalization” — i.e., few-but-real violations. The reported 2/‖w‖ is then a nominal margin with (100·violation%) of points inside it — report it together with the violation fraction, or not at all.
Both, via ξᵢ: ξᵢ is measured in score units (wᵀx + b), whose scale depends on feature units — rescaling a feature changes each ξᵢ and thus the C-price of the same geometric situation. Standardize first, always (geometric law from 8.1).

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Hinge-loss SVM from scratch: minimize (1/2)‖w‖² + C·Σ max(0, 1 − yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b)) by sub-gradient descent on a small dataset; compare the resulting (w, b) and predictions to LinearSVC(C=C) (normalize for the scale convention — compare decision signs and margin geometry, not raw coefficients). Report where your solution and sklearn’s agree and where optimization details diverge.


Solution







Sub-gradient descent on the hinge objective converges to the same margin geometry (same direction; coefficient scale conventions differ between formulations — that’s why you compare normalized geometry). sklearn’s solver is faster and smarter, but you’ve now implemented the objective the whole method optimizes.

Exercise 2. The C-frontier: on overlapping data, sweep C over 6 log-spaced values; for each record (a) training margin-violation fraction, (b) train accuracy, (c) test accuracy, (d) ‖w‖. Plot the panel. Identify the three regimes (underfit-all-slack / balanced / overfit-margin) and connect each to its bias–variance signature (4.4) — C is SVM’s flexibility dial, running opposite to k in KNN or… specify the direction relative to ridge’s λ.


Solution







Small C: everything is slack, ‖w‖ tiny — underfit (bias-dominated). Large C: margin tight, boundary chases the frontier points — variance-dominated. Balanced middle: few violations, stable boundary. Relative to ridge (5.2): C is 1/λ — big C = weak regularization; the dial’s direction is inverted, which trips everyone once.

Exercise 3. Soft margin under label noise: inject 8% label flips into separable data. Compare hard-margin-attempt (C = 1e5) vs CV-tuned soft margin: test accuracy, boundary angle between them, and the fraction of flipped points that became support vectors. Then explain why the tuned soft margin absorbs the noise while the hard attempt contorts around it — and which of the two would you trust under 3.2’s class-overlap realities.


Solution







Flipped labels sit deep in enemy territory; a hard margin bends the boundary extravagantly to accommodate them (or fails); a tuned soft margin prices them as ξ and lets them sit violated — boundary stays where the clean mass of evidence points. Trust the soft margin: label noise is precisely the violation-budget use case, and C is the honest knob declaring how much noise you’ll tolerate.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

C’s direction vs every other penalty: C is 1/λ — larger = less regularized. Writing “higher C = more regularization” in a report is the classic tell of a rushed pipeline.
Violating support vectors: in soft-margin fits, αᵢ is capped at C; points with αᵢ = C are the ξᵢ > 0 violators. Reading dual_coef_ magnitudes against C tells you which SVs are on-margin vs crossing.
LinearSVC has no predict_proba — probability-ish outputs need SVC(probability=True) (Platt scaling, internal CV) or a separate calibrator (3.7); don’t pretend decision_function values are probabilities.
Class weights rescale C per class: class_weight={1: 5} multiplies minority violations’ price — the margin version of imbalance handling (3.1); evaluate with PR metrics.
Hinge loss ⇒ no probabilities and non-smooth optimization: that’s the price of margin sparsity; the logistic comparison (8.5) is exactly hinge-vs-log.
Multiclass: SVC runs OvO internally (8.6) — C’s meaning per binary subproblem, aggregated.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated soft-margin pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


C’s direction flipped: the commentary treats large C as the regularized end; C is the slack price — large C = weak regularization. Fix the narrative (and the grid’s labels) before anyone copies it.
Mixed units, unscaled geometry: the 500-scale feature prices margins in its units; the StandardScaler step is missing — with it, C’s meaning is unit-free.
decision_function ≠ probability: it’s the signed margin score, unbounded both ways. Use SVC(probability=True) + calibration, or quote scores as scores.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Connect the two formulations: show that the ξ-form (min ‖w‖²/2 + CΣξᵢ) is identical to unconstrained hinge minimization (1/2)‖w‖² + CΣmax(0, 1 − yᵢfᵢ) — by substituting ξᵢ = max(0, 1 − yᵢfᵢ) and checking the optimal ξᵢ given (w, b). Then verify numerically: solve both with scipy for a tiny problem and compare (w, b) up to solver tolerance. What does this equivalence buy conceptually (loss view vs constraint view)?


Hint

For fixed (w, b), the constraint set forces ξᵢ ≥ 1 − yᵢfᵢ and ξᵢ ≥ 0; minimizing Cξᵢ picks exactly the hinge value.



Solution

Given (w, b), the smallest feasible ξᵢ is max(0, 1 − yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b)) — substituting and dropping ξ turns the constrained program into unconstrained hinge minimization. The views are dual lenses: the constraint view exposes geometry (margins, SVs, KKT); the loss view exposes optimization (subgradients, SGD, loss comparisons with logistic — 8.5). Solvers like LinearSVC optimize the hinge directly; SVC optimizes the dual of the ξ-form — same optimum, different algebra.

Q2. C vs the bias–variance decomposition: estimate bias² and variance of the soft-margin SVM across C ∈ {0.01, 1, 100} using the multi-training-set protocol (4.4) on overlapping data. Which C minimizes variance, which minimizes bias², and does total error’s minimum sit at the CV-chosen C? Write the sentence connecting C to the decomposition — the SVM’s own bias–variance story.


Solution







Small C: heavy slack tolerance → boundary drifts freely (high variance in position is capped, but bias rises as the fit under-commits). Large C: tight margins fit each sample’s frontier (variance up), bias lower. The CV-chosen C typically sits at the decomposition’s total-minimum — the SVM’s C is its bias–variance dial, in constraint language.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (soft margin × 0.5 splitting × 12.x multiplicity stub). C and feature selection interact: on p = 100 features with 3 relevant, compare (a) SelectKBest(k by CV) → SVC(C by CV), (b) SVC on all features (C by CV), both nested-CV’d. Report test accuracy and which relevant features survive in (a)’s filter (over folds). When does the SVM’s implicit regularization make explicit filtering unnecessary — and when does filtering rescue it?
C2 (soft margin × 3.7 calibration). The C–calibration interaction: fit SVMs at C ∈ {0.1, 1, 10} with probability=True; for each, produce reliability curves and Brier scores, before and after Platt-calibration on a validation split. Does larger C (tighter margins, fewer SVs) help or hurt calibration? Explain via the SV-vote smoothing mechanism (7.3’s averaging intuition applied to support-vector votes) and state your deployment configuration.

title: 8.3 The Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
7. Summary

Soft margin = hard margin + slack budget: min ‖w‖²/2 + CΣξᵢ — the SVM for real, overlapping data.
Hinge loss is the same object unconstrained: zero for far-correct points, linear when wrong.
C is the slack price — 1/λ: larger C = weaker regularization; the inverted direction trips everyone.
Support vectors now include violators; far-correct points still don’t matter.
C is the SVM’s bias–variance dial; CV picks it; margins reported alongside violation fractions.
No native probabilities — calibrate or quote scores as scores.
Linear soft margins in hand, the nonlinear leap costs one substitution: 8.4 Kernel SVM.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text: The kernel trick is the SVM’s superpower: replace every inner product xᵢᵀxⱼ with a kernel function k(xᵢ, xⱼ) that implicitly computes inner products in a vast expanded space — nonlinearity without ever building the features. Circles in, circles classified; dimensions infinite, cost unchanged.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
1. Basic Concept
The dual’s predictions depend only on inner products (8.2): f(x) = Σαᵢyᵢ⟨xᵢ, x⟩ + b. Substitute any valid kernel k:
\[f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i k(x_i, x) + b\]
The RBF (Gaussian) kernel — the default workhorse:
\[k(x_i, x) = \exp(-\gamma \|x_i - x\|^2)\]
— implicitly an infinite-dimensional basis. The classic circle problem, solved:






The explicit feature map, once — to demystify the trick, do it manually for the quadratic kernel:

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
2. Concept Questions

State the kernel trick’s two-part bargain: what must the algorithm never do, and what may it only use?
Why does the RBF kernel create closed, local boundaries while polynomial kernels create open, global ones?
γ in the RBF kernel: what does large γ do to each training point’s influence, and which failure does extreme γ reproduce (7.1)?
What makes a function a valid kernel (the Mercer condition, in one sentence), and name two practical consequences of validity.
SVC.support_vectors_ after an RBF fit: are these points in the original space or the expanded one — and how many coordinates does the expanded space have?



Answers


Never: materialize φ(x) or use any property of features beyond inner products. Only: inner products ⟨xᵢ, xⱼ⟩ (and ⟨xᵢ, x⟩ at prediction) — replace with k(xᵢ, xⱼ) and everything stays valid if k is a real inner product in some space.
RBF similarity decays with distance (Gaussian bump around every SV): boundaries are unions of local closed contours — a point’s class is decided by nearby support vectors. Polynomials are global monomials: boundaries extend to infinity as open curves — decided by global orientation (6.3’s local-vs-global bases, kernel edition).
Large γ → narrow bumps → each training point influences only its own micro-neighborhood → the fit approaches “memorize every point” — a 1-NN with kernels, the same overfitting endpoint (7.1’s k = 1).
Valid = positive semi-definite: Σcᵢcⱼk(xᵢ, xⱼ) ≥ 0 for all coefficients — i.e., it IS an inner product in some Hilbert space. Consequences: the optimization stays convex (a QP), and predictions are consistent geometry (no paradoxical “similar to both classes” pathologies).
Original space — support vectors are training points (stored as-is); the expanded space has infinitely many coordinates for RBF (the map is infinite-dimensional), which is exactly why you never build it.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement the RBF-kernel SVM’s prediction function by hand from a fitted SVC: extract dual_coef_, support_vectors_, intercept_; compute f(x) = Σ αᵢ k(xᵢ, x) + b yourself on a query grid; verify exact agreement with decision_function. Then confirm the kernel matrix your function implies (SVs × queries) matches rbf_gram — the whole model is these numbers.


Solution







A fitted kernel SVM is its support vectors, their dual coefficients, and an intercept — everything else (γ, C) shaped those numbers. This representation is also the deployment format: store ~n_support vectors, evaluate kernels on demand.

Exercise 2. The γ × C landscape: for the circle dataset, grid-search (γ, C) over log grids with 5-fold CV; display the CV-accuracy heat map. Identify the three regimes visible in the map (underfit smooth / well-fit / memorize), and mark the CV optimum. Then state the two-dial tuning recipe — which knob acts like model complexity, which like the fit-price — and their interaction.


Solution







Reading: low γ or low C → underfit (smooth blob, ~50–70%); high γ AND high C → memorize (train-perfect, CV-crippled); the diagonal ridge between them is the operating zone — γ sets per-point locality (complexity), C sets how hard violations are chased (fit price), and jointly they trace the 4.4 U-curve in 2-D.

Exercise 3. Kernel zoo, honestly compared: on three truths (linear, circle, XOR-corner), compare linear / poly(degree 2) / RBF kernels by CV accuracy — plus the “kernel + linear truth” sanity row. Report the 3(kernel) × 3(truth) table. Write the kernel-selection heuristic the table supports, including the role of the linear baseline as a lower-bound guard against needless kernels.


Solution







Reads: linear kernel wins its own truth and never embarrasses elsewhere (the guard); poly2 takes XOR (its basis contains x₁x₂); RBF wins circles and corners (local freedom) but gains nothing on linear truths. Heuristic: always run the linear baseline; reach for RBF when validation says the boundary curves; try poly when domain theory names the interaction order. Kernels are hypotheses about geometry — test them like hypotheses.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

γ and C multiply each other’s effect — the same fit can be reached by (γ↓, C↑) or (γ↑, C↓) along the flat valley; tune jointly on log grids, never independently (4.6).
Scaling is non-negotiable: RBF distance is Euclidean in raw units; unscaled features decide the geometry (8.1’s law, now with teeth — γ’s meaning changes with scale too).
SV count explodes with overlap: RBF SVMs on noisy data can retain most of the training set as SVs — prediction cost and memory scale with it; LinearSVC or trees for huge n.
gamma="scale" (default) is 1/(n·Var(X)) — data-dependent, sensible, but changes between datasets: never port γ across problems.
Probabilities: SVC(probability=True) fits Platt scaling post-hoc (internal CV) — calibrated-ish but slower and slightly different model; quote decision_function for ranking, probabilities only after this step (3.7).
Precomputed kernels: you can pass your own Gram matrix (kernel="precomputed") — the door to custom/domain-specific similarity functions (strings, graphs, alignments) — validity (PSD) is on you.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated kernel pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


γ = 50 on unscaled data: distance² of typical points is tens-to-hundreds → kernel values ≈ e^{-thousands} ≈ 0 — every point isolated, training memorizes (train ≫ test). Scale features; tune γ on a log grid.
One loss → verdict: the linear baseline is a guard, not a rival; on a circle truth it should lose, and kernels don’t “always win” — linear truths punish them (drill 3).
Scores ≠ probabilities: decision_function is the unbounded margin; calibrate (Platt) if probabilities are needed downstream.

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Verify the polynomial-kernel identity on a small case: for x, z ∈ R², k(x, z) = (xᵀz + 1)² equals ⟨φ(x), φ(z)⟩ for φ = (x₁², x₂², √2x₁x₂, √2x₁, √2x₂, 1). Check numerically across random pairs. Then explain why this equivalence means the explicit-map SVM and the kernel SVM are the same model — and construct (conceptually) the case where the explicit map is still preferable (name the resource that becomes the bottleneck).


Hint

Expand (xᵀz + 1)² = (x₁z₁ + x₂z₂ + 1)² term by term; match coefficients to inner products of the φ coordinates.



Solution

(xᵀz + 1)² = (x₁z₁)² + (x₂z₂)² + 2x₁z₁x₂z₂ + 2x₁z₁ + 2x₂z₂ + 1 = x₁²z₁² + x₂²z₂² + (√2x₁x₂)(√2z₁z₂) + (√2x₁)(√2z₁) + (√2x₂)(√2z₂) + 1·1 — exactly ⟨φ(x), φ(z)⟩ for the stated φ. Numerics:






Same model: SVM-in-φ-space with a linear kernel ≡ SVM with (xᵀz+1)² — identical optimum, identical predictions. Explicit map preferred when φ is low-dimensional and you predict millions of times (basis evaluation beats SV-kernel sums) or need φ’s coefficients for interpretation; the kernel wins when dim(φ) is huge (degree 10 → ~66+ dims; RBF → infinite).

Q2. The γ–distance reading: show that for the RBF kernel, the decision function is a signed weighted sum of bumps centered at support vectors, and that γ determines each bump’s radius (∝ 1/√γ). Design and run the diagnostic: for a fitted RBF SVM, plot the decision function along a 1-D slice, mark SV locations, and show how the boundary interpolates between SV classes as γ varies over {0.2, 2, 20}. Write the “γ-as-resolution” sentence a practitioner should carry.


Solution







γ is the resolution dial of a bump-sum representation: 1/√γ is bump width. Low γ: one wide bump family — smooth, nearly-linear boundaries. High γ: a bump per point — the decision function reproduces training labels individually (memorization). Carry the sentence: “γ sets how far one training point’s vote reaches; C sets how expensive it is to disagree — tune them together.”

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (kernels × 5.x high dimensions × 7.4 forests). The nonlinear tabular rematch: n = 200, p = 50, truth = 4 linear signals + 2 interaction signals + 1 radial signal. Compete RBF-SVM (tuned), random forest, and lasso (5.3) by nested CV. Report test error and each method’s capture of the three signal types (importances/coefficient paths). Which inductive bias wins when signals are heterogeneous — and what ensemble-of-diverse-models conclusion does the table support?
C2 (kernels × 8.2 support vectors × 12.x stability stub). SV stability under resampling: fit RBF SVMs (CV-tuned γ, C) on 100 bootstrap resamples; measure (a) the Jaccard overlap of SV sets, (b) prediction agreement, (c) the overlap of top-importance features if any. Compare against a logistic model’s selected-feature stability. Which model’s “explanation artifact” (SV set vs coefficient signs) is more reproducible — and what does that imply about publishing SVM-derived SV analyses?

title: 8.4 Kernel SVM
text:
7. Summary

Kernel trick: predictions need only inner products — swap in k(xᵢ, xⱼ), get the expanded space for free.
RBF = local bumps (closed boundaries, γ = resolution); poly = global monomials (open boundaries); linear = the guard.
Scale features; tune (γ, C) jointly on log grids; the flat valley between underfit and memorize is the target.
Fitted model = support vectors + dual coefficients + intercept — deployable, inspectable, kernel-generic.
Valid kernels are PSD: convexity preserved, geometry consistent, custom similarities welcome.
Nonlinearity now costs a kernel choice, not a basis build — but probabilities, scaling, and SV-cost caveats ride along.
Linear SVM vs logistic, margins vs likelihoods, side by side: 8.5 SVM vs logistic regression.
