title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text: When the formula for an uncertainty is messy or unknown — a median, a difference of AUCs, a ratio — resampling replaces the mathematics with computation: shuffle or resample the data you have, recompute the statistic many times, and look at the spread. It is the bridge between classical inference and the cross-validation you will use for every model.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
1. Basic Concept
The bootstrap treats your sample as a stand-in for the population: draw new samples with replacement, same size as the original, recompute the statistic, repeat. The variability across bootstrap replicates mimics the sampling variability of the statistic.






Let’s do that cleanly for the median — the statistic where formulas hurt:






The permutation test answers a different question — “is this association real?” — by shuffling labels to simulate a world where the null is exactly true, and asking how extreme the real statistic is among the shuffled ones:






The jackknife — leave one out, recompute, look at the spread — estimates bias and SE from n recomputations (cheap, deterministic, less flexible):

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must bootstrap resampling be with replacement, and what would happen without it?
What null does a permutation test simulate, and why don’t we need to know any distribution’s shape?
When does the bootstrap fail even with lots of data? Give one statistic and one data structure.
How does a bootstrap CI for a mean compare to the t-formula CI for near-normal data — and for skewed data?
Conceptually, how is K-fold cross-validation (0.5) a resampling method, and what statistic does it resample for?



Answers


With replacement generates variability — each replicate is a new pseudo-sample whose composition differs (some points twice, some never). Without replacement every replicate is the original sample in a different order — zero variability, zero information.
The null of exchangeability: group labels carry no information, so any shuffling of labels is as probable as the observed one. The p-value counts how often shuffled data produces a statistic at least as extreme as observed — no distributional formula required, only the labels being exchangeable under H₀.

Extreme order statistics — the min/max (bootstrap resamples contain ≤ n distinct values; the max can never exceed the observed max, so its distribution is degenerate). (b) Dependent data — time series or spatial data: i.i.d. resampling destroys the dependence structure that the statistic is about (fixes exist: block bootstrap).

Near-normal: nearly identical (bootstrap ≈ t-interval, slightly wider with percentile method). Skewed: the bootstrap CI inherits the skew of the statistic’s sampling distribution — often more honest than the symmetric t-CI (1.4 Exercise 3).
CV repeatedly partitions the sample, recomputes model performance on held-out parts, and reads stability from the spread — resampling the rows rather than resampling within a statistic’s input. Bootstrap estimates the variability of a statistic; CV estimates the variability of an estimation procedure’s performance.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Bootstrap the difference in medians between two skewed groups (5000 replicates), report the 95% percentile CI, and compare with the CI you’d get from a difference-in-means t-interval. Which pair of estimates is the better summary for skewed data and why?


Solution







For skewed data the medians + bootstrap CI pair is the defensible summary: medians resist the tail, and the bootstrap CI carries the actual (asymmetric) uncertainty. The t-CI on means is dominated by a handful of large values and its symmetric shape misrepresents the uncertainty.

Exercise 2. Implement the permutation test for a difference in means as a reusable function perm_test(a, b, n_perm=10_000, seed=0), then apply it to (a) clearly separated groups, (b) identical distributions. Verify in case (b) that p-values are approximately uniform on (0,1) over 500 repeats — the defining calibration property of a valid test.


Solution







The uniformity check in (b) is the gold-standard self-test of any test implementation: under a true null, p-values must be ~Uniform(0,1), so P(p < α) = α. If your p-values pile up near 0 under the null, your permutation scheme is broken (usually: statistic computed on non-pooled data, or shuffling within groups).

Exercise 3. Bootstrap vs formula SE shootout. For n = 8, 30, 200 samples from a lognormal, compute (a) the t-formula SE of the mean, (b) the bootstrap SE of the mean, (c) the bootstrap SE of the median. Plot/inspect how the three quantities and their stability change with n. Write the two-sentence takeaway.


Solution







Takeaways: (1) formula and bootstrap SE of the mean agree closely — the bootstrap recovers textbook results, validating the machinery; (2) for skewed data the median’s bootstrap SE is smaller and its own sampling distribution is more stable — another argument for robust summaries on skewed biological measurements.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The bootstrap resamples observations, not noise: each replicate should reproduce the original sample size and structure (paired rows stay paired; per-group sizes preserved by stratified bootstrapping).
Percentile CIs under-cover for small n and skewed statistics — improvements (BCa) exist; know that “bootstrap CI” is a family, not one object. Report the method.
Permutation tests require exchangeability under H₀ — with confounded group assignments (e.g. all treated samples run on batch 2), shuffling labels tests the wrong null. Design before inference.
Number of replicates: 1,000–10,000 for CIs; more for tail quantiles. Monte Carlo error of a percentile ≈ \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}\) — at B = 1,000 the 2.5% quantile itself wobbles.
Bootstrap cannot see beyond the sample: it inherits your outliers and your range (the max degeneracy drill). If the sample missed the tails, the bootstrap is confidently wrong about them.
rng.choice vs rng.integers indexing: rng.choice(x, size=(B, n), replace=True) in one call is far faster than a Python loop of resamples — vectorize your resampling like everything else.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated bootstrap has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


replace=False — every “replicate” is just the original data minus one point (a jackknife in disguise); no bootstrap variability.
size=len(data)-1 — replicates must match the original n; smaller samples underestimate the statistic’s variance.
[5, 95] percentiles — that’s a 90% interval labeled as a CI; 95% needs the 2.5/97.5 percentiles. (Minor: a Python loop of 1,000 resamples is fine here but the vectorized form is idiomatic and 100× faster.)







Note the outlier: watch how the bootstrap CI for the mean is stretched rightward while stat=np.median would give a tight, stable interval — run both and compare.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Explain precisely why the bootstrap estimate of a statistic’s SE converges to the true SE as n → ∞, and why the approximation is double (empirical distribution → population, plug-in resampling → true sampling distribution). Where does small n hurt first?


Hint

The bootstrap replaces F (unknown population CDF) with F̂ (empirical CDF). Two questions: how well does F̂ approximate F, and how well does the bootstrap world mimic the real one for your statistic?



Solution

The bootstrap is a plug-in: it pretends F̂ (the empirical distribution — the sample itself) is the truth, then simulates sampling from F̂. By the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem, F̂ → F uniformly as n grows, so for statistics that depend smoothly on the distribution (means, moments, regression coefficients), the bootstrap SE → true SE. The error is two-layered: (1) F̂ ≠ F (sampling error of the original study — unavoidable, shrinks as n grows), and (2) the statistic’s behavior in the bootstrap world ≠ its behavior in the real world (mild for smooth statistics, severe for extremes/discontinuous ones like the max). Small n hurts first through layer (2) for non-smooth statistics and through percentile-CI undercoverage — with n = 10, the empirical distribution has only 10 distinct values and every resample is a sparse remix of them.

Q2. Your permutation test compares a treated group (n = 6) to controls (n = 40). (a) How many distinct label assignments exist, and what is the smallest nonzero p-value the test can ever return? (b) What practical consequences does this have for small-n study design and for reporting “p < 0.001” from a permutation test with 6+40 samples?


Solution


\(\binom{46}{6} = 9{,}366{,}819\) distinct assignments (treated labels are indistinguishable among themselves). The smallest nonzero p is \(1/\binom{46}{6} \approx 1.07 \times 10^{-7}\) — so in principle tiny p-values are attainable. (b) The real constraint is resolution vs replicates: with B = 10,000 random permutations, the add-one p-value has resolution ≈ 10⁻⁴ and Monte Carlo error ~\(\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}\); reporting “p < 0.001” from 10⁴ permutations is not supportable — report “p < 10⁻⁴” or increase B. Design lesson: permutation tests inherit the exact-conditional guarantee but their resolution is bounded by combinatorics and B — small treated groups are fine for moderate p-values, hopeless for “highly significant” claims without huge B (or full enumeration).

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (resampling × 0.5 Data splitting). Implement a bootstrap comparison of two models’ test accuracies: fit both models on each of 200 bootstrap resamples of the training set, evaluate both on the same fixed test set, and build the CI of the accuracy difference. Then explain why this underestimates the uncertainty from training-set variation compared to refitting on fresh splits, and how the “.632 bootstrap” style corrections (4.5) address the overlap problem.
C2 (resampling × 4.6 Hyperparameter tuning preview). You tune a hyperparameter by picking the K-fold CV optimum, then report that optimum’s CV score as the performance estimate. Simulate this procedure under a null (no signal: y random) with 20 candidate values and show the optimistic bias (selected score vs true score on fresh data). Which resampling discipline (nested CV) fixes it, and what does this have in common with the optional-stopping bug of 1.4?

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
7. Summary

Bootstrap: resample rows with replacement, same n, recompute — the spread across replicates estimates uncertainty for almost any statistic.
Permutation test: shuffle labels under exchangeability; the p-value is the rank of the observed statistic among shuffled ones; distribution-free by construction.
Jackknife: leave-one-out; cheap deterministic bias/SE estimates.
Percentile bootstrap CIs match t-CIs for tame data and outperform them for skewed statistics.
Failure modes: order statistics (max), dependent data, non-exchangeable labels, tiny n, and reading more precision out of B replicates than B provides.
Vectorize resampling: one rng.integers/choice call for all replicates.
Uncertainty about a statistic is solved; uncertainty about a model’s predictions is the subject of Part 4 — starting from why held-out data is the only honest judge: Part 2 builds the first models, and Part 4 formalizes their evaluation.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text: Inference answers the question every experiment asks: is this pattern real, or would chance produce it? Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty about a population quantity; hypothesis tests quantify how surprising the data would be under a “nothing is happening” model. Both are built on one idea — the sampling distribution of a statistic.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
1. Basic Concept
The standard error. A sample mean varies from sample to sample with SD ≈ \(s/\sqrt{n}\) — the standard error (SE). Small n means the SE is big means the sample mean is a shaky estimate of the population mean.
Confidence interval. A 95% CI for a mean is approximately
\[\bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where the t-quantile widens the interval for small samples. Interpretation (get this exactly right): if the sampling procedure were repeated many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true mean — it is a property of the procedure, not a 95% probability statement about this particular interval.






Hypothesis test logic. State \(H_0\) (no effect) → compute a statistic measuring departure from \(H_0\) → the p-value is P(data at least this extreme | \(H_0\)). Small p = the null struggles to explain the data. It is not P(\(H_0\) | data).






Errors and power. Two ways to be wrong: Type I — declare an effect under a true null (rate = α); Type II — miss a real effect (rate = β); power = 1 − β, driven by effect size, n, α, and noise.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
2. Concept Questions

A 95% CI is (2.1, 3.9). Is “P(true mean is in (2.1, 3.9)) = 0.95” a correct reading?
Why does a p-value not tell you the probability the null hypothesis is true?
What does the t in “t-test” buy you over a z-test, and when does the distinction vanish?
Your test on n = 5 has p = 0.20. Which conclusions are valid: (a) “no effect exists”, (b) “effect not demonstrated”, (c) “need more data or a better design”?
Why is equal_var=False (Welch) the sensible default for two-sample t-tests?



Answers


No. The interval is now fixed — it either contains the mean or not. The 95% describes the procedure’s long-run success rate across hypothetical repetitions. (Frequentist probability attaches to procedures, not fixed quantities.)
The p-value is computed assuming the null is true; it can’t then assign that null a probability. It is P(data at least this extreme | H₀) — evidence about the data under H₀, not about H₀ given the data. That reversal is exactly Bayes’ rule, and frequentist testing deliberately doesn’t do it (a prior on hypotheses would be required).
t replaces the known population σ with the estimated s, adding uncertainty that widens critical values (t₀.₉₇₅,₄ = 2.78 vs z = 1.96). As df → ∞, t → z; by n ≈ 30–50 the difference is negligible.

and (c) only. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; a high p-value at tiny n is uninformative, not exculpatory. Never conclude “no effect” without a power/equivalence argument.

Real biological groups rarely have equal variances, and Student’s pooled t can inflate false positives under inequality; Welch’s correction keeps Type I error near nominal with negligible power loss — so it’s the robust default.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the two-sample experiment below, compute (a) Welch t-test, (b) the 95% CI of each group mean, (c) the 95% CI for the difference in means (bootstrap is fine). State the decision and the estimate-with-uncertainty sentence you would put in a report.


Solution







Report sentence: “Treatment increased the marker by an estimated 1.5 units (bootstrap 95% CI 0.3 to 2.7; Welch p = 0.02).” The CI is the quantitative claim; the p-value only grades the surprise under “no difference.” Also note the CI excludes 0 exactly when p < 0.05 (two-sided) — consistency check.

Exercise 2. Multiple testing preview, empirically: simulate 100 independent two-group experiments under the global null (α = 0.05 each). (a) Expected number of “significant” results? (b) Empirical probability that at least one is significant? (c) Repeat at α = 0.001. What family-wise lesson emerges?


Solution







At α = 0.05, ~5 false positives per 100-null family and ≈ 99.4% chance of at least one. The family-wise error explodes with the number of tests — the problem Bonferroni and FDR (12.3, 12.4) solve.

Exercise 3. Demonstrate the effect of skew on the t-test/CI: sample n = 10 from a lognormal; bootstrap the sampling distribution of the mean; compare the bootstrap CI to the t-formula CI. Which is trustworthy here, and what sample size restores the t-approximation (test empirically)?


Solution







At n = 10 the mean’s true sampling distribution is strongly right-skewed — the symmetric t-CI is a poor description (and its 95% coverage is off). The bootstrap CI inherits the skew. At n = 100 the CLT has done its work and the two CIs nearly agree. Lesson: t-methods assume approximate normality of the sampling distribution, which skewed small samples violate; alternatives are log-transform, nonparametric tests, or larger n.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

p-value misreadings (all wrong, all common): P(H₀ true) = p; p = 0.03 means “3% chance the result is chance”; p > 0.05 means “no effect”; p = 0.049 vs 0.051 is a meaningful difference. The p-value is one number about one conditional probability — treat it as such.
The t-test compares means; it does not “prove normality” — with n = 5 you cannot even check the assumption well. Prefer Welch + report effect size + CI.
Paired vs unpaired is a design property: repeated measures on the same unit demand paired analysis (ttest_rel); pairing halves the noise only if the pairing is real.
Effect size ≠ significance: at n = 100,000, a 0.1% difference gets p ≈ 0; at n = 5, a huge effect gets p ≈ 0.3. Report effect + CI, let n decide detectability, not importance.
One-sided tests halve the p-value but require pre-registered direction — switching sides after looking at data is p-hacking.
Stopping rules break calibration: “collect until p < 0.05” inflates Type I error far above 5% (the simulation drill adapts to demonstrate this).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Design mismatch: after is generated from before — paired structure. The unpaired test throws away the pairing and most of the power. Use ttest_rel (or test the differences).
Both printed conclusions are wrong: small p is not “96% chance the treatment works” (it’s P(data|H₀), not P(H₀|data) or power), and large p never “proves useless”. Correct sentence: “data would be surprising under no-effect (p = …)”.
Sequential peeking: continuing until significance guarantees eventual “significance” even under a true null — Type I error ≈ 100%. Fix: pre-set n, or use a formal sequential design (alpha-spending); simplest demonstration — fix n and rerun.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive why the SE of a mean is \(s/\sqrt{n}\) using the variance-addition rule from 1.3, and explain the practical arms race it implies: to halve the SE of the mean, how much more data do you need? To halve the noise of each measurement?


Hint

Write Var(x̄) = Var(Σxᵢ/n²) with independence, then take square roots twice.



Solution

With independent \(x_i\) of variance \(\sigma^2\): \(\text{Var}(\bar x) = \text{Var}\!\big(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum x_i\big) = \tfrac{1}{n^2}\,n\sigma^2 = \sigma^2/n\), so \(\text{SE} = \sigma/\sqrt n\) — square-root law. Halving the SE of the mean requires 4× the data; the SE of the mean is about precision of knowledge, and knowledge is expensive. Halving the noise of each measurement (σ) is an instrument/protocol question, not a statistics question — and it pays off in every subsequent analysis. First optimize measurement noise, then buy n.

Q2. Construct and demonstrate the “optional stopping” inflation: under a true null, run the peeking loop (test after every new pair, stop at p < 0.05 or n = 200). Estimate the realized Type I error. Compare to a fixed-n = 200 test. What does this say about A/B test dashboards that highlight “significance” daily?


Solution







Peeking inflates the false-positive rate from 5% to roughly 30–50% — the more checkpoints, the worse. Daily-looked-at dashboards with “significance” badges are exactly this experiment; the fixes are fixed horizons, sequential designs (alpha spending), or Bayesian monitoring with pre-agreed decision rules.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (inference × 0.5 Data splitting). Two models score 0.81 and 0.84 accuracy on the same 250-sample test set. Use the binomial SE machinery to judge whether they differ; then design the evaluation protocol (repeated splits or K-fold, paired comparison per fold) that would let you test the difference honestly. What makes the paired fold-wise comparison better than comparing two independent error bars?
C2 (inference × 2.4 Accuracy of the full model preview). Fit a simple linear regression to 30 noisy points; use the standard errors of slope and intercept (available from scipy.stats.linregress or a small manual computation) to build 95% CIs. Now re-fit on 300 points of the same process. How do the SEs scale, and why does “collect 10× more data” not always shrink practical uncertainty (name the two components: sampling error vs measurement/bias)?

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
7. Summary

Inference = sampling distributions: SE = s/√n; means shrink noise by √n — 4× data per 2× precision.
CI: range of parameter values the data can’t refute (at the chosen level); it’s the procedure that has 95% coverage, not your interval.
p-value = P(data this extreme | H₀); never P(H₀), never “chance of being right.”
Welch two-sample t is the default; paired designs need paired tests; ranks for non-normal data.
Power depends on effect, n, α, noise — underpowered studies “fail” without evidence of absence.
Multiple tests and optional stopping break the 5% guarantee; corrections and fixed protocols restore it.
When assumptions are shaky, resample the data itself: bootstraps and permutation tests — 1.5 Resampling intuition.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text: Every SE, t-test, CI, and F-test in Part 2 rests on assumptions: Linearity, Independence, Normality, Equal variance (of errors). Violations don’t just “break the model” abstractly — each one breaks a specific thing (usually inference, sometimes prediction), and each has a signature plot. This page makes the diagnostics reflexive.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
1. Basic Concept
The assumptions, what each buys, and what its violation costs:









Assumption
Formal statement
Needed for
Violation’s cost




Linearity
\(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0\)
unbiased β̂, meaningful coefficients
biased estimates; everything downstream is about the wrong model


Independence
errors uncorrelated across rows
valid SEs, tests, CIs
SEs wildly wrong (often underestimated); p-values meaningless


Normality
\(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\)
exact t/F reference distributions
only mild at large n (CLT); matters at small n and for prediction intervals


Equal variance
\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid X) = \sigma^2\)
SEs, exact tests
wrong SEs; OLS no longer most efficient



Key triage: prediction needs linearity (systematic structure captured); inference needs all four.
The diagnostic quartet, on one simulated misspecification each:






Reading guide: residuals-vs-fitted should show a structureless horizontal band (curvature ⇒ nonlinearity; funnel ⇒ heteroscedasticity); QQ should hug the diagonal (S-curves ⇒ heavy tails/skew); scale-location should be flat (trend ⇒ variance grows with the mean).

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
2. Concept Questions

Which assumption does a U-shaped residuals-vs-fitted plot violate, and what’s the two-column fix?
Your errors are independent but heteroscedastic. Are your β̂ biased? Your SEs? Name the one-line remedy that fixes the SEs.
Why is normality of errors the least worrying of the four at n = 500, but a genuine worry at n = 8?
Residuals are correlated in time order (a drifting instrument). Which printed numbers become lies, and does the slope estimate itself have to be wrong?
Why must diagnostics use residuals, never the raw y?



Answers


Linearity (systematic curvature left unmodeled). Fix: add \(x^2\) (or a spline basis) — two columns in, assumption restored; refit and re-diagnose (2.8).
β̂: unbiased (linearity intact — OLS is still the right center). SEs: wrong (they assume one σ). Remedy: heteroscedasticity-robust SEs — fit(cov_type="HC3") — or model the variance (GLM, 3.6).
At large n, the CLT makes t/F statistics approximately valid regardless of error shape (influence of each single point vanishes). At n = 8, one outlier is the distribution — the t-reference is fiction, CIs undercover, and no CLT rescue exists.
Every SE, t, p, CI — they all assume independent errors; positive serial correlation makes the effective sample size much smaller than n (n = 200 correlated readings ≈ far fewer independent ones). The slope estimate can remain unbiased but its precision claim is fantasy.
Raw y mixes signal f(x) with error: a “non-normal y” can come entirely from a skewed x-distribution with perfectly normal errors. Residuals isolate ε̂ — the only thing the assumptions speak about.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build diagnose(fit) — a function taking a statsmodels fit and returning a dict of verdicts: residual–fitted curvature score (correlation of residuals with fitted²), funnel score (Spearman |ρ| of |residuals| vs fitted), and normality p-value (Jarque–Bera). Run it on the four synthetic datasets from Section 1 and confirm it flags the right problem in each. What can a verdict dictionary not tell you that the plot can?


Solution







The scores separate the cases (curvature high only for “nonlinear”, funnel only for “hetero”, JB only for “heavy-tail”). What the dict can’t show: patterns a scalar compresses away — e.g. one wild leverage point inside a clean cloud scores fine numerically but is obvious in the plot, and residual-vs-fitted plots reveal which region of x misbehaves. Numbers triage; eyes diagnose.

Exercise 2. The repair menu, demonstrated: for each mis-specified fit below, apply the indicated fix and re-run the diagnostic that failed. (a) quadratic truth + linear model → add x²; (b) heteroscedastic → log-transform y (verify the funnel flattens) and compare HC3 SEs; (c) heavy-tailed → report the HC3 SE alongside classical and note which coefficients lose significance.


Solution







Each repair targets the assumption its diagnostic flagged — and the diagnostics after repair verify the fix rather than trusting it.

Exercise 3. Leverage vs outlier. Construct a 30-point dataset where one point has extreme x (high leverage, y consistent with the line) and another has extreme y at typical x (outlier, low leverage). Fit with and without each point; report slope changes. Which point is more dangerous to the slope? Then connect to Cook’s distance (get_influence().cooks_distance[0]) — which point does it flag?


Solution







Leverage without discrepant y barely moves the fit (it agrees with the line); an outlier at ordinary x drags the line locally but has limited reach. The nightmare is both at once (high leverage AND off-line) — Cook’s distance combines exactly those two ingredients, which is why it, not raw residual size, is the deletion diagnostic.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Diagnostics are for the training residuals, decisions are for the study — after repair (transform, robust SEs), refit and re-diagnose; one pass is not a workflow.
Testing normality with p-values on residuals (Shapiro/JB) is a weak tool: at small n it lacks power, at large n it flags trivial departures. The QQ plot, read as a shape, is more informative than any single p-value.
Independence is the assumption you cannot plot away — it comes from the design (time order, clustering, relatedness). Residual-vs-order plots and HAC/mixed models (the drill) manage known structure; unknown structure needs better data.
Heteroscedasticity has two fixes with different goals: robust SEs fix your uncertainty about β̂ (inference), WLS/GLM/log-transform fix efficiency and prediction intervals (the model). Pick by goal.
Leverage ≠ outlier ≠ influential (Exercise 3): check Cook’s distance (or DFFITS) rather than residual magnitude, especially before deleting anything — deletion is a modeling decision to report, not hygiene.
Don’t diagnose the test set: split integrity (0.5) applies — diagnostics belong to the modeling loop on training data; the test set is spent once.
Multicollinearity (2.5) is sometimes listed as a fifth assumption — it is not an assumption violation (the model can be true!) but a data condition that inflates SEs; diagnose with VIFs, not residual plots.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated validation script has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Normality of y ≠ normality of ε — y’s distribution is dominated by f(x)’s shape; the assumption concerns residuals only. (Here x is uniform, y is U-shaped — the test “fails” for a reason irrelevant to the model.)
Funnel signature is |residuals| vs fitted — correlation of signed residuals with y mostly re-detects the slope, not variance structure. Fix: Spearman(|resid|, fitted), or compare residual SD across fitted-value halves.
Inference on a visibly mis-specified model: the quadratic truth leaves systematic curvature; the classical p-value’s null distribution is wrong. Fix the specification first, then read tests.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the exact variance function of OLS residuals for a binary-style Bernoulli-mean response and show it is inherently heteroscedastic (\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x) = p(x)(1-p(x))\)), peaking at p = 0.5. Use this to explain why linear-probability models always show funnel diagnostics and why the logistic/GLM view (3.2, 3.6) resolves rather than repairs the problem.


Hint

If y ∈ {0,1} with mean p(x), write y = p(x) + ε and compute Var(ε|x).



Solution

y ∈ {0,1}, E[y|x] = p(x) ⇒ ε = y − p(x) takes values −p(x) and 1−p(x), so Var(ε|x) = p(x)(1−p(x)) — maximal (0.25) at p = 0.5, shrinking to 0 at the extremes. The linear-probability model therefore cannot satisfy equal-variance for any σ: the funnel is structural, baked into binary outcomes. No transform or robust SE “fixes” the model; the likelihood that matches the data-generating mechanism (Bernoulli with logit link — logistic regression) makes the variance function part of the model. This is the template for GLMs generally: choose the variance function from the response’s nature, then the mean model — the organizing idea of 3.6.

Q2. A dataset has grouped structure: 30 patients × 5 repeated measurements (150 rows), with patient-level random drift. (a) Demonstrate empirically that OLS SEs are too small (simulate 500 such datasets; compare the empirical SD of β̂ across simulations to the average classical SE). (b) Show that simply averaging each patient’s rows (n = 30) restores honest SEs at the cost of power, and (c) name the two standard remedies that keep all 150 rows (cluster-robust SEs; mixed models) — verify (a)’s lie and one remedy numerically.


Solution







The classical SE assumes 150 independent errors; with 30 patients’ shared drift, effective information ≈ 30-ish units, so the true SD of β̂ is several× the naive SE. Remedies keeping all rows: fit(cov_type="cluster") with patient IDs (fixes inference) and linear mixed models (random patient intercepts — models the structure, often more efficient). Averaging (b) is the transparent sanity check that exposes the lie.

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (assumptions × 2.8 Transforms × 3.6 GLMs preview). For count data generated as Poisson(\(e^{1+0.3x}\)): fit (a) OLS y ~ x, (b) OLS log y ~ x (adding 0.5 to dodge zeros), (c) a Poisson GLM with log link. Compare the coefficient estimates to the truth and run residual diagnostics on (a) and (b). Which problems are repairable by transforms and which are baked into the response’s nature? Write the sentence that motivates GLMs in one breath.
C2 (assumptions × 4.1 Generalization preview). Generate 300 datasets where the true model is quadratic but analysts fit lines. Split each dataset, record (a) the linear model’s test MSE and (b) its slope p-value. What fraction of datasets show a “highly significant” slope alongside clearly worse-than-quadratic test performance? What does this experiment say about the independence of inference validity from predictive adequacy — and why does Part 4’s out-of-sample discipline catch what diagnostics+tests can miss?

title: 2.10 Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
text:
7. Summary

L-I-N-E: linearity (unbiasedness), independence (valid SEs), normality (small-n exactness), equal variance (efficient, valid SEs).
Residuals — never raw y — are the diagnostic subject: residuals-vs-fitted, QQ, scale-location.
Each violation has a repair menu: +x²/splines, transforms, robust/HAC/cluster SEs, GLMs.
Influence ≠ leverage ≠ outlier; Cook’s distance is the deletion diagnostic.
Serial/grouped correlation silently multiplies your p-values’ confidence — design awareness, not plots, is the defense.
Diagnose → repair → re-diagnose; and never diagnose on the test set.
Part 2’s regression toolkit is complete. Part 3 turns to categorical responses, where the equal-variance assumption dies by definition — beginning with what classification is and how it’s scored: 3.1 Classification fundamentals.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text: Regression is the archetypal supervised-learning problem: given inputs \(X\), predict a quantitative response \(Y\) by estimating the underlying function \(f\) with a model \(\hat{f}\) trained on data. Every idea in this course — loss, generalization, bias–variance, tuning — can be seen first through this lens.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
1. Basic Concept
We assume data is generated as
\[Y = f(X) + \varepsilon, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0\]
where \(f\) is the systematic part (what we want to learn) and \(\varepsilon\) is irreducible error (measurement noise, unmeasured variables). We estimate \(\hat{f}\) from training data and measure quality by a loss; for regression, the standard is squared error, whose average on new data is the mean squared error:
\[\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \big(y_i - \hat{f}(x_i)\big)^2\]
Two distinct goals (ISL’s famous dichotomy — know which one you are doing):

Prediction: \(\hat{Y} = \hat{f}(X)\) for new \(X\) — interpretability optional, accuracy paramount.
Inference: which predictors matter, how, and with what uncertainty — a mis-specified-but-interpretable \(\hat f\) can be worse than useless even if it predicts well.







The regression task: from the dots alone, recover an approximation of the curve.
Reducible vs irreducible error. Even a perfect \(\hat f = f\) leaves MSE \(= \text{Var}(\varepsilon)\). Model improvements can only shrink the reducible part. This decomposes (proved via a completing-the-square argument in 4.4 Bias–variance):
\[\mathbb{E}\big[(Y - \hat{f}(X))^2\big] = \underbrace{\big(f(X) - \mathbb{E}\hat{f}(X)\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\text{Var}\big(\hat{f}(X)\big)}_{\text{variance}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\varepsilon)}_{\text{irreducible}}\]

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
2. Concept Questions

Your model’s test MSE is 2.31 and you estimate \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon) = 2.25\). How much room is left for model improvement?
Give one scenario where a highly interpretable but slightly-less-accurate model is the right choice, and one where it is not.
Is \(f\) observable? Is \(\hat f\)? What dataset do you need to evaluate \(\hat f\)?
Why is squared error the conventional loss? Name one situation where it is a poor match.
In \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\), what role does \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0\) play?



Answers


\(\text{MSE} \ge \text{Var}(\varepsilon)\) always, so the reducible gap is \(2.31 - 2.25 = 0.06\) — the model is within 6% of the noise floor. Chasing further gains with the same features is wasted effort; collect better features or accept the limit.
Yes: clinical dosing or credit decisions, where the model must be audited and each coefficient argued. Not: real-time image tagging, where nobody reads the model and only accuracy matters.
\(f\) is never observed; \(\hat f\) is computed from training data. To evaluate it honestly you need data not used in fitting (0.5 Data splitting) — evaluating on training data measures memorization.
Squared error is smooth, differentiable, corresponds to Gaussian-noise MLE (A.2 in the appendix), and treats errors symmetrically — but a single outlier contributes quadratically, so for heavy-tailed or gross-error settings, absolute loss or Huber loss fits better (and then “best” means a different model: median regression).
It makes \(\varepsilon\) noise, not bias: the mean of the error is zero at every \(X\), so all systematic structure lives in \(f\). If violated (e.g. calibration drift), the whole decomposition and OLS theory sit on sand.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Generate \(n = 100\) points from \(y = 1 + 2x + \varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, 4)\). Fit a line with np.polyfit, then report (a) training MSE, (b) fresh test MSE on 10,000 new points, (c) the theoretical noise floor \(\sigma^2\). Which of the two MSEs is closer to the floor, and why — what is the name of that gap?


Solution







Test MSE is closer to the floor but sits above it: training MSE is optimistically biased (the fit adapted to training noise — in-sample optimism), while test MSE = bias² + variance + σ² with small bias² and variance for a well-specified linear model. The excess over 4.0 is reducible error (here: estimation variance, shrinking with n).

Exercise 2. Prediction vs inference framing: you have hours_studied and exam_score data (generated below with a ceiling at 100). Fit a line, predict for hours = 5 and hours = 30, and explain which prediction is trustworthy, which is nonsense, and which word describes the failure (2.2 formalizes it).


Solution







hours = 5 is interpolation — inside the training range (0–12), trustworthy within uncertainty. hours = 30 is extrapolation — 2.5× beyond the observed range; the model silently reports ~175, physically impossible (score caps at 100). The word: extrapolation. Linear models extend the fitted pattern blindly; domain limits must be imposed by the analyst.

Exercise 3. Implement a regress_compare(y_true, y_pred_a, y_pred_b) helper returning MSE, RMSE, and MAE for two competing predictors, and use it to compare the mean-predictor vs the median-predictor on lognormal data. Which loss does each predictor win, and what does that tell you about the mean–median–loss triangle from 1.1?


Solution







The mean-predictor minimizes MSE and the median-predictor minimizes MAE — each wins its own column (check: mean-pred beats median-pred on MSE, median-pred beats mean-pred on MAE). “Which predictor is better” is ill-posed until you name the loss; this is the predictive face of the robustness trade-off from 1.1.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

In-sample (training) MSE is always optimistic — the model was chosen to make it small. The gap between training and test error is optimism, and estimating it is half of Part 4.
Extrapolation is silent: linear models return values outside any observed region with total confidence. Always compare prediction ranges against training ranges.
The noise floor is a feature of the data, not the model — before tuning hyperparameters for hours, estimate \(\sigma^2\) (replicates, domain knowledge, or residual variance from a saturated fit) and ask what’s left to gain (Concept Question 1).
MSE vs RMSE: RMSE is in y-units (reportable), MSE is differentiable-friendly and decomposable (math-friendly). Don’t average RMSEs across folds — average MSEs, then take the root.
y_true - y_pred sign conventions flip between residual-as-truth-minus-fit and fit-minus-truth; squared losses don’t care, but printed residual diagnostics do — know your library’s convention.
Prediction vs inference changes pre-processing rules: dropping a confounded-but-predictive variable is fine for pure prediction and fatal for inference (2.5).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation has three bugs. Run it, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Training MSE labeled “test”: polyfit minimized exactly this quantity — it is the in-sample error and cannot evidence generalization. Fix: split first, evaluate on untouched data.
Averaging RMSEs across folds is not the RMSE of anything (root is nonlinear). Fix: collect fold MSEs, average, then take the square root.
Silent extrapolation to x = 50 when training spanned 0–10. Fix: assert/flag predictions outside the training range, or constrain the domain.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that the function \(c \mapsto \frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - c)^2\) is minimized at \(c = \bar{y}\), and use this to explain why the mean-model’s training MSE equals the sample variance (drill above). What is the analogous statement for the median and MAE?


Hint

Differentiate in \(c\); you already proved the median version in 1.1 Q1.



Solution

\(\frac{d}{dc}\sum(y_i-c)^2 = -2\sum(y_i - c) = 0 \Rightarrow c = \bar y\); substituting back gives \(\frac{1}{n}\sum(y_i - \bar y)^2\), the (population-formula) sample variance. So the intercept-only least-squares model is the sample mean, and its in-sample MSE is the variance — which is exactly why \(R^2 = 1 - \text{RSS}/\text{TSS}\) compares every model against this null (2.4). The MAE analog: constant predictors are minimized by the median, with in-sample MAE = mean absolute deviation.

Q2. A colleague reports: “train MSE 0.9, test MSE 4.1, estimated σ² = 4.0 — my model is optimal, no more work needed.” Evaluate all three numbers as evidence. What additional split or sample-size information would sharpen the claim?


Solution

Test MSE 4.1 ≈ σ² = 4.0 suggests the reducible part is tiny — if the estimate is trustworthy. But (1) a single test split’s MSE has sampling noise (its own SE ≈ σ²·√(2/n_test) under normality — a 100-point test set gives ±0.56 at 1 SE, so 4.1 vs 4.0 is inconclusive); (2) train MSE 0.9 ≪ 4.0 shows substantial in-sample optimism, meaning the model has meaningful variance (complexity) — the test error could still be lowered by regularization or a simpler model family even if it’s near the floor on average; (3) σ² estimated how? If from training residuals of the same model, it inherits the model’s bias (under-specified models inflate apparent σ²). Sharpening: K-fold CV for a stable test estimate, a proper noise estimate (replicates), and n_train/n_test sizes to judge estimation variance.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (setup × 1.3 Probability). Simulate 500 repetitions of: draw n = 25 training points from the Exercise 1 process, fit the line, record test MSE. Plot the histogram of the 500 test MSEs. Relate its center and spread to (a) the noise floor, (b) the sampling variability of \(\hat\beta\) you will quantify in 2.3 — and predict qualitatively how the histogram changes at n = 200.
C2 (setup × 0.4 EDA). Generate data where \(f(x)\) is multiplicative (\(y = 3x\cdot e^{\varepsilon}\), constant relative noise). Show that regressing \(y\) on \(x\) produces the funnel-shaped residuals of 0.4 Q2, then regress \(\log y\) on \(\log x\) and verify the noise is additive there. State the modeling rule this suggests before any model is fit.

title: 2.1 The Regression Problem
text:
7. Summary

Regression = estimating \(f\) in \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\) from data; quality = MSE on data not used for fitting.
\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon)\) is the floor: model work shrinks only bias and variance, never the floor.
Prediction and inference are different games; they impose different rules on feature choice and reporting.
Training MSE is optimism in numbers; test MSE is the only honest currency (Part 4 prices it).
The mean-model is least squares’ null hypothesis; \(R^2\) is measured against it.
Extrapolation is silent failure — police the input range.
With the target defined, 2.2 Simple linear regression builds the first — and still most interpretable — estimator of \(f\).

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text: K-nearest-neighbors regression abandons functional form entirely: to predict a point, average the responses of its k closest training points. It is the prototype nonparametric method — flexible, assumption-light, and the cleanest lens on the flexibility–data trade before Part 4 formalizes it.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The algorithm for predicting at query point \(x_0\):

Compute the distance from \(x_0\) to every training point.
Take the \(k\) nearest.
Predict \(\hat{y} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in N_k(x_0)} y_i\) — their average (optionally distance-weighted).

One hyperparameter, \(k\), controls everything: \(k = 1\) reproduces the training data exactly (maximally flexible); \(k = n\) predicts the global mean everywhere (maximally rigid).






Distance weighting softens the steps without a new hyperparameter family:






Implement it by hand once — the whole method is a NumPy one-liner away:

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does KNN with k = n predict everywhere, and which model from Part 2 is it identical to?
Why does KNN require feature scaling, while OLS arguably doesn’t?
Your KNN has excellent training predictions and poor test predictions. Which end of the k dial are you on, and what single change is the first thing to try?
In 1-D with n = 100 and k = 10, roughly what fraction of the x-range does each neighborhood cover? What happens to that fraction as dimensions grow at fixed n and k?
KNN’s fitted curve is wiggly at k = 5 but smooth at k = 50 — restate that sentence in bias–variance language.



Answers


The global average \(\bar y\) at every query — identical to the intercept-only regression of 2.1/2.2 (whose training RSS = TSS). The two “models” at the extremes of flexibility are the same object.
KNN’s only notion of “near” is a distance metric in raw coordinates; a feature measured in thousands (gene counts) swamps one measured in fractions (GC content), so the neighborhood becomes 1-D along the biggest-scaled axis. OLS multiplies each feature by its own learned coefficient — scale is absorbed by β̂ (up to conditioning) — so it is scale-equivariant, not scale-blind.
Small k (overfitting: variance dominant). First change: increase k — then validate properly (4.6); scaling too if features aren’t comparable.
With uniformly spread points, k = 10 of 100 points spans ~10% of the range. In d dimensions with fixed n and k, the same 10 points live in a shell whose radius explodes (concentration of distances) — neighborhoods become huge relative to any one axis: the curse of dimensionality. KNN degrades toward the global mean unless n grows exponentially in d.
k = 5: low bias (local averages track the true curve) but high variance (each neighborhood’s few points swing the estimate) — wiggly. k = 50: high bias (averages over genuine structure) but low variance (many points stabilize it) — smooth. The dial trades one against the other, exactly the 4.4 decomposition.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement full 2-D KNN regression by hand (vectorized distances, argsort, averaging) and verify exact agreement with KNeighborsRegressor on 20 random queries with k = 7. Then switch to distance weighting in both and re-verify (weights ∝ 1/d, handling d = 0 by falling back to that point alone).


Solution







Agreement to float precision (sklearn’s weighting is the same 1/d scheme). Writing KNN once makes its failure modes concrete: ties, zero distances, and the cost — every query scans all n training points (no “fit” to speak of; the data is the model).

Exercise 2 — KNN vs OLS under two truths. Generate 100 training points under (a) a linear truth and (b) a wiggly sinusoidal truth (same noise). Fit OLS and KNN (k chosen by 5-fold CV over k = 1..30) to each; evaluate both on large fresh test sets. Report a 2×2 table of test MSEs. Which method wins under which truth, and what does that table say about “model choice” as a statement about the world?


Solution







Linear truth: OLS wins (KNN wastes effort estimating zero curvature). Wiggly truth: KNN wins (OLS’s bias dominates). Neither method is “better” — methods are hypotheses about structure; CV chooses the hypothesis the data supports. This 2×2 is the whole model-selection story in miniature (Part 4).

Exercise 3 — the curse, quantified. Generate data with signal only in the first 2 of d features (\(y = x_1 x_2 + \varepsilon\), remaining features pure noise, all scaled comparably). For d = 2, 5, 20, fit CV-tuned KNN and OLS on n = 300 and report test MSE on fresh data. Watch KNN degrade with d while OLS merely gets noisier — then explain in neighborhood-radius language.


Solution







In d = 20, “5 nearest neighbors” are no longer local — they’re scattered across a huge radius, so the average mixes unrelated points (bias explodes), while the useful signal lives in a 2-D slice KNN can’t isolate. OLS degrades gracefully: extra noise features only add mild variance to the coefficient estimates. Nonparametric flexibility is bought with locality, and locality is the first casualty of dimension — the reason Part 5’s regularization exists for wide data.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

No training phase, all query cost: prediction is O(n·d) per point (brute force); KD-trees/ball trees help in low d and stop helping in high d. “The model” is a lookup table — deploy size = training size.
Scaling is part of the model: put the scaler inside the pipeline so CV/tuning refit it per fold (0.5 leakage rule).
k = 1 on training data scores perfectly — reporting it is the canonical overfitting self-own; evaluate on held-out data only.
Ties and even k: with classification (Part 3) even k can produce vote ties; with regression ties are harmless (averages), but distance ties in argsort are resolved arbitrarily — reproducibility note for numeric features with many duplicates.
Weighted KNN interpolates between k-sensitivity and locality: weights="distance" reduces the discontinuity at neighborhood boundaries but doesn’t fix dimensionality.
KNN has no coefficients, no p-values, no global story — it predicts, it doesn’t explain. Using it where inference is the goal is a category error.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated KNN pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Tuning on training error selects k = 1 always (perfect memorization) — hyperparameters must be chosen by CV within the training set.
Unscaled features: distances are dominated by the 10,000-range column; the sin structure in feature 1 is invisible. Fix: StandardScaler in a pipeline.
k=1 training error as quality: by construction zero — it measures memory, not skill. Fix: report CV (tuning) and held-out test error.

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that uniform KNN regression is a linear smoother: \(\hat{y} = S y\) where \(S = D^{-1} W\) with \(W_{ij} = 1\{x_j \in N_k(x_i)\}\). What are the diagonal entries of \(S\) at k = 1, and how does that make the “training error = 0” fact inevitable? Relate the trace of S to an “effective degrees of freedom” and compute it for k = 1 and k = n.


Hint

Each fitted value is an average of a subset of the y’s — write the averaging weights as a matrix.



Solution

\(\hat y_i = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j \in N_k(i)} y_j\) ⇒ \(\hat{\mathbf y} = S\mathbf y\) with row i of S equal to 1/k on the k neighbor columns. At k = 1, each row has a single 1 (the point itself is its own neighbor), so S = I: \(\hat y_i = y_i\) exactly — zero training error by identity, and tr(S) = n = “n effective parameters” (maximal flexibility). At k = n, S has every entry 1/n: \(\hat y_i = \bar y\), tr(S) = 1 (one effective parameter, the mean). The smoother matrix’s trace interpolates between — the KNN analog of polynomial degree. (For OLS, S is the hat matrix H with tr(H) = p + 1 — same bookkeeping, which is how KNN and regression become comparable on a flexibility axis.)

Q2. KNN predictions are discontinuous at neighborhood boundaries; kernel smoothing (Part 6) fixes this by distance-decaying weights. Demonstrate the discontinuity: construct a 1-D dataset where shifting a query point by ε changes its prediction by a jump, measure the jump, and then show the same dataset under weights="distance" yields a continuous prediction path. Why might you nevertheless prefer uniform KNN?


Solution







Crossing the boundary where a far point swaps into the neighborhood changes the average by (y_in − y_out)/k — up to 2σ/k. Distance weighting fades the swap continuously. Uniform KNN is still preferred when: interpretability of “local average of the 5 most similar cases” matters, computation must be cheapest, or the distance scale itself is questionable (weights amplify metric artifacts). Smoothness is a virtue for curve display (Part 6’s smoothing splines are the refined endpoint of this line of thought).

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (KNN × 4.4 Bias–variance preview). Simulate 300 training sets (n = 60) from a known f; for each k in 1..40, fit KNN on every training set and evaluate on a fixed dense grid. Estimate bias² (mean prediction vs f)², variance (SD of predictions)², and total MSE per k; plot all three. Identify the k minimizing total MSE and verify the bias/variance crossover story — you will reuse this exact experimental design on the theory page.
C2 (KNN × 0.5 Splitting × 4.3 CV). Compare two k-selection strategies on 200 fresh simulations: (a) pick k by CV, report that CV value as the error estimate; (b) pick k by CV, then report a nested outer-CV estimate. How big is the optimism of (a), and does it grow with the number of candidate k values? (This prefigures the tuning trap of 4.6.)

title: 2.9 KNN Regression
text:
7. Summary

KNN predicts by local averaging; k is the single flexibility dial from memorization (k=1) to the mean-model (k=n).
Distances make scaling part of the model — scale inside a pipeline, never outside.
It is a linear smoother: tr(S) = effective df; k=1 is the identity map (zero training error, zero information).
The curse of dimensionality inflates neighborhood radius; nonparametric methods need exponentially more data in high d.
KNN vs OLS is bias-vs-flexibility: each wins under the truth it assumes; CV adjudicates.
No coefficients, no inference: KNN predicts, it doesn’t explain.
Before returning to model form, audit the regression machinery’s fine print: 2.10 Regression assumptions.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text: Multiple regression models \(Y\) as a linear function of several predictors at once — which is where regression earns its keep: adjusting for confounders, isolating each variable’s contribution, and predicting from combined structure. It also introduces the two new failure modes that dominate applied work: collinearity and confounding.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The model becomes a vector equation:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p + \varepsilon\]
Fitted by the same least-squares principle, now in \((p+1)\)-dimensional coefficient space: \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf y\) (requires the columns of the design matrix \(X\) to be linearly independent). The key interpretive discipline: \(\hat\beta_j\) is the expected change in \(Y\) per unit of \(X_j\) holding the other predictors fixed — an adjusted association, not a raw one.






Compare each coefficient’s simple (one-at-a-time) estimate with its multiple (adjusted) estimate — the discrepancy is confounding in action:






The F-statistic asks whether any predictor helps: \(H_0: \beta_1 = \cdots = \beta_p = 0\) against the mean-model:

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

In y ~ hours + practice, β̂_hours = 1.8. State the exact operational meaning of that number.
Why can R² rise while every individual p-value falls above 0.05? (Two predictors, strongly collinear, jointly informative.)
What breaks mathematically when two predictors are perfectly collinear (x2 = 2·x1)?
The F-test p = 0.2 but one predictor’s t-test p = 0.03. Possible? What’s going on?
You add a confounder and your key coefficient collapses toward zero. Two explanations — which is the happy one?



Answers


“Increasing study hours by 1 predicts +1.8 in y, for fixed practice problems” — the comparison is between two otherwise-identical subjects. It is not the raw effect of forcing extra hours on a real person (that would include the practice-hours they’d lose — an interaction/mediation issue).
Strongly collinear predictors share their explanatory work: together they lift R², individually neither looks “significant” because each coefficient’s SE is inflated by the redundancy (the model can’t decide which one gets the credit). The F-test (joint) is significant while the t-tests (each alone) are not — the classic collinearity signature.
\(X^\top X\) becomes singular — non-invertible, so \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) doesn’t exist and β̂ is not unique (infinitely many coefficient pairs give identical predictions). Computationally you get huge, unstable estimates; conceptually, the data cannot distinguish the two channels even in principle.
Yes — it’s exactly answer 2’s situation: joint F rejects (the pair helps) while each individual t fails (credit-splitting inflates both SEs). The F-test and the collection of t-tests answer different questions.

Happy: the confounder was inflating the coefficient; your predictor’s adjusted effect is genuinely smaller — this is learning. (b) Sad: the “confounder” is a mediator or a collider, or you adjusted away real signal (overadjustment). Which one depends on the causal structure, not on the regression output.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — the confounder lab. Simulate a classic confounded observational study: hidden z drives both x and y (x = 0.8z + noise, y = 2x + 1.5z + noise). Estimate the effect of x three ways: (a) simple regression, (b) multiple regression adjusting for z, (c) multiple regression adjusting for an irrelevant variable w. Which estimate recovers the truth, and what does (c) demonstrate?


Solution








inherits z’s influence through corr(x, z) and overshoots; (b) recovers 2.0 — adjustment works when the confounder is measured; (c) ≈ (a): adjusting for an unrelated variable changes nothing except a hair of precision. The entire value of multiple regression for inference is (b) — and its limit is that z must have been measured.


Exercise 2 — VIF by hand. Compute the variance inflation factor of each predictor in a 3-predictor model without variance_inflation_factor: regress each predictor on the others, take \(1/(1-R^2_j)\); verify against the library. Then state, numerically, what VIF = 10 does to SE(β̂_j) relative to an uncorrelated design.


Solution







VIF \(j\) = how many times larger \(\text{Var}(\hat\beta_j)\) is than it would be if predictor \(j\) were uncorrelated with the rest; SE inflates by √VIF. VIF = 10 is the common “serious” threshold, but the number to internalize is the mechanism: redundant predictors make individual coefficients unidentifiable in practice even while the model as a whole predicts fine (drill 2).

Exercise 3 — model building discipline. Using the statsmodels formula API on the built-in-style data below, run the classic workflow: (a) fit the full model y ~ x1 + x2 + x3; (b) use a partial F-test (anova_lm) to decide whether x3 earns its place; (c) refit without it if not. Report final coefficients with CIs, and give the one-sentence interpretation of each that a subject-matter reader could use.


Solution







Interpretation template: “holding x2 fixed, each additional unit of x1 predicts +1.2 (95% CI a to b) units of y; similarly for x2 with sign −0.7.” Note what the model doesn’t claim: causality (that needs design) and constancy of the x1 effect across x2 (that’s 2.7 Interaction’s question).

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Adjusted ≠ causal, still. Multiple regression blocks the measured confounders’ backdoors; unmeasured ones survive. The regression is honest; the causal claim needs the design.
Collinearity doesn’t hurt predictions, only interpretations: the fitted surface is stable even when individual coefficients seesaw (drill 2). Report predictions confidently, coefficients humbly.
The F-test tests the joint null — a significant F with null t-tests means collinearity; a null F with a “significant” t is a red flag (multiple testing or a fluke).
Adding predictors always weakly improves in-sample fit (the noise-collector theorem of 2.4); selection — which variables to keep — is a Part 5 topic, and must be judged out-of-sample.
Categorical predictors and interactions slot into this machinery as extra columns — dummy variables (2.6) and products (2.7) — so everything on this page applies to them unchanged.
Too many predictors relative to n (n ≲ 2p) makes OLS unstable or singular: the high-dimensional regime is a different sport (Part 5).
statsmodels vs sklearn: statsmodels gives inference (SEs, tests) and no penalty; sklearn gives prediction machinery and (in LinearRegression) no SEs. Choose by goal — the models are the same math.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Raw coefficients aren’t comparable — dosage spans 0–100 (per-mg effect) while age spans ~40 (per-year effect); the magnitude ranking mixes units with importance. Standardize (z-score) predictors if you need a “which moves y more per SD” statement.
age_celsius_like = 2×age is perfect collinearity — design matrix singular; statsmodels (via pinv) silently returns an arbitrary split, values differ run to run conceptually and SEs explode. Drop the duplicate column; check condition numbers/VIFs when columns might be linear combinations.
“CAUSES” from an observational fit — adjustment does not manufacture randomization. Report the adjusted association; causal language needs the design to back it.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show from \(\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) that if a predictor column is an exact linear combination of others, β̂ is not unique. Then explain why near-collinearity manifests as large coefficient variance: relate \(\text{Var}(\hat\beta) = \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\) to a small eigenvalue of \(X^\top X\) and to the VIF.


Hint

Rotating to the eigenbasis of \(X^\top X\): coefficients along near-null directions are determined by dividing by a tiny eigenvalue.



Solution

Exact collinearity: \(X = X_{-j} c\) for some \(c\) makes \(X\beta = X_{-j}(c\beta_j + \beta_{-j})\); infinitely many β produce identical fitted values, so \((X^\top X)\) is singular and the inverse mapping doesn’t exist. Near-collinearity: diagonalize \(X^\top X = Q\Lambda Q^\top\); the coefficient component along an eigenvector with tiny λ has variance \(\sigma^2/\lambda\) — enormous. The data constrain only the combination of predictors well, not each separately. The VIF is the pairwise-oriented version of the same geometry: \(\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)\) where \(R_j^2\) is how well x_j is explained by the rest; the two views coincide through \(\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\)’s diagonal. Predictions are unaffected because prediction happens in row space, where near-dependence costs little — only coefficient identification is damaged.

Q2. Construct a suppressor variable: a predictor with zero correlation with y that improves the multiple-regression fit and flips another coefficient’s sign. Explain the mechanism in terms of partialled variables: \(\hat\beta_1\) is the slope of y on x₁ after both are cleaned of x₂ — and cleaning can reveal structure that raw correlation hid.


Solution







Mechanism: x2 is a proxy for part of x1’s noise. Controlling for x2 subtracts that noise from x1 (partialling), unmasking x1’s true coefficient; x2 itself picks up −1 from the shared-noise path. The lesson generalizes: raw correlations are projections onto single axes, multiple-regression coefficients are projections after residualization — different objects that can differ in sign or magnitude. (This is also why “delete predictors with insignificant t-stats” is a bad automatic rule.)

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (multiple regression × 1.2 Relationships). Build the full Simpson’s paradox dataset (three groups, positive within-group slopes, negative pooled slope). Show (a) the pooled simple regression, (b) the multiple regression with group dummies (preview of 2.6 — you may hardcode the dummy columns), (c) slope-per-group via interaction (preview of 2.7). Verify (b) recovers the common within-group slope and explain why the dummy adjustment is the paradox’s resolution.
C2 (multiple regression × 0.5 Data splitting × 2.4). On n = 100, compare: in-sample R² of the 10-predictor model vs its 5-fold R², when only 3 predictors are real. Then repeat at n = 1000. Write the “sample size needed per predictor” folklore you observe, and connect it to why Part 5’s penalized methods exist.

title: 2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
text:
7. Summary

Multiple regression estimates each predictor’s association holding the others fixed — an adjusted, not raw, statement.
Adjustment fixes measured confounding; unmeasured confounding survives, and causality still needs design.
Collinearity damages coefficient identification (VIF, inflated SEs, F-vs-t splits) but not prediction quality.
The F-test judges the joint model; t-tests judge individual channels — collinearity decouples them.
In-sample fit creeps up with any added column; adjustment, penalties, and CV are the honest referees.
Design matters: spread predictors, measure the confounders, and mind n vs p.
All predictors so far are numeric; real data has groups and labels — next page: 2.6 Categorical predictors.

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text: Beyond individual coefficients, we judge the whole fit: how close are predictions to reality (RSE), and what fraction of the response’s variation does the model explain (\(R^2\))? Both have in-sample and out-of-sample versions — and the gap between them is the heart of model evaluation.

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
1. Basic Concept
Two classic in-sample summaries of a fit with \(p\) predictors and \(n\) observations:
\[\text{RSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{RSS}}{n - p - 1}} \quad\text{(typical prediction miss, in y-units)} \qquad R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}} \quad\text{(fraction of variance explained)}\]
where \(\text{RSS} = \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\) and \(\text{TSS} = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2\). RSE is absolute (compare to σ), \(R^2\) is relative (compare to the mean-model’s floor of 0 and the perfect fit’s ceiling of 1).






The variance-explained identity. With an intercept, total variation splits exactly:
\[\underbrace{\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{TSS}} = \underbrace{\sum (\hat y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{ESS, explained}} + \underbrace{\sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2}_{\text{RSS, unexplained}}\]






In-sample vs out-of-sample \(R^2\) — the same formula on test data, where it can go negative:

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
2. Concept Questions

Your model’s RSE is 3.2 and y ranges from 40 to 60. Is this a good model? What extra number do you need?
Why is in-sample \(R^2\) never decreased by adding a predictor — even a column of pure noise?
What does out-of-sample \(R^2 < 0\) mean, and which two models does it compare?
RSE divides by \(n - p - 1\) while RMSE divides by \(n\). Which is the honest estimate of σ, and when do they converge?
Your in-sample \(R^2 = 0.9\), test \(R^2 = 0.55\). Name the phenomenon and two standard remedies.



Answers


Depends on σ, not the range alone: RSE ≈ σ means you’re at the noise floor (2.1); RSE ≫ σ means real structure is unexplained. Range (40–60 → SD maybe ~4) gives context: missing 3.2 when the total SD is ~4 is barely better than predicting the mean. You need an estimate of σ (replicates, domain knowledge).
Least squares minimizes RSS, so RSS weakly decreases with any added column — noise columns get tiny fitted coefficients that shave a little RSS. \(R^2\)’s denominator doesn’t move. This monotone creep is why adjusted \(R^2\) (or CV) exists; more in 2.5/Part 5.
The test-set version compares your model against the test set’s own mean: \(R^2_{\text{test}} = 1 - \sum (y_{te} - \hat y_{te})^2 / \sum (y_{te} - \bar y_{te})^2\). Negative = your model predicts worse than just predicting the test mean — the model (fit elsewhere) has negative transfer to this distribution or is simply terrible.
RSE (df-corrected) estimates σ̂ unbiasedly; RMSE(n) is the descriptive in-sample miss. They converge as \(n \gg p\). Report RSE (or test RMSE), not in-sample RMSE, when the audience cares about truth.
Overfitting (in-sample optimism). Remedies: more data, regularization/simpler model (Part 5), and honest evaluation via CV (4.3).

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the cohort-style data below, fit y ~ x and compute in a single pass: RSS, TSS, ESS, in-sample R², RSE, and the df-corrected vs naive RMSE. Verify TSS = ESS + RSS to 8 decimals.


Solution







RSE slightly exceeds naive RMSE because the df correction charges the model for the parameters it fitted. With n = 60, p = 1 the difference is tiny; with n = 8, p = 4 it is violent — one more reason small-n fits deserve RSE, not RMSE.

Exercise 2. Demonstrate the noise-collector theorem: for the data above, append (a) a genuine second predictor correlated with the signal, (b) a pure-noise column, and (c) five pure-noise columns. Track in-sample R² and 5-fold out-of-sample R² across the four models. Which number climbs monotonically, and which tells the truth?


Solution







In-sample R² only ever rises — five noise columns “explain” variance that pure chance aligned with y. CV R² is flat or falling: out-of-sample, the noise coefficients are random directions that add variance, not signal. This single experiment is the entire business case for honest validation (Part 4) and for adjusted metrics/penalties (Part 5).

Exercise 3. Build regression_report(y_true, y_pred, k_params) returning a dict with MSE, RMSE, RSE (df-corrected), MAE, and out-of-sample R² computed against the given y’s mean. Test it in three regimes — good model, underfit model, extrapolated predictions — and write one sentence naming each regime from the numbers alone.


Solution







Reading: “good” has RSE ≈ 1 ≈ σ and healthy positive R²; “underfit” has R² ≈ 0 (no better than the mean); “extrapolated” has negative R² and an RMSE far above σ — the fit is fine but the domain is wrong. Numbers diagnose regimes only when you know what σ and R² = 0 mean.

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

\(R^2\) has no universal “good” — it compares against your response’s variance. In noisy biology, \(R^2 = 0.2\) can be a triumph; in controlled physics, 0.95 can be embarrassing. Context or σ, always.
Out-of-sample \(R^2\) is computed against the test mean — a different denominator than training. Two reported R²s with different test sets are not directly comparable; prefer test RMSE/MSE for comparisons.
Adjusted \(R^2\) charges each predictor with a df penalty: \(1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}\); it can decrease when noise columns join. It’s a better in-sample guide, but CV is the real referee.
Comparing \(R^2\) across transformed responses (\(y\) vs \(\log y\)) is invalid — different denominators, different games. Compare test RMSE on the same scale (back-transform with care: exponentiating log-predictions biases; use smearing or accept the median-level prediction).
RSE estimates σ only under correct specification — a quadratic truth fit with a line inflates σ̂ (2.10); your “noise floor” estimate absorbs your model’s bias.
\(R^2\) says nothing about calibration in y: predictions can be well-correlated with y yet systematically offset; plot ŷ vs y (0.4).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated model report has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Training R² as performance: always the best-case number; report CV or holdout.
R² across different response scales: R²(y) and R²(log y) have different denominators (variance of y vs of log y) — the comparison is meaningless. Compare RMSE on one common scale (here: predict log, exponentiate, RMSE in y-space).
Averaging RMSEs across folds: average fold MSEs, take the root (2.1).

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove TSS = ESS + RSS for least squares with an intercept, starting from \(y_i - \bar y = (\hat y_i - \bar y) + (y_i - \hat y_i)\) and showing the cross-term vanishes. Which first-order condition kills the cross-term, and why does the identity fail without an intercept (or with ridge, Part 5)?


Hint

Expand the sum of squares; the cross-term is \(\sum (\hat y_i - \bar y)(y_i - \hat y_i)\).



Solution

Expand: \(\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2 = \sum(\hat y_i - \bar y)^2 + \sum(y_i - \hat y_i)^2 + 2\sum(\hat y_i - \bar y)(y_i - \hat y_i)\). The cross-term equals \(2\,\hat{y}^\top (I - H) y\)-type expressions; concretely, OLS with intercept implies residuals are orthogonal to the fitted values: \(\sum \hat r_i \hat y_i = 0\) (follows from \(\sum \hat r_i = 0\) and \(\sum \hat r_i x_i = 0\), the two first-order conditions). Hence ESS \(= \sum \hat y_i^2 - n\bar y^2\) and TSS = ESS + RSS. Without an intercept the condition \(\sum \hat r_i = 0\) is lost, so fitted values need not be orthogonal to residuals — and \(R^2\) computed as 1 − RSS/TSS can even go negative in-sample. Regularized fits (ridge) similarly aren’t orthogonal projections, so the decomposition and the tidy R² story are OLS-with-intercept privileges.

Q2. Two models on the same n = 40 dataset: A has in-sample R² = 0.70 with 1 predictor; B has in-sample R² = 0.74 with 8 predictors. (a) Compute adjusted R² for both. (b) Then decide the winner by CV, implementing it. (c) At what sample size would B’s raw R² edge become credible? Answer with code and one paragraph.


Solution








Adjusted R² flips the ranking: B’s 8 parameters must earn their keep and don’t. (b) CV agrees — B adds nothing out-of-sample. (c) The noise columns’ spurious gains shrink like 7/n: only at n in the hundreds does B’s raw-R² edge fall below noise level. Lesson: raw in-sample R² gains of ≈ (extra predictors)/n are the signature of pure chance, not signal.

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (full-model accuracy × 1.5 Resampling). Bootstrap the in-sample R² of the Exercise 2 “x1 + noise5” model (resample rows, refit, recompute R²). Compare its bootstrap distribution to the CV R² distribution. One is centered high and narrow, the other low and honest — explain why resampling rows cannot cure in-sample optimism (the same rows that fit are the rows evaluated), and what this implies for what bootstrap CIs of performance statistics mean.
C2 (full-model accuracy × 2.3 Coefficient accuracy). Generate 200 datasets: n = 30, true slope 0.5, σ = 1. For each, record (a) p-value of the slope, (b) in-sample R², (c) test R² on a fresh 10,000-point set. Estimate: among datasets with p < 0.05, the median test R²; among p ≥ 0.05 likewise. What does this “significance ⇒ magnitude?” experiment teach about the relationship between the two accuracy lenses ([2.3] vs this page)?

title: 2.4 Accuracy of the Full Model
text:
7. Summary

RSE = absolute miss (in σ units); R² = relative variance explained; both in-sample summaries.
TSS = ESS + RSS exactly (with intercept OLS) — R² is the explained share.
In-sample R² rises with any added column; adjusted R² charges for parameters; CV tells the truth.
Out-of-sample R² uses the test mean as its yardstick and can be negative — worse than the mean.
Never compare R² across different response scales; compare same-scale RMSE.
RSE ≈ σ means you’ve hit the noise floor — stop tuning, get better data.
The fit’s average accuracy is settled; next page scales the model to many predictors — with collinearity and confounding in tow: 2.5 Multiple linear regression.

title: 6.3 Basis Functions — The General Recipe
text: Polynomials, steps, splines, sines — all are the same trick: expand \(x\) (or many x’s) into a dictionary of derived columns and run linear regression on the result. This page makes the recipe explicit, shows how the choice of dictionary is the choice of inductive bias, and builds the machinery the rest of Part 6 specializes.

title: 6.3 Basis Functions — The General Recipe
text:
1. Basic Concept
A basis is any set of transformations \(\phi_1(x), \ldots, \phi_K(x)\); the model is
\[\hat y = \sum_{k=1}^K \beta_k\, \phi_k(x)\]
— linear in β, arbitrarily rich in x. The whole game (2.8): the basis encodes what shapes are easy. Compare three dictionaries on one truth:






The Fourier basis nails this truth because sines are in its dictionary — the prior matches the world:

title: 6.3 Basis Functions — The General Recipe
text:
2. Concept Questions

In what sense is a basis a “prior” — and what does the polynomial dictionary believe about functions that Fourier does not?
Your basis has K = 500 columns, n = 200. Which two tools from Part 5 make this survivable, and which basis property do they exploit?
What distinguishes a good basis for a problem from a merely large one? Give one property of Fourier that makes it ideal for periodic data.
Why is basis expansion the standard gateway to kernel methods (8.4)?
Two bases span the same function space. What differs between fits on them — and what never differs?



Answers


The dictionary defines which functions are cheap (few active columns, low effective complexity) vs expensive. Polynomials believe functions are smooth globally and polynomial-ish; Fourier believes in periodicity and frequency sparsity — a truth that is “3 dictionary entries” in one basis is “30 parameters” in another (6.1’s Chebyshev moral at the space level).
Regularization (ridge/lasso on the basis — 5.2, 5.3) and CV to tune it; both exploit that only a few directions typically carry signal (sparsity/low effective rank).
Good = (i) truths of interest are sparse in it, (ii) columns are numerically well-behaved, (iii) evaluation is stable in the region you predict. Fourier is ideal for periodic data because a k-frequency function is exactly 2k columns — perfect sparsity — and the basis is orthogonal on uniform grids.
