Kernel methods compute inner products \(\langle\phi(x), \phi(x')\rangle\) without materializing φ: predictions depend on the basis only through these inner products, so infinite dictionaries (RBF) become computable — the basis view is literally the derivation.
Different fits (coefficients, conditioning, penalty behavior — 6.1 Exercise 2); identical fitted values whenever both bases span the same space and the fit is unpenalized full-rank OLS. Penalties break the equivalence (they’re basis-dependent) — that’s a feature, not a bug.

title: 6.3 Basis Functions — The General Recipe
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build a BasisPipeline comparison harness: for bases {poly-9, hinge at quantile knots, Fourier-K, 12 steps}, compute 5-fold CV MSE on (a) the periodic truth of Section 1, (b) a kinked truth (\(y = |x − 1| + \varepsilon\) on [0, 2]). Report the 4×2 table. State the matching rule between truth geometry and dictionary that the table reveals.


Solution







The table’s diagonal shines: Fourier dominates the periodic truth, hinge/step families dominate the kink (their dictionary contains the kink exactly; polynomials must approximate it globally). The rule: pick dictionaries whose cheap functions look like the phenomena you expect — and verify by CV, since priors can be wrong.

Exercise 2. Random Fourier features, scaled up: generate the RBF-like truth \(y = \exp(-(x-1)^2) + \varepsilon\) on [−2, 2]. Approximate it with RFF bases of size J ∈ {5, 20, 100, 500} (shared rng across sizes), reporting CV MSE for each. Show the MSE falling and stabilizing, then explain (a) what J controls, (b) why the same J would need to grow with input dimension (the connection to 2.9’s curse).


Solution







J is the resolution of the random frequency grid — bigger J covers finer structure (bias ↓) at more parameters (variance ↑), with the knee set by signal smoothness. In d dimensions, covering the frequency space requires J growing roughly exponentially in d — random features inherit the curse; their virtue is making any fixed J cheap for kernels, not escaping dimensionality.

Exercise 3. Basis diagnostics: for the hinge basis at 6 quantile knots on n = 150 uniform x, compute (a) the Gram matrix’s condition number, (b) column norms, (c) pairwise column correlations. Then recompute after standardizing columns. Which diagnostic predicts the OLS coefficient instability, and which predicts ridge’s unequal shrinkage? State the pre-flight checklist for any custom basis.


Solution







Hinge columns are cumulative — each contains the previous plus more — so pairwise correlations near 1 and a huge Gram condition number are inherent to the basis. That predicts (a) unstable raw OLS coefficients and (b) ridge shrinking later columns most (they carry the smallest marginal new information). Checklist: column norms comparable (else standardize), condition number sane (else orthogonalize/regularize), no near-duplicate columns (else lasso coin-flips — 5.3).

title: 6.3 Basis Functions — The General Recipe
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The dictionary IS the model: two practitioners with the same estimator but different bases built different inductive biases — document your basis like you’d document your features.
Unstandardized, unregularized custom bases are where numerical demons live: check norms, condition numbers, and column correlations before trusting coefficients (Exercise 3’s checklist).
Basis leakage: quantile knots, cutpoints, standardization constants — anything fitted to X must be fit per-fold (0.5); a transformer class (or SplineTransformer/KBinsDiscretizer in a pipeline) is the enforcement.
Penalties are basis-relative: ridge-on-Fourier is frequency-shrinkage; ridge-on-steps is neighbor-averaging. Same α, different prior — never port tuning across bases.
Interactions multiply: basis-expanding several features jointly explodes columns combinatorially (2.7, 5.6); additive-by-feature expansion (GAM-style, 6.7) is the controlled alternative.
Extrapolation behavior is basis-inherited: Fourier extrapolates periodically, steps flatline, polynomials explode, RFF oscillates. Choose the failure mode you can live with.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “feature engineering” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Knots from full data — quantile knots fitted on test rows leak (0.5). Fit the basis transformer on training folds only.
Stacked correlated bases — hinge + powers triple-count the same smoothness; coefficients become uninterpretable mixtures and penalties arbitrary. Choose one dictionary (or pre-declare the composite basis as the model).
Step basis extrapolation: all cumulative dummies saturate at 1 → the fit extrapolates as the last bin’s constant plus penalty residue; also indexing trickery in the print. Either clip to range or pick a basis whose extrapolation mode is intended.

title: 6.3 Basis Functions — The General Recipe
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that any linear smoother with hat matrix H = B(BᵀB)⁻¹Bᵀ satisfies tr(H) = K when B has full column rank K, and use it to compare the effective complexity of the Section 1 three fits at their CV-chosen sizes. Then explain why two different bases with equal tr(H) can still produce different test errors — what does tr(H) not capture?


Hint

Rank–trace identity for idempotent matrices; then think about which K directions each basis spends its budget on relative to the truth.



Solution

H = B(BᵀB)⁻¹Bᵀ is the orthogonal projector onto span(B): idempotent with rank = K, so tr(H) = K — every full-rank basis with K columns spends exactly K effective parameters, regardless of dictionary. Two K-column bases differ in where their K directions point: Fourier’s are frequency-localized, steps’ are space-localized; test error equals the truth’s energy outside the spanned subspace plus σ²·K/n-style variance — and the energy mismatch term is basis-dependent even at equal tr(H). Complexity is bookkeeping; alignment with the truth is the physics.

Q2. The null-space trick: construct a basis for x ∈ [0, 1] whose first two columns have (near-)zero variance across the data but capture all of y’s signal — e.g., \(\phi_1 = \sin(40\pi x)\) evaluated only… no; instead use a two-point signal: y depends on \(\mathbb{1}(x > 0.5)\) while your candidate basis is {x, x²} (polynomials). Quantify by simulation how many polynomial degrees are needed before CV MSE approaches the 1-column hinge-at-0.5 fit. What does this gap measure about basis mismatch, and how would you detect it in practice (you don’t know the truth)?


Hint

The kink at 0.5 is invisible to low-degree polynomials; watch the CV curve as d grows and compare against any local/step basis’s flat performance.



Solution







Polynomials only approach the hinge’s error around d ≈ 15–25 — they must synthesize a step from smooth monomials, spending dozens of parameters on what the hinge does with one. The gap between a flexible generic basis and a small aligned one is a basis-mismatch tax. In practice (truth unknown): fit several dictionary families at matched complexity, and treat a large CV gap between them as a discovery about the truth’s geometry (sharp jumps favor local dictionaries; periodicity favors Fourier; smoothness favors everything).

title: 6.3 Basis Functions — The General Recipe
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (bases × 5.3 lasso). Sparse dictionaries meet sparse penalties: on the Section 1 periodic truth, expand with a large Fourier dictionary (K = 20 frequencies) and fit LassoCV. Report the selected frequencies against the truth’s {1, 3} — does L1 recover frequency sparsity? Then repeat with 20 random frequencies (mismatched dictionary) and compare both CV MSE and selection interpretability. Write the sentence linking dictionary alignment to lasso’s recovery guarantees (5.3’s irrepresentable intuition).
C2 (bases × 7.1 trees preview × 9.2 PCA). Adaptive vs fixed vs rotated bases: fit (a) a depth-5 tree, (b) a 12-cutpoint step basis + OLS, (c) PCA-on-features + linear model, to a truth with diagonal structure (y depends on x₁ + x₂, both noisy). Compare CV MSE and interpret each fit’s structure. Trees find the diagonal split greedily; the step basis (axis-aligned) cannot; PCA rotates toward it — write the three-way trade-off (adaptivity vs stability vs interpretability) your table implies, as a preview of Parts 7 and 9.

title: 6.3 Basis Functions — The General Recipe
text:
7. Summary

Basis expansion is the universal recipe: pick a dictionary, regress linearly — the dictionary is the inductive bias.
Matched dictionaries (Fourier↔︎periodic, hinge↔︎kinks, steps↔︎regimes) buy order-of-magnitude efficiency; CV is the check.
Effective complexity is tr(H) = K — but alignment with the truth determines test error at equal K.
Diagnose any custom basis: column norms, Gram condition number, duplicate columns — then standardize/regularize.
RFF randomizes infinite dictionaries into finite ones; J trades bias for variance, dimension-for-dimension cursed.
Penalties and bases interact — ridge-on-Fourier is frequency shrinkage; document both.
The most useful local dictionary gets continuity constraints next: 6.4 Regression splines.

title: 6.5 Smoothing Splines
text:
Instead of choosing where to put knots, put a knot at every data point and pay a penalty for roughness. The smoothing spline minimizes
\[\sum_i (y_i - f(x_i))^2 + \lambda \int \big(f''(t)\big)^2 dt\]
— fit the data, but pay for wiggling. One continuous dial, λ, replaces knot placement: the elegance that makes this the statistician’s smoothing benchmark.

title: 6.5 Smoothing Splines
text:
1. Basic Concept
The minimizer of that criterion is a natural cubic spline with knots at every distinct x — the penalty converts “how many knots” into “how much bending,” λ trading fidelity against roughness: λ = 0 interpolates, λ = ∞ returns the least-squares straight line.






UnivariateSpline’s s is a sum-of-squared-residuals allowance (not λ itself): s ≈ nσ² targets the truth’s smoothness. Tune it by CV like any hyperparameter:

title: 6.5 Smoothing Splines
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must the roughness penalty use the second derivative (and not the first or the function itself)?
λ = 0 and λ = ∞: state both endpoints precisely, including what the penalty’s null space contributes.
UnivariateSpline’s s is not λ. What is the relationship, and why does the “s ≈ nσ²” heuristic make sense?
What are the effective degrees of freedom of a smoothing spline, and how does it behave as λ moves?
Your data has 80 points but you know the first 10 are from a different regime (batch artifact). Why is a single global λ the wrong tool, and what are the two standard remedies?



Answers


Penalizing f itself would fight the data’s level; f′ would penalize any slope (linear functions cost infinitely). f″ is the curvature — zero for lines (so lines are free, matching the penalty’s null space) and growing with wiggliness: it measures exactly what “too wiggly” means.
λ = 0: pure interpolation — the natural cubic spline through every point (n df). λ = ∞: f″ ≡ 0 forced → f is any straight line, fitted by least squares (2 df). The linear functions sit in the penalty’s null space and are never penalized.
The criterion balances RSS + λ·∫f″²; s bounds the RSS directly, so s ≈ n·(per-point noise variance) reproduces the λ that an honest bias–variance trade would pick when σ² is known — a heuristic starting point, still tuned by CV.
df(λ) = tr(S_λ) for the smoother matrix S_λ — a continuous quantity sliding from n (λ=0) to 2 (λ=∞). Report it alongside any smoothing-spline fit: it is the model’s honest complexity.
A global λ imposes one smoothness everywhere, but the artifact region needs different smoothness (or exclusion). Remedies: (a) regime-wise smoothing (fit separately / include regime covariates), (b) adaptive/variable-knot penalty methods — or fix the data issue upstream.

title: 6.5 Smoothing Splines
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The σ² connection, tested: for σ ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 1.0} (sinusoid, n = 80), tune the smoothing parameter by 5-fold CV and report the chosen s in units of nσ². Does the optimal s/n track σ²? Then verify the converse use: given a well-tuned fit, estimate σ² as RSS/n and check it against the truth.


Solution







The optimal s/n rises roughly with σ² — noisier data tolerates (needs) rougher-penalized, smoother fits. And the tuned fit’s residual variance estimates σ² (slightly downward — the smoother absorbs some noise, the classic df-shrunk underestimate; honest versions divide by n − df).

Exercise 2. Effective df, measured properly: compute the smoothing spline’s hat matrix by evaluating fits at fixed design points across many y-draws (S_λ via covariance: E[ŷ] = S_λ f under fixed x, σ known) — or, cheaply, via spl.get_coeffs() and the B-spline basis. Simpler and rigorous: for 300 draws of y = f + ε at the same x, estimate df(λ) = Σᵢ Cov(ŷᵢ, yᵢ)/σ². Trace df against λ for λ ∈ {small, medium, large} and confirm the slide from n toward 2.


Solution







The covariance estimator (the same E[df] = Σ Cov(ŷᵢ, yᵢ)/σ² used for the lasso in 5.3 Q2) slides smoothly from ≈ 50 down toward the linear model’s 2 — smoothing splines genuinely are a continuous family of models between interpolation and the mean line, with df as the honest complexity meter.

Exercise 3. Confidence bands for the smooth: using the bootstrap (resample rows, refit at fixed λ, percentile bands — 4.5), build 95% bands for the smoothing-spline fit at σ = 0.3. Overlay the pointwise band and check its coverage of the truth across x (fraction of grid points where truth lies inside). Then explain why these are confidence bands for the function and not prediction intervals for new points — and widen one into the other.


Solution







The bootstrap band quantifies uncertainty of the estimated curve (mean response) — narrow, and its truth-coverage is the confidence-band claim. New observations add irreducible σ on top: the widened band is the prediction interval, the same mean-vs-new-point distinction as 2.2 Exercise 3, now for curves.

title: 6.5 Smoothing Splines
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

s vs λ confusion is the top UnivariateSpline trap: s bounds residual mass (so it scales with n and σ²), while the textbook λ multiplies roughness. Translate once, tune by CV, document which you report.
Replicate x values: smoothing splines assume unique x; with repeated x, average within duplicates or use weights (w=) — UnivariateSpline errors otherwise.
Weights ≠ frequencies alone: w multiplies each residual’s penalty; for known heteroscedastic variances pass w = 1/σᵢ — the weighted criterion from 2.10’s repair menu.
Effective df should accompany every smooth: a fit is not described by λ/s alone; “smoothed with 7.3 df” is the reproducible statement.
Boundary behavior: natural-spline structure keeps tails linear, but tail estimates still lean on few points — report where the data actually supports the curve (or shade the bands honestly, Exercise 3).
Multivariate smoothing splines exist (thin-plate splines) but explode computationally with dimension — the practical route to multiple smooths is the additive model (6.7).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated smoother has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Duplicate x: the interpolating structure needs distinct abscissae. Average duplicates (with combined weight) or jitter-and-disclose.
s as λ: s = 0.001 allows almost no residual mass → near-interpolation regardless of n; the allowance must scale like nσ² (then be tuned).
Weights inverted: w multiplies each squared residual — high-variance points should get small w. Passing variances upweights the noisiest points, exactly backwards (2.10’s WLS logic).

title: 6.5 Smoothing Splines
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Sketch the variational argument: among all twice-differentiable f minimizing RSS + λ∫f″², argue the minimizer must be a natural cubic spline with knots at the data points. (Hint: on any interval between consecutive x’s, the Euler–Lagrange condition for the integrand (f″)² forces f⁗ = 0 — a cubic; the boundary conditions at the extreme data force naturality.) What role does λ play in this derivation, and what does the result not tell you (name one thing CV still must decide)?


Hint

Variation f → f + εg vanishing at data points; integrate ∫f″g″ by parts twice; the ODE f⁗ = 0 emerges between knots with natural boundary conditions f″ = f‴ = 0 at the ends.



Solution

Perturbing f by smooth g with g(xᵢ) = 0 and setting the first variation to zero: ∫(f″g″)dx + λ∑-terms give, after integrating by parts, ∫f⁗g = 0 for all admissible g between consecutive data — hence f⁗ ≡ 0 there (cubic pieces). At the boundary intervals the natural conditions f″ = f‴ = 0 appear (no outside data to balance them), making the spline natural. λ scales the trade-off inside this fixed family — the family itself is λ-independent. What the derivation doesn’t decide: σ² / the absolute scale of residual tolerance (where on the λ-path to stop) — that is CV’s job, exactly as in Exercise 1; theory gives the shape of the model space, validation picks the point in it.

Q2. Reinsch/GCV without GCV: the generalized cross-validation score is \(\text{GCV}(\lambda) = \frac{n\,\text{RSS}(\lambda)}{(n - \text{df}(\lambda))^2}\). Implement GCV for the smoothing spline using the covariance-based df estimator (Exercise 2, at reduced R for cost), sweep λ, and compare GCV-chosen s against 5-fold-CV-chosen s over 100 simulated datasets. Report agreement rates and which is cheaper. When do they disagree systematically (heteroscedastic data)?


Solution







GCV is the closed-form cousin of CV (cheaper: one fit per λ, not per fold) and typically lands within a notch of CV on homoscedastic data. Under heteroscedasticity GCV’s implicit uniform-σ assumption biases the choice — the same fragility as every analytic criterion vs the empirical honesty of cross-validation.

title: 6.5 Smoothing Splines
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (smoothing × 5.2 ridge × 6.4). Prove-by-construction the identity: a smoothing spline is ridge regression on a rich spline basis (fine knot grid) with a penalty tailored to the basis. Implement ridge-on-SplineTransformer (many knots), tune α by CV, and compare against UnivariateSpline tuned by CV: fitted curves, effective df, CV MSE. Where they differ, explain via the penalty’s form (coefficient shrinkage vs derivative integral) and boundary handling.
C2 (smoothing × 3.6 GLM × 6.7 preview). Smoothing for non-Gaussian responses: binary outcome with smooth logit truth logit(p(x)) = sin(2πx). Fit (a) a Gaussian-error smoothing spline to the 0/1 y (wrong likelihood), (b) a binned-response spline (bin x into 15 cells, smooth the empirical logits), (c) plain logistic with polynomial basis. Compare CV log-loss. This ad-hoc tour is exactly the problem generalized additive logistic models solve properly — write down what (b) gets right and where it still falls short of a true GAM.

title: 6.5 Smoothing Splines
text:
7. Summary

Smoothing splines: knots everywhere, roughness penalized — knot placement becomes one continuous dial.
The minimizer is a natural cubic spline through the data; λ slides df continuously from n to 2.
s (residual allowance ≈ nσ²) vs λ (roughness weight): know which your library exposes; tune by CV either way.
Report effective df — the honest complexity of a smooth.
Bands: bootstrap for the function; add σ for new points.
GCV is the cheap analytic dial; heteroscedasticity breaks it — CV stays the referee.
One smooth of one variable is a toy; real data has many x’s: additive models — 6.7 GAMs — after the local-regression way station: 6.6 Local regression.

title: 6.1 Polynomial Regression — Beyond the Line
text: Part 2’s line was a choice, not a law. Polynomial regression keeps the entire linear-model machinery — closed forms, t-tests, pipelines — but lets the fitted curve bend by replacing \(x\) with powers of itself. This page is where “linear in the parameters, flexible in the features” becomes a design principle (2.8 revisited with modeling intent).

title: 6.1 Polynomial Regression — Beyond the Line
text:
1. Basic Concept
Replace \(x\) with the basis \(\phi(x) = (x, x^2, \ldots, x^d)\) and fit least squares on the expanded design. The model is still \(\hat y = \phi(x)^\top\beta\) — linear in \(\beta\), polynomial in \(x\). Degree \(d\) controls flexibility; everything from 4.1’s U-curve applies with \(d\) as the dial.






A cleaner estimator than raw polyfit: PolynomialFeatures + standardization inside a pipeline (raw powers of large \(x\) are numerically poisonous — 2.8):

title: 6.1 Polynomial Regression — Beyond the Line
text:
2. Concept Questions

Your true function is cubic but you fit degree 7 with n = 20. Name the disease, its symptom in the coefficients, and its cure.
Why does standardizing x before squaring change anything — isn’t \(x^2\) the same information as \((x/2)^2\) up to scaling?
A polynomial fit looks perfect on [0, 1] and predicts −40 at x = 1.1. Which basis property makes polynomials uniquely catastrophic extrapolators?
Orthogonal polynomials: what numerical problem do they solve, and do they change the fitted curve?
You have two candidate degrees with CV MSE 8.1 and 8.3. Which two considerations decide, and what rule from 4.6 applies?



Answers


Overfitting (variance-dominated). Symptom: huge, alternating-sign high-order coefficients (they encode noise wiggles). Cure: lower the degree, or regularize the expanded features (ridge on the basis — 5.2), or collect data.
The fit is invariant (same column space) but the penalty and numerics are not: with raw scales, \(x^2\)’s column norm dwarfs \(x\)’s, so ridge shrinks them unequally and the normal equations are ill-conditioned. Standardization makes each basis column a fair citizen.
Polynomials are global bases: a coefficient fitted to wiggle inside [0, 1] must express that wiggle via powers that explode outside it — the curve has nowhere to go but vertical. Local bases (steps, splines — 6.2, 6.4) keep misbehavior local.
Ill-conditioning of the Vandermonde matrix \([1, x, x^2, \ldots]\): near-collinear columns make coefficient estimates numerically unstable. Orthogonal polynomials decorrelate the basis — same fitted values, far more stable coefficients.
The gap is within noise (check the SE of the CV difference); prefer the simpler degree unless the extra flexibility earns its keep — the one-standard-error rule, plus interpretation cost.

title: 6.1 Polynomial Regression — Beyond the Line
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Model-selection theater, then honesty: for the quartic truth \(y = 1 - 2x + 0.5x^2 - 0.1x^3 + 0.01x^4 + \varepsilon\) (σ = 2, n = 50), fit degrees 1–10 and report (a) training MSE, (b) 5-fold CV MSE, (c) true test MSE on 20,000 fresh points. Identify the CV-argmin and the true-argmin; how often (over 200 data draws) does CV pick the exactly-optimal degree ±1?


Solution







CV lands within ±1 of the true degree in most draws, and its chosen model’s true error is statistically indistinguishable from the oracle’s — degree selection is one of the friendlier hyperparameters. The residual gap between the two rows is selection noise, priced and familiar (4.6).

Exercise 2. The conditioning autopsy: fit degree 8 on x ∈ [0, 100] with (a) raw powers via np.polyfit, (b) standardized powers via the pipeline. Compare the leading coefficients and the fitted values’ SD across 100 bootstrap resamples of the training data. Which parameterization’s coefficients are reproducible, and what does that mean for reporting “the x³ effect”?


Solution







The raw parameterization’s leading coefficient wobbles by orders of magnitude — collinearity of powers makes each coefficient an unstable mixture of all others. The standardized basis (or orthogonal polynomials) spreads the work evenly, so coefficients — and any story attached to them — become reportable. Fitted values were never in danger; your interpretations were.

Exercise 3. Extrapolation guard-rail: build a PolyModel class wrapping the pipeline with (a) predict(x_new) that refuses (with an informative error) points outside the training range, (b) a slope(x) method returning the derivative \(f'(x) = \sum k c_k x^{k-1}\) evaluated via the fitted coefficients. Fit on the sinusoid, verify the derivative against np.gradient at three points, and demonstrate the refusal at x beyond range.


Solution







The class turns two recurring lessons — range-policing (2.1) and derivative-style interpretation — into reusable machinery. The slope check against a numerical derivative validates the standardized-coefficient chain rule.

title: 6.1 Polynomial Regression — Beyond the Line
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

**np.polyfit‘s coefficient order** (highest first) versus PolynomialFeatures’ (lowest first) — mixing the two conventions is a classic silent bug.
include_bias=True adds the constant column: pair it with LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False) or you get a redundant intercept (harmless with OLS, wasteful with penalized fits).
Extrapolation is the polynomial’s worst subject — global basis, exploding tails; guard-rails or local bases (6.4).
Degree ≠ complexity exactly: a degree-9 fit with ridge (α tuned) can behave like a degree-3 fit — flexibility is jointly set by basis size and penalty (5.2).
Weights: noisy heteroscedastic data wants weighted least squares on the basis (LinearRegression can’t; use sample-weighted estimators) — otherwise high-variance regions dictate the global curve.
Numerical creep: degrees above ~15 on raw scales produce garbage even when predictions look fine — check np.linalg.cond of the design, or just standardize/orthogonalize.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated fit has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Bias column + intercept double-counts the constant: OLS survives (pseudo-inverse absorbs it), but ridge would split the intercept across both — and the coefficient table now lies about which constant is which.
pf.fit_transform(X_te) re-fits the transformer on test data — a different expansion than training used. Always transform, never fit_transform, on non-training data (or just use the pipeline).
1-D x into cross_val_score — sklearn expects 2-D features; the explicit reshape (or pipeline over the original frame) is required.

title: 6.1 Polynomial Regression — Beyond the Line
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that fitting degree-d polynomials by OLS is a linear smoother: \(\hat{y} = H^{(d)} y\) where \(H^{(d)}\) is the hat matrix of the expanded design. Use this to (a) explain why training error strictly decreases in d, and (b) compute the effective degrees of freedom as tr(\(H^{(d)}\)) = d + 1 — verifying both claims numerically on a small dataset.


Hint

OLS fitted values are projections; nested column spaces give nested projections; trace of a projection = its rank.



Solution

\(\hat y = X_d (X_d^\top X_d)^{-1} X_d^\top y \equiv H^{(d)} y\); the column spaces are nested \(span(X_1) \subset span(X_2) \subset \cdots\), and projections onto superspaces can only shrink residuals — training error is monotone down. \(H^{(d)}\) is idempotent of rank d + 1, so tr = d + 1 — the effective df that Cp charges for (5.1Cp — same identity).






This linear-smootherness is what lets polynomials, splines, and KNN be compared on one complexity axis (2.9 Q1) — the tr(H) bookkeeping runs the whole show.

Q2. Chebyshev rebalancing: for x ∈ [−1, 1], compare the condition number of the Vandermonde matrix under (a) raw monomials \(x^k\) and (b) Chebyshev polynomials \(T_k(x)\), for d = 10. Then verify that OLS on the Chebyshev basis yields identical fitted values (up to tolerance) with far better-conditioned normal equations. What does this imply about the information content of the two bases — and about which part of the analysis (fit vs interpretation) benefits?


Hint

Both bases span the same degree-d polynomial space; conditioning differs, span doesn’t.



Solution







The condition number improves by orders of magnitude while fitted values coincide to float precision: the span is identical, only the coordinate system changed. Interpretation benefits most — coefficients on Chebyshev basis functions are stable, meaningful amplitudes of oscillation, whereas raw-monomial coefficients are numerically arbitrary mixtures. Same moral as 2.8’s standardization, taken to its mathematical conclusion.

title: 6.1 Polynomial Regression — Beyond the Line
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (polynomials × 4.4 decomposition). Produce the degree-wise bias²/variance decomposition (300 training sets, n = 30, sinusoid truth) twice: once for raw polyfit, once for ridge-on-standardized-basis with α chosen per training set by CV. Overlay both total-MSE curves. Where does regularization move the optimal flexibility, and what does that say about degree as a hyperparameter when a penalty is present?
C2 (polynomials × 5.6 high dimensions). Multiply the basis: with p = 8 raw features expanded to all degree-2 monomials and interactions, you have p′ = 44 columns (count them via PolynomialFeatures). For n ∈ {30, 100, 400}: fit (a) OLS on the expanded basis, (b) lasso on the expanded basis, reporting nested test MSE and support size (counting interaction terms). At which n does the interaction term \(x_1 x_2\) (built into the truth with coefficient 2) get selected reliably? What does this say about interaction hunting as a function of sample size — extending 2.7 C2?

title: 6.1 Polynomial Regression — Beyond the Line
text:
7. Summary

Polynomials = linear models on a power basis: full inference machinery, one flexibility dial (degree).
Train error always falls with degree; test error U-curves; CV chooses — and usually lands near the truth.
Standardize (or orthogonalize) the basis: conditioning protects coefficients, penalties, and your interpretations.
Global bases extrapolate catastrophically; police the range or move to local bases.
tr(H) = d + 1: polynomials, splines, and KNN speak the same effective-df language.
Ridge-on-basis decouples flexibility from degree — the penalty is the modern dial.
The most local basis of all: cut x into intervals and fit constants — 6.2 Step functions.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text: BART keeps boosting’s “sum of small trees” architecture but replaces sequential greedy fitting with a Bayesian posterior: a prior over tree shapes and leaf values, MCMC sampling over the space of tree ensembles, and — the payoff — honest uncertainty intervals on predictions from a nonlinear, interaction-friendly model. No BART library runs in Pyodide, so this page builds the Bayesian machinery the model rests on, hands you the concepts, and flags where the production implementations live.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
1. Basic Concept
The BART model:
\[y = \sum_{m=1}^M g(x; T_m, M_m) + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]
— M small trees (T = shape, M = leaf values) with a regularizing prior: shallow trees favored (deep splits penalized), leaf values shrunk toward 0, σ² given its own prior. Fitting = MCMC over (T₁…T_M, M₁…M_M, σ²), sampling tree grows/prunes/swaps and leaf draws.
The Bayesian core you can run here: a conjugate Bayesian linear model — prior + likelihood → posterior → credible intervals. This is the identical inference object BART produces, just with a linear basis instead of trees:






Posterior sampling — the MCMC connection — via direct draws from that conjugate posterior:

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does BART’s tree-shape prior (prefer shallow, shrink leaves) accomplish, in regularization language (5.2)?
Contrast fitting: boosting finds one greedy sequential ensemble; BART samples many ensembles from a posterior. What does the second buy at prediction time?
Why is BART’s uncertainty interval meaningfully different from a bootstrap band (4.5) — even though both are intervals around predictions?
The sum-of-trees form with M small trees resembles boosting’s Σνhₘ. What replaces boosting’s learning rate and residual chasing?
Name two practical reasons BART remains niche despite its uncertainty output — and the niches where it wins anyway.



Answers


A prior favoring shallow trees and shrunken leaves is L0-on-structure + shrinkage-on-values simultaneously: the model starts regularized, and the data moves it only as far as evidence pushes — the Bayesian rendering of “keep trees weak” (boosting enforces it by construction via depth limits and ν).
A posterior predictive distribution: every future prediction can carry its own interval, and new-observation uncertainty is separate from fit uncertainty (the σ² layer). Boosting gives a point prediction; intervals must be bolted on (4.5-style), with weaker guarantees.
Bootstrap bands reflect resampling variability of a procedure, assuming the model; posterior credible bands reflect conditional uncertainty given the prior and likelihood — they can differ when the prior matters, and they natively separate parameter-uncertainty from observation-noise layers.
The prior plays ν’s role (shallow+shrunk = small steps are likely a priori), and MCMC’s grow/prune moves play residual-chasing: the chain revises trees wherever the current ensemble’s residuals are largest, stochastically rather than greedily.

MCMC compute: thousands of tree-ensemble draws vs one greedy pass — slow on big n/p; (b) implementation maturity/deployment tooling (boosting libraries are industrial; BART’s are research-grade, R-centric). It wins where uncertainty-qualified predictions are the product — clinical dosing, causal-effect estimation with interactions, small-n scientific inference.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Full conjugate workflow: given X (n = 50, 3 features incl. intercept), y, prior N(0, τ²I) with τ = 2, σ² = 1: compute (a) posterior mean and covariance, (b) 95% credible intervals for each β, (c) the posterior probability that β₂ > 0 (via draws). Compare the interval for β₂ against the frequentist OLS CI (statsmodels). Where do they differ, and which prior choice drove the difference?


Solution







With τ = 2 the prior is weak — Bayesian and OLS intervals nearly coincide (the data dominates). Shrink τ and the Bayesian intervals contract toward 0 by assumption, while OLS stays data-only; the difference between the two outputs is exactly the prior’s influence — know what you chose. The P(β₂ > 0) statement is the Bayesian bonus: direct probability claims about parameters, no null-hypothesis machinery.

Exercise 2. The sum-of-trees prior, simulated: implement a toy “BART-lite”: fit B = 200 tiny ensembles where each ensemble is 5 depth-2 trees fit on bootstrap data with leaf values shrunk by a factor κ ∈ {0.2, 1.0}; predict as the average. Measure test MSE and the SD of predictions across ensembles at fixed points, for both κ. Shrinkage (small κ) is the prior doing regularization — verify its variance/accuracy signature and connect it to boosting’s learning rate ν (7.5).


Solution







κ = 0.2 (strong prior shrinkage) tames each tree’s contribution — lower variance across ensembles, often better test MSE on noisy truths; κ = 1 lets each tree speak at full volume (variance up). This is ν-as-prior: BART’s leaf-shrinkage prior plays precisely boosting’s learning-rate role, but inside a sampling framework where the “right” amount is informed by the data through σ² and the marginal likelihood.

Exercise 3. Uncertainty layers, separated: using the conjugate model, produce three intervals for a new observation at a test point x₀: (a) the posterior interval of the mean f(x₀), (b) the predictive interval of a new y, (c) the OLS-style interval ignoring parameter uncertainty (just ±1.96σ̂). Plot all three and compute coverage of each over 500 simulated datasets. Which layer does each interval answer — and which would you show a patient (a new individual) vs a review board (the model’s claim)?


Solution








answers “where is the function here,” (b) “where will this patient land,” (c) pretends the fit is certain — it undercovers whenever parameter uncertainty is real (small n). BART’s headline feature is delivering (a) and (b) for nonlinear tree ensembles — the same layering, no conjugate shortcut required.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Priors are design decisions: BART’s defaults (depth-limiting probabilities, β-shrinkage quantiles, σ prior) encode “sparse, weak interactions” — check them against your problem instead of outsourcing the choice to the library default.
MCMC diagnostics are mandatory: run multiple chains, check mixing of σ² and tree counts; BART’s credible intervals are only as trustworthy as the chain’s convergence — the Bayesian tax for the uncertainty feature.
BART is not fast: minutes on n = 1,000 where boosting takes milliseconds; parallel chains help but the algorithm is inherently sequential. For speed-uncertainty trade-offs, quantile-regression forests are the cheaper cousin.
Variable selection leanings: BART underuses weak features under strong priors (like all shrinkage) — presence in the model ≠ importance; use inclusion frequencies across MCMC draws as the diagnostic.
Causal inference is BART’s flagship niche (treatment-effect estimation with exchangeability assumptions): the posterior over heterogeneous effects is exactly what applied micro is after — but the causal validity lives in the design, as always (2.2 Q2).
Binary/count responses: BART extends via probit/logit link versions (MCMC gets latent-variable steps) — the additive-GAM-to-GLM move (6.7) replayed in Bayesian key.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “Bayesian model” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Precision/convention flip: the conjugate posterior is (XᵀX/σ² + I/τ²)⁻¹ — multiplying by τ² (instead of dividing) strengthens the prior as τ² grows, backwards. Get the precision algebra right; it’s the entire estimator.
Posterior SD ≠ rescaled mean: it’s √diag(posterior covariance). Hand-waving SDs make every downstream interval fiction.
Predictive intervals need σ²: new observations add the noise layer — parameter uncertainty alone undercovers new points (Exercise 3’s layer separation).

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the conjugate update: prior β ~ N(0, τ²I), likelihood y ~ N(Xβ, σ²I) ⇒ posterior N(μₙ, Σₙ) with Σₙ = (XᵀX/σ² + I/τ²)⁻¹, μₙ = ΣₙXᵀy/σ². Verify that as τ² → ∞ you recover OLS and as τ² → 0 you recover β = 0 — the two endpoints matching ridge’s λ → 0/∞ (5.2 Q2). Then compute the posterior probability P(β_j > 0) via draws and show it equals Φ(μⱼ/√Σⱼⱼ) — no simulation needed.


Hint

Complete the square on β in the joint density; Gaussian arithmetic; the marginal of a Gaussian is Gaussian.



Solution

Joint ∝ exp(−‖y − Xβ‖²/2σ² − ‖β‖²/2τ²); expanding in β and completing the square gives precision Λ = XᵀX/σ² + I/τ² and mean μₙ = Λ⁻¹Xᵀy/σ². Limits: τ² → ∞ removes the prior term → Λ = XᵀX/σ², μₙ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy = OLS; τ² → 0 forces μₙ → 0. Since marginals of Gaussians are Gaussian, β_j | y ~ N(μⱼ, Σⱼⱼ), so P(β_j > 0) = Φ(μⱼ/√Σⱼⱼ):






The closed form is the sampling-based one at infinite draws — Bayesian inference for conjugate models is exactly computed, and BART’s MCMC exists because tree ensembles forfeit conjugacy, not because sampling is inherently superior.

Q2. BART vs boosting uncertainty, head-to-head design: on 200 simulated datasets (n = 60, smooth truth), compare three interval producers — (a) boosted trees + residual ± band, (b) bootstrap-banded forest (4.5), (c) the conjugate Bayesian interval on the correct basis — by nominal-95% coverage of the truth and of new points. Which achieves nominal coverage for the function, which for observations, and what structural feature does (c) have that (a)/(b) must borrow? Write the practical guidance you’d give before someone reaches for bands.


Solution







The correctly-specified Bayesian interval hits nominal coverage for both layers because it carries the two uncertainty sources separately. Boosted trees ± residual band covers observations roughly but has no parameter-uncertainty layer (function claims undercoverage); bootstrap bands estimate procedure variability (often near-nominal for the function on stable learners) but can’t separate the layers without adding σ̂. Guidance: decide which claim you’re making first — function vs new point — then pick the machinery that natively states it; and remember (c)’s advantage came from knowing the basis, i.e., from model correctness, which no interval machinery can grant.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (BART × 7.5 boosting × 4.5 bootstrap). The uncertainty triathlon on one dataset: point predictions from boosting, bootstrap bands from a forest, and (on the correct linear basis, as BART-stand-in) posterior bands. Compare widths and calibration of the three intervals for both functions and new points over 200 simulations. Write the decision tree a practitioner should follow: “if you need ___ and can assume , use ” — three branches, honestly conditioned.
C2 (BART × 2.5 confounding × 12.x stub). Treatment effects, BART’s home turf: simulate an observational study with a binary treatment, confounders, and heterogeneous effects (effect varies with x₁). Using the conjugate Bayesian machinery on a basis that includes treatment × covariate terms, compute the posterior distribution of the effect at several x₁ values. Report the effect curve with credible bands, and state precisely what design assumption (unconfoundedness) the bands still require — the Bayesian machinery quantifies uncertainty, not identification.

title: 7.7 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
text:
7. Summary

BART = boosting’s sum-of-small-trees, fitted by MCMC under a regularizing prior — the Bayesian answer to nonlinear tabular regression.
The prize: posterior predictive distributions — function-uncertainty and new-observation uncertainty as separate, honest layers.
The conjugate Bayesian model is the runnable core: same updates, same credible intervals, closed-form (drills).
Priors replace boosting’s ν; MCMC replaces greedy residual-chasing; tree-depth preferences replace depth caps.
Costs: MCMC compute, implementation maturity, and mandatory chain diagnostics.
Niche of strength: small-to-mid n, uncertainty-qualified predictions, causal effect estimation — not the 100M-row leaderboard.
Part 7 closes with the full arc: one greedy algorithm → ensembles → sequential → Bayesian. Next, geometry takes the stage: 8.1 Geometry essentials.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text: A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, splitting the data into ever-purer regions. It is the first model in this course that learns its own basis functions — the adaptive step functions of 6.2, with cutpoints chosen by greedy RSS/impurity reduction — and the atom from which the most successful tabular learners (Parts 7.3–7.6) are built.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
1. Basic Concept
Growing a tree = recursive binary splitting: at each node, search every feature × every cutpoint for the split that most reduces impurity — RSS for regression, Gini or cross-entropy for classification:
\[\text{Gini}: \; G = \sum_k \hat p_k (1 - \hat p_k), \qquad \text{RSS} = \sum_{i \in R} (y_i - \hat y_R)^2\]
Grow deep, then prune back (cost-complexity: minimize RSS + α·|leaves|) — because a fully grown tree interpolates its training data (4.1).






Classification trees and their region structure:

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why grow deep and then prune, rather than stopping early at “no split looks useful”?
The greedy split at the root maximizes immediate impurity reduction. Construct (in words) a truth where this misses the optimal first split.
What exactly does min_samples_leaf trade, and how does it differ in spirit from max_depth?
A tree needs no feature scaling — why, and which earlier models contradicted that requirement?
Your tree’s regression fit is piecewise-constant, so predictions within a leaf don’t move. Name two modeling consequences.



Answers


Early stopping is myopic: a split that looks useless now enables a powerful split one level down (the XOR/interaction structure of 2.7). Grow-full-then-prune evaluates subtrees globally against data via cross-validated α — a better search over tree sizes than greedy stopping.
Two features where the best pair of splits is diagonal but each single split is weak: e.g. class = “x1 XOR x2 > 0”. Any first axis-parallel split leaves both children 50/50 (zero impurity gain), so greedy stops — while a diagonal cut at 45° separates perfectly. Trees can still represent XOR with two levels, but greedy search needs luck (or the data volume) to find it.
Both limit complexity, but min_samples_leaf enforces a data-density guarantee (every prediction rests on ≥ m observations — stable leaf means, honest confidence), while max_depth caps interaction depth regardless of density. Deep-but-wide and shallow-but-narrow are different failure shapes.
Splits compare features via ordered thresholds — invariant to any monotone rescaling. Ridge/lasso/PCA/KNN all depended on magnitudes/distances (5.2, 0.5); trees don’t, which is also why they’re forgiving with mixed units.

The response is discontinuous at every split — an artifact unless the world truly steps (6.2); (b) smooth trends are approximated as staircases — many leaves needed for accuracy, and derivatives are zero inside leaves. Model averaging (7.3) smooths both problems.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Pruning, done properly: grow a full tree on noisy regression data (n = 150), extract the cost-complexity path, and select α by 5-fold CV over the path. Report (a) leaves and test MSE for the unpruned tree, (b) for the CV-pruned tree, (c) for the true-model oracle (degree-known step fit). Then state what pruning bought and what it cost.


Solution







Pruning removes the interpolation tail (hundreds of leaves → a handful), recovering most of the achievable accuracy; the cost is a few hundredths of MSE vs the theoretical best plus one CV loop. This grow-then-prune is the template every ensemble in this part inherits.

Exercise 2. The greedy trap, demonstrated: build the diagonal-separability truth — classes split by the line x₁ + x₂ = 0 with noise — and fit trees of depth 1, 2, 4. Plot boundaries and report test accuracy. Then fit a rotated model: tree on features (x₁+x₂)/√2, x₁ (a basis trick from 6.3). Write the lesson about axis-parallel bias and what fixes it (rotation, ensembles, or kernels — 8.4).


Solution







A single depth-1 stump on raw features is near a coin flip (the diagonal truth gives no axis-parallel purchase); depth 4 stitches four axis-parallel cells into a staircase approximating the line. One rotated feature makes a stump near-perfect. Axis-parallel greediness is the tree’s bias; basis rotation, oblique trees, ensembles of perturbed trees, or kernel methods are the standard remedies — each paying a different price.

Exercise 3. Impurity zoo: fit classification trees with criterion="gini" vs "entropy" on the same 6 datasets (varying class overlap and balance), comparing test accuracy and tree size (leaves). Then implement Gini by hand for a node with class proportions p and verify against tree.compute_feature_importances-style arithmetic on one split: predict the impurity drop of a candidate split manually and confirm it matches the reduction the fitted tree realized at that node (via tree_.impurity).


Solution







Gini vs entropy: cosmetic — the criteria are nearly proportional for two classes; neither fixes greediness or axis-alignment (the real tree biases). The hand computation is the whole learning algorithm in four lines: weighted impurity drop, maximized over splits.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Instability is the defining flaw: resample the data and the root split can move to a different feature entirely — small structural changes, big prediction changes. This is precisely what bagging (7.3) exploits and cures.
Impurity-based feature importances are biased toward high-cardinality/continuous features and unreliable under correlated features (7.4 covers the fix: permutation importance).
No extrapolation: regression trees predict leaf means — flat outside and between (2.1’s warning at its extreme); time-trended data needs care (or linex tricks).
Unbalanced classes: deep trees isolate rare-class pockets happily; use class_weight="balanced" or stratified evaluation (3.1).
random_state matters more than it should: tie-breaking among equally-good splits is random — pin seeds for reproducibility, but note ties indicate the data doesn’t care which split it got.
Interpretation caveat: a single small tree is genuinely interpretable (export_text); a deep tree is a maze — “interpretable model class” ≠ “this particular 500-leaf object is readable.”


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated tree has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unpruned default tree: train R² = 1.0, test R² collapses — the interpolation pathology; prune (ccp_alpha via CV) or cap depth/leaves.
Pointless scaler: trees are scale-invariant; the transform is dead weight that will silently bite later (transforming serving data with a scaler the model never needed). Drop it — knowing why is the point.
Extrapolated “trend”: the tree returns a leaf mean for x = 5 — the last leaf’s constant, dressed as a forecast. Refuse out-of-range queries or switch to a basis that extrapolates deliberately (6.4).

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Regression trees are adaptive step functions — show it: prove that a depth-d tree partitions the feature space into ≤ 2^d rectangles and predicts the mean of each. Then verify numerically that for a single feature, the depth-1 stump’s chosen threshold equals the RSS-minimizing split over all candidate cutpoints (compute both by brute force). What does the greedy-vs-exhaustive distinction cost when splits interact (2.7)?


Hint

Induction on depth for the partition; for the stump, each candidate cut creates two means — compute RSS directly.



Solution

Each internal node splits a rectangle into two rectangles by one threshold, so depth-d yields ≤ 2^d disjoint rectangles, and each leaf’s prediction is its training mean — a piecewise-constant function (6.2 with data-chosen boundaries). For the stump:






They match to the candidate grid. Greediness costs nothing at the stump (exhaustive over one variable’s cutpoints is cheap); the bill arrives with interactions: the best pair of splits may look worthless individually (2.7’s XOR), and greedy trees find such structures only when data volume makes intermediate gains real — the honest argument for deeper search or ensembles.

Q2. Cost-complexity pruning as a regularization path: relate the ccp objective RSS(T) + α|T| to ridge’s penalty (5.2) — what is the “norm” being constrained (|T| = leaf count = L0-style), and why does the α-path exist as a finite sequence of distinct trees (verify: len(path.ccp_alphas) ≪ 2^leaves)? Then plot test MSE vs α on one dataset and mark the CV choice — identifying the U-curve of 4.1 in tree space.


Solution

ccp penalizes the L0 “norm” of the tree (number of leaves) — combinatorial regularization, vs ridge’s smooth L2. The key fact: as α increases, the optimal subtree changes only at O(#internal nodes) critical values — the whole pruning path is computable in one pass (that’s what cost_complexity_pruning_path returns), not a search over 2^leaves subsets.






Same U-curve, same CV discipline — pruning is regularization where the penalty counts leaves instead of coefficient mass, and the path algorithm is what makes it tractable.

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (trees × 6.2 step functions). Face-off in their home game: truth = a true threshold (y = 1 + 2·1(x > t) + noise, t unknown). Compare (a) hand grid-searched 2-bin step (6.2 Exercise 3), (b) depth-1 stump, (c) depth-3 tree, by threshold-recovery error and test MSE over 200 simulations. Connect the stump’s threshold variance to 6.2 Q2 and state why ensembles of trees (7.3) both stabilize predictions and blur individual thresholds — is that blur a scientific loss?
C2 (trees × 5.x no other fixes). Trees in p ≫ n: n = 80, p = 500, 8 true signals. Fit a pruned tree, lasso-linear, and a random forest (7.4, teaser) with nested CV. Compare test MSE and which true features land in the top-10 importances. Which method’s feature ranking would you trust for follow-up, and does the tree’s axis-parallel greediness help or hurt under sparse signal?

title: 7.1 Decision Trees
text:
7. Summary

Trees = greedy recursive partitioning: impurity-drop splits, grow deep, prune by cost-complexity.
Adaptive axis-parallel step functions: no scaling needed, interactions reachable in depth, boundaries always rectangular.
Default = interpolation: pruning (ccp_alpha via CV) is not optional.
Greedy search misses XOR-style structures at shallow depth; basis rotation or ensembles compensate.
Single trees are unstable — a flaw so central that the next three pages turn it into a superpower.
Piecewise-constant predictions: no extrapolation, no smoothness — fine for regimes, wrong for trends.
The fix for instability without losing adaptivity: average many trees — 7.2 Advantages & limitations first catalogues what we’re averaging.

title: 7.4 Random Forests
text: Random forests = bagged trees (7.3) plus random feature subsampling at every split. The extra randomness decorrelates the trees — attacking the ρσ² floor that plain bagging can’t touch — and produced the most reliable off-the-shelf learner for tabular data of its era.

title: 7.4 Random Forests
text:
1. Basic Concept
Two randomness sources per tree: (1) a bootstrap sample (7.3); (2) at each split, only max_features (mtry) randomly-chosen features may be considered. The second is the forest’s signature — trees are forced to disagree:






The mtry dial, swept: decorrelation vs per-tree quality:






OOB comes free, and feature importances are one attribute away:

title: 7.4 Random Forests
text:
2. Concept Questions

State precisely what max_features does at each split, and why forcing trees to be weaker can make the forest better.
Standard defaults: mtry = √p for classification, p/3 for regression. What trade produces each?
Why don’t random forests overfit when you add more trees — and which earlier ensemble violated that?
OOB error vs CV error for a forest: when do they agree, and what procedure detail (not the error estimate itself) makes them differ?
Two features are near-duplicates. What happens to (a) impurity importances, (b) the model’s predictions?



Answers


Each split may only consider mtry randomly-drawn features; if the strong feature isn’t in the draw, the tree must split on something else — producing a different tree. Individually worse (weaker splits), collectively decorrelated: in ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B terms, ρ drops enough that the (1−ρ)/B term’s collapse dominates.
The trade is per-split quality vs decorrelation. Classification: √p candidates usually include enough signal to keep splits decent while decorrelating across p choices. Regression: p/3 — regression signals are typically spread over more features, needing wider draws.
Adding trees only averages more draws from the same randomized procedure — Var → ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B monotonically decreasing, no overfitting term in B. Gradient boosting (7.5) fits trees sequentially to residuals, so more trees keep changing the function — and can overfit.
They estimate the same quantity (test error of the procedure) by the same principle (out-of-sample rows). They differ in mechanics: OOB uses ≈ 0.368B trees per row and bootstrap-sized training sets, CV uses full ensemble and (K−1)/K-sized sets — so numbers differ by a few percent while conclusions rarely do.

Impurity importances split the credit arbitrarily between the twins (each mirrors the other; whichever is drawn first takes the share) — importances are diluted and unstable; (b) predictions are essentially unaffected — the forest uses the shared signal whichever twin carries it. Interpretation is where duplicates hurt, not prediction.

title: 7.4 Random Forests
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The decorrelation dividend, isolated: build a wide dataset where ONE feature is strongly informative and 19 are weak-but-real (so plain bagging’s trees all grab the same one). Compare bagging (max_features = p) vs forest (max_features = √p): test MSE, and the average pairwise correlation between member-tree predictions. Verify that the forest’s gain tracks the ρ drop — the ρσ²-floor argument made empirical.


Solution







The forest’s trees disagree more (lower ρ) even though each is individually handicapped — and the test MSE tracks ρ almost mechanically. This one experiment is the random forest’s raison d’être.

Exercise 2. Importance forensics: on data with (a) one signal feature, (b) its near-duplicate twin, (c) 18 noise features, compare impurity importances vs permutation importances (permutation_importance computed on a held-out set). Report both rankings’ treatment of the twins and the noise. Which importance answers “which feature does the model use” and which answers “which feature helps predictions”?


Solution







Impurity importance splits credit between twins (whichever is drawn first claims the split, starving the other) and inflates noise features with many split opportunities. Permutation importance on held-out data answers the deployment question — breaking f1 breaks predictions because f0 alone (fitted with a twin present) doesn’t fully carry the mapping — while correctly zeroing noise. The two questions are different; quote the one you mean.

Exercise 3. The honest forest workflow: build Pipeline(StandardScaler-optional, RandomForest) — deliberately without scaling (defend the choice) — tune max_features and min_samples_leaf by inner CV, evaluate by outer nested CV, and report OOB alongside. Apply to a 600-feature, 100-row problem (5.6 territory). Write the three-sentence summary comparing the forest to your Part 5 linear winners on accuracy, assumptions, and interpretation.


Solution







Summary template: “The random forest matched the penalized linear models’ nested-CV accuracy without linearity or scaling assumptions, at the cost of coefficient interpretability; its per-feature importances are advisory, and its OOB estimate tracked nested CV within noise. On n = 100, p = 600 data both families are viable; the choice is driven by the shape of the signal (sparse-linear → lasso; interaction-rich → forest) rather than by leaderboard deltas.”

title: 7.4 Random Forests
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

OOB is not a license to tune on everything: OOB can pick hyperparameters weakly, but heavy tuning against OOB re-inflates selection optimism (4.6); nested CV for claims.
Impurity importance’s bias: favors continuous/high-cardinality features and splits credit arbitrarily under correlation — permutation importance on held-out data is the defensible default (Exercise 2).
n_estimators is compute, not tuning: more trees monotonically help (plateau); tune max_features, min_samples_leaf, max_depth — the variance/correlation dials.
Regression forests can’t extrapolate (leaf means, 7.2): trending time series need detrending or different tools.
Probabilities: forest class fractions average many noisy leaf estimates — better than one tree, still not calibrated; check reliability (3.7).
Missing values: classic sklearn forests need imputation; HistGradientBoosting (7.6) handles NaN natively — a practical deciding factor in messy pipelines.
Class imbalance: forests inherit tree biases; class_weight="balanced" or stratified sampling — then evaluate with AUC/PR (3.1, 3.1.5).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated forest has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Five trees: more trees monotonically improve — B is a compute setting (≥ a few hundred); report the plateau, not a 5-tree straw model.
B is not a tuning parameter — sweeping it on test burns the test set for nothing. Fix B by compute budget; tune max_features/min_samples_leaf by inner CV.
Importances ≠ causation (and are unreliable under correlation): if features 5/6 are near-duplicates of feature 0, impurity importance fragments across them. Use permutation importance on held-out data, disclose correlation structure, and claim “model relies on,” never “causes.”

title: 7.4 Random Forests
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the forest’s OOB prediction for row i: the average over trees whose bootstrap sample excluded i, and show its expected training-set size per OOB prediction is ≈ 0.368B trees on ≈ 0.632n rows. Then verify empirically that OOB error estimates the error of the 0.632n-trained forest, not the full-data forest, by comparing OOB against honest test error as n grows (n ∈ {50, 200, 800}) — the 4.5 Q1 mismatch, in forest clothing. At which n is OOB’s pessimism negligible?


Hint

Each row is OOB with probability (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → e⁻¹; the OOB prediction averages only the trees that didn’t train on it.



Solution

OOB row i uses trees B_b with i ∉ bootstrap_b: a fraction (1−1/n)ⁿ ≈ 0.368 of B trees, each trained on a bootstrap of all n rows excluding i’s influence — effectively ≈ 0.632n-row models.






The OOB gap shrinks as n grows — at a few hundred rows it’s negligible, at n = 50 it’s a visible pessimism tax. Report OOB as the free monitor; spend a holdout or CV when the claim matters.

Q2. Why does mtry = 1 sometimes win? Construct a truth with exactly one strong feature and many weak ones; sweep mtry ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, p} and plot test error. Explain the U-shape via ρ and per-tree quality (the 7.3 formula: variance floor = ρ(mtry)·σ²(mtry) with both terms mtry-dependent). Then state the symptom-based default: if your forest at default mtry underperforms a single pruned tree, which direction do you move mtry and why?


Solution







With one loud feature, small mtry forces many trees to miss it (bad individual splits — high bias) but the trees that do use it are nearly independent (low ρ); large mtry gives strong trees that are near-clones (ρ → 1, bagging-floor). The optimum balances the two — and with a single dominant feature, small mtry wins because decorrelation matters more than split polish. Symptom default: if the forest loses to a single pruned tree, per-tree quality is being sacrificed — raise mtry toward p (bagging limit) and re-tune min_samples_leaf.

title: 7.4 Random Forests
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (forest × 5.6 high-dimensional). Forest vs lasso rematch with mixed truth: n = 120, p = 300, where 6 features are sparse-linear, 3 contribute only through interactions, and 1 has a threshold effect. Nested-CV both (lasso on raw features; forest), report test MSE and each method’s recovery of the three signal types (linear coefficients for lasso; importances for forest). Which truth components favor which method — and what ensemble-plus-lasso combined workflow would you pre-register?
C2 (forest × 3.6 GLM × 6.7 GAM). Interpretability triangulation: on a truth with one smooth effect + one interaction + one threshold, fit forest, GAM, and GAM+interaction-term. Compare CV MSE and each method’s recovery of the smooth component (correlate forest partial-dependence and GAM’s \(s_1\) with truth). Write the reporting rule: which model for the coefficient table, which for the black-box check, and what agreement between forest-PD and GAM smooths certifies about the additive assumption (6.7 C2’s triangulation, formalized).

title: 7.4 Random Forests
text:
7. Summary

Forest = bagged trees + mtry-limited splits: decorrelation attacks the ρσ² floor bagging can’t.
mtry is the key dial (√p classification, p/3 regression defaults): too small starves splits, too large clones trees.
n_estimators is compute; more trees never overfit — boosting will break that rule next page.
OOB: free internal validation, tracks CV closely, slightly pessimistic at small n.
Importances: impurity-based ones fragment under correlation; permutation-on-held-out is the defensible kind — and neither is causal.
Inherited from trees: no extrapolation, scale-invariance, uncalibrated probabilities; new superpowers: interactions and nonlinearity by default.
The sequential alternative: fit trees to residuals and climb — 7.5 Gradient boosting.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text: XGBoost and LightGBM industrialized gradient boosting: second-order (Newton) objectives, histogram-based split finding, built-in regularization, native missing-value handling, and engineering that made 10⁶-row datasets routine. sklearn’s HistGradientBoosting* implements the same core ideas natively — so this page teaches the concepts on a guaranteed-available implementation, then translates to the two libraries’ idioms.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
1. Basic Concept
What modern boosters add to 7.5’s recipe:

Second-order fitting: splits and leaf values use gradient and Hessian (Newton-style), not just gradients.
Histogram binning: features are binned (~255 bins) — split finding becomes histogram counting instead of sorting: orders of magnitude faster.
Leaf-wise vs level-wise growth: LightGBM grows the leaf with the largest loss reduction (asymmetric trees); classic boosting grows level-by-level.
Native NaN handling: missing values learn which branch to take — no imputation.
Penalized objectives: explicit L1/L2 on leaf values, min_child_weight — regularization built into the split criterion.

sklearn’s histogram booster — the always-available baseline:






The same fit in LightGBM and XGBoost idioms:

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does second-order (Hessian-using) splitting buy over 7.5’s first-order version — and where does the Hessian come from for log-loss?
Why is histogram binning approximately lossless for split finding, and what does it cost?
LightGBM’s leaf-wise growth can produce deeper, asymmetric trees. What risk does that add, and which hyperparameter (num_leaves) tames it?
Native NaN handling: why is “learn the best branch for missing” better than mean-imputation for predictive purposes — and what caveat does it carry for deployment?
num_leaves vs max_depth: which is the honest complexity knob for leaf-wise trees, and why?



Answers


Newton steps use curvature: leaf values become Σgᵢ/(Σhᵢ + λ) — the optimal value for the local quadratic approximation, so each tree fits more per step and convergence needs fewer trees. For log-loss, per-point Hessian is p(1−p) (the Bernoulli variance) — the same quantity GLM IRLS used (3.3).
Split rankings rarely change under fine binning: the best threshold within a bin matters less than choosing the right bin boundary — 255 quantile-ish bins capture essentially all real split structure. Cost: splits snap to bin edges (harmless in practice) plus one preprocessing pass.
Leaf-wise growth keeps splitting the highest-loss leaf, producing deep lopsided branches that can overfit isolated pockets — num_leaves caps the total leaf count directly (LightGBM’s complexity knob; typical 15–255).
Learned NaN routing lets each split use the best empirical guess per node (often better than any global imputation), and requires no imputation model to maintain. Caveat: the routing is fitted to training-time missingness patterns — if deployment missingness differs (new reasons for NaN), routing generalizes no better than imputation would (12.x-style shift caution).
num_leaves. In leaf-wise growth, depth is a poor complexity proxy (one deep branch ≠ many leaves); the leaf count bounds the model’s degrees of freedom directly — max_depth remains only as a safety rail.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Three implementations, one protocol: fit sklearn-GBM (7.5’s GradientBoostingRegressor), HistGradientBoostingRegressor, and LightGBM on the same 20k-row regression problem, each tuned lightly (early stopping where supported) inside a 5-fold CV. Report the CV MSE table and fit times. Write the selection paragraph: when do the industrial implementations earn their dependency?


Solution







Accuracy is a wash (all implement the same algorithm family at sane settings); time separates them — histogram methods are one to two orders faster at 20k rows, and the gap widens with n. The paragraph: “We use HistGradientBoosting/LightGBM for any dataset beyond a few thousand rows, reserving exact GradientBoosting for small problems where its simplicity aids teaching or debugging.”

Exercise 2. Native-NaN vs imputation, honestly: inject 20% missing completely-at-random into one feature (MCAR) and 20% missing depending on y (MNAR-ish: mask feature where y = 1) on a classification task. Compare HistGB-native-NaN vs mean-imputation pipelines by CV AUC in each scenario. Where does native handling shine, where does it not save you (what does the MNAR case teach about missingness mechanisms, connecting to 9.3)?


Solution







Under MCAR, native NaN routing and imputation tie (both recover the feature’s info). Under y-dependent missingness, the missingness itself is signal — native NaN handling captures it (missingness-pattern splits), while blind mean-imputation erases the pattern and can bias the feature. The deep lesson (Part 9.3’s territory): imputation is a modeling decision about why values are missing, not a preprocessing reflex.

Exercise 3. The complexity-knob audit: for LightGBM, sweep num_leaves ∈ {7, 15, 31, 63, 127} (with min_child_samples fixed) and separately max_depth ∈ {3, 5, 8, −1} at fixed num_leaves, reporting CV AUC and tree statistics (average depth via the booster). Which knob’s sweep moves performance, and how do the two interact? Write the tuning-order recipe you’d follow on a new tabular problem.


Solution







num_leaves moves the needle (it caps the model’s true complexity); max_depth only bites when it clips num_leaves (tiny depths) — otherwise it’s a safety rail. Recipe: fix learning_rate modestly (0.05), tune num_leaves + min_child_samples by CV, set max_depth as a guardrail, scale n_estimators with early stopping, and only then consider feature_fraction/bagging dials (7.5’s subsample, renamed).

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The dial dictionary translates: sklearn-GBM max_depth ↔︎ LightGBM num_leaves (complexity), subsample ↔︎ bagging_fraction, colsample ↔︎ feature_fraction, min_samples_leaf ↔︎ min_child_weight/samples — carrying names across libraries without remapping semantics is the #1 tuning bug.
Early stopping APIs differ per version: LightGBM/XGBoost have changed callback/eval-set conventions repeatedly — pin versions and read your installed signature (help(model.fit)), not blog posts.
NaN routing + feature_fraction interplay: features with NaNs get “free” informative splits — check whether missingness itself is predictive before crediting the feature (Exercise 2).
Histogram binning + tiny data: on n < ~1000 the exact (sklearn-GBM) splitter can match or beat histogram methods — industrial speed matters when data is big.
Determinism: identical seeds give identical forests, but GPU/histogram orderings can vary across hardware — document versions for reproducibility (4.6’s protocol hygiene).
Interpretability exports: all three expose importances (split/gain) with the same 7.4 caveats; prefer permutation/SHAP-style attributions on held-out data for anything you publish.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated LightGBM pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Accuracy as headline at 10% prevalence: ~0.90 achievable by predicting the majority — use AUC/AP (3.1).
num_leaves = 127 unchecked: leaf-wise growth will grow deep pockets on minority-class noise; cap by CV (typical 15–63 at this n) and watch min_child_samples.
Test-set early stopping: the eval_set must be a validation split carved from training — the test set is spent once, at the end.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Newton leaf values: for a leaf with examples {gᵢ, hᵢ} (gradients, Hessians) and L2 penalty λ, derive the optimal leaf value w* = −Σgᵢ/(Σhᵢ + λ) and the resulting split-gain formula used by XGBoost. Verify numerically for a log-loss leaf (compute gᵢ, hᵢ from pᵢ) that w* equals the local log-odds correction — connecting to the Newton/IRLS machinery of logistic regression (3.3 Q1).


Hint

Minimize Σ[gᵢw + ½hᵢw²] + ½λw² in w; the gain formula is ½·(GL²/(GR+λ) + GR²/(GR+λ) − G²/(G+λ)) minus γ per leaf.



Solution

Quadratic-in-w leaf objective: Σgᵢw + ½Σhᵢw² + ½λw² minimized at w* = −Σgᵢ/(Σhᵢ + λ). For log-loss, gᵢ = pᵢ − yᵢ and hᵢ = pᵢ(1−pᵢ) — the IRLS weights. Verification:






The leaf update is one IRLS step on the leaf’s members — modern boosting is Newton boosting, which is why it converges in fewer, better-fitted trees than the first-order original.

Q2. Histogram approximation audit: on one dataset, compare exact-split boosting (sklearn GradientBoostingRegressor) against histogram boosting (HistGB) at increasing max_bins (31, 127, 255), tracking CV MSE. Verify that MSE decreases toward the exact method’s and stabilizes well before 255 on a smooth feature, then construct a feature where binning bites (extremely spiky/multi-modal with narrow gaps) and show 31 bins lose to 255. What’s the practical bin-count policy?


Solution







Smooth features: 127 bins ≈ 255 ≈ exact (split choices are coarse-grain stable). The spiky truth exposes binning: narrow ridges fall between coarse bin edges, and 31 bins measurably lose. Policy: default 255 (the library default) is nearly free; drop bins only for speed on huge n — and check exact-vs-histogram once on your data before trusting a leaderboard delta.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (libraries × 7.3–7.5 family tournament). The full Part 7 bake-off on one honest protocol: single tree, random forest, sklearn-GBM, HistGB, LightGBM, XGBoost — same dataset (10k rows, 20 features, mixed signal types), identical outer 5-fold nested CV, light inner tuning. Produce the accuracy-vs-fit-time scatter and write the deployment recommendation for (a) a laptop-scale research problem and (b) a 100M-row scoring pipeline — justifying each choice by the measured frontier, not reputation.
C2 (libraries × 5.6 p ≫ n × 12.4 FDR stub). Boosters in the wide regime: n = 150, p = 2,000 with 10 signals. Compare LightGBM (with feature_fraction < 1) against lasso and the random forest — nested CV MSE plus each method’s top-20 recovery overlap with truth. In p ≫ n, which inductive bias (sparsity-linear, decorrelated trees, sequential trees) wins, and does the answer change when the signal becomes interaction-heavy? Write the pre-registered analysis plan you’d commit to before seeing the response.

title: 7.6 Modern Boosting Libraries
text:
7. Summary

Modern boosters = 7.5’s algorithm + Newton leaf values + histogram splits + native NaN routing + leaf-wise growth.
HistGradientBoosting (sklearn) implements the core with zero extra dependencies; LightGBM/XGBoost add ecosystem and raw speed.
num_leaves is the complexity knob (leaf-wise trees); max_depth is a guardrail; early stopping must use a validation split, never the test set.
Learned NaN branches are a predictive feature — and a missingness-mechanism assumption (9.3).
Hyperparameter names don’t translate across libraries; translate semantics, then tune on your data.
Accuracy at sane settings is a tie between implementations; speed, data volume, and deployment constraints decide.
Part 7’s sequence — trees → bagging → forests → boosting → libraries — is one idea (adaptive step functions) refined four ways. Next, margins meet kernels: Part 8, SVMs, starting with 8.1 Geometry essentials.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text: When positives are rare (1% disease, 0.1% hits in a screen), ROC-AUC keeps flattering weak classifiers — the huge negative pool absorbs false alarms invisibly. The precision–recall curve and its area (AUPRC / average precision) put the cost of false alarms in a sparse world back in the picture.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
1. Basic Concept
Sweeping the threshold from strict to loose traces a curve in precision (PPV = TP/(TP+FP)) vs recall (TPR) space. The area under it — computed as sklearn’s average precision,
\[\text{AP} = \sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1})\, P_n\]
i.e., each precision value weighted by the increase in recall it purchased — is the standard scalar (AUPRC).
Two facts make AUPRC the right lens under skew:

The baseline is the prevalence, not 0.5: a random classifier’s PR curve hovers at precision = prevalence. AUPRC = 0.55 at 1% prevalence is massive; AUC = 0.55 would be negligible.
False positives are priced in the metric: at low prevalence, each FP slashes precision immediately (denominator TP+FP), while in ROC-land an FP just nudges FPR by 1/(huge N).

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is a random classifier’s PR baseline the prevalence while its ROC baseline is the diagonal?
Two datasets have identical classifier quality; one has 1% prevalence, one 30%. Which metric is comparable across them — AUC, AP, or neither?
AP = 0.35 at 5% prevalence: translate that into “how much better than random” in one sentence.
Your model’s PR curve is strictly below the prevalence line everywhere. What does that tell you, and what single transformation rescues the model?
Why does AP have no nice probabilistic interpretation like AUC’s concordance probability?



Answers


Random scoring means precision ≈ prevalence at every recall level (each retrieved batch is prevalence-random), so the PR “curve” is the horizontal line y = prevalence. In ROC space, random scoring moves TPR and FPR together — the diagonal.
AUC (it’s a within-pair probability, prevalence-independent in expectation). AP is prevalence-dependent by design — its baseline moves with prevalence — so absolute AP values don’t transfer across datasets with different class balance. Neither is a substitute for reporting the dataset’s prevalence alongside.
Random retrieval gets precision 0.05; this model’s precision-recall trade is worth AP = 0.35, i.e. its average precision across recall levels is 7× the random baseline — strong for a 1-in-20 problem.
Precision below prevalence at all recalls means the score is anti-ranked: top-scored items are less likely to be positive than random. Negate the scores (or flip the sign of the decision function) and the same information becomes a good model — always check this before discarding a model.
