AUC counts a specific, symmetric random experiment (draw one of each, who wins?). AP is a weighted sum of precisions with data-dependent weights (recall increments) — a different, asymmetric summary with no single natural random-pair story; its “meaning” is operational: expected precision averaged over recall levels you choose to chase.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. By hand, build the full precision–recall table for the ranked list below (compute P@k, R@k for every k), compute AP from the table, and verify against average_precision_score. Then state the single threshold (top-k) you would choose if the budget allows exactly 3 follow-ups, and its precision.


Solution







The budget answer is a decision the curve exists to inform: with 3 slots you catch 2 of 5 positives (precision 0.67); the curve lets management see exactly what the 4th and 5th slot would buy.

Exercise 2. Prevalence surgery: fix one classifier and one score distribution; vary prevalence from 0.5% to 40% by subsampling negatives, and plot AUC and AP against prevalence. Which curve moves, which holds steady, and what does this experiment say about comparing your AP to a published AP from a different cohort?


Solution







AUC is flat (prevalence-free by construction); AP falls as prevalence falls — the baseline sinks with it. Consequence: AP values are cohort-specific; compare APs only within the same prevalence regime, or convert to “multiple of prevalence baseline” (AP / prevalence) for a rough cross-cohort normalized statement.

Exercise 3. Metric face-off on a realistic screen: build a 1%-positive dataset with a mildly informative score; compute (a) accuracy at 0.5, (b) balanced accuracy, (c) AUC, (d) AP, (e) precision at recall = 0.5. Rank the metrics by how usefully each describes the model for a screening manager who can only follow up 50 samples. Justify the ranking in two sentences per metric.


Solution







Usefulness ranking for the manager: (e) precision@recall-0.5 — an operating point, exactly what “we follow up 50” means; (d) AP — the full-curve summary, prevalence-anchored; (c) AUC — ranks well but abstracts away the FP flood; (b) balanced accuracy — treats classes symmetrically when the budget doesn’t; (a) accuracy — tells the manager nothing (it’s the prevalence in disguise). The general law: the closer a metric sits to the actual decision (budget, costs, threshold), the more decisions it can improve.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Three names, one thing (mostly): AUPRC (area under PR curve), AP (sklearn’s interpolated area), mean average precision (mAP — averaged over queries, the retrieval convention). sklearn’s average_precision_score uses the recall-increment weighting — not the trapezoidal rule — so hand-trapezoiding your PR points gives slightly different numbers (the worked table uses the sklearn definition; the trapezoid variant appears in Appendix A.7’s worked example).
AP is not comparable across cohorts with different prevalence (Exercise 2) — report prevalence next to every AP, always.
The last point of the PR curve: precision_recall_curve appends the anchor (recall 0, precision 1); the thresholds array is one shorter — off-by-one errors when zip()-ing live here.
Interpolated “best PR” curves (as in some leaderboards) paint an upper envelope that no actual threshold achieves; be explicit which convention you report.
AUPRC noise: with few positives the curve is jagged and AP’s sampling variance is large — bootstrap it (1.5) before declaring one model better than another.
PR wins under skew; ROC still wins for: cost-symmetric ranking questions, prevalence-robust reporting, and comparing against chance (0.5) — the metrics answer different questions; report both under skew.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “screen performance” report has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Accuracy at 1% prevalence ≈ 0.99 for anything — replace with AP/precision@budget and always print the prevalence.
PR machinery on 0/1 predictions: at most two distinct thresholds exist; the “curve” is a line and trapz is not the AP definition (and on hard labels it’s meaningless). Feed continuous scores to average_precision_score.
Cross-cohort AP comparison without prevalences: their cohort may be 30% positive (AP baseline 0.30) while yours is 1% (baseline 0.01) — 0.07 may be the stronger result. Normalize (AP/prevalence) or recompute both on a common prevalence.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove the AP formula \(\text{AP} = \sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1})P_n\) equals the precision averaged over the recall axis for the step-function PR curve, and show that for a single threshold operating point (R₀, P₀) the formula contributes \(R_0 P_0 = TP_0 / N_+\) — connecting AP to the raw hit count. What does this imply about AP’s sensitivity to the last positives retrieved (high recall, low precision region)?


Hint

Write each recall increment as ΔTP/N₊ and multiply by precision = TP/(TP+FP) at that step.



Solution

\(R_n - R_{n-1} = \Delta TP_n / N_+\) and \(P_n = TP_n/(TP_n + FP_n)\), so each term counts positives gained weighted by their purity; summed, AP = (1/N₊) Σ ΔTP·P = mean precision per positive retrieved. For a model that puts all TPs first at one shot: one increment with \(R_0 = TP_0/N_+\), \(P_0 = 1\), contributing \(TP_0/N_+\) = fraction of positives found perfectly. Consequence: the tail matters — retrieving the final positives at precision ~prevalence adds \((R=1 - R_{prev}) \times \text{prevalence}\)-ish mass; with 5 positives, each late hit adds ~0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02. AP rewards getting most positives cleanly; it is forgiving of the last scrappy recoveries exactly in proportion to how few positives remain — a feature under skew, and the reason AP > AUC Rankings shuffles rarely change AP’s tail.

Q2. Your team must choose between Model A (AP = 0.21, AUC = 0.85) and Model B (AP = 0.24, AUC = 0.80) at 2% prevalence, with a fixed budget of 100 follow-ups per 10,000 screened. Design the decision experiment: what single metric or plot settles it, how do you quantify uncertainty (bootstrap), and how should the budget constraint enter the comparison? Implement it.


Solution







The budget turns the comparison into precision@k (top-100 hits) — AUC and AP both summarize the whole curve, but only k = 100 will be operated. The bootstrap CI on the hit difference says whether B’s sharper head is real or noise (here B wins at the operating point despite losing on AUC — a decisive, budget-aware answer). Generalize the pattern: choose the metric that mirrors the deployment constraint, then attach uncertainty to that metric, not to a curve-wide scalar that no one will ever operate.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (AUPRC × 3.1 metrics × 1.4 inference). Generate 200 resampled test sets (bootstrap the same test data) and compute AP and AUC distributions for one fixed model. Which metric’s CI is wider at 1% prevalence, and does the ordering of two competing models (by either metric) survive the uncertainty? Write the reporting rule that follows: when do you need the bootstrap before comparing two classifiers, and what sample size of positives makes single-number AP comparisons defensible?
C2 (AUPRC × 12.x multiple testing preview). A biomarker screen tests 20,000 candidates and reports “14 significant hits.” Reinterpret the screen as a classifier: define scores, prevalence, and AP for the hit list, then compute the precision you’d need for the list to beat random selection by a factor of 10. Connect to the FDR viewpoint: precision of a hit list at fixed size is 1 − FDR of that list — the two vocabularies are the same object seen from the ranking and the testing side.

title: 3.1.5 AUPRC for Skewed Datasets
text:
7. Summary

Under class skew, PR curves price false alarms honestly; ROC’s huge negative pool hides them.
AP = Σ Δrecall × precision: mean precision weighted by positives gained; baseline = prevalence.
AUC stays comparable across prevalences; AP does not — report prevalence beside every AP.
Below-baseline PR curve = anti-ranked scores: flip before you discard.
The metric that mirrors the deployment constraint (precision@budget) beats any curve-wide scalar for decisions.
With few positives, bootstrap AP differences before believing them.
With both metric families in hand, ask the orthogonal question — why not just use linear regression on 0/1 labels? — 3.2 Why not linear regression for categories?

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text: Instead of modeling P(y|x) directly (discriminative — logistic), generative classifiers model how each class generates data — P(x|y) and P(y) — then flip the conditioning with Bayes’ rule. Three classical instances span the assumption spectrum: LDA (Gaussian, shared covariance), QDA (Gaussian, per-class covariance), Naive Bayes (conditionally independent features).
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
1. Basic Concept
Bayes’ rule chooses the class maximizing the posterior:
\[P(y = k \mid x) = \frac{P(x \mid y = k)\, P(y = k)}{\sum_j P(x \mid y = j)\, P(y = j)}\]
LDA assumes each class is Gaussian with its own mean μₖ but one shared covariance Σ. Plugging in and simplifying, the log-posterior becomes linear in x — hence linear discriminant. QDA gives each class its own Σₖ; quadratic terms survive — quadratic boundaries. Gaussian Naive Bayes assumes independence within each class (diagonal covariance): one variance per feature per class, no correlations — crude but fast and parameter-poor.






When the classes’ covariances genuinely differ, QDA earns its extra parameters:






Naive Bayes by hand — the whole method in ten lines, then verified against sklearn:
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does the “naive” in Naive Bayes assume, and why is it catastrophic for correlated features even when each feature is individually informative?
LDA vs QDA: state the parameter-count trade (in d dimensions, per class) and the sample-size rule of thumb that follows.
Why do generative models need fewer training samples to reach a given accuracy when their assumptions hold — and what happens when the assumptions don’t hold?
LDA’s boundary is linear. Which two simplifications of the Bayes-optimal rule produce that linearity?
Your features are 5,000 gene counts with strong correlations. Which of the three would you reach for first, and what would you need to check before trusting QDA?



Answers


Features are conditionally independent given the class (diagonal class covariance). With correlated informative features, NB double-counts the same evidence: two correlated genes each “voting” for the class push the posterior toward certainty twice — overconfident probabilities, badly calibrated posteriors (accuracy can survive; the probability values don’t).
LDA: one shared Σ = O(d²) parameters total + d means per class; QDA: full Σₖ per class = O(k·d²). With d = 50, LDA’s Σ has 1,275 entries shared; QDA’s two have 2,550 estimated separately. Rule of thumb (ISL): small n or a shared-covariance belief → LDA; large n or visibly different covariances → QDA. (Between them sits “regularized QDA”/shrinkage covariance.)
Modeling the joint densities adds structure the data needn’t discover: with correct assumptions, the estimate converges at parametric rates and out-of-sample accuracy rises quickly with n (fewer effective parameters than a discriminative search over boundaries). When wrong, the bias is baked in — and generative models typically converge to the wrong boundary no matter how much data arrives, while flexible discriminative methods would eventually find the truth.

Gaussian class densities; (b) equal covariance matrices — the quadratic terms x^TΣₖ⁻¹x then coincide across classes and cancel in the log-ratio, leaving a linear score.

Gaussian NB with correlation-aware caution… honestly: none of the three directly. NB’s independence assumption is badly violated (double counting). QDA in d = 5,000 estimates 12.5M covariance entries per class — singular without regularization; you’d need heavy shrinkage (reg_param) or feature reduction first (or logistic regression with penalties — Part 5). The check before QDA: n ≫ d and covariance stability, neither plausible here.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement LDA’s classification rule from scratch for two classes: estimate μ̂₀, μ̂₁, pooled covariance Σ̂, priors; classify by sign of the linear score \(x^\top \Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1 - \mu_0) - \tfrac12(\mu_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_1 - \mu_0^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_0) + \log(\pi_1/\pi_0)\). Verify 100% agreement with sklearn on training data, then perturb one class’s covariance and show where LDA and QDA begin to disagree.


Solution







The hand version IS sklearn’s rule (up to internal scaling). Once covariances differ, the shared-Σ score is no longer Bayes-optimal and QDA’s quadratic terms capture the elliptical structure — visible as disagreement concentrated far from the boundary.

Exercise 2. The NB double-counting experiment, quantified: build truth where P(y=1|x) depends on a single latent z, and expose it through k increasingly correlated copies (ρ = 0, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0 between copies). For each ρ, fit GaussianNB and logistic regression; report (a) accuracy, (b) the mean predicted probability for true positives (overconfidence meter). Which model’s accuracy degrades with ρ? Which model’s probabilities degrade?


Solution







Accuracy stays similar across ρ for both (the information content doesn’t change much), but NB’s predicted probabilities inflate toward 1 as correlation grows — the same evidence counted twice. Logistic regression, discriminative, never assumed independence and stays calibrated. Lesson: choose the model by what you consume — rankings (NB fine) or probabilities (NB dangerous under correlation).

Exercise 3. Generative vs discriminative sample-efficiency sweep: fixed true model = two Gaussians with equal covariance (LDA’s world, so its assumptions hold). For n per class in {5, 15, 50, 200}, fit LDA and unpenalized logistic on 100 independent training sets, evaluate each on a fixed test set, and plot mean test accuracy vs n. Which converges faster? Then repeat with unequal covariances and re-read the curves.


Solution







Equal covariance (LDA’s assumptions true): LDA leads at every n — the generative parametric payoff. Unequal: LDA’s advantage evaporates/reverses as its bias caps its ceiling while logistic keeps climbing. The generative-vs-discriminative trade, drawn to scale.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

LDA’s shared covariance is a modeling claim — check it (visual covariance ellipses, Box’s M in spirit) before trusting its SEs/probabilities; QDA when ellipses differ, and reg_param when n is small.
QDA in high dimensions is numerically fragile: per-class covariance matrices go singular (d > n per class); sklearn’s reg_param adds ridge-like stabilization — tune it, don’t disable it.
NB posteriors are overconfident under any correlation — never quote its probabilities without calibration checks (3.7); its rankings survive much better than its values.
Class priors matter: LDA/NB use empirical priors; in case–control samples the priors are sampling artifacts — correct with priors= (sklearn) or logit-offset (3.3 C2).
LDA is also a projector: its scalings give the k−1 discriminant axes — a supervised alternative to PCA for visualization (9.2 contrast: PCA is unsupervised, ignores y).
Multiclass comes free: all three handle k > 2 natively (no one-vs-rest machinery) — a quiet advantage over the logistic formulations of 3.3.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated classifier has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


NB probabilities quoted as risks: three near-copies of one signal triple-count the evidence; predicted risks inflate toward 1. Report rankings, or recalibrate (3.7), or drop duplicate features / use logistic.
Case–control priors as prevalence: class_prior_ here reflects the sampling design (here 50/50), not biology. Set GaussianNB(priors=...) to real prevalence or correct downstream.
QDA on 6 samples: covariance estimates are garbage (reg_param=0 doesn’t even stabilize); the 1.00 “score” is training-set self-evaluation. Fix: more data, reg_param tuned by CV, or LDA.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive LDA’s linear score from the Gaussian log-densities: write \(\log P(x|k) + \log \pi_k\) for class k, subtract the two classes’ expressions, and show every quadratic term cancels under Σ₀ = Σ₁. Then state precisely which direction the discriminant points (Σ⁻¹(μ₁−μ₀)) and why it is the Fisher optimal projection (maximizing between-class over within-class variance).


Hint

Expand −½(x−μₖ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μₖ); the xᵀΣ⁻¹x piece is class-independent.



Solution

log P(x|k) = −½(x−μₖ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μₖ) + constₖ. The difference log P(x|1) − log P(x|0) = xᵀΣ⁻¹(μ₁−μ₀) − ½(μ₁ᵀΣ⁻¹μ₁ − μ₀ᵀΣ⁻¹μ₀) — the xᵀΣ⁻¹x terms cancel because Σ is shared. The decision score is linear with direction w = Σ⁻¹(μ₁−μ₀): the class separation, whitened by within-class covariance — which is exactly Fisher’s criterion argmax wᵀ(μ₁−μ₀)/√(wᵀΣw). Two views, one vector: the generative derivation and the optimal-projection problem have the same solution, which is why LDA doubles as both a classifier and a supervised projector.

Q2. You have d = 2,000 features, n = 200 samples, two classes with correlated features. Design the analysis pipeline: which of LDA/QDA/NB/logistic is even feasible as-is, what preprocessing must precede it, how you’d validate the choice (0.5 + 4.6 discipline), and what failure mode each option guards against. Demonstrate with a simulation: compare the candidates’ CV accuracies and calibration under p ≫ n.


Solution

Feasibility triage: QDA — infeasible (4M covariance parameters/class, singular). LDA — pooled Σ is 2000×2000 from 200 samples: singular; needs shrinkage or feature reduction. GaussianNB — feasible (2 diag variances per class) but assumes away the correlations and p ≫ n overconfidence. Logistic with L2 penalty — feasible and standard. Pipeline: standardize → (optionally) reduce dimension (feature screening inside CV only, or PCA) → fit penalized logistic / shrunk-LDA / NB inside a Pipeline → nested CV for model choice, calibration curve at the end.






Typical outcome: penalized logistic ≈ shrunk LDA > NB on accuracy, and only logistic/LDA give trustworthy probability directions; NB’s accuracy is respectable while its probabilities are inflated. The p ≫ n moral: the choice is not “which classifier” but “which regularization + which validation” — the subject of Part 5 and Part 4 respectively.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (generative × 2.6 categorical). Extend the Bayes classifier to mixed feature types: one Gaussian feature and one binary feature per class (model the binary one with class-specific Bernoulli probabilities — the “independence” NB way). Implement the joint log-posterior by hand, verify on simulated data against GaussianNB-on-dummified input where possible, and explain where a fully-Naive treatment misprices the joint evidence of (Gaussian, binary) pairs that are correlated within class.
C2 (generative × 4.4 bias–variance preview). Organize the three classifiers on a flexibility axis: NB (diagonal, k·d params) → LDA (shared full Σ) → QDA (per-class Σ). Simulate data under each of the three data-generatings in turn; for each, sweep the three models across n ∈ {20, 100, 500} and record test accuracy. You should reproduce the classic picture: the correctly-specified model dominates at small n; all converge at large n unless misspecified. Bring the resulting 3×3×3 table to 4.4 and map each cell onto bias/variance language.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes
text:
7. Summary

Generative = model P(x|y)P(y), classify by posterior; fewer effective parameters, stronger assumptions.
LDA: shared Gaussian covariance → linear boundary + Fisher projection; QDA: per-class covariance → quadratic; NB: conditional independence → diagonal, fast, fragile probabilities.
LDA/QDA need n ≫ d and covariance stability (shrinkage/reg_param); NB needs feature independence to be honest.
Priors are parameters: sampling designs (case–control) must be corrected before quoting posteriors.
Correlated features double-count in NB — rankings survive, probabilities don’t.
Generative wins small-n under true assumptions; discriminative catches up and overtakes when assumptions fail.
The remaining classical classifier is assumption-free neighborhood voting: 3.5 KNN classification.
crumbs: 3.4 Generative Classifiers: LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text: Logistic regression was not a one-off trick — it is one instance of a general recipe: pick a response distribution, a link between its mean and the linear predictor, fit by maximum likelihood. That recipe — the GLM — handles counts, rates, proportions, and skewed positives with the same coefficient-interpretation and inference machinery as Part 2.

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
1. Basic Concept
A GLM has three ingredients:

Random component — the response’s distribution family: Gaussian (linear regression), Binomial (logistic), Poisson (counts), Gamma (positive skewed), etc.
Systematic component — the linear predictor \(\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots\)
Link function — \(g(\mu) = \eta\), connecting the mean μ to the predictor. Identity for Gaussian; logit for Binomial; log for Poisson.

The log link makes coefficients multiplicative: \(e^{\beta}\) is a rate ratio per unit of x. Fitting maximizes the family’s likelihood (IRLS again — same engine as 3.3).






Why not just OLS on counts? Three failures, demonstrated live:






Offsets — exposures enter as a fixed coefficient: counts per differing library sizes model as \(\log \lambda = \eta + \log(\text{depth})\), i.e., modeling the rate not the raw count:

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
2. Concept Questions

Name the three ingredients of a GLM, and identify all three for (a) linear regression, (b) logistic regression, (c) Poisson regression.
β = 0.25 with a log link. State the effect in rate-ratio language, and in plain words if the baseline rate is 2.0.
Why does the Poisson assumption Var = mean matter inferentially — and what is the standard diagnostic when counts are more spread than that?
What does an offset do, when is it required, and why is log(depth) the offset rather than depth itself?
Your response is a proportion of successes out of varying n per row. Which GLM family and what structural detail of the fit?



Answers



Gaussian; η = β₀+β₁x; identity. (b) Bernoulli/Binomial; η; logit. (c) Poisson; η; log. Every classical regression is this triple — memorize the table, and new response types stop being new methods.

Each +1 in x multiplies the mean rate by e^0.25 ≈ 1.284 (+28.4%). At baseline 2.0: new rate ≈ 2.57 — the absolute jump grows with the baseline, which is exactly what multiplicative language encodes.
Poisson’s Var = mean enters the likelihood AND the SEs: if real counts are overdispersed (Var ≫ mean, near-universal in biology), GLM SEs are too small and p-values overconfident — by the same mechanism as 2.10’s equal-variance violation. Diagnostic: Pearson χ²/df ≫ 1; remedies: quasi-Poisson (robust SEs) or negative binomial — the default in differential-expression pipelines (Part 12’s T2 workflow).
An offset is a predictor with its coefficient fixed at 1: log λ = η + log(depth) ⇒ λ = depth × e^η — modeling rate per unit exposure. Required whenever observation effort/size varies (depths, person-years, areas). The log appears because the model is multiplicative: rate × exposure = count on the log scale becomes addition.
Binomial with a logit link, as a 2-column response (successes, failures) — sm.GLM(y, X, family=sm.families.Binomial()) with y = [successes, failures] per row — so each row’s variance follows its own n. A plain 0/1 logistic (3.3) is the n = 1 special case.

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Recover a rate model end-to-end: simulate hospital readmissions where each patient has an exposure (days, 1–30) and a covariate x (age, 30–80) with log-rate = −4 + 0.03·age. Fit the Poisson GLM with offset, interpret both parameters in plain words, predict the expected readmission count for a 65-year-old admitted for 10 days, and verify against the true rate.


Solution







Reading: baseline rate ≈ e^−4 ≈ 0.018/day at age 30 (intercept’s reference); each decade multiplies the daily rate by ≈ 1.35. The offset does the bookkeeping for follow-up time — the model speaks in rates, the data arrive as counts.

Exercise 2. Overdispersion forensics: generate counts with Var = 4× mean (negative binomial), fit (a) Poisson GLM, (b) quasi-Poisson (sm.families.Poisson() + scale='X2' — Pearson-scaled SEs), (c) negative binomial GLM. Compare the slope estimates (all ≈ unbiased) and the three SEs, and report each model’s p-value for the slope. Which models “know” the truth about uncertainty?


Solution







All three slopes agree (the mean model is fine); the Poisson SE is the liar — small p-value manufactured by pretending Var = mean. Quasi-Poisson (scaled SEs) and negative binomial (explicit variance function) restore honest uncertainty. In biology, always run the dispersion diagnostic before trusting a Poisson p-value.

Exercise 3. GLM diagnostics, Poisson edition: for the Exercise 1 setup, build the randomized-quantile or deviance-residual diagnostics: plot deviance residuals vs fitted and vs age; QQ-plot them; verify approximate normality of deviance residuals under correct specification. Then inject a mis-fit (drop the offset) and show which diagnostic screams first.


Solution







With the offset, deviance residuals look like N(0,1) noise (dispersion ≈ 1); without it, dispersion explodes (counts without their exposure correction look wildly inconsistent) and the residual-vs-fitted panel develops structure. The first diagnostic to scream: the dispersion ratio — it is the Poisson world’s heteroscedasticity check (2.10 analog).

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Log-link counts and zero observations: log(0) never appears in the model (the link acts on the mean, not on y) — but a manual log(y+1) OLS “fix” changes the estimand and breaks at different y’s. Model the counts with the right likelihood instead.
Overdispersion is the default state of biological counts — quasi-Poisson or negative binomial before any p-value is read (Exercise 2); the Poisson is a special-case claim, not a default.
Rate ratios vs risk ratios: with log links, e^β multiplies rates; converting to risk differences/ratios needs the baseline and horizon — the same translation discipline as 3.3’s odds ratios.
Offsets vs exposure covariates: an offset has coefficient fixed at 1; leaving exposure out entirely (or as a free coefficient) answers a different question — model the design, don’t average over it.
Complete separation’s cousin — zero cells: grouped binomial tables with all-success/all-failure strata destabilize fits; the same regularization/futility logic as 3.3 Exercise 2.
GLM SEs are inverse-Hessian (asymptotic): valid for n reasonably large; small-sample counts (few events) need exact/penalized methods — the rare-event caveat again.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated count analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


log(y+1) OLS: changes the estimand (now modeling log-counts, with the +1 bias), mishandles the count nature, and mixes depth in as a free coefficient on the wrong scale. Model rates with log link + offset.
Depth ignored: dose effect is confounded with sequencing effort — samples with higher depth have more counts regardless of dose. Fix: offset=np.log(depth) (or include log-depth as a covariate with free coefficient if effort itself needs modeling).
Dispersion unchecked: with Poisson SEs, significance claims are premature. Run Pearson chi²/df, scale or go negative binomial if ≫ 1.

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the Poisson GLM’s IRLS update and show its working response is \(z = \eta + (y - \mu)/\mu\) and its weight is \(w = \mu\). Use this to explain (a) why zero-count observations get high weight in the fit relative to OLS’s treatment of residuals, and (b) why the variance structure (w = μ) automatically produces the funnel-shaped raw residuals of Exercise-drill 2 — and why that funnel is correct behavior, not a violation.


Hint

For Poisson, Var(y) = μ; the IRLS weight is Var⁻¹ evaluated at the current μ; the working response is the linearization of the link.



Solution

With g = log, g′(μ) = 1/μ: working response z = g(μ) + (y − μ)g′(μ) = η + (y−μ)/μ; IRLS weight w = 1/(g′(μ)²Var) = μ. (a) A zero count at μ = 4 gives working residual (0−4)/4 = −1 — the same pull as a count of 8 (+1): the link scales residuals by 1/μ, so relative misses weigh equally; OLS would treat the count-0 miss (−4) as four times the count-8 miss — inverting the information content for heteroscedastic counts. (b) Raw residuals y−μ have SD √μ by construction: the funnel in raw residuals is the model passing its own variance assumption; only deviance/Pearson residuals (normalized) should look homoscedastic. Diagnosing raw GLM residuals with OLS eyes inverts the verdict.

Q2. A colleague fits a Poisson GLM to single-cell UMI counts (dropped-out, overdispersed, zero-inflated) and reports significant genes via Poisson p-values. Design the critique experiment: simulate zero-inflated negative-binomial counts with (a) no real genes and (b) 100 truly differential genes; run the Poisson pipeline; report false-positive rate and sensitivity. Then state which layer of the pipeline each problem (overdispersion, zero-inflation) belongs to, and what the standard production answer is (negative binomial with empirical dispersion — the DESeq2/edgeR view, previewing Part 12’s T2 workflow).


Solution







The Poisson pipeline flags null genes far above 5% (overdispersion + zero-inflation inflate the statistic) while missing many true effects. Layering: overdispersion is a variance-function misspecification (fix: NB/quasi-likelihood); zero-inflation is a mean-process mixture (fix: ZINB hurdle models, or aggregates/normalization strategies). Production pipelines (DESeq2/edgeR) use empirical-Bayes negative binomial dispersions across genes — the principle: share variance information across the feature family rather than trusting per-gene Poisson. Full treatment in 12.6 (T2).

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (GLM × 3.3 logistic × 2.7 interaction). Poisson model a count response with treatment × sex interaction on the log-rate scale. Show numerically that the interaction coefficient is a ratio of rate ratios — and that a significant multiplicative interaction can correspond to nearly identical absolute rate differences at low baselines. Produce the two-panel plot (rate ratio and rate difference by baseline) that would let a reviewer see both languages at once.
C2 (GLM × 2.4 model accuracy × 4.3 CV preview). Define and compute an out-of-sample deviance (or Poisson log-loss) for the readmission model of Exercise 1 across 5 folds, and compare in-sample vs CV deviance. What plays the role of R² here (hint: compare against the intercept-only GLM’s deviance)? This “explained deviance” is how GLM model accuracy is reported — practice computing it honestly.

title: 3.6 Generalized Linear Models
text:
7. Summary

GLM = family × linear predictor × link; logistic and linear regression are members; Poisson (counts, log link) is the workhorse you didn’t know you needed.
e^β = rate ratio; offsets convert counts to rates when exposure varies.
OLS on counts predicts negatives, misweights residuals, and misstates variance — the likelihood is the fix, not a transform.
Overdispersion (Pearson χ²/df ≫ 1) is biology’s default; quasi-Poisson/negative binomial before believing p-values.
Diagnostics: deviance residuals (not raw), dispersion ratio as the first alarm.
p ≫ n and rare events strain GLM SEs — regularization and exact methods await in Part 5.
Every model so far needs the same referee: how well does it predict new data, really? Part 4 begins: 4.1 The generalization problem.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text: K-nearest-neighbors classification votes: a query’s class is the majority class among its k nearest training points. No assumptions about distributions or boundaries — the data is the model. Combined with 2.9’s regression twin, this page completes the neighborhood-methods toolkit and its biases.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
1. Basic Concept
The algorithm at query \(x_0\):

Find the k nearest training points (any distance metric — Euclidean by default).
Output the majority class (or, usefully, the vote fraction as a probability estimate).

k is the flexibility dial: k = 1 draws maximal boundaries around every point (train accuracy 100%); k = n predicts the majority class everywhere.






The vote fraction doubles as a (crude) probability estimate — coarser as k grows:






Vote by hand once:

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is k = 1’s training accuracy always 100%, and what is the only thing its test performance demonstrates?
KNN “probabilities” from vote fractions take k+1 distinct values. What are the consequences for (a) calibration curves, (b) threshold tuning granularity?
Which KNN failure mode is shared with every distance-based method (2.9) and fixed identically?
In a 3-class problem with k = 4, what happens on ties, and name two resolutions.
Odd k is folk-wisdom for binary problems. Why does it not fully protect against ties in practice?



Answers


Each point is its own nearest neighbor, so training predictions are the training labels verbatim. Zero training error demonstrates memorization capacity — nothing about generalization; only held-out performance means anything (0.5).

Calibration plots show ≤ k+1 distinct predicted values — a step function, no fine calibration possible; (b) thresholds between adjacent vote levels do nothing — decision granularity is coarse (with k = 5, you cannot build a 60%-threshold classifier). Use larger k for finer probability resolution, or distance weighting.

Feature scaling — distance domination by large-range features. Fix identically: StandardScaler inside a pipeline, fitted per-fold (2.9, 0.5).
With k = 4, a 2–2 vote tie is possible (and 1–1–2 in 3 classes). Resolutions: use odd k; break ties by distance-weighted votes, by the closer class-sum, or by sklearn’s default (order/prior-based choice — check the docs, don’t assume).
Distances can tie exactly (identical/duplicated points, integer coordinates), and multiclass problems create majority-less splits at any k. Odd k reduces, not eliminates, ambiguity — know your library’s tie rule.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement multiclass KNN by hand with (a) majority vote, (b) distance-weighted vote (weights 1/d, aggregate per class, argmax), and verify both against sklearn on 25 random queries. Report one query where the two methods disagree and explain the neighborhood geometry that caused it.


Solution







Disagreements happen when the majority class sits marginally farther on average: uniform vote follows the count, weighted vote follows the close points. Both are defensible; the choice is part of the model.

Exercise 2. Boundary-artifact tour: for two Gaussian classes, plot k = 1, 3, 15 decision boundaries; then report test accuracy for each on a large fresh sample, together with train accuracy. Produce the k-vs-error table (train, test) and identify the overfitting/underfitting regions — then argue from the table which k you’d ship, and what extra experiment would firm that up.


Solution







k = 1: perfect train, visibly worse test (islands around single points). Test error bottoms in the mid-k range then climbs as neighborhoods straddle the true boundary. To ship a k: repeat across splits/CV and pick by mean test (or CV) error — the table from one split is indicative, not decisive (4.3).

Exercise 3. Curse-of-dimensionality face-off: signal in 3 of d dimensions (d = 3, 30, 300), n = 400 training points, KNN (CV-tuned k) vs penalized logistic regression; report CV-chosen k and test accuracies. Explain the k-trend with d and the reason logistic degrades gracefully — then state the dimension threshold past which you’d stop considering plain KNN for this data shape.


Solution







CV-chosen k grows with d (the only useful neighborhoods are huge), and KNN’s accuracy sags as neighborhoods stop being local; logistic’s linear score ignores the junk dimensions’ distances entirely and loses only mild precision from estimating extra coefficients. Threshold judgment call: for this linear-signal shape, KNN stops competing around d ≈ tens-to-hundreds — the exact number depends on signal strength and n, which is why the honest answer is “measure it by CV,” not folklore.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Evaluate with predict_proba, decide with costs: vote fractions are the model’s probability surrogate; their coarseness (Concept Question 2) makes fine thresholding impossible — a reason to prefer logistic when calibrated probabilities matter.
Scaling, always, inside the pipeline — the single most common KNN bug in the wild, shared with 2.9.
Multiclass ties: sklearn breaks count ties deterministically (order-dependent); make k odd per problem, prefer distance weighting, or aggregate with weights="distance" for smoother ties.
Duplicated points make distance ties and destabilize neighbor identity — deduplicate or add tiny jitter; also watch duplicated rows leaking across train/test (0.5 bug #3).
Prediction cost scales with training size (no model compression); KD-tree/ball-tree speedups decay in high d — for deployment-sized training sets, KNN is a service, not a function.
KNN’s boundary is not learnable features — nothing interpretable comes out; if a stakeholder asks “why classified so?”, the answer is a list of neighbor cases (which is sometimes exactly the right answer — case-based reasoning).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated classifier has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Train = test evaluation: k = 3 on its own training data reports memorization-flattered accuracy. Split first (0.5).
k tuned on training accuracy: k = 1 (or small) always wins that sweep — tune by CV within training.
Unscaled features: distances dominated by read counts (0–50,000); biomarker (the true signal, 0–1) is invisible. StandardScaler inside a pipeline.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that KNN’s training-set leave-one-out (LOO) error can be computed without refitting for every k simultaneously: sort each point’s distances once, then for each k count label agreement with the k-th neighbor set. Implement it and verify against cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(k), cv=KFold(n_splits=n))-style LOO for k = 1..15 on a small dataset. Why does the naive LOO shortcut not apply to logistic regression?


Hint

Removing a training point changes the neighbor sets only for queries near it; for the left-out point itself, its k neighbors are found among the remaining n−1 regardless of k.



Solution

For point i left out: its neighbors are drawn from the other n−1 points, and the k-NN prediction for i is determined by i’s distance ranks among those n−1 — computable from one sort of row i. Sweep k along the sorted row and tally agreement; one O(n²) pass yields LOO errors for every k. Verification:






Logistic refits coefficients on every LOO fold — leave-one-out changes the global fit, so no per-row shortcut exists. KNN’s locality (each prediction touches k points) is exactly what makes its LOO cheap; parametric fits are global and must be redone.

Q2. KNN’s vote fraction estimates P(y=1|x) with variance ≈ p(1−p)/k and bias whenever the class probability varies within the neighborhood. For 1-D data with a sharp probability transition at x = 5, quantify both effects empirically: for k ∈ {5, 25, 125}, estimate the bias of the vote-fraction estimate at x = 4.9 (true p ≈ 0.72) and its Monte-Carlo variance across 2,000 training sets. State the k that minimizes MSE at that point and how it shifts with the transition’s sharpness.


Solution







Small k: near-zero bias (neighborhood stays on one side of the transition), high variance. Large k: variance shrinks but bias grows as the neighborhood averages across the transition. The MSE-optimal k sits where the two curves cross — and as the transition sharpens (larger slope in the sigmoid), the bias term grows for every k, pushing the optimal k smaller. This local bias–variance diagram is the pointwise version of the global picture in 4.4.

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (KNN × 3.1 metrics × 3.7 preview). On a moderately imbalanced two-Gaussian problem, compare KNN (CV-tuned k), logistic, and LDA on both ROC-AUC and PR-AP, and plot both curve families on one figure per model. Which model’s advantage shrinks the most under the PR lens, and how does the coarse vote-fraction ladder of KNN explain its curve’s shape?
C2 (KNN × 4.6 tuning × 2.9). Jointly tune k and the distance-weighting scheme (uniform/distance) with GridSearchCV over a pipeline, then compare against tuning k alone at fixed uniform weights — honest nested estimates both times. Quantify the extra optimism the wider grid buys and state when the extra hyperparameter is worth its selection cost (connect to the selection-inflation experiments of 4.6).

title: 3.5 KNN Classification
text:
7. Summary

KNN classifies by neighborhood vote; k sets the smoothness, vote fractions are coarse probability estimates.
k = 1 memorizes (train acc 1.0); k = n = majority class; test error is U-shaped in k.
Scaling inside a pipeline is non-negotiable; ties, duplicates, and even-k quirks need explicit policy.
The curse of dimensionality caps KNN’s reach; linear/penalized models degrade more gracefully in high d.
LOO errors for all k come free from one distance sort — locality has computational perks.
Pointwise, vote-fraction MSE balances bias (wide neighborhoods across transitions) against variance (few voters).
Several classifiers now produce scores; the question becomes comparing and calibrating them: 3.7 Classification model comparison.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text: Instead of shrinking coefficients, shrink the feature space: summarize correlated predictors by a few derived directions, then regress on those. PCR builds directions from the predictors alone (PCA); PLS builds them using y. Both trade interpretability of individual coefficients for stability under extreme collinearity — and their contrast is a masterclass in supervised vs unsupervised thinking.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
1. Basic Concept
PCR recipe: standardize X → PCA on X → keep the first M principal components → regress y on those M scores. The only new hyperparameter is M. PLS recipe: same pipeline, but directions are chosen to maximize covariance with y, not variance within X.






PLS, same data — and a first contrast:






The pathological case — signal hidden in a low-variance direction, where the two methods diverge:

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
2. Concept Questions

PCR with M = p (all components, after standardizing) reproduces which estimator exactly? What does that make M, in bias–variance language?
Why must PCA inside PCR be fit on training folds only? Which page’s law is this?
PLS’s first direction maximizes Cov(Xw, y). In one sentence, why can that find the tiny-variance signal that PCR’s first component cannot?
You interpret “component 1 loading +0.5 on gene A” — what stops you from reading it as “gene A’s effect is +0.5”?
Ridge also damps low-variance directions (5.2 SVD view). What is PCR’s version of the same move, and what’s the essential difference?



Answers


OLS on standardized features: keeping all p orthogonal components loses no information, and the regression on full PCA scores equals OLS. M is a pure flexibility dial — M = 0 is the mean-model, M = p is OLS (4.4’s dial again).
PCA is fitted from X — including validation rows’ means/structure; fitting it on all data leaks fold information into training (0.5, 4.3). The Pipeline mechanic enforces it.
PCR ranks directions by X’s internal variance; PLS’s criterion explicitly includes y, so a direction with little X-variance but strong y-relationship wins PLS’s first slot while it lands at the bottom of PCR’s list.
Components are rotations: loadings mix all features with sign/convention freedom, and the component’s coefficient (not the loading) carries the y-relationship, itself shrunken by the regression on scores. Individual-feature effects are unrecoverable without rotating back — interpret the component as a measurement direction, not a mechanism.
PCR truncates small-variance directions (keeps M, drops the rest); ridge damps them smoothly (factor s²/(s²+λ)). Same SVD backdrop (5.2 Q1), hard vs soft; both are blind to y when choosing what to suppress — PLS is the supervised cousin.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. PCR vs OLS under extreme collinearity: n = 50, p = 10, built from 2 latent factors + noise (so the effective rank is ≈ 2–4). Compare: OLS, PCR with M chosen by CV, and ridge with α chosen by CV. Report nested test MSEs via the outer-loop discipline of 4.6. Rank them and explain the ordering in terms of what each does to the noisy small directions.


Solution







OLS trails badly (10 nearly-collinear columns: maximal variance waste), PCR and ridge land close — both suppress the small directions, one by truncation, one by damping. When the effective rank is tiny, M ≈ 2–4 and PCR is essentially “ridge with a hard cutoff.”

Exercise 2. The supervised-vs-unsupervised contrast, swept: construct the Section 1 pathological geometry at three signal-to-noise ratios (tiny-direction coefficient c ∈ {5, 20, 60} with direction SD 0.1). For each, compute CV-MSE of PCR(M=1), PCR(M chosen by CV), PLS(M=1). At which c does PCR’s CV finally pick M = 2 — and what does that tell you about using X-internal criteria to hunt y-relevant structure?


Solution







Only when the tiny direction’s signal grows loud enough does CV promote M = 2 (and PCR’s error collapses to PLS-like levels) — the X-internal criterion needed rescue from the y to notice relevance. PLS(1) is insensitive to c’s scale (it locks onto the covariance immediately). Moral: unsupervised compression is a bet that variance = relevance; PLS/weak supervision is the hedge.

Exercise 3. Interpretation audit: fit PCR (M = 2) on a dataset with known truth (y = 3x₁ − x₄ + noise, all features independent so loadings are readable). Report (a) the component loadings, (b) the regression coefficients on components, (c) the reconstructed per-feature coefficients β̂ = V·γ (rotate back), compared to OLS’s coefficients. Then explain to a collaborator why (c) is legitimate for describing the fitted model while per-feature p-values remain unavailable.


Solution







Rotation back through V is exact algebra for the fitted model — the two parameterizations predict identically, so (c) is the honest per-feature description of what PCR actually fit (and with independent features it lands close to OLS, modulo the dropped components’ shrinkage). What’s not available: standard errors/p-values per feature — the components were data-chosen, and the truncation shares information across features (5.1’s post-selection caution, rotated).

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The Pipeline discipline is existential here: PCA is fitted from X, so fitting it before splitting leaks validation structure into training — the most common PCR bug in the wild (0.5).
Standardize before PCA unless features share natural units and scale: PCA’s variance-ranking is unit-dependent (5.2’s standardization law, inherited).
M is chosen by CV, not by scree plots: “keep components covering 90% variance” optimizes X-description, not y-prediction — the whole lesson of Exercise 2.
PLS with M = p ≈ OLS but is numerically optimized sequentially; don’t treat its M = p endpoint as an identity to 12 decimals.
PLS’s coefficients and loadings are even harder to read than PCR’s (directions tilted toward y, deflation between steps); report predictions and component meanings, not per-feature stories.
Scaling of y matters in PLS (its criterion is covariance-based): unlike PCR, y-scaling shifts PLS’s path — set scale=True defaults consciously.
Both are linear-in-components: nonlinear structure needs basis expansion first (2.8) or the tree/kernel machinery of later parts.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated PCR pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


PCA fit on all rows: test-set means/variances/components shaped the training inputs — leakage (4.3). PCA goes inside the pipeline.
Scree-chosen M: variance covered in X ≠ prediction of y; M is a hyperparameter for CV (Concept Question 3, Exercise 2).
No standardization: columns with big units dominate components; PCA on raw features ranks measurement choices, not structure. StandardScaler first.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove PCR’s M = p equivalence with OLS (after standardization): the PCA scores are X·V where V is the orthogonal loading matrix, and regressing y on X·V with all p components yields coefficients γ = Vᵀβ̂_OLS, so predictions V·γ = β̂_OLS·X exactly. Then explain why the equivalence breaks when M < p is chosen by CV on the same data used to report OLS’s R² — and what that asymmetry means for comparing methods on training data.


Hint

Rotations preserve column spaces: span(XV) = span(X). For M < p, the fitted models are different projections — and any comparison computed in-sample is dominated by each model’s own optimism.



Solution

With standardized X = USVᵀ, scores Z = XV span the same space as X; OLS on Z fits the same projection of y, hence identical fitted values/R² (γ = Vᵀβ̂ rotates back exactly). For M < p, PCR projects y onto a subspace — a different, shrunken model; comparing its training R² to OLS’s is meaningless because each number carries its own optimism (p + 1 vs M + 1 parameters’ worth, per 4.1 Q1). All method comparisons must happen out-of-fold — the asymmetric lesson being that in-sample tables systematically flatter the most flexible method (OLS) precisely where regularization is needed most.

Q2. PLS’s first direction solves \(\max_w \text{Cov}^2(Xw, y)\) subject to ‖w‖ = 1 (NIPALS essentially does power iteration on XᵀyyᵀX). Verify numerically on a small problem: compare sklearn’s first x_weights_ to the dominant eigenvector of XᵀyyᵀX (standardized), and to the OLS direction β̂_OLS/‖β̂_OLS‖. When do the PLS and OLS directions coincide (construct the case), and what does the mismatch measure?


Hint

XᵀyyᵀX = (Xᵀy)(Xᵀy)ᵀ is rank one → its dominant eigenvector IS Xᵀy (∝ the OLS direction when columns are standardized and uncorrelated).



Solution

For a single component, PLS’s criterion has closed form w ∝ Xᵀy — exactly the OLS direction’s shape. With uncorrelated standardized columns, XᵀX = I makes Xᵀy the OLS coefficient vector itself, so PLS(1) and OLS point the same way; correlations tilt PLS toward high-covariance blocks and away from OLS’s precision.






The alignment to XᵀyyᵀX’s eigenvector is exact (both are ±Xᵀy); the OLS alignment is exact only under uncorrelated design — the discrepancy is PLS trading OLS’s per-coordinate optimality for direction stability under collinearity, which is precisely its selling point.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (PCR/PLS × 5.2–5.4). The shrinkage family reunion: on one collinear dataset (effective rank 3, p = 20), compare ridge, lasso, net, PCR(CV-M), PLS(CV-M) by outer-nested CV. Then produce the “complexity profile” of each chosen model: ridge’s effective df, lasso’s support size, PCR/PLS’s M. Rank methods by (a) accuracy and (b) interpretability of the complexity measure. Which pair would you present to a review board that demands “number of dimensions used” — and why does that question favor PCR/PLS even at equal MSE?
C2 (PCR × 9.2 PCA stub × 4.4 bias–variance). Measure PCR’s bias–variance decomposition across M (the 4.4 multi-training-set protocol, M ∈ 1..p on a low-rank truth). Confirm the U-curve in M, identify whether bias or variance dominates at M = 1 for (a) latent-factor truths (Section 1 style), (b) the pathological low-variance-signal truth. The two panels are the argument for PLS — write the caption.

title: 5.5 PCR and PLS
text:
7. Summary

PCR: PCA on X, regress on the top M scores; M = p recovers OLS, M is the flexibility dial.
PLS: directions chosen by covariance with y — supervised compression that finds low-variance signal PCR cannot.
Both need standardization, in-pipeline fitting, and CV-chosen M (never scree).
Hard truncation vs ridge’s soft damping — same SVD stage, different smoothing of the same idea.
Component loadings are rotations, not effects; per-feature inference stays unavailable (or rotated and caveated).
The pathological direction experiment is the method-selection decision tree in miniature: variance-blind (PCR/ridge) vs y-aware (PLS/lasso).
When p truly dwarfs n — thousands of features, dozens of rows — every choice here gets sharper consequences: 5.6 High-dimensional data.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text: When predictors outnumber good ideas, you must choose a subset — for prediction parsimony, for interpretability, or for cheaper deployment. Feature selection is where statistics meets 4.6 Tuning: a feature set is a hyperparameter, and selecting it on the data you report on is the oldest self-deception in the field.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three families of selection:

Subset selection — search discrete subsets (best-subset by enumeration, forward/backward stepwise), score each by Cp/AIC/BIC or CV.
Filter methods — rank features by a univariate statistic (correlation, F-score), keep the top k.
Embedded methods — selection as a by-product of fitting (lasso’s zeros, 5.3; trees’ split choices, Part 7).

Mallows’ \(C_p\) scores a model with \(d\) fitted parameters by trading fit against size:
\[C_p = \frac{1}{n}\big(\text{RSS} + 2\,d\,\hat\sigma^2\big)\]
— training error plus a \(2\sigma^2/n\)-per-parameter optimism charge (the quantity derived in 4.1 Q1).
Best subset by brute force, scored by \(C_p\), on a small truth:






Filters and CV-tuned selection — the honest one-line production version (selection inside the folds, per 4.3):

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does adding \(2d\hat\sigma^2\) to RSS (per 2.4) make \(C_p\) a fairer comparator than raw RSS?
Forward vs backward stepwise: name one setting where each fails to find the best subset.
Why can’t you compute p-values from the final selected model in the usual way, after the selection used those same p-values?
What is selection instability, and what does it predict about two labs running identical stepwise on their own data?
Your filter keeps the 5 features with the strongest marginal correlation with y. Name two kinds of variables this rule can miss.



Answers


Raw RSS only falls as features join (2.4’s noise-collector theorem). \(C_p\) adds the expected optimism, ≈ 2σ²d/n, so models are compared on their estimated test error — noise columns now lose.
Forward fails when a variable is useless alone but essential in pairs (its first step never picks it; the famous XOR-style trap). Backward fails when p ≥ n — the full model can’t even be fitted (singular design).
The selection step picked the covariates because they looked good in this sample; the post-selection p-values then test “is this good-looking feature good?” on the same data that chose it — double use of the evidence. Valid post-selection inference needs special machinery (or sample splitting: select on half, infer on the rest).
The set of selected features varies wildly across resamples of the same population when features are correlated. Prediction: each lab reports a different “top biomarkers” list with similar performance — a reproducibility red flag that screams correlated features + overfit selection.

Suppressor/joint variables — useless marginally, essential jointly (their combination carries the signal). (b) Low-marginal-but-nonlinear contributors, or features whose signal cancels a confounder’s — anything where the marginal projection hides the conditional effect (2.5 Q2’s suppressor story).

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement forward stepwise from scratch: start empty; at each step add the feature whose inclusion most reduces RSS; stop when no addition improves \(C_p\). Run it on the Section 1 dataset. Report the selected set and each step’s Cp. Which step would BIC (heavier penalty, \(\log n\) per parameter) have stopped at?


Solution







Forward picked the true pair, then stopped when Cp plateaued. Under BIC’s \(\log n\)-per-parameter penalty the second variable sometimes fails to clear the bar at small n — penalty choice is a statement about how much you fear false positives vs missed variables.

Exercise 2. Selection-on-training vs leakage: build a 20-feature, 5-signal dataset (n = 150). Evaluate two pipelines by nested CV: (a) SelectKBest(k=5) fitted on all data first, then CV the logistic model on the pre-filtered matrix; (b) the identical selection inside the pipeline via GridSearchCV. Report both accuracies and the gap — this is feature-selection leakage priced in dollars.


Solution







The leaky number is a mirage: the CV folds’ validation rows voted on which features matter. With weaker signal or fewer samples the gap widens; with abundant signal it vanishes — which is exactly why the bug survives in careless labs (4.3’s rule 6).

Exercise 3. The filter-vs-joint failure, constructed: build data where x₁ and x₂ are independent noise marginally uncorrelated with y, but y depends on their product (interaction: \(y = 2\,x_1 x_2\,u\), u noise). Run SelectKBest(f_regression, k=2) — check whether either is chosen; then fit a model with the engineered feature \(x_1 x_2\) included and compare test MSE against the filter+OLS pipeline. State the design lesson in one sentence.


Solution







Marginal filters are projections onto single axes (2.5): interaction signal lives in the product direction, invisible to any per-feature score. Lesson: filters are cheap shortlists for enormous p, never the final selection procedure — and interaction-aware search or embedded methods (lasso on an engineered basis, trees) must take over where marginal views end.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Selection is part of the model. Anything chosen from the data — features, transformations (2.8), bin edges — must be re-derivable inside each CV fold, or your performance number describes a model that never existed.
Stepwise p-value thresholds (“add if p < 0.05”) are not tests and don’t control any error rate; they’re heuristics with unknown operating characteristics. Prefer explicit penalties (Cp/AIC/BIC) or CV — quantities with definitions.
Post-selection inference is a real research area (selective inference, data carving) because naive SEs after stepwise/lasso are wrong in ways that matter. The pragmatic default: split-sample — select on half, fit and infer on the other half, at the cost of power.
Selection frequency is the report: with correlated features, print selection frequencies across bootstraps/subsamples (drill 4) instead of one cherry-picked set; a feature selected 55% of the time is a different claim from 99%.
Filters buy speed at truth’s expense: at p = 500,000 univariate screens are the only affordable first pass — but always validate the shortlist jointly, and expect to miss interaction/suppressor structure (Exercise 3).
Unstable selection often means collinearity (2.5): when two features share signal, subset selection coin-flips between them; ridge-style shrinkage or elastic net’s grouping (5.4) is the structural fix.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Selection before CV — the folds’ validation labels picked the features. Selection belongs inside the pipeline.
Downstream CV of a pre-filtered matrix inherits bug 1; the number is inflated by the selection’s peek at every row.
Univariate p < 0.05 over 15 features is ~0–1 expected false positives with NO FDR guarantee — that’s raw multiplicity (12.4 preview); FDR requires explicit q-value/BH procedure over the full tested set.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that selecting the single feature with the largest |t-statistic| from M pure-noise features yields a feature whose in-sample |correlation| has expected value ≈ √(2 log M / n), and verify by simulation for n = 50, M = 1000. What does this tell you about “the top feature explains R² of the selected model” claims?


Hint

The max of M i.i.d. half-normals scales like √(2 log M) — the same order statistic that drove 4.6 Q1’s selection bonus.



Solution

Under the null each sample correlation is ≈ N(0, 1/n); the largest |r| among M is the max of M half-normal draws, whose expectation ≈ √(2 log M / n). Simulation:






≈ 0.38 correlation with pure noise — an in-sample R² near 0.14 for a feature that has nothing. Any “top feature” narrative built on in-sample fit of selected candidates inherits this order-statistic fiction; out-of-sample evaluation is the only corrective.

Q2. Design the stability-selection procedure: given a selection algorithm, sample B subsamples (half the rows), record each feature’s selection frequency, and keep features selected in ≥ π (say 0.6) of subsamples. Implement it for forward selection on the Section 1 data (with correlated features added), report the frequency table, and explain (a) why high threshold controls false selections, (b) why correlated true features can also fail the threshold — and what that asymmetry means for your final claim.


Solution








A noise feature must beat the field in 60% of half-samples — vanishingly unlikely under the null (each has ~50% coin-flip chances, compounded downward). (b) x1 and x3 are both true (x3 inherits signal through correlation) yet each is selected only when the subsample’s noise favors it over its twin — both can hover near 50% and miss a 0.6 threshold. The asymmetry: the procedure certifies unique contributors and abstains on interchangeable ones — which is honest reporting (say “x1 or its proxy x3”), not a flaw.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (selection × 4.6 tuning × 12.x stub). Unify the three selection paradigms on one dataset: k chosen by CV (filter), λ chosen by CV (lasso, 5.3 — implement with LassoCV), and Cp-based best subset — all nested inside a common outer 5-fold loop measuring the whole procedure’s test MSE. Which procedure’s outer error is lowest, and how does the ranking change if you compare their inner best scores instead? This experiment is the practical proof of “selection procedures must be evaluated as procedures.”
C2 (selection × 1.5 resampling). Bootstrap the entire selected-model pipeline (resample rows → re-run forward selection → predict at a fixed x₀) and produce a predictive distribution rather than a feature list. Then compare its 95% interval to the naive interval from the one selected model (formula SEs, ignoring selection). Quantify the undercoverage of the naive interval empirically over 200 true-data draws — this is post-selection uncertainty made visible.

title: 5.1 Feature Selection
text:
7. Summary

Selection has three families — subset, filter, embedded — and one law: selection is data-dependent, so it lives inside validation loops.
Cp/AIC/BIC convert fit into estimated test error; CV does it without σ̂² or parametric assumptions.
Forward fails on joint variables; backward fails when p ≥ n; filters fail on suppressors and interactions.
Post-selection p-values are fiction; use split-sample selection or specialized selective inference.
Selection instability across resamples is diagnostic (collinearity) and reportable (selection frequencies).
The max-of-M order statistic manufactures in-sample stars from pure noise — 4.1 everywhere.
Continuous selection — penalties instead of subsets — is smoother and scales to p ≫ n: 5.2 Ridge regression.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text: Genomics asked statistics a question it wasn’t built for: 20,000 features, 40 samples. In the p ≫ n regime every rule from Part 2 inverts — OLS fits perfectly and means nothing, R² = 1 is the default state of noise, and the disciplines of Parts 4–5 stop being best practice and become survival equipment.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three structural facts define the regime:

Interpolation is guaranteed: p ≥ n means a hyperplane through every training point exists — training error = 0 always (4.1).
Classical inference collapses: OLS SEs need df = n − p − 1 > 0; with p ≥ n there are no residual degrees of freedom, so no σ̂², no t-tests, no F-tests.
Selection is unavoidable: you cannot “use all features” — some reduction (penalty, components, filters) is mathematically mandatory.

The R² = 1 noise miracle, witnessed:






The regime’s survival kit, applied to a realistic simulation (n = 60 patients, p = 400 genes, 6 truly active):

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why exactly are there no residual degrees of freedom when p ≥ n, and which downstream quantities die first as p approaches n?
Your colleague reports an OLS on 200 samples with 500 covariates and “significant” adjusted R² of 0.95. Name the three disqualifications.
Why does CV become more important in p ≫ n — and what special care does stratification/selection need here?
Lasso can select at most n features when p ≫ n. You need “the” biomarker panel of 12. Is lasso’s 12-feature selection from 5,000 candidates trustworthy as a discovery list?
Distance-based methods (KNN, 2.9) fail hardest in high dimensions. Why, and which Part 5 tools repair them?



Answers


df = n − (p + 1); it hits 0 at p = n − 1. σ̂² = RSS/(n − p − 1) becomes 0/0 or negative → every t-test, F-test, CI, RSE, and Cp/AIC penalty built on σ̂² dies in sequence.

p > n: the fit interpolates — R² is 1 by construction, not by skill; (2) adjusted R²’s formula assumes p ≪ n and is garbage in this regime; (3) “significant” claims require SEs, which don’t exist (Concept 1). The 0.95 is the interpolation identity wearing a suit.

Because model selection (which penalty, which features, which M) now carries the whole burden — with no unpenalized fallback, tuning choices dominate the outcome, so the selection must be honest and repeated (4.3). Selection stability across folds/resamples must be reported because single supports are noise.
No. It’s one arbitrary draw from a near-tie set of correlated candidates (5.1 instability, 5.3 twins); the defensible products are (a) its predictive performance (nested CV), (b) selection frequencies across resamples — never a fixed “panel of 12” narrative.
High-dimensional distances concentrate: nearest and farthest neighbors converge (2.9’s curse), so neighborhoods stop being local. Repair: reduce dimension first (PCR directions, 5.5), or select features so distances are computed in the signal subspace — both are Part 5 tools.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The p/n frontier, mapped: fix n = 100 and sweep p ∈ {10, 50, 100, 200, 500} with a fixed 5-signal truth (signals in the first 5 features when p allows; extra features pure noise). For each p, report OLS train R², OLS test R², and RidgeCV’s test R². Where does OLS’s train R² hit 1.0, and how does each method’s test performance degrade with p? State the “usable dimensionality” rule of thumb this table supports.


Solution







Train R² pins to 1.0 exactly at p = n; OLS’s test R² turns negative beyond and stays dead. Ridge degrades gracefully, retaining real predictive value even at p = 5n. Rule of thumb: unpenalized regression is defensible while p stays a small fraction of n (and effects are strong); the moment p/n ≳ 0.5, penalized methods are the toolset, full stop.

Exercise 2. Selection stability at genomic scale: n = 50, p = 300, 8 true genes. Run LassoCV selection on 100 bootstrap resamples; report (a) how often each true gene is selected, (b) how often each of the top-5 most frequently selected noise genes is selected, (c) the median support size. Then compute the overlap of consecutive supports (Jaccard). Write the two-sentence methods paragraph reporting this honestly — the paragraph your genomics paper needs.


Solution







True genes are selected often (but not always — power at n = 50); several noise genes cross 20–40% selection by chance, and consecutive supports overlap only partially. Honest paragraph: “Lasso selection at CV-chosen penalization was repeated across 100 bootstrap resamples. Features are ranked by selection frequency; we report the full frequency table rather than a fixed panel, noting that individual supports are unstable under resampling (median support size X, mean pairwise Jaccard Y). Predictive performance was assessed by nested cross-validation.”

Exercise 3. The full high-dimensional workflow, end to end: n = 80 patients, p = 600 genes, outcome binary (case/control, 40/40), driven by 5 genes with moderate effect. Build and honestly evaluate: standardize → lasso-logistic (C tuned by inner CV) → outer 5-fold stratified CV → report AUC, plus selection frequencies per gene across outer folds. Then answer: which single number in your report is the performance claim, and which artifact is the exploratory output?


Solution







The performance claim is the outer-CV AUC with its SD — that number prices the whole procedure including feature selection. The gene list (and its frequencies) is exploratory: it generates hypotheses for validation in fresh cohorts, and its instability across folds is exactly why frequencies, not a fixed list, get reported. Conflating the two — quoting the AUC and presenting the support as discovered truth — is the p ≫ n era’s signature overreach.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

No unpenalized fallback exists: in p ≥ n, “just fit OLS” is not an option, so the entire modeling decision space is Part 5’s — penalty family, strength, and preprocessing are the model.
Batch effects and unwanted variation are high-dimensional biology’s confounders: they correlate with thousands of features at once and dominate PCA/lasso if uncorrected — normalization/combat-style adjustment precedes everything (and must itself live inside CV for honest evaluation).
Multiplicity is ambient: 20,000 genes ⇒ 20,000 implicit tests even before you “test” anything; every marginal screen needs FDR machinery (12.4 stub), and lasso-style joint selection needs stability reporting (5.1).
Prediction ≠ discovery, twice over: the selected genes are not validated by the model’s AUC (they rode along with it); conversely, a well-validated model can consist mostly of non-causal tags. State which claim each result supports.
Effective sample size may be smaller than n: correlated samples (related patients, batches, repeated measures) shrink n below its nominal value exactly when you need every row — the grouped-splitting discipline of 4.3 applies to the units, not rows.
Double descent’s home turf: at p ≈ n test error peaks, and overparameterized interpolators can descend again (4.4 Q2) — a real phenomenon, but not a license: the descent region’s gains are model-specific and modest relative to just collecting more samples.
Reporting standards: n, p, prevalence, penalty family, tuning grid, inner/outer CV protocol, selection frequencies, and a null-simulation calibration check. If any is missing, the result isn’t reproducible.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “biomarker study” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


OLS at p ≫ n: the 1.0000 train R² is the interpolation identity; no SEs exist; the fit is meaningless.
Screen-then-fit on the same rows: with a null outcome, this manufactures “hits” with inflated in-sample R² — the entire result is the selection’s shadow (5.1 Exercise 2).
Discovery claim from marginal p < 0.05 over 800 tests: expect ~40 false positives at this rate; no FDR control, no validation, no stability — nothing supports the word “identified.”

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the expected training R² under the null for OLS with n rows and p ≤ n−1: using E[RSS] = (n − p − 1)σ² (errors dominate), show E[R²] ≈ p/(n − 1). Verify by simulation across a p-sweep, and connect the formula to (a) the adjusted-R² penalty, (b) why train R² = p/n-lookalikes certify nothing in high dimensions.


Hint

TSS ≈ (n−1)σ² under the null; RSS ≈ (n−p−1)σ²; R² = 1 − RSS/TSS → p/(n−1).



Solution

Under the null (y independent of X), OLS consumes p + 1 df on noise: E[RSS] = (n − p − 1)σ², and TSS ≈ (n − 1)σ², so E[R²] = 1 − (n − p − 1)/(n − 1) = p/(n − 1).







Adjusted R² subtracts exactly this noise inflation (that’s its whole job — and why its derivation assumes p ≪ n). (b) In the p ≈ n regime the “explained variance” of a null fit approaches 1 — every in-sample goodness number is the complexity charge in disguise, and only out-of-sample estimates retain meaning.


Q2. You must choose between two p ≫ n studies to trust: Study A reports a 15-gene panel selected by lasso with CV AUC 0.84; Study B reports the same genes independently validated (AUC 0.71) in an external cohort of 200 samples. Construct the argument (with a mini-simulation if useful) for why B’s lower AUC is the stronger scientific claim, and design the combined analysis you’d actually run given both datasets (selection in A, frozen evaluation in B, then pooled refit with stability reporting).


Solution

A’s 0.84 prices selection adaptivity but lives on n = 40-ish effective samples and resampling within one dataset — its CI covers optimistic territory (selection bonus + small-n noise + any batch structure). B’s 0.71 is a pre-registered (frozen-panel) evaluation on fresh rows: no selection degrees of freedom, so 0.71 is a claim about the world, not the procedure. Simulation sketch:






The transfer number typically sits below the internal number (selection + small-n optimism) yet carries more evidential weight. Combined analysis: tune/choose on A (or pooled inner folds), freeze, evaluate on B untouched; finally refit on all data and report per-gene selection frequencies across resamples — with the two datasets’ batch structures declared. The hierarchy of evidence: frozen external validation > internal nested CV > internal CV of the selected model > anything with “significant” and p ≫ n in the same sentence.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (p ≫ n × 5.2–5.5 family reunion). At n = 60, p = 800 (latent-factor truth, 8 active features, duplicate-block structure): run the complete Part 5 tournament — ridge, lasso, net, PCR, PLS — each tuned inside an outer CV. Deliver (a) the accuracy table, (b) each winner’s complexity measure (effective df / support size / M), (c) selection stability for the sparse methods. Write the discussion paragraph: which method would you pre-register for the next cohort, and what information would justify changing?
C2 (p ≫ n × 12.4 FDR stub × 3.1.5 AUPRC). Connect the two selection languages: run a marginal screen (p-values for 1,000 features under a sparse truth), apply BH-FDR at q = 0.05 to get a “significant” set, then run LassoCV selection on the same data. Compare the two feature sets (size, truth overlap) and their precision (fraction true). Show that lasso’s support behaves like a data-adaptive FDR-thresholded set — and identify the condition (strong signal, weak correlation) under which the vocabularies coincide, previewing Part 12’s formal treatment.

title: 5.6 High-Dimensional Data
text:
7. Summary

p ≥ n: interpolation guaranteed, R² = 1 meaningless, residual df gone — inference and unpenalized fitting are off the table.
E[train R²] ≈ p/(n−1) under the null: in-sample numbers measure complexity, not discovery.
Survival kit: penalized regression (ridge/lasso/net), direction methods (PCR/PLS), filters — all inside honest nested CV.
Selection in this regime is unstable by nature; report frequencies and validation, never fixed panels as discoveries.
Frozen external validation outranks every internal number; batch/unwanted variation and unit-level splitting are design-level duties.
The p ≫ n workflow’s product is a calibrated claim: performance for prediction, hypotheses for discovery, never both from one number.
Part 5 closes the classical toolkit. Next the models bend shape — polynomials, splines and smoothing in Part 6 — then trees, SVMs, and unsupervised structure beginning with the PCA depths at 9.2 PCA.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text: K-means partitions data into k groups by minimizing within-cluster distance to centroids: pick k centers, assign points to the nearest, move each center to its cluster’s mean, repeat. It is fast, scalable, universally available — and explicitly assumes spherical, equal-sized groups. Knowing exactly what it optimizes tells you exactly when it lies.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
1. Basic Concept
The objective (inertia):
\[\min_{C_1, \ldots, C_k} \sum_{j=1}^k \sum_{i \in C_j} \|x_i - \mu_j\|^2, \qquad \mu_j = \text{mean of cluster } j\]
Lloyd’s algorithm alternates assign↔︎update until convergence — each step never increases inertia, so it converges (to a local optimum; hence n_init restarts):






Lloyd’s algorithm, by hand:

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does K-means implicitly assume spherical, equal-variance, equal-size clusters — derive each from the Euclidean-distance-to-centroid criterion?
