Why must centroids be initialized well (n_init, k-means++), and what does Lloyd’s convergence guarantee not include?
Elbow vs silhouette vs gap statistic for choosing k: state what each measures and their shared blind spot.
Your feature is “income” in dollars and another is “age” in years. What happens to the clustering, and why is this the same disease as 9.1 Exercise 1?
K-means on data with one categorical feature encoded as integers (0, 1, 2)? What breaks, and what are the two standard repairs?



Answers


The criterion cares only about distance to the centroid (a single point): (a) elongated clusters get split (a long ellipse has far corners even with one true group — variance in every direction costs); (b) unequal variances misassign (the wide cluster’s points sit “closer” to the tight neighbor’s centroid); (c) unequal sizes bias boundary placement toward the big cluster (6.2-style bias, Voronoi edition).
Lloyd’s converges to a local optimum — bad inits (two centers in one true cluster) converge to poor partitions that still satisfy the fixed point. n_init restarts take the best; k-means++ seeds centers far apart probabilistically — better optima, fewer restarts.
Elbow: inertia vs k, look for the bend (subjective; inertia always falls). Silhouette: mean (b−a)/max(a,b) per point — cohesion vs separation (−1..1, computable, biased toward convex shapes). Gap statistic: inertia vs its null-expectation under uniform sampling (principled, costlier). Shared blind spot: all measure spherical-metric fit — none can tell you the true k for structured/non-spherical data.
Dollars dominate Euclidean distance by units — income decides everything, age is invisible. Same disease: unscaled features weight the metric; standardize (or weight features deliberately).
Integer-coded categories fabricate arithmetic: category 2 is “twice” category 1 and between 0 and 3 — the centroid becomes a meaningless average label. Repairs: one-hot the categorical (then distances are Hamming-ish on that block) or use k-modes/mixed-type distances (9.6).

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Init sensitivity, quantified: for the 3-blob data, run K-means with n_init=1 over 200 different random seeds; record the final inertia and cluster quality (ARI). Plot the histogram of inertias — how many distinct optima exist, and what fraction of seeds found the global one? Then rerun with k-means++ (init="k-means++") and report the same. What does n_init=10 default buy you?


Solution







Random init finds the global optimum only some fraction of the time — the rest converge to split-cluster/merge-cluster locals with visibly worse inertia. k-means++ seeding (far-apart probabilistic starts) hits the global basin nearly always, which is why it’s the modern default and why n_init remains as insurance.

Exercise 2. Choosing k with three judges: for data with a planted k* = 4 (unequal weights), compute for k ∈ 2..9: (a) inertia (elbow by eye + second-difference knee detection), (b) mean silhouette, (c) a mini gap statistic (compare inertia to the mean inertia of uniform data in the same bounding box, B = 20 draws). Report the table and each judge’s verdict. Where do they disagree, and which do you trust for the final claim — with what supporting evidence?


Solution







The three judges typically agree on the planted k here, but through different evidence: silhouette peaks (separation quality), gap spikes (vs null), inertia elbows (rate change). When they disagree: silhouette/gap answer “is this partition defensible”, the elbow answers “where do returns vanish” — for a claim (“there are 4 groups”), demand the stability evidence of 9.1 Exercise 2 on top: no single index crowns k.

Exercise 3. Break it three ways, then fix what’s fixable: (a) two moons (hand-rolled crescents), (b) three clusters with wildly different variances, (c) one big uniform blob with 5% far outliers. For each: K-means k = true-k ARI, then the best repair among {more clusters + merge, K-means on PCA-2 (9.2), scaling tweaks, or “wrong tool — use a different family”}. Write the diagnosis-to-algorithm mapping sentence for each.


Solution








Non-convex truth: K-means’ Voronoi cells cannot represent crescents — change algorithm family (spectral, DBSCAN), not hyperparameters. (b) Shape/size assumption: Gaussian mixtures relax K-means’s hard spherical prior while staying in the centroid family. (c) Outliers hijack centroids (a single far point is its own “cluster’s” gravity) — outlier removal/detection is a preprocessing obligation. The mapping sentence: diagnose which assumption fails — convexity, variance-equality, or outlier-freedom — and switch algorithms at that assumption, not at the accuracy number.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

K-means is a special case of a Gaussian mixture (equal spherical covariances, hard assignment) — GMMs (Exercise 3b) are the generalization when clusters differ in shape/size/weight.
n_init and random_state belong in every report: K-means’ local optima make runs incomparable otherwise; report the initialization scheme, restarts, and convergence criterion.
The k-choice is a claim: “k = 4 subtypes” enters papers; support it with stability + external validation (9.1 Q2, 9.6), not the elbow alone.
Feature weighting is hidden tuning: scaling up a feature weights it in every distance — deliberate weighting (domain-informed) is legitimate; accidental weighting (units) is the 9.1 disease.
Empty clusters: a centroid can lose all its points; sklearn relocates it — but your hand-rolled version (Exercise 0’s update) needs the guard (we kept the old center).
K-means on PCA scores (9.2) is standard for wide data (denoised, decorrelated distances) — but it clusters the projection: structure in discarded components is invisible (C2 of 9.2’s batch caution).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated clustering has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


n_init = 1 with no initialization report: the run is a lottery ticket on local optima. Use k-means++ with n_init ≥ 10 and report stability (9.1 Exercise 2).
Integer-coded category in Euclidean space — the Concept Question 5 breakage: one-hot (or k-modes); the category now dominates distance by its arbitrary spacing.
Inertia as quality: it only ever decreases with k and says nothing about validity — report silhouette/stability alongside, and interpret inertia only comparatively at fixed k and features.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove Lloyd’s algorithm never increases inertia, and that it converges in finitely many steps: (a) the assignment step (each point to nearest centroid) cannot increase inertia for fixed centers; (b) the update step (centroid = cluster mean) minimizes within-cluster squared distance for fixed assignments; (c) finitely many partitions ⇒ termination. What does this proof not promise — and which quantity’s monotonicity would an observer track to detect a buggy implementation?


Hint

Each step is an exact coordinate-wise minimization of the same objective; monotone decrease + finite states ⇒ convergence.



Solution


For fixed centers, nearest-centroid assignment minimizes each point’s contribution — inertia weakly decreases. (b) For fixed assignments, each Σ‖xᵢ − c‖² over a cluster is minimized at c = mean — weakly decreases again. (c) Inertia strictly decreases unless the partition repeats; partitions are finite ⇒ termination at a local optimum. Not promised: global optimality, a bound on iterations, or correctness of k. The tracked quantity is inertia per iteration — it must be monotone non-increasing; any increase means an implementation bug (misaligned assignment/update, or empty-cluster handling).


Q2. K-means vs GMM on unequal variances, theory and measurement: a GMM with full per-cluster covariances reduces to K-means when all covariances = σ²I and responsibilities are hard. Construct data where K-means and a fitted 2-component GMM disagree (variance ratio 4:1), fit both (GaussianMixture if available, else compare K-means on raw vs per-cluster-standardized features as the poor-man’s GMM), and report ARI vs truth for each. What does the GMM’s soft responsibility fix that hard assignment cannot?


Hint

Hard assignment sends wide-cluster points at the boundary to the tight cluster; soft responsibilities weigh by each cluster’s density — variance-aware.



Solution

K-means’ Voronoi boundary equidistant in raw space ignores that one cluster is supposed to be wider; a GMM’s responsibility compares densities — a point moderately far from the wide cluster’s mean is still probably wide-cluster. With equal-variance assumption dropped, the boundary curves around the tight cluster.






GMM’s soft responsibilities also give graded membership — points near boundaries are honestly uncertain instead of hard-assigned, which downstream pipelines can propagate. The general lesson: K-means is the spherical hard special case; each relaxation (covariance, softness) buys validity on a wider cluster family at the cost of parameters and compute.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (K-means × 5.6 × 9.2). Wide-data clustering protocol: n = 200, p = 500 (5 planted clusters, strong batch direction). Compare pipelines: (a) raw → K-means; (b) scale → K-means; (c) scale → PCA-5 → K-means; (d) scale → batch-corrected → PCA-5 → K-means. Evaluate ARI vs biological truth AND vs batch. Write the pipeline decision and the audit that justified it — the realistic omics workflow in miniature.
C2 (K-means × 9.6 × 12.x stub). The k-selection multiplicity experiment: run the full k-selection circus (elbow, silhouette, gap, stability) on null data (no clusters) for k ∈ 2..9, 100 datasets. How often does each judge declare some k “clearly best”? Implement the correction (require judge agreement + stability + effect-size floor) and measure the false-discovery rate of “we found k clusters” claims. This is Part 12’s logic wearing unsupervised clothes.

title: 9.4 K-means Clustering
text:
7. Summary

K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distance to centroids: Lloyd assign/update, monotone, local-optimum.
Assumptions: spherical, equal-variance, equal-size clusters in Euclidean space — each breakage has a named failure mode.
k-means++ + n_init manage initialization; report the setup or the run isn’t reproducible.
k is chosen by converging evidence — elbow + silhouette + gap + stability — and it’s a claim, not a setting.
Categorical codes, unscaled units, outliers, non-convex shapes: each is a diagnosed assumption violation with a mapped repair.
GMMs generalize; spectral/density methods change families; the diagnosis-first rule routes you.
Clusters need validation, comparison, and honesty about selection — the practical centerpiece: 9.6 Practical clustering issues, after hierarchical trees of clusters in 9.5.

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text: PCA finds the orthogonal directions along which the data varies most, and re-expresses it in those directions. It is simultaneously a dimension-reduction tool, a decorrelation machine, a visualization device, and the algebraic backbone of ridge (5.2) and PCR (5.5) — the most reused object in applied statistics.

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
1. Basic Concept
PC1 = the unit vector w maximizing Var(Xw) = wᵀΣw subject to ‖w‖ = 1 — the solution is the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix; subsequent PCs are the next eigenvectors, orthogonal to the rest. Equivalent view: PCA is the SVD of the (centered) data matrix.






Scores, loadings, and the reconstruction — the three objects to keep straight:

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
2. Concept Questions

PCA is unsupervised — state precisely what it does not look at, and recall the page where that blindness cost it (5.5).
Why must features be centered before PCA? Scaled? When is scaling the wrong choice?
Your PC1 has loadings (−0.7, +0.7, 0.05, 0.1). Interpret it — and state the two sign/scale caveats.
What does “PCA loses information” mean numerically, and which quantity measures exactly what’s lost per component?
PCA on raw counts (skewed, huge-variance features) found “PC1 = one gene.” Diagnose, and name the two standard fixes.



Answers


It never sees y. Consequence: PCs rank by X-variance, which may be irrelevant to the response — the low-variance-signal pathology (5.5 Exercise 2), and the supervised alternative (PLS) exists for exactly this.
Center: PCA finds directions through the origin of the data cloud — uncentered, PC1 points at the mean (garbage directions). Scale: PCA’s criterion is variance — without scaling, big-unit features own the components; scale whenever features have arbitrary units. Wrong to scale: when features share a natural unit and their variances ARE the signal (e.g., same-assay measurements) — then raw-covariance PCA respects the physics.
“A contrast: feature 1 loads negative, feature 2 positive, equally; features 3–4 uninvolved” — PC1 is roughly feature2 − feature1. Caveats: (a) sign is arbitrary (−w is the same component — sklearn flips signs by its own convention); (b) loadings are unit-scaled — interpret the pattern (ratios, signs), not absolute numbers.
Reconstruction error: ‖X − X_M‖² = Σ_{j>M} λⱼ (sum of discarded eigenvalues) — PCA drops exactly the orthogonal variance along dropped directions, and explained_variance_ratio_ is the kept fraction. Loss is orthogonal-projection loss: the best rank-M summary possible (Eckart–Young: PCA is optimal in Frobenius norm).
Diagnosis: unscaled, skewed data — the huge-variance gene dominates PC1 by units, not biology. Fixes: log-transform skewed features (0.4), then standardize. Then PC1 becomes a pattern, not a unit artifact.

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. PCA by hand, via covariance eigendecomposition and via SVD: center a dataset, compute Σ = XᶜᵀXᶜ/(n−1), take np.linalg.eigh, and compare its eigenpairs to sklearn’s PCA output (match signs, compare explained ratios). Then do it via np.linalg.svd and verify the identity λⱼ = sⱼ²/(n−1). Owning this equivalence demystifies every PCA discussion in the course.


Solution







Three roads, one decomposition. Eigen-route exposes “eigenvectors of covariance”; SVD-route exposes “best rank-M projection” (Eckart–Young); sklearn emits the latter. Any PCA claim you’ll ever read reduces to objects you just computed.

Exercise 2. The scree decision, done with eyes: on a dataset with a planted structure (3 latent factors + noise, p = 12), plot (a) explained-variance ratios, (b) cumulative variance, (c) the reconstruction error as M grows. Mark where the scree “elbows” and where reconstruction error flattens. Then verify against the truth: M = 3 captures the planted structure. Finally, state when the elbow is ambiguous and which tool arbitrates (6.5’s dial logic, transplanted).


Solution







Planted rank shows as the scree’s cliff (huge λ₁₋₃, noise-floor λ₄₊). Ambiguous elbows (gradual decay) happen when signal and noise variances blend — then the choice is a bias–variance trade like any M-selection (5.5 CV-tunes M; 9.6 stability-checks it), and visualization is a legitimate “M = 2 by fiat” use.

Exercise 3. Biplot discipline: on the 4-feature cohort-style data below, produce (a) PC1/PC2 score scatter, (b) loading vectors overlaid, (c) each feature’s correlation with PC1/PC2 as a table. Interpret PC1 in a sentence a domain reader could accept, and identify which feature the biplot says is redundant (nearly collinear with another) — verify by direct correlation. Note explicitly what a biplot cannot tell you (name the supervised question it ignores).


Solution







The biplot’s geometry: features pointing the same direction are correlated (expr1/expr2 nearly overlap — redundancy visible before any correlation call); features opposing are anti-correlated; scores near a loading tip have high values of that feature. What it can’t say: anything about y — PCA is blind to outcomes by construction (5.5), and “PC1 = severity” needs external validation (9.1’s reification trap).

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

PCA on the covariance vs correlation matrix: scaling = correlation-PCA; raw = covariance-PCA — a modeling choice with the 9.1 assumption weight (Exercise units; Q2b).
PCA is not feature selection: components are combinations of all features — sparse variants (sparse PCA) exist if you need actual feature drops (5.1’s selection, rotated).
Outliers own variance: one extreme point can be PC1; robust PCA (or inspection before fitting) for dirty data (2.10 leverage, unsupervised edition).
PCA inside pipelines: fit on training folds only — the leakage law (0.5); Pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(), model) is the mechanical guarantee (5.5 Exercise 3).
Interpretation limits: loadings are basis vectors of a rotated coordinate system — components can mix causally unrelated features; correlations between scores and external variables are the validation, not the discovery (9.1 Q3).
Sign and rotation freedom: eigenvectors are sign-arbitrary; with near-equal eigenvalues, subspaces rotate freely — small data perturbations can “swap” PCs (stability diagnostics again, 9.6).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated PCA pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Unscaled PCA: the 1000-mean feature’s variance dominates — PC1 is a units artifact. Standardize (or justify raw-covariance PCA by shared units).
Choosing the component by correlation with y: (a) that’s supervised selection wearing PCA clothes — the honest tool is PLS/PCR-with-CV (5.5); (b) with 2 components the “choice” is trivial anyway. Keep PCA unsupervised and use all M components downstream, or justify M by variance/CV.
Two different PCAs for train/test: bases must match — fit the transformer on training data, transform test (the Pipeline law, 0.5).

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove PCA’s optimality (Eckart–Young): among all rank-M approximations C of centered X, PCA’s reconstruction X·V_M·V_Mᵀ (V_M = top-M right singular vectors) minimizes ‖X − C‖_F. Verify numerically that no other rank-2 orthogonal projection of a fixed dataset achieves lower reconstruction error, and connect the result to the SVD identity λⱼ = sⱼ²/(n−1) from Exercise 1.


Hint

Eckart–Young: truncating the SVD at rank M minimizes Frobenius error; PCA’s subspace IS the top-M right singular subspace.



Solution</summary»
By the SVD X = USVᵀ, the best rank-M approximation in Frobenius norm is U_M S_M V_Mᵀ (Eckart–Young theorem) — keeping the M largest singular values. PCA’s projection X V_M V_Mᵀ is exactly this object; the discarded error is Σ_{j>M} sⱼ² = (n−1)Σ_{j>M} λⱼ.






PCA and truncated SVD coincide to float precision; any other rank-2 projection loses strictly more — PCA is the unique best low-rank linear summary (up to rotation within the subspace). This optimality is in X’s own geometry — nothing about y (5.5’s recurring caveat).

Q2. PCA stability under correlated noise: generate data with a planted PC1 and increasing noise correlation among the noise features; measure (a) the angle between refit PC1 across bootstrap resamples and (b) the explained-variance-ratio stability, as noise correlation grows. Show PC subspace stability degrading before the variance ratio does — then write the reporting rule: which PCA claims need stability analysis (subspace interpretation) and which are robust (aggregate variance summaries)?


Solution







As noise features correlate, their collective variance competes with the planted direction: the top eigenvector’s identity wobbles (angles grow) even while the explained-variance summary barely moves. Reporting rule: interpreting “what PC1 means” requires subspace stability (bootstrap angles, 9.1 Exercise 2’s logic); quoting “PC1 captures X% variance” is comparatively robust. Two claims, two evidentiary standards.

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (PCA × 7.4 forests × 3.6 GLM). Representation learning bake-off: on wide data (n = 150, p = 100, mixed linear/nonlinear signals), compare downstream classifiers trained on (a) raw features, (b) PCA-20 scores, (c) PCA-5 scores — nested CV. When does compression help (noise dilution) and when hurt (nonlinear signal spread across PCs)? Connect to 5.5’s PCR findings and write the dimension-reduction routing rule: raw vs compressed, by signal type and n/p ratio.
C2 (PCA × 9.4 K-means × 12.x batch stub). The cluster-on-PCs pipeline: cluster (K-means, k = 3) on (a) raw scaled features and (b) the top-3 PC scores of wide data with planted clusters and a planted batch direction. Measure agreement with true biological clusters vs with batches, both pipelines. Does PCA-to-3 dims remove the batch artifact or preserve it (hint: batch is a variance direction)? Write the caution about “we clustered in PC space, so it’s denoised” — and the correct order of operations (batch audit before, not after, compression).

title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis
text:
7. Summary

PCA = eigendecomposition of covariance = SVD of centered data: directions of maximal variance, orthogonally.
Three objects: scores (data in PC space), loadings (the rotation), explained-variance ratios (the budget).
Center always; scale unless units are meaningful; fit inside pipelines; the outcome-blindness is structural.
Reconstruction loss = dropped eigenvalues; PCA is the optimal rank-M summary (Eckart–Young) in X’s geometry.
Scree picks M when the cliff is real; CV picks it when it’s a bias–variance trade.
Interpretation claims need subspace stability; variance claims are sturdier.
PCA compresses; the next problem is what to do when the data is incomplete — 9.3 Missing values and matrix completion.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusterings instead of one partition: start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the closest pair (agglomerative), or split recursively (divisive). The output — a dendrogram — shows structure at every scale simultaneously, letting you choose k by cutting the tree rather than committing upfront.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
1. Basic Concept
Agglomerative nesting (AGNES): repeatedly merge the two closest clusters, where “cluster distance” is defined by the linkage:

single: min pairwise distance (chains; finds long straggly shapes)
complete: max pairwise distance (compact, tight balls)
average: mean pairwise distance (compromise)
ward: merge minimizing total within-cluster variance increase (the K-means-flavored default)







Cutting the tree at different heights = different clusterings:

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
2. Concept Questions

What does a dendrogram’s height encode, and why is “cut at height h” equivalent to “keep the k merges below h”?
Single linkage’s chaining failure: describe the mechanism, draw it mentally on two crescents, and name the truth-shape it’s designed for.
Ward linkage vs K-means: state the precise relationship (what Ward merges minimize) and when their outputs can differ.
Inversion (a later merge at smaller height than an earlier one): which linkage can produce it, and what does it break (both interpretationally and computationally)?
The dendrogram is n−1 merges tall. What does that structure guarantee about hierarchy — and what real data property violates it (making the tree partly fiction)?



Answers


Height = the distance between the two merged clusters (linkage-defined). Cutting at h keeps only merges with height ≤ h; the remaining connected components are exactly the k clusters — height-cuts and k-cuts are two views of one tree.
Single linkage merges by the closest pair — a chain of close steps connects two genuinely distinct groups through intermediate points (“chaining”). It’s designed for elongated/straggly truths (its home game), and it’s robust to scale-ordering.
Ward merges the pair whose union minimizes the increase in Σ within-cluster squared deviation — exactly K-means’ criterion applied hierarchically. Outputs differ: greedy hierarchical order ≠ K-means’ global refinement; a final K-means pass on Ward’s clusters often improves them (7.1 greedy-vs-refit echo).
Inversions occur with centroid/median linkage (distances of merged clusters can shrink) — they break the monotone dendrogram (heights must be non-decreasing upward) and the fcluster-style cutting (no clean level cut exists). Ward/single/complete/average are inversion-free.
The tree guarantees a strictly nested hierarchy: every pair of clusters is disjoint or nested. Real structure violates it — overlapping groups (cells share states), multi-scale co-existing structures — so forcing data into a tree loses cross-cutting structure (the same nesting assumption 6.2’s trees and 7.1 decision trees make, here about clusters).

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Implement single and complete linkage from scratch (the merge loop with a live distance matrix), verify against scipy.linkage on a 12-point dataset, and demonstrate the chaining/compactness contrast on the bridge dataset from drill 2. Which lines of your implementation encode the definition of each linkage?


Solution







The two lines selecting block.min() vs block.max() ARE the linkage definitions — everything else is bookkeeping. scipy computes them with optimized updates (Lance–Williams), but the semantics you’ve now written by hand are identical.

Exercise 2. Linkage zoology on structured truths: build four truths — (a) blobs, (b) two crescents (non-convex), (c) long straggly chains, (d) tight balls of unequal size — and run all four linkages (single/complete/average/ward), scoring ARI at the true k. Report the 4×4 table. Verify: single wins crescents/chains, ward wins balls/blobs, complete resists chaining. Write the linkage-selection sentence.


Solution







The table’s diagonal is the lesson: single linkage owns chains/crescents (chaining is a feature there); ward owns blobs and unequal balls (variance criterion matches); complete guards compactness against bridges; average splits the difference. Selection sentence: “choose the linkage whose merge semantics match the cluster shape your domain expects — then verify with the dendrogram and stability (9.6).”

Exercise 3. Dendrogram forensics: for the bridge dataset, produce dendrograms under single and complete linkage side by side. Read from each: at what height do the two blobs separate, and what does the single-linkage tree claim about the bridge points (which merge last/never at low height)? Then cut both trees at k = 2 and draw the partitions. Write the two-sentence guidance for reading a dendrogram before trusting its cuts.


Solution







Reading discipline: (1) scan the top merges first — the last few merge heights encode the strongest separations (a tiny final height = weak global structure); (2) check for chaining (single linkage with long mid-height ladders means bridges are being absorbed). Only then do cuts mean what you hope. The single-linkage tree here absorbs the bridge into one cluster at low heights; complete linkage’s top merge separates the blobs cleanly — same data, opposite stories, chosen by linkage semantics.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Complexity: naive agglomerative is O(n³) (or O(n² log n) with heaps) and O(n²) memory — the practical ceiling is ~10–20k points; for larger n, use K-means (9.4) first, then hierarchically cluster the centroids, or sample.
Ward on non-Euclidean inputs: ward assumes Euclidean distances (it’s a variance criterion); with correlation or custom distances, use average/complete — or accept that ward’s “variance” is undefined on your metric.
fcluster criteria: “maxclust” (k clusters) vs “distance” (height cut) answer different questions — height cuts transfer across datasets (a meaningful similarity scale), k-cuts don’t.
Dendrogram orientation illusion: reordering leaves changes nothing about the tree — don’t read neighborliness into leaf adjacency across branches (only within the last merges).
Stability still applies: bootstrap the rows, re-cluster, compare trees (cophenetic correlation / ARI at the cut) — hierarchical trees are as resample-sensitive as K-means labels (9.1 Exercise 2).
No reallocation: once merged, never split/switch — early greedy mistakes are frozen into the tree (agglomerative’s original sin; divisive or refined approaches pay to escape it).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated hierarchical pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Ward needs Euclidean geometry — its merge criterion is a variance increase, undefined on correlation distances. Use average/complete linkage on non-Euclidean metrics (or embed the metric first).
Threshold imported from elsewhere: distance cuts are meaningful in this dataset’s similarity scale — read the target height off this dendrogram (or cut by k with justification).
Leaf adjacency isn’t similarity: dendrogram leaves are ordered for drawing; only tree structure (nested merges, heights) carries information.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive Ward’s merge criterion: show that for two clusters A, B, the increase in total within-cluster Σ‖x − μ‖² from merging them equals \(\frac{n_A n_B}{n_A + n_B}\|\mu_A - \mu_B\|^2\). Use this to prove ward linkage merges the pair whose centroids are closest weighted by harmonic-mean-ish sizes — and explain why this makes ward prefer merging small clusters early (the unequal-size behavior of 7.2’s ledger).


Hint</summary»
Total within-cluster SSE change = SSE(A∪B) − SSE(A) − SSE(B); expand each SSE around the union mean via the parallel-axis identity.



Solution</summary»
With the identity SSE(A∪B) = SSE(A) + SSE(B) + (n_A n_B/(n_A + n_B))‖μ_A − μ_B‖², the merge cost is exactly the size-weighted centroid distance. The weight n_A n_B/(n_A+n_B) is maximized at balanced sizes: merging two small clusters costs little (small weight), merging two large ones costs plenty — so ward grows big clusters late and prefers consolidating small ones early. Consequence: on unequal-size truths, ward’s trees can consolidate the minority cluster with noise fragments before facing the big cluster — the hierarchical face of K-means’ equal-size tendency.

Q2. Cophenetic correlation as a tree-quality summary: define the cophenetic distance between two points as the height of the merge where they first join; the cophenetic correlation is the correlation between these heights and the original distances. Implement it (scipy.cluster.hierarchy.cophenet), compute it for all four linkages on one dataset, and interpret: what does a high cophenetic correlation certify (and not certify)? Then show a dataset where cophenetic correlation is high but the clustering at true k is wrong — separating “faithful tree” from “correct partition.”


Solution







High cophenetic correlation certifies the tree faithfully represents the pairwise distances — the embedding into tree-heights lost little. It does not certify that the tree’s clusters match the true groups: concentric rings give a faithful tree whose k = 2 cut slices by radius, not ring — tree fidelity and partition correctness are different virtues, exactly the internal-vs-external validation split of 9.1 Q1.

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (hierarchical × 9.2 PCA × 7.4). Wide-data hierarchy: n = 150, p = 200 (5 planted clusters + noise directions). Compare ward-hierarchies built on (a) raw scaled distances, (b) PCA-5 scores, (c) forest-proximity-derived distances (1 − P(same leaf) from a random forest) — ARI at true k plus dendrogram stability under bootstrap. Which distance matrix produces the most faithful tree, and what does the proximity-distance result say about learning metrics from models (7.4)?
C2 (hierarchical × 6.2 steps × 4.6 tuning). Cut selection as hyperparameter tuning: treat the dendrogram cut height as a hyperparameter and select it by a downstream supervised proxy (e.g., cluster-label agreement with a known covariate split, or downstream regression R² using cluster dummies). Implement cut-selection by downstream-CV on data where the true k is known; compare against silhouette-chosen cuts. When does downstream-supervised cut selection find the truth better — and what selection-inflation guard (4.1) must accompany it?

title: 9.5 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
7. Summary

Hierarchical clustering = a tree of nested partitions: merges by linkage (single/complete/average/ward), read at any scale.
Dendrogram heights are merge distances; cuts at height h or into k clusters are two views of one object.
Linkage semantics are shape hypotheses: single→chains, ward→compact variance balls, complete→tight anti-bridge, average→compromise.
Ward = K-means’ criterion hierarchically (size-weighted centroid distance); their outputs relate but greedy order ≠ global refinement.
Faithful trees (cophenetic correlation) can still cut wrong — tree fidelity ≠ partition correctness.
No reallocation, nesting assumption, O(n²) memory: know the ceiling; hybridize for scale.
All structure-finding needs the practical layer — stability, k-selection discipline, mixed data, validation: 9.6 Practical clustering issues.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text: Python is the substrate everything else in this course is written in. Before touching NumPy, pandas, or scikit-learn, your reflexes in core Python — types, functions, comprehensions, error messages — need to be automatic. This page drills exactly those reflexes, with a bias toward the numerical/data style of Python rather than web or scripting styles.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
1. Basic Concept
Python is a dynamically typed language: names are labels attached to objects, not boxes with fixed types. For numerical work you mostly live with four scalar types (int, float, bool, str) and four container types (list, tuple, dict, set).
One fact causes more numerical bugs than anything else: Python float is IEEE-754 binary floating point, so most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly.






The second fact to internalize: / is always true division; // is floor division; % is the remainder.






A function is defined with def, returns with return (no return means it returns None), and can take default arguments:






Comprehensions are the idiomatic way to transform collections. If you are writing a for loop whose only job is to build a list, you should usually write a comprehension instead:






f-strings format values into text — you will use them constantly to report results:

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
2. Concept Questions
Answer from memory first, then open each answer to check.

What does 10 / 4 evaluate to, and what type is the result?
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 False? Name the underlying cause.
What is the difference between a list and a tuple? Give one practical consequence.
What does a function return if you never write return?
In f"{x:.2f}", what does the .2f part do?



Answers


2.5, a float. In Python 3, / always produces a float, even for whole-number results (8 / 2 is 4.0).
0.1 and 0.2 have no exact representation in binary floating point (IEEE-754). Their nearest representable values don’t sum to the nearest representable 0.3. Compare with a tolerance (math.isclose) instead.
Lists are mutable, tuples are immutable. Consequence: tuples can be dictionary keys and elements of sets; lists cannot. Also, accidentally mutating a tuple raises an error, which can protect data.
None.
Format x as a fixed-point number with exactly 2 digits after the decimal point (rounding half-to-even on the decimal representation).

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict each line’s output before running. These rebuild reflexes — do them until automatic.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Write a function celsius_to_fahrenheit(c) that converts a temperature and returns the result rounded to 1 decimal place. Then use it in a comprehension to convert [0, 37, 100].


Solution








Exercise 2. Given the DNA string below, compute (a) its length, (b) GC content as a percentage with 1 decimal, (c) its reverse complement. Use one comprehension and one dictionary somewhere.


Solution







Note: reversed(seq) + join is O(n); building a string with += in a loop is O(n²) — a classic performance trap.

Exercise 3. FizzBuzz, data edition: for integers 1–20, print Bio if divisible by 3, Stats if divisible by 5, BioStats if divisible by both, otherwise the number — as a single list of strings.


Solution







Order matters: check the compound condition (% 15 == 0) first, otherwise the simple cases win. Same idea as writing mutually exclusive if/elif branches.

Exercise 4. Parse this mini-FASTA (a real task shape in bioinformatics) and report each sequence’s length and GC%:
>gene1
ATGGCC
>gene2
GCGCGCGCGT


Solution







sum(b in "GC" for b in seq) works because True/False sum as 1/0 — an idiom worth owning.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls
Pitfalls that bite numerical/data Python specifically:

Mutable default arguments are created once, at function definition — not at each call. def f(x, acc=[]) shares the same list across all calls. This is the single most common “haunted function” bug.
is compares identity, == compares value. Never write x is 5 — it happens to work for small ints in CPython and breaks everywhere else.
Floats in loops accumulate error. Summing 10 million floats with + loses precision; use math.fsum or better, NumPy (np.sum uses pairwise summation).
Chained comparison is a feature: 0 < x < 1 means (0 < x) and (x < 1). Nice, but it changes short-circuit semantics.
Names resolve at call time, not definition time (closures see the current value of outer variables, a classic loop-closure bug).
Everything is an object: 1 and True compare equal (1 == True), and bool is a subclass of int. So [1, 2].count(True) counts True, not 1… except it counts both, because True == 1. Watch out in data cleaning.


Read & Refactor AI Code
The following AI-generated snippet looks reasonable but contains three bugs. Run it, observe the wrong behavior, find the bugs, and fix them in the editor.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Mutable default argument. The default list is created once, so the second call appends to the first call’s list. Fix: default to None and create the list inside.
is with floats. Identity comparison, not equality; 30.0 is not the same object as the literal in the function. Fix: ==, or better math.isclose for computed floats.
// instead of /. Floor division silently truncates the mean. Fix: /.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Explain precisely why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in terms of binary representation. Why is 0.5 stored exactly but 0.1 not?


Hint

Write 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 as sums of powers of 1/2. Which terminate?



Solution

IEEE-754 doubles store numbers as ±m × 2^e with a 53-bit significand. A decimal fraction is exactly representable only if it is a dyadic rational — a fraction whose denominator is a power of 2. 0.5 = 1/2 is dyadic: exact. 0.1 = 1/10 needs denominator 2 × 5; the factor 5 is impossible in binary, so 0.1 rounds to the nearest 53-bit binary fraction: 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827.... Adding the two rounded values 0.1 + 0.2 gives a value whose rounded nearest double is 0.30000000000000004, one ulp above 0.3’s nearest double. Consequence for practice: never test float equality; test abs(a-b) < tol or math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=0.0). For exact decimal money/counting semantics use decimal.Decimal or integers.

Q2. What does this print, and why?








Hint

Closures capture variables, not values. When do the lambdas look up f?



Solution

[9, 9, 9]. Each lambda closes over the variable f; by the time they are called, the loop finished and f holds 3, so every call computes 3*3. Fix by binding at definition time: lambda f=f: f*f (default argument evaluated immediately), or use a factory function def make(f): return lambda: f*f. The same late-binding logic explains why a list of functions that reference a module-level config variable all change behavior when you reassign that variable.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (functions × strings × loops → bioinformatics). Write translate(seq) that translates a DNA string to an amino-acid one-letter string using the standard genetic code, handling (a) lowercase input, (b) a trailing partial codon, (c) stop codons marked *. Test on ATGGCCATTGTAATGGGCCGCTGAAAGGGTGCCCGATAG (you can hardcode just the codons you need, or a 64-entry dict). When you reach 0.2 NumPy, consider which parts of this problem could be vectorized — and which fundamentally cannot (hint: the lookup table is not arithmetic).
C2 (this page × 1.1 Descriptive statistics). Write a pure-Python function summary(xs) returning a dict with n, mean, median, min, max, computed without importing anything. Then check: what happens with an empty list, a list of one element, and a list containing None? Design your function’s error behavior deliberately (raise ValueError? skip None?) — this is exactly the design decision pandas makes for you with skipna=True.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
7. Summary

Python names point to objects; types live on the objects, not the names.
/ is true division, // floors, % gives the remainder; floats are IEEE-754 binary — compare with math.isclose, never ==.
Comprehensions > loops for building collections; f-strings > string concatenation for output.
Functions returning None by default and mutable default arguments are top sources of silent bugs.
is checks identity; == checks equality; empty containers are falsy.
Closures look up variables at call time — late binding breaks loop-generated functions.
Pure-Python numeric loops are slow: the moment you have arrays of numbers, you want 0.2 NumPy, which pushes loops into compiled code and changes how you express numerical ideas entirely.

title: 0.3 pandas
text: NumPy arrays are fast but anonymous — columns have no names, rows have no identity, and mixed types are impossible. pandas adds labels. It is the Python twin of R’s data frame (the tidyverse’s tibble), and it will be your main tool for loading, cleaning, and summarizing data before any model sees it.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
1. Basic Concept
A DataFrame is a rectangular table: each column is a Series (a labeled 1-D array with one dtype), and rows share an index. Think: dict of columns + shared row labels.






Two selectors, two jobs. loc selects by label, iloc by integer position, and both use [rows, columns]:






groupby is the split–apply–combine engine and probably the single most used pandas verb:






merging joins two tables on a key — the same mental model as SQL joins:

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
2. Concept Questions

What is the difference between df["expr"] and df[["expr"]]?
When do loc and iloc give different answers for the same-looking call?
Why does df[df["expr"] > 10]["expr"] = 0 silently fail to change df?
What does how="left" in merge guarantee, and what can it create?
What does df.groupby("tissue")["expr"].transform("mean") return, and how is it different from .mean()?



Answers


df["expr"] returns a Series; df[["expr"]] returns a one-column DataFrame. Many methods (.T, joining, multiple columns) behave differently on the two.
When the index labels are not 0..n-1 (e.g. after filtering, or a named index). loc["S2", ...] finds the row named S2; iloc[1, ...] finds the second row whatever it’s called.
Chained indexing: the first bracket may return a temporary copy, so the assignment can land on a copy that’s then discarded (the classic SettingWithCopyWarning). The correct form assigns through one loc call: df.loc[df["expr"] > 10, "expr"] = 0.
Left merge keeps every row of the left table; rows with no match on the right get NaN in the right columns (a merge “fan-out” can also multiply rows if the key is duplicated on the right).
transform("mean") returns a Series the same length/index as df — the group mean broadcast back to each row — so you can subtract it to center within groups. .mean() returns one row per group.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
We’ll build one small cohort table and predict outputs before running each cell.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. From the cohort df above: build a summary table with one row per group showing mean age, mean marker, and patient count, then add a column is_old (age > 50) and recompute the table splitting on both group and is_old.


Solution







The agg(col=("source", "func")) named aggregation syntax produces clean column names in one pass — no renaming afterwards.

Exercise 2. Merge a measurements table with a demographic table (left join), count missing matches, and fill missing site values with "unknown".


Solution







P03 exists in measurements but not demographics → left join keeps it, site becomes NaN. This exact pattern (merge → count NaN → decide policy) is 90% of real data integration.

Exercise 3. Given the wide expression table below (rows = genes, columns = samples), compute each gene’s mean and variance, keep genes with variance above 2.0, and melt the survivors into long format (gene, sample, value).


Solution







Wide ↔︎ long reshaping (melt / pivot) is the pandas equivalent of tidyverse’s pivot_longer / pivot_wider. Most plotting and modeling tools want long format.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Chained assignment is the #1 pandas bug. df[df.a > 0]["b"] = 1 may write to a temporary copy. Always: single loc call → df.loc[mask, "b"] = 1. (pandas 3.0’s copy-on-write makes chained assignment fail loudly; the pyodide pandas here is 2.x, where it can still silently no-op.)
inplace=True is deprecated style. It mutates the object you may not own and prevents method chaining. Prefer df = df.dropna() or df.dropna(subset=["marker"], inplace=False).
Index is not “row number”. After filtering, .iloc[0] and .index[0] diverge. Reset with reset_index(drop=True) when position and label must agree again.
merge can silently multiply rows if the key is duplicated on either side — always check len(result) vs len(left) and result["key"].value_counts().
== on a column with NaN gives False, never NaN: df[df["x"] == np.nan] matches nothing. Use df["x"].isna().
Object dtype columns are slow (Python objects, not arrays). Convert strings to category when few distinct values; parse dates with pd.to_datetime immediately.
groupby drops groups containing NaN keys by default (dropna=True) — a silent row-loss channel in reports.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated analysis has three bugs. Run it, observe, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Chained assignment: high may be a copy, so the mark never lands in df (see the printed 0). Fix with df.loc[df["value"] > 10, "site"] = "HIGH".
NaN never equals NaN: count is 0 despite two NaNs. Fix: df["value"].isna().sum().
Loop + manual dict is slower, noisier, and easier to get wrong than groupby; also the loop’s .mean() results are fine here but the pattern invites index bugs. Fix: df.groupby("site")["value"].mean().

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. A colleague merges a 20,000-row measurements table with a 200-row annotation table and the result has 23,117 rows. Diagnose the likely causes and give a defensive merge recipe.


Hint

What does validate= in merge do? What does a duplicated key do to row counts?



Solution

The key is duplicated: an m-to-many join multiplies rows (each left row matches every right row with the same key). Diagnosis: anno["gene"].value_counts().head(), compare len(left), len(right), len(merged); check merged["gene"].is_unique. Defensive recipe: merged = meas.merge(anno, on="gene", how="left", validate="m:1") — raises instead of fanning out; or deduplicate anno.drop_duplicates("gene") first; assert len(merged) == len(meas) afterwards. Choosing validate is documentation and a runtime guard.

Q2. Explain the difference between apply, transform, and agg on a groupby object, and why apply is the dangerous one. Give a task where apply is genuinely required.


Solution

agg collapses each group to one value (len = n groups). transform returns one value per input row (len = n rows, group statistic broadcast back). apply returns whatever your function returns — a scalar, a Series, or a DataFrame — so pandas has to guess how to assemble results, which is slower and produces surprising shapes/indexes. Use agg/transform whenever possible; reach for apply when you need genuinely per-group multi-row computation, e.g. fitting a per-group linear model and returning its coefficients as a Series: df.groupby("site").apply(lambda g: pd.Series(np.polyfit(g["x"], g["y"], 1), index=["slope", "intercept"])). In modern pandas, prefer groupby(...).filter(...) for row selection and named agg for summaries to keep types predictable.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (pandas × 0.4 Visualisation). Take the cohort df and produce, in long format, everything needed to plot marker distributions per group: which table shape does matplotlib’s ax.boxplot want (list of arrays) and which does a pandas .boxplot(by=...) want? Convert between wide and long to produce the same figure both ways — internalize why “tidy/long” is the interchange format and “wide” is a display choice.
C2 (pandas × 1.2 Relationships). For the cohort data, compute the correlation matrix of the numeric columns (df.corr(numeric_only=True)), then compute it within groups (df.groupby("group").corr(numeric_only=True)). Under what real-world condition can the pooled correlation have the opposite sign from every within-group correlation (Simpson’s paradox)? Construct a 3-line synthetic example demonstrating it.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
7. Summary

A DataFrame is labeled columns of Series sharing an index; dtypes tells you what you actually have.
loc = labels, iloc = positions; filtering is df.loc[mask, cols] — one call, no chaining.
groupby + agg/transform covers split–apply–combine; transform broadcasts back to row shape.
merge(how="left", validate="m:1") with NaN-counting afterwards is the safe join recipe.
NaN: use .isna(), skipna defaults, and decide drop-vs-fill deliberately.
Wide is for humans, long is for machines; melt/pivot convert between them.
Numbers on a page lie less than pictures — next page turns these tables into plots that reveal structure before you model it: 0.4 Visualisation & EDA.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text: Training error is a promise the model makes to itself; test error is the promise it keeps to you. The gap between them — optimism — grows with model flexibility and shrinks with data. This page makes the gap visible, measurable, and predictable: the organizing problem of statistical learning.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three error quantities, precisely:

Training (in-sample) error: average loss on the data the model was fitted to. Always optimistic — the fit adapted to this data’s noise.
Test (out-of-sample) error: average loss on fresh data from the same process. The honest quantity — what deployment will see.
Generalization gap (optimism): test − training. Grows with flexibility (more parameters, smaller k, deeper trees…), shrinks with n.

The signature experiment — one figure that contains the entire course:






The same story with a continuous flexibility dial (KNN’s k) — train error rises monotonically with k while test is U-shaped:

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is training error guaranteed non-increasing in polynomial degree, while test error is not?
State the direction of each effect on optimism: doubling the number of fitted parameters; doubling n; increasing noise σ.
Your colleague reports train MSE 0.02, test MSE 0.21, σ² ≈ 0.09. Diagnose the model in one sentence and name the two standard remedies.
KNN’s k and polynomial degree are both flexibility dials — which direction is “more flexible” in each, and why are their U-curves mirror images?
A model with training error above the noise floor tells you what, immediately?



Answers


Least squares projects y onto a growing column space: each added polynomial term can only reduce RSS (2.8 Q1). Test error pays for each parameter twice — once through variance in estimating it — so beyond the true structure it climbs.
More parameters → more optimism; more n → less (each parameter is better pinned, and the fit has less room to chase noise); larger σ → more optimism in absolute terms (more noise available to chase) while the noise floor itself also rises.
Overfitting: the gap (0.19) is ≫ the distance to the floor (0.12) — the model has high variance. Remedies: reduce flexibility (lower degree, larger k, regularization) or gather more data; verify by CV either way.
Polynomials: flexibility ↑ with degree (more terms). KNN: flexibility ↑ as k ↓ (locality). So the KNN U-curve is traversed right-to-left relative to the polynomial’s — mirror images of the same phenomenon.
Underfitting (bias-dominated): the model can’t even reach the noise floor, so no amount of validation care will help — increase flexibility before optimizing anything else. It’s the cheap, immediate diagnostic people forget.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. The optimism experiment, quantified: for degrees 1–10, repeat 200 times (fresh n = 30 training sets, fixed large test set), and record the mean training MSE, mean test MSE, and the mean gap. Plot all three vs degree. Verify the two qualitative laws: training error falls in degree, and the gap grows in degree; then check quantitatively how much of the test curve’s left side is bias (mean prediction ≠ truth) vs variance (prediction wiggles across training sets).


Solution







Degree 1: bias² dominates (a line can’t trace a sine). Degree 9: variance dominates (curves swing wildly between training sets). The decomposition is 4.4 previewed with your own data.

Exercise 2. Data-volume rescue: fix the degree-9 overfitting disaster by scaling n (30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000). Report test MSE at each n. Then replot the degree-1-vs-9 test comparison across n. Write the two-sentence law: when does flexibility stop hurting, and what never stops hurting?


Solution







Degree 9’s test error falls toward the degree-1 level (and past it, eventually) as n grows — variance is curable with data, since each coefficient gets pinned by more points. Degree 1’s error never improves past its bias floor — no amount of data fixes a wrong model shape. Flexibility’s danger is finite; underfitting’s is permanent.

Exercise 3. p ≫ n theater: n = 25 samples, 200 pure-noise features, pure-noise labels. Fit (a) plain OLS, (b) ridge with α = 10 (Part 5 preview — Ridge(alpha=10)), (c) KNN with k = 10. Report train and test R²/MSE for each. Which method’s training behavior is the most honest? Connect each to a bias/variance profile.


Solution







OLS: train ≈ 0 (interpolates 25 points with 200 features), test astronomically bad — pure variance. Ridge: shrinkage caps coefficients, train ≈ 1, test ≈ 1 — behaves like the null model, honest by constraint. KNN: train worse than OLS (local averaging can’t interpolate as aggressively), test near the floor — local smoothing is naturally low-variance here. Ranking the training numbers by honesty: KNN/Ridge ≫ OLS; the training number only fools those who forget what it measures.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Optimism is predictable in size: for linear models, in-sample optimism ≈ (2σ²/n)·(number of parameters) — the engine behind Cp/AIC/BIC and adjusted R². It’s why 2.4’s noise columns added ≈ (k/n) worth of fake R².
The test set is a budget: every look spends it (0.5); adaptive “tune on test, report test” can make a noise-only pipeline score near-perfectly (try it once, to be cured forever — 4.2).
Selection inflates: choosing the best of M models by its CV score reports an extreme order statistic — the winner’s CV score is biased up by roughly (SD of the noise) × E[max of M standard normals]. More candidates = more inflation (4.6).
Modern caveat — double descent: beyond the interpolation threshold (p ≳ n), test error can fall again for some overparameterized models (the deep-learning regime). The classical U-curve is the right mental model for classical models; hold it loosely at the extremes.
Data leakage resurrects optimism invisibly: preprocessing fit before splitting, duplicates across splits, features derived from the outcome — every one shrinks the apparent gap while worsening the real one. The gap being small is good news only if the pipeline earned it.
In-sample diagnostics ≠ out-of-sample validity: residual plots (2.10) certify the fit’s assumptions; only held-out data certifies predictions.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “experiment” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Three models, one test set, argmax on test: the winner’s score is an order statistic — biased up even though each individual estimate was unbiased. Select on training-side CV.
Selected-on-test then reported-on-test: the number is now a selection number, not an estimate. Report on data untouched by selection.
Split-shopping: with enough tries, some split flatters any model; keeping the flattering one is p-hacking with a random seed (1.4’s peeking loop in evaluation clothing).

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. For a linear model with n training points and p parameters, the expected optimism of the training MSE is approximately \(\frac{2\sigma^2}{n} p\). Verify this by simulation (σ = 1, p ∈ {1, 5, 20}, n = 100, truth = zero signal or mild signal), then use it to explain (a) why Cp/AIC-style criteria subtract \(2p\hat\sigma^2/n\) from training error, and (b) why the approximation degrades when p approaches n.


Hint

Optimism = E[test error] − E[train error] for the fitted rule; for linear smoothers with hat matrix H, trace-based arguments give the 2σ²p/n form (Mallows’ Cp derivation).



Solution







Agreement is close while p ≪ n. As p → n, the fit interpolates: training MSE → 0, the hat matrix saturates (H → I, df → n), and the linear approximation’s assumptions (moderate leverage) break — optimism explodes non-linearly rather than tracking 2pσ²/n. The formula is a small-p law; the U-curve is the whole truth.

Q2. A pipeline reports “CV error 0.31” as the performance of the selected model, where selection was: 12 candidate models evaluated by the same 5-fold CV, winner = smallest. Design and run the experiment measuring the selection inflation: simulate null data (no signal) where every model’s true error equals σ², run the selection, record the winner’s CV score; compare its average to σ² and to the average of a fixed model’s CV score. Then derive the practical rule (report the winner’s score from a fresh outer CV, or correct by the expected order statistic).


Solution







Even with zero signal, the winner of 12 candidates reports ≈ 0.8–0.9 — selection alone manufactures a fake improvement over the fixed model’s ≈ 1.0. This gap is pure selection inflation and it grows with the candidate count and CV noise. Rules: (1) estimate the selected pipeline’s performance by wrapping selection itself inside an outer CV (nested — 4.6); (2) or subtract the expected order-statistic bonus (knowable by simulation under the null — exactly what you just built).

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (generalization × 2.9/3.5 KNN). Build the full 2-D map: for n ∈ {25, 100, 400} and k ∈ {1, 3, 10, 30, 100}, record train and test MSE (regression) or error (classification) on a fixed truth. Produce a heatmap of test error over (n, k) and draw the ridge of optimal k. How does optimal k scale with n, and what does the map predict about KNN’s viability when you can only collect 25 more samples?
C2 (generalization × 3.7 comparison). Six classifiers, one dataset, twenty replications: record each model’s CV accuracy per replication, then compute (a) each model’s mean, (b) the winner-per-replication’s average score, (c) the fixed pre-registered model’s average. Quantify (b) − (c) as measured selection inflation in a non-null setting, and check whether it’s larger or smaller than your null-data estimate from Q2 — then explain the direction.

title: 4.1 The Generalization Problem
text:
7. Summary

Training error is an optimistic estimator; the optimism grows with flexibility and shrinks with n.
The U-curve (test error vs flexibility) is the field’s central picture: underfit left, overfit right, noise floor below.
Flexibility dials point opposite ways (degree ↑, k ↓) but the physics is one: bias² + variance + σ².
Selection among many models inflates the winner’s score — order statistics, not skill.
Test sets are budgets; CV is the renewable subscription (next pages); leakage is counterfeit currency.
Underfitting (train error above σ²) is permanent without more flexibility; overfitting is curable with data or constraints.
The first remedy for optimism is the simplest split of all: 4.2 The validation set approach.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text: The simplest honest estimator: hold out a chunk of data, fit on the rest, evaluate once on the holdout. It is the prototype of every validation scheme — and its weaknesses (variance, wasted data, single-number confidence) are exactly the weaknesses the rest of Part 4 exists to fix.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
1. Basic Concept
Protocol: split rows into training and validation sets (say 70/30). Fit the model on training. Compute the metric once on validation. That number estimates out-of-sample error.






The weaknesses, demonstrated rather than described. First, variance: the estimate depends heavily on which rows land in validation:






Second, bias from smaller training: validation-error estimates are pessimistic because the model is trained on only 70% of the data — deployment would use 100%:

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
2. Concept Questions

Your validation MSE is 0.31 on one 70/30 split. What is the (approximate) standard error of that single number if σ² ≈ 0.09 and n_validation = 60 — and what does it say about reporting “0.31” to three decimals?
Why is validation error said to overestimate the error of the final model refit on all data?
Which two competing pressures determine the validation fraction, and what happens at the extremes (10% vs 50% holdout)?
You use the validation set to pick among 15 models, then report the winner’s validation MSE. Which error from 4.1 have you committed, and what’s the minimal fix?
For a time-ordered dataset, what must change in the protocol, and why is a random split actively wrong?



Answers


SE(MSE) ≈ σ²·√(2/n_val) ≈ 0.09 × √(2/60) ≈ 0.0164. So 0.31 ± 0.033 (95%): the third decimal is noise; report 0.31 ± 0.02 or the CI — or average over splits (4.3).
The validation model trained on 70% of data; with less data its error is higher than the refit-on-100% model’s (4.1’s data-rescue law). The estimator is pessimistically biased for the deployment model.
Big validation → precise estimate but badly undertrained model (pessimistic, wasteful); small validation → near-deployment training but noisy estimate. 20–30% is the customary compromise; CV removes the trade-off.
Selection on the validation set converts it into a second training set — the winner’s number is an order statistic, inflated. Minimal fix: a third, untouched test split; the full fix is nested CV (4.6).
Time-ordered data needs forward chaining: train on the past, validate on the future (random splits let the model train on the future — temporal leakage). Metrics then answer “how well do we predict tomorrow,” the only deployment-honest question.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Validation-vs-truth calibration: for a fixed data-generating process, compute (a) the true test MSE of a model trained on 70% of n = 150 (evaluated on 100k fresh points), and (b) the distribution of single-split validation estimates over 300 seeds. Report the mean of (b) vs (a), the SD of (b), and the fraction of 95% intervals (estimate ± 1.96·SE, SE from validation residuals) that contain (a). Is the validation estimator centered where it claims?


Solution







The per-split mean matches the truth (the estimator is centered for the 70%-trained model); within-split SEs describe split-to-split scatter well (coverage ≈ 0.93–0.95). The two failure modes to remember: it’s centered for the smaller training set (pessimism for deployment), and single-split numbers carry ±SE-sized error bars people rarely print.

Exercise 2. The learning-curve use case: for n_train ∈ {15, 30, 60, 120} (from a pool of 600), estimate test MSE by validation on a fixed 200-row holdout, replicating each size 100 times. Plot mean ± SD vs n_train. Identify where the curve flattens (“more data stops helping”) and connect to 4.1 Exercise 2’s law — what does the flatten point say about how much more data to collect?


Solution







The curve falls steeply then flattens: past the elbow, additional samples buy little — the residual error is dominated by noise floor + bias, not estimation variance. The flatten point is the empirical answer to “how much data is enough,” and it shifts left or right with model flexibility (simpler models flatten earlier).

Exercise 3. Validation-set selection inflation, in miniature: 20 candidate polynomial degrees (1–20) evaluated on ONE validation split; record the winner’s validation MSE. Repeat over 300 datasets; report the mean winner-vs-fixed-degree-3 validation ratio under a sinusoidal truth where degree 3 is genuinely near-optimal. Compare with selecting by 5-fold CV instead (averaged within each dataset). How much does honest selection reduce the inflation?


Solution







CV-based selection picks degrees closer to optimal and its winners’ true errors are lower — the single validation split’s noisier estimates select flashy degrees (selected-on-noise). The deeper lesson though: in both cases the winner’s own selection score must not be reported as performance; the numbers here are TRUE errors of refit winners, which is why they’re comparable at all.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

One number, no error bar — the validation estimate’s SE is computable from the validation residuals (drill 4) and should be printed; most published single-split numbers would fail that audit.
The holdout is a budget too: every model evaluated on it spends it (0.5); “validation” that saw 15 models is a training set wearing a costume.
Pessimism by undertraining — correction strategies exist (e.g., learning-curve extrapolation), but the clean fix is CV, which refits on (K−1)/K of data per fold.
Stratification for classification, grouping for clustered data, temporal order for time series — the split’s design is part of the estimator (0.5).
Post-selection refit: after choosing on validation, refit on ALL data before deployment — but then the validation number describes the pre-refit model, not the deployed one; only CV/nested schemes price the full pipeline.
Validation on a different distribution than deployment (site shift, prevalence shift) measures the wrong thing — the split cannot fix a sampling problem (3.7 C2).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated pipeline has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Pre-split scaling leaks validation statistics into training inputs (0.5). Scale inside the training fold only.
Selection and report on the same holdout: winner’s score is an order statistic (4.1 Q2). Reserve a third split, or select by CV.
Score transplant: the validation number belongs to the 70%-trained model; the deployed all-data model’s performance was never estimated. Estimate the full pipeline honestly (CV over the entire choose-and-fit procedure).

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the SE of a validation MSE estimate: given validation residuals e_i with mean-zero assumption violations aside, SE = sd(e²)/√(n_val). Compare, by simulation, this plug-in SE to the observed SD of validation MSEs across 500 splits. When do they disagree (name the distributional cause), and what does the disagreement do to naive “± SE” error bars?


Hint

e² has a skewed distribution (χ²-like when errors are Gaussian); its mean’s SE uses e²’s own variance — but heavy tails or heteroscedasticity make the plug-in unstable.



Solution







Under Gaussian errors the plug-in SE is unbiased for the across-split SD (they estimate the same sampling variability); they diverge when errors are heavy-tailed (e² ’s variance is dominated by rare huge residuals, so the plug-in is itself noisy — sometimes 2× off) or heteroscedastic (validation mix shifts). Consequence: treat “± SE” bars on single-split estimates as approximate, and prefer averaging across splits, which makes the across-split SD directly measurable.

Q2. Your deployment population drifts: the validation set was drawn from distribution P, deployment sees Q (same relationship, different x-mix). Design a simulation where the validation estimate is unbiased for P and biased for Q, quantify the bias as a function of the drift’s magnitude, and derive the reporting rule for validation estimates under anticipated drift (report per-stratum estimates or reweight to Q’s mix — never the pooled number alone).


Solution







The validation number is a perfectly good estimate of error-on-P and a biased estimate of error-on-Q; the bias grows with how much Q’s x-mass sits outside (or disproportionately inside) regions where the model misfits (here: extrapolation region x > 1). Rule: validation estimates are distribution-conditional; under anticipated drift, report stratified/reweighted errors — the pooled MSE is a weighted average with weights (P’s) that deployment doesn’t have. This is covariate shift, and it converts “validation” from a statistic into a design decision.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (validation × 0.5 stratification × 3.1.5 AUPRC). On a 1%-positive dataset with n = 1000, compare unstratified vs stratified 70/30 validation for estimating AUPRC: 200 splits each, report the spread (SD and IQR) of the estimates. Which procedure’s estimate would you publish, and what sample size of positives would make the unstratified version tolerable (verify empirically)?
C2 (validation × 4.3 CV preview). Using the same dataset and model, run the head-to-head: 200 independent single 70/30 splits vs 5-fold CV (repeated 40 times) as estimators of the same quantity. Compare (a) bias (vs a huge fresh test truth), (b) variance across repetitions, (c) total compute (fits per estimate). You should find CV’s variance advantage at 5× the compute — the explicit price list that makes 4.3’s conventions legible.

title: 4.2 The Validation Set Approach
text:
7. Summary

Validation = fit on one part, evaluate once on an untouched part — the prototype of honest estimation.
Its estimate is noisy (single split) and pessimistic (smaller training); both defects are measurable and both are CV’s motivation.
The validation set is a budget: selection on it converts it to training; keep a third split or use nested CV.
Print uncertainty: plug-in SEs from validation residuals, or split-to-split SDs — never a bare 3-decimal number.
Split design (stratify, group, temporal order) is part of the estimator, not an implementation detail.
Estimates are distribution-conditional: drift between validation and deployment breaks the number, not the math.
The fix for both defects — reuse every row for validation while keeping folds clean — is cross-validation: 4.3 Cross-validation.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text: The bootstrap replaces distributional theory with computation: resample your data, refit, and read uncertainty off the spread. Beyond CIs for statistics (1.5), it prices models: coefficient stability, prediction intervals, and the famous .632 correction for optimistic resubstitution error.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
1. Basic Concept
Mechanics for model assessment: draw B bootstrap samples (n rows, sampled with replacement) from the training data; fit the model on each; the collection of B fitted models approximates the sampling variability of the fitting procedure.






The same machinery gives prediction uncertainty — both of the fitted mean and of a new observation:






The .632 estimator — fixing the optimistic resubstitution error. A bootstrap sample omits ≈ 36.8% of rows (since \((1-1/n)^n \to e^{-1}\)); those out-of-bag rows are honest test cases for the bootstrap-fit model:
\[\text{Err}^{(.632)} = 0.368 \cdot \text{Err}_{\text{train}} + 0.632 \cdot \text{Err}_{\text{OOB}}\]

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must resampling be with replacement — and what fraction of rows does a bootstrap sample typically miss, to first order?
The .632 blend uses the resubstitution error (optimistic!) with weight 0.368. What is the logic of including it at all?
Bootstrap CIs for a model’s coefficients vs the formula SEs of 2.3: when do they agree, and what does it mean when they don’t?
Is the bootstrap valid for time-ordered rows? Name the assumption it needs and the standard fix when it fails.
A model’s OOB error ≈ its 10-fold CV error. Which property of the procedure makes those two estimates target (nearly) the same quantity?



Answers


Replacement generates variability between replicates (each row appears Poisson(1) times; some twice, some never). Missed fraction → \(e^{-1} ≈ 0.368\) — the “out-of-bag” set, which is what makes OOB evaluation possible.
The resubstitution error is the lower anchor (the fit’s error on data it memorized); OOB is closer to honest. Their weighted mix interpolates toward the true error — for stable learners with mild optimism the blend lands closer to truth than OOB alone, whose training sets are smaller (n distinct ≈ 0.632n, inflating OOB error). Advanced Q1 covers the .632+ refinement.
Under the model’s own assumptions (linear, homoscedastic, independent), bootstrap SEs converge to the formula SEs — agreement validates both. Divergence means the assumptions are wrong (heteroscedasticity, outliers, small-n skew) — the bootstrap is measuring the world as it is; the formula measures the world as assumed (2.3 Q2).
It needs exchangeability — rows i.i.d. from one distribution. Time series violate it (resampling destroys temporal dependence → SEs too small). Fixes: block bootstrap (resample contiguous blocks), or model-based resampling of residuals.
Both estimate the expected error of models trained on ≈ 63–80% of the data (bootstrap: ≈ 0.632n distinct rows; 10-fold CV: 90%) evaluated on unseen rows — the training-set-size mismatch is the main difference, and both are slightly pessimistic for the final refit-on-all-data model (4.2).

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Bootstrap vs formula SE shootout under violations: generate data with heteroscedastic noise (\(\sigma \propto x\)) and heavy-tailed noise (t₂), n = 40. For each, compute the OLS formula SE of the slope and the bootstrap SE (B = 3000). Report the ratio. Which violation breaks the formula SE more, and what does the bootstrap’s larger value correspond to in reality?


Solution







The bootstrap SE exceeds the formula SE in both regimes — it prices the real error structure (heteroscedastic variance, outliers that sometimes land in a resample and swing the fit). The formula assumes one σ and thin tails; its number is a statement about the assumed world. When they diverge, trust the bootstrap and reach for robust SEs or a different likelihood.

Exercise 2. Implement the full .632 vs cross-validation comparison: for the k-NN regression setup above (and also k = 1 and k = 25), compute (a) resubstitution error, (b) .632 estimate, (c) 5-fold CV, and (d) the true test error on 20,000 fresh points. Tabulate all four per k. For which k does .632 come closest to truth, and what does the resubstitution column look like at k = 1 (why does that row explain the entire motivation of the estimator)?


Solution







At k = 1, resubstitution is exactly 0 — the estimate that motivated .632. The .632 blend lands near truth for moderate-k stable learners; note its known weakness: for severely overfitting learners the resubstitution anchor (0 at k = 1) drags the blend down (optimistic) — the .632+ correction reweights by relative overfitting rate. CV remains the workhorse; .632 matters when CV is too expensive or training sets are tiny.

Exercise 3. Prediction intervals by bootstrap: for the linear fit, build three bands at x = 0.5: (a) bootstrap CI of the mean response (vary coefficients), (b) bootstrap prediction interval (add simulated residual noise to each bootstrap prediction), (c) the classical t-based prediction interval from statsmodels (get_prediction). Compare widths and centering. Which band is honest for “where will the next point land”?


Solution







Band (a) is narrow (coefficient uncertainty only); bands (b)/(c) are wider by roughly 2σ·1.96 — the irreducible noise of a new point (2.2 Exercise 3). Bootstrap (b) matches classical (c) closely under correct specification and inherits the empirical residual distribution when it isn’t (skew, outliers) — its advantage in exactly the settings where the classical t-interval is fiction.

title: 4.5 The Bootstrap
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The bootstrap resamples rows — paired/multilevel data must resample the unit (patient), not the visit; otherwise the resamples invent independence that isn’t there (the 2.10 Q2 lesson in resampling clothing).
Order statistics and extremes break it (the max degeneracy drill) — any statistic living at the sample boundary needs parametric or smoothed variants.
B matters, but differently per use: SEs stabilize by B ≈ 500–1000; 95% percentile CIs need B ≈ 2000+ (the 2.5% tail quantile is noisy); never report more digits than B supports.
The bootstrap estimates variability of the procedure, not the specific fit — that’s a feature (matches deployment, where a new sample gets a new fit) and a warning (it cannot tell you about the one fit you shipped beyond its procedure-level behavior).
Bootstrap model selection is optimistic — choosing hyperparameters by OOB score then reporting that OOB score overfits the resamples exactly like CV-selection does (4.6).
.632+ exists because .632 is optimistic for overfitting-heavy learners (Exercise 2’s k = 1 row); it reweights the blend by an estimated relative-overfitting rate — implement only if you must explain it; CV is usually simpler.
